title: Pocket
pitch: Poker for humans and agents: WebMCP gives each player’s copilot live, seat-safe game state and returns its advice to the table, while the human makes every move.
about_excerpt: Poker for humans and agents: WebMCP gives each player’s copilot live, seat-safe game state and returns its advice to the table, while the human makes every move. Like Comment Story Updates Pocket - WebMCP Poker Live Game With Staged Recommendation Bring Your Own Copilot in Multiplayer WebMCP Copilot in a Live Hand Inspiration Most web applications are built for people. When an AI agent tries to help someone use one, it often has to reconstruct what is happening from the page, or depend on the user to explain everything correctly. I wanted to explore a different model: what does an application look like when a user can bring their own agent with them, and the application is designed to work with it? Poker turned out to be a great environment for testing that idea. A poker decision can depend on public information like the board and pot, private information like your hole cards, the complete history of the hand, exact rules about which actions are legal, and a game state that may change while an agent is still thinking. There are also multiple people interacting with the same application, each with a different view of what they are allowed to know. But there is another kind of context too: information that belongs to the player rather than the poker application. Your agent might know how you like to play, strategies you've been working on, your appetite for risk, previous hands you've discussed, or your own observations about the people you're playing with. Pocket shouldn't need to own that information in order for it to be useful. That led to Pocket: a playable Texas Hold'em game where every seat can have two minds - the player and their AI copilot. What it does Pocket lets you play Texas Hold'em against bots or with other people while using a compatible AI agent as a copilot during the hand. Normally, asking an AI for poker advice means explaining your cards, the board, pot, stacks, previous betting, and what you can do next. Pocket already knows all of those things, so it exposes them directly through three WebMCP tools: get_current_situation gives the agent the exact current game state, including the player's private cards, board, pot, stacks, whose turn it is, and the legal actions with precise raise limits. get_hand_history gives the agent Pocket's authoritative record of how the hand reached the current situation. stage_recommendation lets the agent send its recommended move and explanation back into Pocket's Copilot panel. That creates a full application → agent → application loop. Pocket supplies the facts about the game, the agent reasons over them, and its recommendation comes back into the interface where the player is actually making the decision. The important part is that Pocket doesn't have to be the agent. A user can bring an agent that has its own context, preferences, memory, or way of reasoning and combine that with authoritative state supplied by the application at the moment it's needed. Pocket knows the table. Your agent can know you. That separation is especially interesting to me from a privacy perspective. Personal strategy, notes about other players, previous conversations, and other private context don't need to become part of Pocket's user profile or database just so an AI feature can use them. The application can expose what it knows, while personal context can remain with the user's chosen agent. I also deliberately did not give the agent a tool for folding, checking, calling, or raising. It can recommend a move, but the player still has to make it. The goal is a copilot, not an autopilot. How I built it Pocket is built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. At the center is a Texas Hold'em game engine that owns the authoritative state of each hand and determines which actions are currently legal. One of the most important architectural decisions was creating a seat-safe view of that state. The engine itself needs to know everyone's cards, but a player's interface, and their copilot, should only receive the information that particular player is entitled to see. The visible game and the WebMCP tools are both derived from that same player-safe state. That means the agent isn't getting a privileged version of the game behind the scenes. I kept the WebMCP surface intentionally small. The three tools basically correspond to three useful questions: What is happening right now? How did we get here? What does the agent recommend? Pocket also tracks the game, hand, and state version. When the agent returns a recommendation, Pocket verifies that it still belongs to the current situation before displaying it. If someone has acted and the table has moved on, the old recommendation is rejected instead of being presented as current advice. Beyond the WebMCP integration, I built bot games, real-time multiplayer rooms, persistent game sessions, responsive table layouts, game history, visible copilot activity, and a deterministic demo flow so the complete interaction can be experienced reliably. Pocket is deployed on Vercel, with unit, integration, and browser tests covering the poker flow, privacy boundaries, WebMCP contracts, multiplayer behavior, and the end-to-end demo. Challenges I ran into Keeping private information private Poker made the permission problem impossible to ignore. The engine has to know everyone's cards, but a particular player obviously shouldn't. I didn't want to expose the raw game state and trust the agent not to use fields it wasn't supposed to see. Instead, I built a seat-specific projection that only contains information available to that player. There were some less obvious cases too, like showdown, where cards that were private earlier in the hand may legitimately become public. Multiplayer also made this feel like more than a theoretical concern. Every player can occupy the same shared game while still having a different private view of it, and potentially a completely different copilot with its own private context. Keeping recommendations synchronized with a live game Poker state can change quickly, and the game doesn't stop while the agent is thinking. A recommendation could be correct when the request starts but already be stale by the time it comes back because another player acted or the hand moved to the next street. I solved that by explicitly versioning the state and binding each recommendation to the game, hand, and exact state it was created from. Pocket validates that again before showing the recommendation. Keeping the WebMCP lifecycle stable This caused one of the more frustrating bugs during development. The table's React state changes constantly as players act, turns advance, and cards are dealt. My first implementation tied the WebMCP tool registration too closely to that changing state, which meant tools could be repeatedly removed and registered during normal gameplay. I eventually separated the stable tool lifecycle from the changing game data. The tools stay registered while the table is active, but read the latest authoritative state whenever they are invoked. Deciding what the agent should actually be allowed to do I could have exposed a tool that lets the agent make the poker move itself. Technically, that would have been pretty easy. But that isn't the interaction I wanted Pocket to demonstrate. There is an important difference between giving an agent useful capabilities and handing over every consequential action. stage_recommendation became that boundary: the agent can participate visibly in the live application, but the final move still belongs to the player. Making the integration visible without turning Pocket into a developer demo A technically correct tool exchange isn't automatically understandable to the person using the product. I spent a lot of time iterating on how the table, game history, player controls, WebMCP activity, and Copilot panel fit together. I wanted someone looking at Pocket to understand that an agent is actually participating in the application without making the entire product look like a tool inspector. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Pocket doesn't just demonstrate an agent calling a tool. It demonstrates a much richer relationship between an application, a user, and the agent that user chooses to bring with them. Pocket is a real multiplayer game with real hidden information, changing state, history, rules, permissions, and decisions. That gave me a chance to explore several things I find genuinely exciting about WebMCP in one product. A player's copilot doesn't have to guess what is happening from the screen. Pocket can give it the exact state of the game and the exact actions that are legal. At the same time, that agent only receives the private information its player is entitled to see. In a multiplayer game, every person can be looking at the same shared table while their agent receives a different, permissioned view of it.  Inspiration 

 Designing a home is joyful, as each member of the family has their own ideas and preferences. Interior designers help clients walk through this process by showing multiple plans and different furniture arrangements. However, this process can become lengthy and repetitive. 

 This project was inspired by the idea of making that process simpler and helping users design the layout provided by their real estate developer while allowing them to view the design from different viewing angles. 

 What it does 

 HouseSpaceAI helps users design the layout provided by a real estate developer and visualize it from different viewing angles. 

 The main goals while building it were: 

 
 Simple to use 
 Faster and more accurate results 
 Design the dream 
 

 How we built it 

 I used different approaches to solve the problem: 

 
 Image to 3D: 
I first tried converting an image directly into a 3D layout, but this affected the accuracy. 
 Image to 2D floor plan to 3D: 
I then tried converting the image into a 2D floor plan first and then into 3D. This improved the accuracy by a bit. 
 

 There are still some issues with furniture orientations and sizes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was maintaining accuracy while converting a provided layout into a usable 3D representation. 

 
 Direct image-to-3D conversion affected accuracy. 
 Adding an intermediate 2D floor-plan step improved accuracy, but it was still not perfect. 
 Furniture orientation and sizing remain areas that need further improvement. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Built a working concept for turning a real estate-provided layout into an interactive design. 
 Explored different approaches to improve the accuracy of the generated layout. 
 Focused on making the experience simple and faster for users. 
 Created a way to view the designed space from different angles. 
 

 What we learned 

 Building this project gave me experience with new libraries such as WebMCP and tools that make connections with the browser. 

 I also learned how different approaches to image and floor-plan processing can affect the accuracy of a 3D representation. 

 I still feel that not having a Codex Plus connection was a disadvantage, as it would have helped me test the product more extensively. 

 What's next for HouseSpaceAI 

 The opportunities are limitless. HouseSpaceAI can potentially be used by: 

 
 Real estate developers 
 Interior designers 
 Individuals designing their own homes 
 

 The goal is to continue improving accuracy, especially furniture orientation and sizing, while making the experience faster and easier so more people can design their dream spaces.

title: Open Racer Racing Line Editor
pitch: An open-source racing line editor that lets AI agents create track layouts through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An open-source racing line editor that lets AI agents create track layouts through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Racing Line 3D View Codex using WebMCP Inspiration I built the first version of the racing line editor about six years ago. I wanted a tool to prepare for karting and learn unfamiliar tracks. I studied onboard videos and drew every braking point, apex, and acceleration zone by hand. I kept wondering whether an AI could help me. Last year, I returned to the project and added a 3D WebGL view. Claude and Codex helped me bring it back to life. The editor was also recognized in the 2025 Google Maps Platform Awards. What it does The racing line editor lets you draw and edit racing lines on a satellite map. Points can represent braking, acceleration, or transition. Lines can be saved locally and viewed in 3D. In the demo, Codex reads an existing full-circuit line. Two shorter layouts are missing. Through WebMCP, it reads the circuit, the reference line, and the editor guidance. It then creates both missing layouts directly in the editor. How I built it For this challenge, I separated the editor from the older Open Racer application and rebuilt it as a standalone open-source app. It uses Vite, React 19, JavaScript, Google Maps Platform, and Paper.js. Lines are stored locally with IndexedDB and can be exported as JSON. There is no backend or sign-in. The WebMCP tools use the same editor state as the visible controls. Agents can inspect the track, read line-creation guidance, edit points, undo changes, and save or load lines. I use Vitest for unit tests, Playwright for browser tests, and GitHub Pages for deployment. The hardest part A racing line is more than coordinates. Point order matters. The line must stay on the drivable surface, and one circuit can contain several layouts. The challenge was giving the agent enough context while keeping every change visible and understandable to the user. What I learned Structured WebMCP actions reduce guessing. They make agent changes more predictable and easier to verify.  Aliigo Action Layer 

 Project name 

 Aliigo Action Layer (AAL) 

 Elevator pitch 

 Aliigo Action Layer makes online business knowledge actionable and future-ready for both people and AI. Using WebMCP, it turns a business’s approved information and capabilities into clear tools that AI assistants can use to find answers, recommend services, prepare bookings or quote requests, and guide customers to the next step—without having to guess their way through the website. 

 One-line version 

 Turn your business knowledge into actions that both customers and AI assistants can use. 

 Tagline 

 Built for people. Ready for their agents. 

 

 Inspiration 

 Aliigo started from a simple problem: businesses already have valuable knowledge scattered across their websites, service pages, FAQs, policies, booking systems, and other public sources, but that information is often difficult for search engines, AI systems, and even customers to understand consistently. 

 We have been building Aliigo around the idea that a business should be able to organize and control the knowledge that represents it, make that knowledge easier for Google and AI systems to understand, and put it to work through a Business Agent that can answer visitor questions. 

 WebMCP suggested the next logical step. 

 If a business can make its knowledge understandable to AI, why should its customers’ agents still have to guess their way through buttons, forms, menus, and page layouts? 

 That led to Aliigo Action Layer . 

 The idea is to give a normal business website a structured action layer for AI agents while keeping the human experience intact. Instead of replacing the website, WebMCP lets us make the same website usable by both people and their agents. 

 The long-term inspiration is simple: 

 Make businesses easier to find, understand, choose, and act on. 

 

 What it does 

 Aliigo Action Layer makes online business knowledge actionable. 

 Instead of asking an AI agent to interpret a website visually and guess how to complete a task, the site exposes structured, business-specific tools that describe exactly what the agent can do. 

 For example, a wellness business can expose tools that let an agent: 

 
 understand available services; 
 find an appropriate service for a customer’s need; 
 check available times; 
 prepare a booking. 
 

 A printing business can expose a different set of capabilities: 

 
 find appropriate print products; 
 check artwork requirements; 
 compare relevant options; 
 prepare a quote request. 
 

 The important part is that these are not separate one-off integrations. 

 Aliigo Action Layer uses the same underlying business capability model to expose the appropriate tools for different types of businesses. 

 The agent can prepare an action while the website shows the result to the human for review and confirmation. 

 The experience becomes: 

 Human intent → Agent uses structured tools → Website shows the prepared action → Human confirms 

 This keeps the human in control while giving the agent a much more reliable way to help. 

 

 How we built it 

 We built Aliigo Action Layer as an isolated WebMCP experiment, separate from the production Aliigo platform but designed with a future integration path in mind. 

 The application uses a reusable business-definition and capability layer. 

 Each business defines: 

 
 its identity; 
 approved business knowledge; 
 products or services; 
 policies; 
 available actions; 
 structured data required for those actions. 
 

 A WebMCP adapter then translates those capabilities into business-specific tools exposed through the browser. 

 We deliberately kept the WebMCP layer separate from the UI and business logic. 

 Conceptually: 
 Business knowledge
 +
Business capabilities
 ↓
Aliigo Action Layer
 ↓
WebMCP tools
 ↓
AI agent
 
 The same application can switch between different example businesses and expose a different toolset without rebuilding the underlying architecture. 

 We also added visible shared state so that when an agent prepares a booking or quote request, the result appears immediately in the human-facing interface. 

 The current challenge implementation is intentionally self-contained and deterministic. It does not require production Aliigo infrastructure, customer data, external APIs, authentication, or payment systems. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was thinking differently about what a website interface is for. 

 Traditional web development assumes that the human is the only actor navigating the interface. Even AI-assisted browsing often follows the same model: the agent tries to understand the page, find the correct control, and interact with it. 

 WebMCP changes that assumption. 

 We had to decide which parts of the business should become explicit tools, what information each tool should accept, and which actions should remain under direct human control. 

 Another challenge was avoiding generic tools. 

 A tool such as execute_action may be technically flexible, but it gives an agent very little useful business context. We found that tools become much more meaningful when they describe actual business capabilities such as: 

 
 find_services 
 find_available_times 
 prepare_booking 
 check_artwork_requirements 
 prepare_quote_request 
 

 We also had to design around an emerging standard. WebMCP is still experimental, so feature detection, browser compatibility, graceful fallback behavior, and keeping the implementation close to the current specification were important. 

 Finally, we had to resist turning the challenge project into the full Aliigo platform. The goal was to demonstrate the idea clearly and reliably without reproducing the much larger production architecture. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are most proud that Aliigo Action Layer demonstrates something broader than a single WebMCP-enabled form. 

 The same underlying architecture can represent very different businesses and expose different agent capabilities based on what each business actually does. 

 A wellness studio can become bookable by an agent. 

 A printing company can become quote-ready. 

 Both use the same underlying model. 

 We are also proud of the human-agent interaction pattern. 

 The agent does not simply disappear into the background and perform an opaque task. It prepares a structured action, and the website reflects that action back to the human. 

 That creates a collaborative experience rather than an autonomous black box.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: TabulaFlow
pitch: Auditable local-first data workflows where people and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Auditable local-first data workflows where people and AI agents collaborate through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Data preparation tools are visually dense, stateful, and risky for agents to operate through generic browser automation. An agent can target the wrong dataset, repeat a mutation, lose track of the current revision, or expose sensitive values while inferring state from tables and graph coordinates. TabulaFlow explores a better model: one visible data workflow shared by people and agents, with precise semantic operations and explicit human authority. What it does TabulaFlow is an auditable, local-first data workbench built around Source → Prepare → Compose . Source imports Excel, CSV, JSON, JSONL, and NDJSON while keeping local data in the browser. Prepare profiles data quality, manages ordered transformation recipes, creates deterministic Formula columns, applies protected filters, and supports human-reviewed qualitative coding. Compose validates and chains Append, Join, Difference, Aggregate, Filter, Distinct, Pivot, and Unpivot operations. WebMCP exposes stable, strict tools for agents to inspect, validate, mutate, export, and monitor the same application state shown to the user. People retain control of local file selection, agent-upload consent, destructive confirmation, semantic declassification, and qualitative interpretation. Why WebMCP is a strong fit Generic browser automation must guess from visual coordinates and transient UI state. TabulaFlow instead exposes a semantic agent API through WebMCP. Agents can discover action-specific contracts, target stable dataset and node IDs, dry-run changes, reject stale revisions, replay idempotently, poll asynchronous operations, and cancel before commit. This creates a better user experience because agent work is visible in the normal product, recorded in a shared privacy-safe activity ledger, and governed by the same validation and transaction boundaries as direct user actions. People and agents can now collaborate on multi-step data preparation and graph-based composition without hiding mutations inside an opaque autonomous workflow. How we built it Frontend: React 19 and Vite Analytical engine: DuckDB-Wasm in a dedicated browser worker Agent interface: document.modelContext.registerTool() with stable dispatcher tools and strict action-specific JSON Schemas Persistence: IndexedDB flow metadata, recipes, graph positions, and activity events Safety: optimistic workspace revisions, idempotency keys, protected-value bindings, bounded redacted previews, writer serialization, asynchronous lifecycle, cooperative cancellation, and visible user confirmations Hosting: ChatGPT Sites-compatible production bundle The current contract exposes 17 stable WebMCP tools and 60 bounded Source, Prepare, Compose, and qualitative-coding action routes. What people and agents can do together Agents can inspect schemas and quality, validate candidate changes, maintain recipes, create Compose operations, promote results, export datasets, and report evidence-backed qualitative coding suggestions. Users can see and review the same state, undo transformations, reject unsafe actions, and retain exclusive authority over sensitive boundaries. How we used AI Codex and ChatGPT supported implementation, debugging, regression testing, live WebMCP QC, documentation, and demo preparation. The human owner set product direction, reviewed trade-offs, controlled releases, and accepted or rejected changes. Testing instructions Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Download the synthetic fixture from the public repository at examples/webmcp-demo.csv . Import it manually in Source. No login is required. Call the capabilities, workspace-state, and workflow-guide tools. Inspect the dataset and data profile through Prepare. Add a Formula column named weight_gap_kg with [chargeable_weight_kg] - [actual_weight_kg] . In Compose, validate and create an Aggregate grouped by service , with count and average actual-weight metrics. Inspect the operation schema, preview, and quality. Demonstrate stale-revision rejection, idempotent replay, cancellation, or the shared activity ledger. Do not confirm deletion or reset. Full walkthrough: https://github.com/jacobcalvyn/TabulaFlow/blob/main/docs/DEMO.md Challenges and accomplishments The hardest work was making a complex data mutation surface agent-safe without duplicating application logic. We hardened strict schema discovery, protected recipe round-trips, privacy-aware previews, atomic tool publication, asynchronous cancellation, response pagination, and local-file recovery boundaries. The result passed live WebMCP regression coverage across Prepare and all eight Compose operation types, alongside repository tests and production build checks. Built during the challenge TabulaFlow's WebMCP integration, safety contracts, Formula workflow, Compose parity, agent upload consent, qualitative-coding boundary, and demo materials were implemented and hardened during the challenge period. Dated evidence is available in docs/HACKATHON.md and the Git history. Known limitations Browser imports are capped at 50 MB, 100,000 rows, and 1,000 stored columns. Local file permissions may require explicit re-linking. Formula columns intentionally exclude window, rank, LOD, regex, and nondeterministic current-time functions. WebMCP requires a compatible browser implementation. title: BeatMCP
pitch: A live collaborative beat canvas where people and AI agents build four-bar instrumentals together through WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A live collaborative beat canvas where people and AI agents build four-bar instrumentals together through WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 BeatMCP 

 BeatMCP is a collaborative beat-making canvas built for the WebMCP Challenge. 

 Inspiration 

 Making music with AI often feels disconnected: you describe a beat, wait for a result, then try to explain what feels wrong. I wanted a more natural workflow where a person keeps creative control while an agent can contribute directly inside the same music workspace. 

 The core question was: what if an agent could use a music-making web app through structured controls instead of guessing how to click through the interface? 

 What it does 

 BeatMCP is a four-bar, 64-step beat canvas where a person and an agent can build an instrumental together. 

 The studio includes drums, bass, piano, guitar, bell, keys, pad, and lead lanes. Users can set tempo and key, program steps manually, and shape a beat in a shared timeline. 

 Agents can use WebMCP tools to: 

 
 read the current pattern and musical state 
 set tempo, key, and scale 
 write drum, bass, melody, and chord patterns 
 create chords on Piano, Keys, and Pad lanes 
 humanize timing and velocity 
 reset a beat, start playback, and begin a live composition session 
 list playable instruments and save/reuse patterns 
 

 A key feature is live composition. When an agent writes a new layer, BeatMCP auditions the first new sound in sequence—such as kick, bass, chords, then melody—while the changed steps flash on the grid. This makes the agent's creative process visible and audible instead of hiding everything until the end. 

 How we built it 

 BeatMCP is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand, Tone.js, and the @mcp-b WebMCP libraries. 

 
 Next.js and React power the browser experience. 
 Zustand keeps the beat, tracks, tempo, key, and pattern state synchronized. 
 Tone.js synthesizes drums and instrument voices in the browser. 
 WebMCP exposes structured tools directly from the page so agents can work with the same musical controls as users. 
 The studio uses a 64-step master timeline so a beat can develop across four bars rather than being limited to one short loop. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest part was making the human-agent collaboration feel trustworthy in real time. 

 Browser audio needs an initial user gesture, so we designed the flow around one Start click before an agent can begin live composition. We also had to prevent overlapping transport loops, keep WebMCP tool discovery fresh after page reloads, and make agent edits understandable through visual flashes and queued sound auditions. 

 Another challenge was avoiding a traditional “AI generates everything” interaction. We wanted the agent to be musically useful without replacing the producer's judgment. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that WebMCP is most compelling when the agent has precise, meaningful controls and the person can immediately understand the consequences of each action. 

 For music, that means an agent should not just return text or a finished file. It should be able to set a key, place a kick, write a chord, audition a sound, and respond to human feedback in the same live workspace. 

 Why WebMCP 

 BeatMCP becomes meaningfully better because agents can use the web app directly through structured tools. The agent reads the real state of the beat and changes the same instrument lanes the person sees and hears. 

 That creates a collaborative workflow: the agent handles musical structure and repetitive programming, while the person decides what feels right.

title: Dust Off
pitch: An AI piano teacher that listens to your playing, gives feedback, and creates lessons you can practise anytime.
about_excerpt: An AI piano teacher that listens to your playing, gives feedback, and creates lessons you can practise anytime. Like Comment Story Updates Screenshot of site Inspiration A MIDI keyboard can sit unused because its owner doesn’t know what to practise or whether they’re improving. Dust Off turns that instrument into a shared workspace with an AI teacher that can demonstrate, respond to real playing, and prepare the next exercise. What it does Dust Off helps beginners learn through short, interactive exercises. The agent highlights notes with finger numbers, plays a demonstration, and reads the student’s notes, timing, and velocity to give feedback. It can also save personalised lessons. These stay in the library, where the app demonstrates, listens, and grades independently. Students can use a physical MIDI controller, computer keyboard, or on-screen keys. How we built it We built Dust Off with plain JavaScript, Web Audio, Web MIDI, and WebMCP, hosted on Netlify. WebMCP tools such as show_notes, play_notes, listen, and save_lesson let the agent work directly with the piano page. The page handles musical timing and analysis, while the agent decides what to teach. Lessons and practice observations are stored locally. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was browser compatibility: Codex’s in-app browser supported WebMCP calls but did not grant MIDI access, while Chrome supported our MIDI controller. We built a small local Node.js relay that forwards Chrome’s hardware input into the same Codex piano page where WebMCP operates. Real testing also exposed duplicate events from mirrored MIDI ports, premature phrase endings while beginners searched for keys, and outdated performance results after a listening window closed. Accomplishments that we're proud of We demonstrated a complete interaction with a real MIDI keyboard: the agent taught an exercise, demonstrated notes, read physical playing, gave feedback, and saved a personalised lesson. We also completed an independent chord lesson and reviewed its results with the agent. What we learned Musical timing belongs in the application, not in model round trips. WebMCP works well when tools represent meaningful actions—demonstrate a phrase, analyse a performance, save a lesson—rather than individual clicks. Testing with a real beginner also showed how important patience and clear feedback are. What's next for Dust Off We want to simplify hardware setup, improve phrase capture and progress tracking, and make saved lessons easier to share across browsers. We’ll also expand exercises for chord transitions, rhythm, and even touch while keeping practice approachable for beginners. title: NextPlay
pitch: Call the play. Lock your vision. Let AI replan the rest.
about_excerpt: Call the play. Lock your vision. Let AI replan the rest. Like 1 Comment Story Updates NextPlay Call the play. Lock your vision. Let AI replan the rest. Inspiration Basketball play design is collaborative by nature: a coach sketches an idea, tests the timing, changes a screen or route, and keeps refining until the sequence works. But most AI tools break that workflow. They generate a diagram, description, or recommendation somewhere outside the actual product. Once the coach edits the board, the AI no longer understands the current state—or which decisions are intentional and must not be overwritten. We built NextPlay around a simple question: What would a basketball tactics board look like if the coach and an AI agent could work on the same live play? WebMCP made that possible. Instead of relying on screenshots or a hidden copy of the play, the page exposes structured tools that let the agent read and modify the exact state the coach is viewing. What It Does NextPlay is a browser-native basketball tactics board for human–AI collaboration. A coach can ask an agent to create a sideline out-of-bounds play for a right-corner three. The agent: Reads the current formation, clock, actions, locks, and revision. Adds six structured basketball actions. Validates the play against deterministic execution constraints. Animates the result directly on the court. Then the coach can intervene through the normal interface. In our core demo, the coach: Moves A3’s screen to the right_elbow . Locks A3. Locks O2’s route in A4. Shortens the clock from 4.2 seconds to 2.0 seconds. That creates a clock-overflow error because A6 finishes too late. The agent then rereads the live page, sees the coach’s edits and locks, and retimes only the unlocked pass and shot in A5 and A6. A3 and A4 remain unchanged, the repaired play passes all seven validation checks, and the final animation completes within the new two-second clock. That second turn is the heart of NextPlay: the AI does not start over or overwrite the coach. It adapts around the coach’s decisions. Why WebMCP Matters The important state in NextPlay is live and page-local: Current player positions The action timeline The shortened clock The selected action Coach-made edits Locked actions Validation results The current play revision A generic assistant would have to infer that state from pixels, manipulate small controls, or work from an outdated description. NextPlay instead exposes exactly five semantic WebMCP tools: get_play_state add_play_actions validate_play animate_play update_play_action There is deliberately no agent tool for locking or unlocking actions. Locks are a coach-only authority boundary. This means the coach remains in control while the agent handles structured construction and replanning. How We Built It NextPlay is built with React, TypeScript, Zustand, Zod, Vite, and Vercel . We designed the application around one architectural rule: Every persistent mutation—whether initiated by the coach or the agent—must pass through the same command and transaction layer. The WebMCP tools do not maintain a separate copy of the play. Their handlers call the same application commands used by the visible coach interface. As a result, agent changes immediately appear on the: Court Timeline Action inspector Validation panel Activity rail Each successful content mutation increments the play revision exactly once. Write tools can include an expected revision, allowing NextPlay to reject stale updates when the page has changed since the agent last read it. We also implemented atomic action batches. When the agent creates the initial play, all six actions are accepted together or none are committed. The validation engine checks deterministic structural properties such as: Whether all actions fit within the clock Whether one player has incompatible overlapping actions Whether referenced players and actions are valid Whether possession order is consistent Whether the play contains the required inbound pass and shot Whether locked coach actions were preserved NextPlay does not claim that a play is tactically optimal, likely to score, or physically realistic. It validates the structure and timing of an animated tactical diagram. Challenges We Faced Preserving Human Authority The hardest product question was not how to let the agent edit the play—it was how to stop the agent from erasing intentional human decisions. We solved this with coach-only action locks. Before every agent mutation, NextPlay snapshots locked actions and verifies that they remain unchanged. Attempts to modify a locked action return an ACTION_LOCKED error without changing the play revision. Keeping the Agent and Interface Synchronized It would have been easy to build a demo where the agent edits hidden JSON while the UI displays something similar. Instead, we made the visible application state the source of truth. Tool success is returned only after the updated state has been committed through the same data model used by the coach interface. Handling Stale Agent State A coach may change the play after the agent reads it. Without concurrency protection, the next agent write could accidentally overwrite a newer version. Revision-aware writes let the application detect that situation and ask the agent to reread the play before continuing. Making Validation Honest We wanted the validator to be useful without making exaggerated basketball claims. That required carefully separating deterministic facts like timing, possession order, references, and lock preservation from subjective questions like whether the play would fool a real defense. Building a Reliable Live Demo A hackathon project has to work repeatedly, not just once. We reduced the scope to one polished sideline out-of-bounds scenario, kept the WebMCP surface to five tools, added strict runtime schemas, tested fresh-context production flows, and included an honest manual fallback for browsers that do not support WebMCP. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that giving an agent more autonomy is not always the same as making it more useful. In collaborative software, an agent needs three things: Semantic access to the real application state. Clear authority boundaries defining what it may change. Observable, revision-aware actions that both the user and the system can verify. WebMCP turns the page from a visual interface the agent must guess at into a structured collaboration environment. We also learned that the most compelling agent experiences are not single-prompt generation demos. They are iterative workflows where a human changes the constraints and the agent successfully adapts without losing prior intent. What We Are Proud Of NextPlay demonstrates a complete human–agent loop: Intent → structured construction → validation → animation → human intervention → constraint violation → agent repair The coach remains the decision-maker. The agent accelerates execution. That is the interaction model we believe will matter far beyond basketball: humans defining intent and protecting critical decisions while agents operate directly inside live, structured applications. title: Trellis, a Personal WebMCP Marketplace
pitch: Tested WebMCP tools for sites that never shipped any. Install in one click.
about_excerpt: Tested WebMCP tools for sites that never shipped any. Install in one click. Like Comment Story Updates A catalog of tested WebMCP tools for sites that have not shipped any, plus the extension that installs them and the agent that writes them for you. Why I built it I have spent this year putting WebMCP tools onto a production site. The problem is who has to ship it. WebMCP only works if the site adds it. That is the right design, but it splits the web in two. A few sites will offer tools. The rest will still use actuation. We created a way to use the protocol on sites that have not adopted it, and an argument aimed at those sites: here are the tools for your pages, here is proof they work, here is a user already calling them. What it does Point the extension at a site. It asks a public catalog whether anyone has published tools for that hostname, shows you what they would touch, and on your say-so installs them into the page's real WebMCP surface. From there they are ordinary tools. Chrome's own agent sees them, my extension sees them, and I drive them today with a browser extension with an agent-in-browser on Chrome and with Codex. Nobody uploads code. A tool is a name, a description, an input schema, and steps from a fixed set of nine operations. One interpreter runs them, and it cannot reach the network, touch storage, or point at anything the tool did not declare. Every tool is run against the real page before publishing, and both its result and everything it touched are recorded. What I learned Single page apps were the hard part. A site like that never reloads, so tools installed on the home route are still in the agent's list after the user clicks into a product page, pointing at elements that are gone. Browsers only announce a real page load. A route change inside a single page app arrives as a separate event, and if you do not listen for it you never learn the page changed. So the extension listens for both: a real load reinstalls everything, a route change only re-decides which tools still apply. The catalog makes that cheap, because the answer for a hostname is one lookup it can repeat on every route change with no help from the site. The other lesson was about who gets to write a tool. Use agents to write the code, host them locally, and inject them via an extension you own. Then any webmcp enabled site you have crawled can use the webmcp api and tools for now. The honest limit is that as pages change, you'll need to recrawl. about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered runtime tool for coding agents. Find ended sessions, explain leftover processes, and prepare cleanup while destructive actions stay controlled by human. Like Comment Story Updates wyd tui wyd webmcp Inspiration Coding agents often leave browsers, MCP servers, dev servers, and other processes running after a session ends. ps tells me what is running, but not who started it or whether it is safe to remove. I built wyd to answer that. What it does wyd connects running resources to the coding-agent session and project that created them. For this challenge I added wyd web and six WebMCP tools. A browser agent can find ended sessions, inspect leftovers, explain process provenance, focus resources in the UI, and prepare a cleanup proposal. Cleanup itself is intentionally left to the human. How I built it wyd is mostly Rust. The web dashboard uses the same runtime/provenance engine as the CLI and TUI. WebMCP tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , and agent actions update the same UI state the human sees. The hosted demo uses deterministic synthetic data. Challenges The main challenge was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do. I separated investigation from execution: WebMCP can explain and prepare cleanup, but cannot perform destructive actions. I also separated ownership from lifecycle state. A process can belong to an ended session and therefore be both confidently owned and a leftover candidate. What I learned Structured tools work much better than asking an agent to scrape a UI. title: 2D WebMCP - agent-friendly, screen reader accessible canvas
pitch: Blind people already use AI to use 2D UIs, but they have to jump through hoops to verify the output. This project makes verification easier using WebMCP, so blind users get AI's full benefit.
about_excerpt: Blind people already use AI to use 2D UIs, but they have to jump through hoops to verify the output. This project makes verification easier using WebMCP, so blind users get AI's full benefit. Like 2 Comment 1 Story Updates 6 screenshot of chatGPT and the in app browser with the user requesting "prove it" and a flow editor on the right. Inspiration Screen reader tech has sophisticated ways of navigating web content, but reading complex UI such as diagrams, maps, charts, boards, slides, etc can quickly break down. With enough engineering investment, these applications can be exposed accessibly, often through alternative presentations (for example a visually hidden table of data), but even then they require a lot of navigation and working memory to understand the whole picture. AI can make this easier by interpreting and operating on the user's behalf, but there’s still a gap in the verification step. Spot-checking a result can mean laboriously retracing a complex UI, asking a sighted person, or trusting the agent without an independent way to verify its work. The same people who get the most out of AI cannot always get the proof they need to trust it. A study of 16 programmers who use screen readers backs this up, showing that the most time-consuming part of their workflow was verifying agent output. Participants had a hard time tracking the scope and location of changes, verifying results across multiple views and determining if the agent had completed every requested task. What it does The application itself is a multi-purpose 2D flow diagram editor. Users can add, edit, and delete nodes, create or delete connections to represent workflows and sequences. It is keyboard accessible and screen reader accessible, insofar as a UI like this can be. WebMCP plays several important roles: it exposes tools to create and edit complex flows and deep link to a part of the UI for evidence of an action; effectively a shortcut to evidence that a change took place. It works with a text or image prompt to generate complex, inspectable flows. The response that includes fields for changes in the application’s state , so that agents and screen reader users can verify the change. The list of state changes can support other evidence the agent gathers from the UI state (via screenshotting or the accessibility API diffs), but most importantly, they can be inspected by a screen reader user to get confidence. Impact An assistive technology user can hand off a complex task without giving up the ability to fully understand the result. Verification is fast and reliable and doesn’t replay the same complexity the agent abstracted away. This improves user confidence, removes barriers, and unlocks creativity. How I built it I built a workflow editor with a 2D editable canvas that exposes tools to agents (and proximately to screen readers) via WebMCP. These include evaluation, editing, and undo tools, as well as a focus management tool. I used the webmcp-evals CLI to run evals and iterate on the tool definitions that worked well in this context and domain. Once I had the evals in place I was able to iteratively improve using Codex to increase the scores. What I learned Using evals and iterating on those helped me arrive at 100% completion rates with 2% of requests retrying due to errors; 9.52s (p50) duration. More data here . The webmcp-evals tooling drove vast improvements over my initial efforts. These gain we largely driven by reducing tool calls and better tool descriptions along with a more interpretable schema for the agent reducing errors and retries. Early on I attempted to add detailed output that included a serialized output schema, but it had little impact on the results compared to simpler response strings, and cost roughly 45% additional input tokens per trial (very little change in output tokens). I adjusted my responses accordingly, and continued to iterate. What's next I'm continuing to work with screen reader users to iterate and improve on the UX, and intend to write up the results. Research Blind screen-reader users have described the cognitive burden of working with two-dimensional artboards even when object details and coordinates are available: “It’s too much information and not enough at the same time.” Schaadhardt, Hiniker, and Wobbrock, Understanding Blind Screen-Reader Users’ Experiences of Digital Artboards · Evidence discussion Accessible tables are familiar and necessary, but they can still make overview and comparison difficult. One participant facing 393 rows said: “I can’t really get a snapshot.” Zong et al., Rich Screen Reader Experiences for Accessible Data Visualization · Evidence discussion Blind users already test and cross-check AI rather than treating it as automatically reliable. One participant advised: “Just play with it. Don’t rely on them.” Alharbi et al., Misfitting With AI: How Blind People Verify and Contest AI Errors · Evidence discussion Built With chatgpt codex react typescript webmcp Try it out 2d-webmcp.netlify.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Cameron Cundiff Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Cameron Cundiff posted an update — Sep 03, 2026 05:35 PM EDT iterated with evals to improve correctness and latency; added auto layout to the created diagram. title: svgent Agent Stage
pitch: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video.
about_excerpt: A studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. The agent in your browser writes and directs, you approve, the page renders SVG and video. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Stage: two showcase scripts rendered by svgent, a terminal and an app Inspiration svgent is a client-only studio for fictional coding-agent sessions. A script describes a chat window or a terminal, with typing, thinking, tool runs, approvals and choices, and the studio renders it to SVG, PNG, GIF and MP4. People use it for READMEs, docs, talks and posts, where a recording of a real session would leak secrets and could not be re-shot or translated. Before this, the studio's AI assist was copy and paste: copy a prompt into a chat, paste the JSON back. WebMCP replaces that with tool calls on the page. The page can also answer with facts a language model cannot see: how long a page runs, when each message lands, what the frame looks like at eleven seconds. The agent works on the stage itself, not on a guess about it. What it does Agent Stage is the studio with WebMCP site tools. The agent in ChatGPT's built-in browser writes the script, sets the surface, look, camera and pages, measures the result, looks at a frame, proposes rewrites, and asks to export. The person keeps the decisions: rewrites and exports wait on a card, every string the script puts on the stage is listed, and each change can be undone. load_script validates a script and previews it at once. direct_camera turns on a deterministic follow camera. inspect_timeline returns per-message timing and a review. snapshot_frame returns a PNG of any moment. fit_duration lands a page on an exact length and reports what it changed. propose_patch puts rewrites on a card. approve_proposal exists only while a proposal is pending and waits for the person's click. export asks first. The rail shows every call. The "Every word on the stage" list holds every string the script puts on the stage, including what a collapse or a page turn hides. The tool descriptions tell the agent to treat what it knows from the conversation as private and to use stand-ins for real names, unless the person relaxes that on the page or in the chat. Credentials never pass. A loaded script keeps only the fields that render. Looks, fonts, images and camera go through their own tools. Live: https://agent.svgent.zakideee.dev/ Code: https://github.com/zakideee/svgent (the page is apps/webmcp/ ) How we built it 13 tools on document.modelContext , with navigator.modelContext as the fallback, registered with an AbortSignal for teardown. approve_proposal is registered only while a proposal is pending. Results are plain objects plus an MCP-style content array (text, and an image part for frames). The studio package gained a small imperative handle: read, replace and patch the project, seek, play, export, render a frame, spotlight a message. An agent's edit goes through the same state the person's controls use, so undo, autosave, validation and preview all see it. Text layout and rasterization run in WASM (boundsvg) in the browser. The animated SVG is CSS keyframes with no JavaScript. There is no server; nothing leaves the tab except the files the person downloads. The submission is apps/webmcp/ : the WebMCP tools, the agent rail, the privacy default, the showcase scripts and the share card, plus the studio handle ( StudioHandle , chrome , renderFrame , spotlight ) and one preview aspect-ratio fix. The studio, scene and render packages predate the challenge. Challenges we ran into ChatGPT's browser exposes document.modelContext , Chromium exposes navigator.modelContext , and the API can appear after the page has loaded. Registration prefers the document, polls for a late API, and reports the outcome in the rail. A dynamic tool ( approve_proposal ) that unregisters itself while a call is in flight fails that call. It now stays registered for a short grace period after the proposal resolves. A script an agent writes from a conversation can carry real names, paths, hosts and keys from that conversation. The privacy default, the script allowlist and the "every word" list exist for that. Accomplishments that we're proud of The whole loop runs in the ChatGPT desktop app (built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Sol) and in Chromium with WebMCP enabled, and the demo video is a recording of it. The agent edits through the same state as the person's controls, so undo, autosave, validation and preview treat both alike. Four of the showcase scripts are problems agent-app users have: a clip for the team channel without the secrets; a reproduction of a decline that was missed, when recording is not allowed; three slides that walk a colleague through choices and approvals; a README hero for your own MCP server. What we learned A page can hand an agent facts it cannot infer (timing, frames, what would render), and that is worth more than letting the agent guess well. Approval and visibility have to be part of the tools, not a note in a prompt. What's next for svgent Agent Stage A deny list of the person's own words (names, hosts, projects) checked on the page, next to the pattern-based hints. The same tools on the other surfaces the studio renders, and on the CLI for headless use. The demo video was recorded in the ChatGPT desktop app. Waits are sped up where marked. The narration is a synthetic voice. about_excerpt:
AegisDesk is a human-in-the-loop AML investigation workspace that helps financial institutions detect, investigate, and resolve compliance alerts faster.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 What inspired me
I built AegisDesk after seeing how fragmented AML compliance workflows really are. Financial crime investigators often juggle multiple disconnected systems—alert queues in one tool, transaction data in another, document requests over email, and audit trails buried in logs. This fragmentation slows investigations, creates gaps in auditability, and forces analysts to piece together context manually. 

 At the same time, I became interested in WebMCP and human-in-the-loop automation. The idea of giving AI agents structured tools while keeping humans in control of sensitive decisions felt like the right fit for compliance work, where accountability and explainability matter more than raw automation speed. 

 AegisDesk is my attempt to bring those two ideas together: a single workspace for AML investigations that uses explainable, human-controlled automation instead of black-box decisioning. 

 What I learned
Building AegisDesk taught me several things: 

 Human-in-the-loop is non-negotiable in compliance. Automation can handle repetitive tasks, but high-risk decisions—like escalating a case, approving a transaction, or filing a report—must remain under explicit human control. WebMCP's confirmation gate pattern (gateDecision before mutating actions) became central to the design. 

 Auditability is a feature, not an afterthought. Every action in AegisDesk is written to an append-only activity log, with a real-time activity rail for investigators to see what's happening. This wasn't just about compliance requirements; it also made debugging and collaboration easier during development. 

 Edge-native architecture can work for serious workloads. Running the entire backend on Cloudflare Workers—with D1 for structured data, R2 for documents, and Durable Objects for real-time activity streaming—proved that you don't need a traditional cloud stack to build production-grade compliance tooling. 

 Explainability beats cleverness. Investigators need to understand why a tool returned certain results. Simple, transparent screening tools with clear inputs and outputs are more useful than complex models that can't be interrogated. 

 How I built it
AegisDesk is built as a single Cloudflare Worker serving both the API and SPA: 

 Backend: Hono app on Cloudflare Workers, with 10 WebMCP tool endpoints for case management, screening, document handling, rules, and activity. All mutating actions pass through a confirmation gate before execution. 

 Data layer: D1 (aegisdesk-db) for cases and rules, R2 (aegisdesk-docs) for document storage, and a Durable Object (ActivityRoom) for real-time activity streaming and replay. 

 Frontend: React/TypeScript SPA with components for the case queue, case detail modals, rules management, and an activity rail that shows live updates via WebSocket. 

 Audit trail: An append-only activity log (worker/src/activity-log.ts) captures every action and fans out to the Durable Object for real-time broadcasting. 

 Optional integrations: Alpaca (for trading data) and Notion (for external audit pages) are wired in but designed to cleanly skip if credentials aren't configured. 

 The development workflow used wrangler dev for local testing and iterative fixes, with each verified change reflected in the bundle hash. A live demo is deployed at https://aegisdesk-api.otemaach.workers.dev . 

 Challenges I faced
Balancing automation and control. Early versions leaned too far toward automation. I had to pull back and add explicit confirmation gates for sensitive actions, even when it made workflows slightly slower. The trade-off was worth it for compliance use cases. 

 Real-time activity without complexity. Getting WebSocket handshakes, Durable Object connections, and activity replay to work reliably on the edge took several iterations. The final design uses a simple /ws endpoint and a single ActivityRoom DO per session. 

 Fragmented data problem. AML investigations inherently involve multiple data sources. Instead of trying to unify everything, I focused on making the workspace a control plane where investigators can trigger screening, request documents, and add notes while maintaining a single audit trail. 

 Deploy vs. source drift. The deployed Worker version fell behind the local source during development (proven by bundle-hash mismatch). This highlighted the need for a more disciplined deploy process before demos or submissions. 

 Testing sensitive flows. Some flows (like approve/reject final submit) were intentionally blocked on live demo data, so I relied on integration tests and local wrangler dev to verify the correct code paths without risking real compliance actions. 

 AegisDesk is still evolving, but it's proven that you can build a secure, auditable, human-in-the-loop AML workspace on edge infrastructure—and that compliance teams benefit more from explainable tools than from opaque automation

title: Polaris Chat
pitch: Polaris Chat brings a Creators live community into one place. With WebMCP, streamers can ask their favorite AI Agent (like Codex) what they missed and get useful answers from the chaos of chat.
about_excerpt: Polaris Chat brings a Creators live community into one place. With WebMCP, streamers can ask their favorite AI Agent (like Codex) what they missed and get useful answers from the chaos of chat. Like Comment Story Updates 01-polaris-chat-hero 02-unified-workspace 03-webmcp-shared-workspace 04-producer-queue 05-human-agent-loop contact-sheet Inspiration Polaris Chat started from a problem I experience as a creator: when you stream to multiple platforms, every community is moving at once. Chat messages, technical issues, viewer questions, follows, subscriptions, and other community moments can all compete for attention while you are still trying to entertain the audience. But also seeing big creators struggle with keeping up with all their Chats. The idea behind Polaris Chat is simple: bring those communities into one calm workspace. For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to push that idea further. Instead of putting another chatbot next to the dashboard, I wanted ChatGPT to become a quiet producer working inside the same workspace as the creator. The goal was not to let AI take over the stream. The goal was to help the human notice what matters. What it does Polaris Chat is a public interactive preview of a future multistream creator workspace for Twitch, YouTube, Kick, TikTok LIVE, and X Live. The challenge edition* uses deterministic simulated livestream activity, so it requires no creator accounts, OAuth credentials, provider APIs, or private data. At the center of the experience is the Producer Queue . Using WebMCP, ChatGPT can: inspect the current Polaris workspace; read recent Chat and community activity; identify technical problems, unanswered viewer questions, and meaningful community moments; add existing items to the shared Producer Queue; assign priorities; focus the visible workspace on the most important source; read changes made by the human and adapt on the next turn. The creator can still handle, dismiss, reopen, or reprioritize every queue item manually. ChatGPT cannot send messages, moderate viewers, connect accounts, authorize providers, or control a livestream. How I built it Polaris Chat existed as a private product project before the challenge, including its brand, five-platform vision, and core Chat, Activity, Platform Hub, and Settings concepts. For this challenge, I created a separate public implementation specifically for WebMCP rather than exposing the private production repository. The challenge edition includes: a deterministic five-platform Producer Rush scenario; synthetic Chat and Activity fixtures; a persistent browser-based Producer Queue; human queue controls and source focusing; deterministic Reset Demo behavior; responsive desktop, tablet, and mobile layouts; eight WebMCP tools registered directly from the top-level application. The WebMCP tool set includes: get_live_workspace_snapshot list_recent_chat_messages list_recent_community_events get_producer_queue add_producer_queue_item update_producer_queue_item focus_workspace_item set_workspace_filter The tools use narrow schemas, bounded inputs, and explicit read-only or untrusted-content annotations where appropriate. One important design choice was to treat livestream Chat as untrusted data, never instructions . A viewer can type anything into Chat, including something that looks like a prompt, but that content cannot redefine tool behavior or directly trigger actions. The public preview is deployed on ChatGPT Sites and the challenge source is published separately under the MIT License. Challenges The biggest challenge was deciding how much autonomy the agent should have. It would have been easy to make the demo look more dramatic by letting ChatGPT reply to viewers, moderate users, or perform external actions. Instead, I intentionally kept the WebMCP tools narrow and reversible. The agent can help manage attention, but the creator remains responsible for the actual community interaction. Another challenge was preserving the feel of a real product while removing everything that should not exist in a public hackathon demo. The production direction for Polaris includes real provider integrations, but the challenge build had to be completely safe to publish. That meant replacing real runtime dependencies with deterministic simulated state while keeping the experience believable. WebMCP also changed how I thought about AI integration. I learned that the interesting part is not simply giving an agent more tools. The useful part is giving the agent a small set of understandable actions tied to the exact interface the human is already using. What I learned The biggest lesson from this project is that human-agent collaboration becomes much more useful when both sides share visible state. In Polaris Chat, the agent does not operate in a hidden workflow. When ChatGPT adds something to the Producer Queue, the creator sees it. When the creator marks something handled, ChatGPT can see that change on the next turn. That simple loop— agent acts → human acts → agent adapts —ended up becoming the most important part of the project. Polaris Chat is ultimately about attention, not automation. Every community. One North Star. Small disclaimer I started this project two months ago, but it came over-engineered and too complicated since I had no knowledge when it came to coding, and I purely relied on ChatGPT 5.5. So with a lot of trial and errors (and 5.6 Sol + Tibos resets) I was able to polish what was a private only app into what is now The Polaris Chat. The Challenge Edition* This is a clone of the real project that is strictly focused on integrating WebMCP, although after everything I learned about how it actually works, it will be a feature that helps my product stand out from all the others. If you read this far, thank you for your time.
