title: Signoff - the agent proposes, you decide
pitch: A refund-approval queue where the agent proposes decisions with written reasons - and the tool that applies one doesn't exist until a human approves it.
about_excerpt: A refund-approval queue where the agent proposes decisions with written reasons - and the tool that applies one doesn't exist until a human approves it. Like Comment Story Updates The refund queue: risk signals and proposals Tool console: get_policy called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the apply_proposal tool doesn't exist in the registry until a human approves the agent's proposal - enforcement lives in tool existence , not a runtime permission check. Inspiration Working a refund queue is judgment sandwiched between drudgery: read the ticket, weigh the amount against the risk, write a defensible reason, repeat forty times. The judgment is the human's job. The reading, weighing, and drafting shouldn't be. What it does The agent reads a written refund policy and every request's evidence, proposes approve / deny / partial decisions with a written reason each, and stages them as cards next to the requests they concern. Nothing applies until a human clicks Approve - and apply_proposal , the tool that actually applies a decision, is registered only while at least one approved-but-unapplied proposal exists. Approve nothing, and the tool to apply anything simply isn't in the agent's list. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, no framework. Every tool and every UI button call the same mutation through one invoke() chokepoint that also writes the shared activity log. apply_proposal dynamically registers/unregisters via an AbortController tied to whether a pending approved proposal exists - a permission boundary expressed as which tools exist, not as an instruction a model could ignore. Challenges we ran into Two rounds of adversarial testing against real Chrome (not headless mocks) found two distinct bugs in that dynamic-registration path: first, a self-abort race where the tool's own disarm logic cancelled the very call it was running under; then, after fixing that with a deferred abort, a second race where a fast Approve → Revoke → re-Approve cycle could silently desync the tool from Chrome's real registry - no error, but the tool had actually vanished. Root-caused via page.mouse.click() (real coordinate clicks reproduced it 12/15 times; Playwright's polling clicks never did), then fixed by tracking and synchronously draining any stale pending abort before re-arming. Accomplishments that we're proud of An approval boundary enforced by the browser's own tool registry, not by prompt instructions - and proven against the actual WebMCP bridge under adversarial, rapid-clicking conditions, not just the happy path. What we learned "It passed headless Playwright" and "it's correct against real Chrome" are different claims. The riskiest bugs in a dynamic-tool-registration pattern only show up under real, synchronous, same-tick timing. What's next A written audit trail export per decision, and richer risk-signal explanations sourced from order history across the whole account, not just the single request. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: Shipment Document Check
pitch: Checks shipment documents, helps an agent prepare the right fixes, and keeps approvals and final decisions with the person reviewing the pack.
about_excerpt: Checks shipment documents, helps an agent prepare the right fixes, and keeps approvals and final decisions with the person reviewing the pack. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 The starting shipment pack, with five documents, nine checks and the WebMCP review workflow in one place. The agent has prepared two corrections for exporter-owned documents. Both remain staged until a person approves them. The Bill of Lading remains locked while the application prepares an unsent correction request for the carrier. The goods descriptions are shown side by side so a person can review the evidence and confirm the final decision. Inspiration Export shipments involve several documents, and those documents are not all controlled by the same person. The exporter prepares some of them, while others come from a bank, carrier or public authority. What interested me was that finding a mismatch is only half the job. The reviewer also needs to know who is allowed to correct it. An exporter can fix its own invoice, but it cannot rewrite a Bill of Lading issued by a carrier. Some differences are also unclear enough that a person still needs to make the final decision. I built Shipment Document Check to explore how an agent could help with this work without being given permission to change everything. What it does The application reviews one fictional shipment pack containing five documents: Letter of Credit Commercial Invoice Packing List Bill of Lading Certificate of Origin It runs nine consistency checks and starts with five findings. For documents controlled by the exporter, the agent can prepare a correction. The correction is shown in the page, but a person must approve it before it is applied. For documents issued by a carrier or authority, the original document stays locked. The agent can prepare a correction request, but it cannot change the document or send the request. There is also a goods-description difference that needs human judgement. The agent can show the evidence and record a proposed decision, but a person must confirm it. After the approved corrections and confirmed decision, the preflight is run again. Seven of the nine checks pass. The remaining two issues still need action from the external issuers. How WebMCP is used I did not want to add another chatbot inside the application. Instead, the page exposes six WebMCP tools directly to a compatible browser agent: get_pack_state get_finding_evidence stage_exporter_corrections draft_external_correction_requests stage_human_decision rerun_preflight These tools give the agent a clear set of actions instead of making it guess from buttons and page text. The agent and the person reviewing the shipment work with the same visible state. When the agent stages a correction or decision, it appears in the page for review. Approval is deliberately kept outside the agent's control. The application also contains an instruction hidden inside a fictional trade document. That text is treated as document content, not as an instruction the agent should follow. How I built it The project is a client-side React and TypeScript application built with Vite. The shipment data and all nine checks are deterministic. React useReducer manages the workflow, and Zod validates the document data and WebMCP tool inputs. The WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools and the manual interface use the same reducer actions, so the agent cannot bypass rules that apply in the page. There is no backend, login, database, OCR service or document upload. Everything in the shipment pack is fictional and stays in the browser. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was keeping the agent useful without giving it too much control. A staged correction must not be mistaken for an approved correction. A drafted request must not be mistaken for a sent request. The WebMCP result and the visible page also need to show the same workflow state after every action. It was equally important to prove that locked documents are actually protected. If the agent tries to modify the carrier-issued Bill of Lading, the application returns DOCUMENT_LOCKED and leaves the document unchanged. What I am proud of The project has only six tools, and each one has a clear purpose. The final result is also honest. The application ends with seven passing checks and two issues still waiting for external action. It does not pretend that every problem can be solved automatically. What I learned This project changed how I think about agent access. Giving an agent more control does not always make the product better. In this case, the useful part is the separation of responsibilities. The agent handles repetitive checking and preparation. The application enforces the rules. The person keeps control over approvals and judgement. What is next A future version could accept real documents, use OCR and support different shipment rules. Before adding those features, I would want to do a proper privacy and security review. For this challenge, I kept the project small, deterministic and limited to fictional data. title: AgentReady.js: Instant WebMCP for Every Website
pitch: Turn any website into safe, structured WebMCP tools with a single script tag. Progressive enhancement for AI agents with built-in human-in-the-loop safety.
about_excerpt: Turn any website into safe, structured WebMCP tools with a single script tag. Progressive enhancement for AI agents with built-in human-in-the-loop safety. Like 3 Comment Story Updates Send "Search for Keyboard" in WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector Watch the AgentReady tool calling logs Fill the form using WebMCP Find a product Inspiration The promise of autonomous AI agents browsing the web has collided with a painful reality: modern agent browsing relies heavily on computer vision, screenshot parsing, or dumping massive DOM trees into LLM context windows. This approach is slow, brittle, and expensive. When an agent consumes raw HTML or high-resolution screenshots, the signal-to-noise ratio is dismal: $$\text{Efficiency Ratio} = \frac{\text{Semantic Information}}{\text{Token Overhead}} \ll 1$$ The emerging WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) standard solves this by allowing web applications to declare structured, high-level tools directly to AI clients via document.modelContext. However, expecting developers to rewrite millions of legacy websites and single-page apps (SPAs) with custom WebMCP implementations will take years. We asked ourselves: Why can't existing websites become instantly agent-ready with zero code changes? That question inspired AgentReady.js — a progressive-enhancement JavaScript runtime that extracts semantic meaning from standard HTML and instantly exposes safe, structured WebMCP tools to any AI browser or in-page agent. What it does With a single tag, AgentReady.js transforms any standard web page into an AI-accessible powerhouse: Automatic Semantic Discovery & Synthesis: Scans the DOM tree, analyzes forms, buttons, navigational structures, and accessibility attributes (aria-label, placeholder, label), and automatically derives typed JSON Schema tools (e.g., transforming a search form into search_products({ q, category, max_price })). 7 Core Built-In Primitives: Provides foundational tools including get_page_context, find_on_page, read_target, activate_target, set_field, fill_form, and submit_form. Multi-Platform WebMCP Bridge: Exposes all synthesized and registered tools natively via document.modelContext (and navigator.modelContext), while providing an identical in-page shim (getTools() and executeTool()) so ChatGPT desktop browsers, Chrome 149+, Firefox, and in-page AI companions work seamlessly. Three-Tier Progressive Enhancement: Level 0 (Zero Code): Drop in the script; tools are synthesized automatically. Level 1 (HTML Metadata): Refine tools using declarative data-agent-* attributes. Level 2 (Native Tooling): Register bespoke business logic via window.AgentReady.register({...}). Human-in-the-Loop Safety Engine: Quarantines sensitive fields (passwords, tokens, CVVs, cc-* credit card data) and pauses consequential actions (purchases, deletions, form submissions) with an interactive Approve / Decline panel. How we built it AgentReady.js is crafted with modern TypeScript and Bun for high performance and zero external runtime dependencies: ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Web Browser │ └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘ │ ┌────────────┴────────────┐ │ AgentReady.js │ │ (Zero-dependency Shim) │ └────────────┬────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ │ Semantic Analyzer │ │ Safety Policy │ │ Runtime Adapter │ │ • WeakRef Cache │ │ • Regex Redactor │ │ • document. │ │ • Form Synthesis │ │ • Token Budget │ │ modelContext │ │ • MutationObserver│ │ • Approval Dialog │ │ • In-Page Fallback│ └───────────────────┘ └───────────────────┘ └───────────────────┘ Runtime & Adapter Layer (src/runtime.ts): Listens to native engine events, dynamically registers schemas, and manages tool life cycles. When native WebMCP is absent, it seamlessly provides spec-compliant getTools() and executeTool() methods. Semantic Engine & Stable Ref Pool (src/semantic.ts): Indexes interactive elements using WeakRef to eliminate memory leaks. Elements are queried via natural language token matching without mutating the original DOM. Dynamic Resynthesis (src/index.ts): Leverages a debounced MutationObserver (\Delta t \approx 100\text{ms}) to detect route transitions in SPAs and re-synthesize available tools on the fly. Shadow DOM Inspector (src/inspector.ts): An isolated UI widget attached via Shadow DOM with closed encapsulation, preventing CSS collisions with host websites while rendering real-time execution logs and safety confirmation dialogs. Strict Testing Suite: Over 43 automated unit tests run with Bun's test runner, combined with full end-to-end Playwright tests on real Chrome. Challenges we ran into 1. The Dynamic SPA Problem & Memory Leaks Single Page Applications (SPAs) frequently tear down and rebuild DOM subtrees. Storing direct references to DOM nodes caused memory leaks, while relying on static selectors resulted in StaleElementReference failures. Solution: We implemented an ephemeral reference registry backed by JavaScript WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry, pairing fuzzy text queries with structural paths to gracefully recover when elements re-render. 2. Output Budgets and Context Poisoning LLMs can easily be overwhelmed if a tool returns an entire table containing thousands of rows. Solution: We designed a strict output-budget clamp enforcing an upper bound: $$L_{\text{output}} \le 1500 \text{ characters}$$ This truncates large payloads gracefully while informing the agent that additional pagination or targeted querying is required. 3. Divergent Browser Implementations During testing across Chrome 149+ builds and ChatGPT's in-app browser, we encountered differing WebMCP draft implementations (e.g., JSON schema strings vs. parsed schema objects, document.modelContext vs. navigator.modelContext, and register-only environments). We engineered a resilient normalization layer that detects engine quirks and provides a consistent interface across all clients. Accomplishments that we're proud of True Zero-Configuration: Simply adding immediately enables a ChatGPT browser or WebMCP agent to navigate, search, add products to cart, and prepare checkout on a standard e-commerce storefront. Radical Token Reduction: Replacing raw HTML DOM dumps with structured JSON tool schemas achieves up to a 90% reduction in token consumption per interaction turn: $$\text{Token Savings} = 1 - \frac{\text{Tokens} {\text{WebMCP Tool}}}{\text{Tokens} {\text{Raw DOM}}} \approx 85\% - 95\%$$ Zero-Compromise Security: Full proactive redaction of type="password", autocomplete="cc-*", hidden CSRF tokens, and sensitive credential fields ensures agent actions remain transparent and strictly supervised. Lightweight Footprint: The entire runtime bundles into a standalone, minified script under 25 KB with zero third-party dependencies. What we learned Semantic HTML is AI's Best Friend: Modern accessibility primitives (aria-*, label, form method, semantic button labels) already contain almost all the structural metadata needed to synthesize high-quality AI tool definitions. Building for accessibility naturally creates AI-ready applications. Deterministic Tools Beat Autonomous Spelunking: Agents provided with 5–8 high-level, strongly-typed semantic tools consistently outperform agents forced to guess low-level click coordinates or query selectors. Safety Must Be Default, Not Configurable: Autonomous tools that can submit forms or make payments must demand human confirmation at the platform level, making safe behavior the default rather than an afterthought. What's next for AgentReady.js: Instant WebMCP for Every Website Framework Adapters & Components: Native bindings and wrapper components for React, Vue, Svelte, and Next.js for even easier declarative tool mapping. Multi-Modal Spatial Grounding: Integrating semantic bounding box data so agents combining visual and WebMCP modalities can visually correlate tools with UI components. Public CDN & npm Package: Distributing @agentready/core via npm and global CDNs (Cloudflare, cdnjs, unpkg) for one-line deployment across the web. Community Tool Templates: Pre-built semantic profiles for popular web platforms like Shopify, WordPress, WooCommerce, and Webflow to instantly expose rich store and CMS actions out of the box. pitch: A WebMCP-powered returns desk that lets AI agents search orders, evaluate return eligibility, compare resolutions, and prepare RMAs for human approval.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-powered returns desk that lets AI agents search orders, evaluate return eligibility, compare resolutions, and prepare RMAs for human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 discovers 6 WebMCP tools 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Returns Desk main UI 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 search_orders real tool call

 discovers 6 WebMCP tools 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Returns Desk main UI 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 search_orders real tool call 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 HTML report 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 discovers 6 WebMCP tools 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Returns sound simple, but the actual workflow is usually not. 

 A customer asks, “Can I return this order?”, and suddenly a support operator has to find the order, read the right return policy, check the return window, look at the item condition, compare different resolutions, draft a response, and sometimes prepare an RMA. 

 We wanted to explore what this workflow would look like if the website was designed not only for humans, but also for AI agents. 

 Instead of asking an agent to read the page, guess which button to click, and simulate a human user, we wanted the website to expose its real capabilities directly. 

 That is where WebMCP became a really good fit for the project. 

 

 What it does 

 Returns Desk is a WebMCP-powered returns workspace for small e-commerce teams. 

 It exposes six WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_orders 
 get_return_policy 
 check_return_eligibility 
 compare_resolution_options 
 draft_customer_message 
 submit_rma_for_approval 
 

 An agent can use these tools to move through a real returns workflow step by step. 

 For example, a user can ask the agent to find order ORD-1001 , check whether it is eligible for return, and compare the available resolution options. 

 The agent can then call the website tools directly instead of trying to operate the UI like a human. 

 The main idea is simple: 

 AI handles the repetitive work, while humans stay in control of important decisions. 

 

 How we built it 

 We built the frontend with React and TypeScript, and deployed the application with Cloudflare Workers. 

 The WebMCP layer exposes the same business capabilities that already exist in the application, instead of creating a separate demo-only flow. 

 That means the human-facing UI and the agent-facing tools are connected to the same returns logic. 

 We also tried to keep the policy and eligibility logic as deterministic as possible. 

 Instead of asking an LLM to freely interpret every return case, the application uses structured rules such as return windows, final-sale restrictions, item condition, and available resolution options. 

 For write-related actions, we added an approval boundary so the agent can prepare a request without silently completing a consequential action. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was deciding what should actually become a WebMCP tool. 

 At first, it is easy to think in terms of UI actions like “click this button” or “open this page”. 

 But that would miss the point of WebMCP. 

 We realized the tools should represent meaningful business capabilities instead, such as check_return_eligibility or compare_resolution_options . 

 Another challenge was deciding where automation should stop. 

 We wanted the agent to be genuinely useful, but we did not want it to silently perform important write actions. 

 That led us to separate read and decision-support tools from approval-related actions. 

 We also had to test the production site in a real WebMCP environment and make sure ChatGPT could actually discover the tools, not just see them in source code. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are especially proud that Returns Desk works as both a normal website and an agent-ready website. 

 A human can still use the UI normally, but an AI agent can discover structured capabilities through WebMCP. 

 We successfully exposed six WebMCP tools in the production site and verified that they can be discovered through ChatGPT Desktop Site Tools. 

 We are also proud of the human-in-the-loop design. 

 The agent can handle order lookup, policy retrieval, eligibility checks, resolution comparison, and preparation work, while important actions still remain reviewable by a human. 

 Another thing we are proud of is keeping the demo safe and repeatable. 

 The project uses isolated demo data, so no real payments, refunds, emails, shipments, or customer accounts are affected. 

 

 What we learned 

 The biggest thing we learned is that making a website “AI-ready” is not the same as adding a chatbot. 

 The more interesting question is: 

 What capabilities should the website expose so an agent can understand and use it reliably? 

 WebMCP made us think much more carefully about tool design, schemas, responsibilities, and safety boundaries. 

 We also learned that a good agent workflow depends heavily on the tools underneath it. 

 Clear tools make the workflow easier to understand, test, and trust. 

 This project also helped us connect a lot of engineering pieces together: frontend, backend logic, APIs, structured tools, deployment, and agent interaction. 

 

 What's next for Returns Desk 

 The current version is built around a deterministic demo returns workflow. 

 The next step would be connecting it to real commerce infrastructure. 

 Possible future integrations include: 

 
 Shopify orders and inventory 
 real return and refund systems 
 shipping and return-label providers 
 merchant-configurable return policies 
 customer support platforms 
 richer approval and audit workflows 
 

 We would also like to explore more advanced agent workflows where an agent can handle most of the repetitive returns process while keeping merchants informed and in control. 

 The long-term idea is to make Returns Desk an agent-ready operations layer for e-commerce returns, not just another support dashboard.

title: TLDW | Too Long Didn't Watch
pitch: For those who want to Cut Through The Noise to Get to The Signal in their YouTube videos.
about_excerpt: For those who want to Cut Through The Noise to Get to The Signal in their YouTube videos. Like Comment Story Updates Step 1 Processing Result Icon Inspiration In a world of AI there is too much noise, this is a simple tool to leverage that very same AI to help cut through the noise to get to the signal of your YouTube videos. What it does TLDW is one web page where you paste a YouTube link and gets the captions, with the moment each line was said. An AI agent opening the page finds two WebMCP tools instead of buttons: get_transcript(url) hands it the captions as timestamped segments, and render_explainer(slides, url) draws whatever the agent wrote back onto the page, every timestamp a link that opens the video at that second, then reads it aloud. The thinking runs on the visitor's own ChatGPT plan, in their own session. How its built Built entirely with AI, Both tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool, with navigator.modelContext as a fallback for older builds, each with a JSON schema an agent can read. Errors are returned, never thrown, so a failure arrives as a result the agent can act on. Every fetch has three outcomes, not two: ok, not_measured with a reason, or a structured error, because a tool that cannot tell a failed measurement from a real zero will report the first as the second. Captions come from a transcript API first with a direct fetch behind it, held in memory for ten minutes and never written down. The page is served by a Cloudflare Worker. Read-aloud uses the browser's own voices by default with a voice picker; one opt-in experimental entry renders a natural voice on our server and streams it back. An agent whose browser has no WebMCP yet can paste the same slides into a Render box on the page and get the identical result. It was built from nothing in one evening, live on stream, by a fleet of AI bodies run by one human, with two independent reviews on every change. Challenges We (Myself and my AI Team) only had ~8 total hours for this as that's when I found out about the competition, then immediately started live streaming the start to finish. We had about ~3 hours of prep while waiting for the reset then 5 hours to build. The spec moved while we built: our first registration was on navigator.modelContext only, and Chrome's stable build binds document.modelContext, so the tools registered and nobody could see them. YouTube refuses caption fetches from a server, so the free path failed silently until we made refusal a first-class result and put a transcript API in front of it. Agents that fetched the captions then answered in chat instead of drawing on the page, until the tool text put the obligation before the data. And the browser's speech queue armed from the speak call rather than from what was drawn, so a slide with the wrong shape left a full explainer on screen and nothing to play. Each one was found by a second reader, not by the author. Accomplishments that we're proud of We got it done 40mins past the buzzer but fortunately there was a 12 hour extension, so we polished the video and made minor edits to the description etc (also generated by AI) The tool work on a free ChatGPT account, the desktop app's built-in browser, and with one sentence: explain this video and render it on the page. The page registers two tools, the agent calls them, the explainer appears with timestamps that jump into the YouTube video if you want to watch a particular segment in full, and it also comes with a reads aloud bar with play back controls and voice selection that uses your browser supported voices and 2 x experimental neural voices. The public repository has one clean history, one identity, and passed a whole-history scan by a stranger before it went public. What we learned The hard part was restraint. Every instinct said add a summarizer, add a model, add a key, and each one would have made it slower, costlier. The second lesson was the error surface: an agent is not a human staring at a stack trace, it reads your failure and decides what to do next, so a tool that throws ends the conversation and a tool that returns a readable error lets the agent try something sensible. The third was the voices, Chrome free supports free neural style voices as well as system voices, the ChatGPT browser uses only the free system voice. We are experimenting with some neural voices but the render time is slower, there could be an option to use something like Elevenlabs but then that would mean have to charge a fee for the service or run ad's on the page. It would be good if the ChatGPT could somehow enable support for the Chrome voices as those are pretty good. What's next for TLDW | Too Long Didn't Watch This is TLDW v1 .v2 & v3 will be better. I didn't want to create something that Notebook LM already does so keeping it video focused is the lane I'll stay in for now. v2 would be more generating more interactive lessons / explainers with interactive kinetic elements maybe a quiz at the end and then perhaps v3 would be the ability to generate a Summarized Explainer Video about the video on the fly. and then later another version of the product for teachers that uses the same logic and flow to help produce lesson plans and explainers on the fly for all students at all levels with all styles of learning requirements. title: Ukebaco — file requests your agent can open and answer
pitch: Collect files from people who have no Google account, straight into your own Drive. With WebMCP your agent opens the upload page, then answers "has Acme sent this month's invoice yet?"
about_excerpt: Collect files from people who have no Google account, straight into your own Drive. With WebMCP your agent opens the upload page, then answers "has Acme sent this month's invoice yet?" Like Comment Story Updates The problem Every small business collects files from people who are not their colleagues: monthly invoices from subcontractors, ID documents from new hires, photos from event participants. Those people do not have an account on your system and will not make one. So the files arrive by email, one at a time, named "scan001.pdf", and somebody spends their Friday renaming them into the right folder and ticking names off a list. Ukebaco ( https://ukeba.co ) is the boring fix: you publish one link, anyone can upload without signing in to anything, and the file lands directly in your Google Drive™ — sorted into a folder tree you defined, renamed from the answers the sender typed, and recorded as a row in a Google Sheets™ ledger. It has been live and taking real payments since 2026-09-03. What WebMCP adds The tedious part was never the uploading. It is the two questions that bracket it: Before: "set up a page to collect September invoices from my 12 subcontractors, PDF only, due the 30th, folder per company." After: "has Acme sent theirs yet? what about the rest?" Both are now sentences you say to the agent in the tab where you are already signed in. The dashboard registers four tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() : Tool What it does create_link Creates the public upload page: fields to ask, folder tree, file-naming rule, deadline, PIN, allowed extensions. Returns the URL to share. list_links The owner's links with status, destination folder and ledger URL. search_submissions Who sent what, when, and the Drive URL of each file. Matches company name, folder path, receipt number, file name. set_link_active Stops or resumes a link. The URL survives; submissions are refused. create_link is the interesting one. Creating a good file request is a form with about fifteen decisions in it — that is precisely the shape of task people abandon halfway. Described in one sentence to an agent, it becomes one tool call. Folder templates, file-name templates and field types are inferred from a natural-language description and normalised in a pure, unit-tested layer before they ever reach the API. search_submissions is the one people use every day. "Has this month's invoice come in from X" is a question the ledger can answer, but only if you open the spreadsheet and scroll. The tool answers it in place, and returns the Drive URL so the next sentence can be "open it". Why WebMCP is the right fit — and not a remote MCP server We built both, so this is an informed answer. WebMCP let us add agent control without inventing a single new credential . execute runs inside the owner's signed-in tab, so fetch carries the existing session cookie and the server identifies the user with the same getSession() it already used. There is no token to issue, store, rotate, revoke or leak. Log out, and the tools go with the tab. If you are not signed in, the dashboard redirects to /login and no tools are ever registered. For a product where the whole value proposition is "your files stay in your own Drive", adding a new long-lived credential to reach that Drive would have been the wrong trade. The second reason is that the server does not get more permissive because an agent is asking. Plan limits and paid features (PIN, deadline, email verification) are enforced by the same /api/links route as the UI; when the plan does not allow something it returns 402 and the tool relays that sentence verbatim to the agent. There is deliberately no "agent path" through the paywall. We shipped a remote MCP server too ( POST /api/mcp , with Ukebaco acting as its own OAuth 2.1 authorization server — dynamic client registration, PKCE, a consent screen and refresh-token rotation) so ChatGPT and Claude can reach the same four tools from outside the browser. It works, and it took roughly six times as much code as the WebMCP path, almost all of it in issuing and revoking credentials. That comparison is the strongest argument for WebMCP we can make: for a signed-in web app, WebMCP is the version of this feature you can actually maintain. The part we deliberately kept human Agents get the repetitive half. People keep the half that should stay deliberate. Choosing an existing Drive folder stays in the Google Picker, which an agent cannot drive. Our OAuth scope is drive.file only, so Ukebaco can see the folders it created and the ones you personally handed it. An agent cannot widen that, and we did not add a tool that pretends otherwise. Everything a submitter typed is marked untrustedContentHint . Submitters are third parties: the company name, the note in a text field and the file name are strings a stranger wrote. They are data to be shown, never instructions to be followed. This is the one place where an agent-readable file-collection service is genuinely dangerous, and it is annotated at the source. readOnlyHint on list_links and search_submissions , so the agent knows which two of the four tools cannot change anything. Calls from tools carry X-Ukebaco-Client: webmcp , and link creation records which route it came from. When an agent creates a link, the audit trail says so. How we built it Next.js 15 on Firebase App Hosting; Firestore for metadata only (90-day TTL); files go from the submitter's browser straight to Drive's resumable session URI and never touch our servers. The WebMCP layer is split in two so the interesting part is testable: src/lib/webmcp-tools.ts — tool definitions, JSON Schemas, and the normalisation of whatever the agent sends (labels in any language become valid field ids; folder templates are resolved against the fields that actually exist; a date becomes an end-of-day deadline). No I/O. Covered by unit tests. src/components/WebMcpTools.tsx — registration and fetch . Feature-detects both document.modelContext and the older navigator.modelContext , unregisters on unmount, and if registration fails the dashboard carries on as an ordinary web page. src/lib/link-service.ts — one decision layer shared by the dashboard API, the WebMCP tools and the remote MCP server, so the three routes cannot drift apart. What is new in the challenge window Ukebaco itself predates the challenge. Everything agent-facing — the four tools, the pure tool layer and its tests, the shared link service, the remote MCP server and its OAuth authorization server — was written on 2026-09-04, inside the submission period. See the commit history and ADR-0002 / ADR-0003 in docs/adr/. Try it Sign in at https://ukeba.co with any Google account. The free plan needs no payment details and gives you a working link. Open the dashboard in ChatGPT's in-app browser and ask it to make you a file request. What's next Per-tool consent that the owner can set once ("agents may search, but never create"), richer folder inference from a single sentence, and dropping the Chrome origin-trial header the day WebMCP ships unflagged. pitch: An AI agent completing real-world multi-step errands across three independently-owned websites with zero backend integration, zero API keys, and pure WebMCP discovery.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent completing real-world multi-step errands across three independently-owned websites with zero backend integration, zero API keys, and pure WebMCP discovery.

 Completed Itinerary — Verified cross-merchant receipts with zero backend API keys

 Merchant 2: Luxe Grooming Studio — Calendar slot discovery & appointment booking 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Merchant 3: Paper & Ink Bookstore — untrustedContentHint protection against prompt injection 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Today's agentic web demos fall into one of two traps: 

 
 Brittle Screen Scraping : Agents using vision or accessibility trees to click coordinates and type blindly into DOM elements, which break the moment a CSS class, layout, or modal changes. 
 Walled-Garden Aggregators : Agents restricted to closed ecosystem APIs where independent neighborhood businesses must surrender 30% take rates and hand over customer relationships to centralized platforms. 
 

 When the W3C and Chrome WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext ) emerged, we saw the foundation for a third, better future: the open web itself as the native agent runtime . 

 We asked ourselves: Could an AI agent coordinate a real-world multi-stop morning errand across three completely independent, standalone neighborhood businesses—a specialty coffee shop, a boutique grooming studio, and an indie bookstore—with zero backend integration, zero proprietary API keys, and pure on-page tool discovery? 

 That question led to Open Web Concierge . 

 

 What It Does 

 Open Web Concierge is an autonomous multi-vendor assistant that plans, negotiates, and executes unified errands across the open web while keeping the human firmly in control. 

 
 Dynamic Instruction-Driven Scoping : The user speaks naturally (e.g., "I want an iced cold brew with oat milk" , "Book a haircut with Marcus at 11:15" , or a multi-stop Saturday routine). The agent dynamically parses intent and activates only the merchant services requested, gracefully omitting non-relevant stops with zero wasted spend. 
 User Identity Profile & Live Form Reflection : The Concierge maintains the user's default credentials (Name, Email, Mobile No., Gender). As the agent navigates each merchant website, it emits live synchronization events over a shared errand bus—allowing the user to watch the merchant's counter form or booking calendar populate live on screen with an active sync indicator. 
 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Security Gates : The agent never silently commits funds. Before finalizing any transaction, a modal confirmation gate halts execution, presenting itemized pricing, timing, and merchant verification for explicit user approval. 
 Live Cross-Side Checkout Reflection : Once authorized, dual-layer real-time synchronization ( BroadcastChannel and reactive storage) immediately posts the confirmed order to the merchant's Active Barista Queue , Client Appointment Log , and Front Register Holds across independent windows and tabs. 
 Auditable Receipts : Upon completion, the Concierge compiles an itemized trip log with verifiable order IDs and costs, exportable as Markdown or JSON. 
 

 

 How We Built It 

 We built the application as a production-grade multi-page web ecosystem using React 19 , Vite 6 , and Tailwind CSS , adhering strictly to the Chrome & W3C WebMCP specification: 

 
 Merchant Tool Registration on document.modelContext :

 
 Artisan Roast Café ( /cafe/ ) : Exposes check_menu ( readOnlyHint: true ) and order_coffee (with strict parameter schemas and customer contact info). 
 Luxe Grooming Studio ( /salon/ ) : Exposes check_availability ( readOnlyHint: true ) and book_slot for stylist and calendar scheduling. 
 Paper & Ink Bookstore ( /bookstore/ ) : Exposes search_catalog ( untrustedContentHint: true ) and reserve_book for front-desk holds. 
 Concierge Orchestration Hub ( / ) : Exposes get_errand_briefing and log_completed_step . 
 
 Prompt Injection Defense via Chrome Hints :

 
 Following WebMCP security guidelines, search_catalog marks query results with untrustedContentHint: true . This informs the consuming LLM that merchant book blurbs and user reviews are untrusted third-party content, neutralizing indirect prompt injection vectors. 
 
 Idempotency Protection :

 
 Implemented client request tokens ( clientRequestId ) cached in a 15-second sliding window to prevent accidental double-billing or duplicate holds from rapid agent loops. 
 
 Bi-Directional Errand Bus :

 
 Combined the HTML5 BroadcastChannel API ( webmcp_errand_bus ) with reactive window storage listeners to ensure sub-millisecond, cross-tab synchronization between the Concierge hub and open merchant tabs without requiring an intermediary WebSocket server. 
 
 Built-in WebMCP Inspector :

 
 Included an interactive on-page drawer allowing judges and developers to inspect live registered schemas, test parameter validation, and trigger manual tool executions. 
 
 

 

 Challenges We Faced 

 
 Contextual Linguistic Disambiguation : Natural language is messy. In a prompt like "Book a haircut with Marcus" , the word "book" is a scheduling verb, not a request for literature. We engineered a contextual parser that accurately distinguishes verbal actions ( "book an appointment" ) from literary nouns ( "read a book" , "buy a novel" ) to prevent erroneous merchant activations. 
 Zero-Flicker Live Form Population : Connecting cross-tab React state to live agent actions without causing form resets or race conditions required decoupling tool discovery from UI input bindings, synchronizing through a predictable broadcast event contract. 
 Eliminating "AI Slop" Aesthetics : We committed to an authentic, human-crafted design language. We eliminated all emojis, avoided generic gradient pills, and designed a neutral, high-contrast dark palette ( #0C0C0C , #121110 , #141414 ) inspired by Swiss editorial typography and physical ledger boards. 
 Cross-Window Consistency : Ensuring that checkouts made in the Concierge immediately reflect in the merchant's Barista Queue or Appointment Log across separate browser tabs and embedded multi-views required implementing dual-channel sync ( BroadcastChannel with storage event fallbacks). 
 

 

 What We Learned & The Future of the Open Web 

 WebMCP represents a paradigm shift for web development. For the last 15 years, the web has been pressured into walled gardens and mobile app silos because machines couldn't reliably interact with standard HTML. 

 By standardizing document.modelContext , the open web becomes the agentic web . A local family-owned bakery or indie bookstore can become fully AI-operable in an afternoon simply by exposing standard tools on their existing website. No platform monopolies, no 30% tolls, and no closed ecosystems—just humans, agents, and merchants collaborating over the open protocols of the web.

pitch: An agent-native WebMCP layer for Jennifer Furniture enabling AI agents to search 14,000+ catalog items, eliminate generative visual hallucinations, and execute 1-click room-fit checkouts.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native WebMCP layer for Jennifer Furniture enabling AI agents to search 14,000+ catalog items, eliminate generative visual hallucinations, and execute 1-click room-fit checkouts.

 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 1-Click Direct Checkout: Automated Shopify Cart Permalink pre-loading bundled items and promotional discounts. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Jennifer Furniture WebMCP Co-Pilot: Native AI agent interface for conversational and spatial commerce. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Multimodal room input: Customers provide room photos with spatial, dimensional, and budget constraints. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Zero-hallucination room staging: Visual Asset Bridge renders authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 System Architecture: Customer Intent → ChatGPT Agent → WebMCP Visual & Spatial Tools → 1-Click Shopify Checkout. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 1-Click Direct Checkout: Automated Shopify Cart Permalink pre-loading bundled items and promotional discounts. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Jennifer Furniture WebMCP Co-Pilot: Native AI agent interface for conversational and spatial commerce. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Multimodal room input: Customers provide room photos with spatial, dimensional, and budget constraints. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Zero-hallucination room staging: Visual Asset Bridge renders authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 System Architecture: Customer Intent → ChatGPT Agent → WebMCP Visual & Spatial Tools → 1-Click Shopify Checkout. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 1-Click Direct Checkout: Automated Shopify Cart Permalink pre-loading bundled items and promotional discounts. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Shopping for home furniture online has a fundamental visual and spatial disconnect: 

 
 A customer uploads a photo of their living room and asks: "Which sofa from this website will look beautiful in this room, fit between my walls with proper walking clearance, and stay under my $ 2,500 budget?" 
 Standard AI chatbots fail because they either hallucinate fictional 3D furniture models that do not exist, or they just return a list of text links without understanding the room's physical layout or visual aesthetics. 
 

 We built Jennifer WebMCP to turn Jennifer Furniture's Shopify Plus store (14,447 catalog products) into an agent-native spatial shopping engine . By implementing the experimental WebMCP standard, AI agents in ChatGPT and Google Chrome can natively interact with the catalog, evaluate room spatial clearance, extract authentic visual assets, and generate 1-click direct checkouts. 

 

 What it does 

 Jennifer WebMCP exposes a suite of structured tools directly to AI agents via /api/mcp/manifest : 

 
 find_products_by_constraints :
Searches Jennifer Furniture's 14,447 catalog items by price budget ($B \le $ 2,500$), dimensions, room category, and fabric types. 
 get_product_visual_asset (The Visual Bridge) :
Solves the core problem of AI visual hallucinations. Instead of describing furniture in plain text, WebMCP fetches the canonical high-resolution Shopify CDN photography, converts it into a byte-level base64 data URI, and supplies explicit geometry-preservation prompt anchors for GPT-4o Vision and diffusion models. 
 calculate_room_fit_and_clearance :
Evaluates spatial boundaries and perimeter walkway clearance $d_{\text{clearance}}$: 
 

 d clearance = W room − ( W sofa + 2 × d margin ) 

 Verdict = { "OPTIMAL_FIT" , if  d clearance ≥ 36  inches   "ACCEPTABLE_FIT" , if  30  inches ≤ d clearance < 36  inches   "RESTRICTED_WALKWAY" , if  d clearance < 30  inches 

 
 build_coordinated_room_bundle :
Pairs the chosen sofa with a matching ottoman and accent chair, automatically applying a promotional 15% bundle discount: 
 

 P bundle = 0.85 × ∑ j = 1 3 P j 

 
 create_checkout_handoff :
Generates an official direct Shopify Cart Permalink that pre-loads all selected items and discounts into a 1-click instant checkout. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 WebMCP Platform : Next.js 14 App Router and TypeScript deployed live on Vercel ( https://jennifer-webmcp.vercel.app ), serving OpenAPI 3.1.0 JSON-RPC manifests at /api/mcp/manifest . 
 Multimodal Visual Asset Bridge : Dedicated edge endpoint ( /api/tools/visual-asset ) proxying Shopify CDN assets into base64 visual anchors with geometry preservation rules. 
 Storefront Voice & Web Client : Lightweight zero-dependency SDK ( public/widget.js ) registering WebMCP tools on the client window.WebMCP object for browser-based agents. 
 Shopify Plus Commerce Engine : Direct integration with Shopify Storefront API and cart permalink architecture for frictionless checkout handoff. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Eliminating Generative Hallucinations in Room Staging :
When vision models try to place a sofa into a user's photo using only text, they frequently alter the cushions, armrests, or fabric color. We built get_product_visual_asset to feed byte-level pixel data directly into the model's multimodal prompt, anchoring the generation to the authentic product. 
 Standardizing Agent Tool Schemas :
Ensuring that complex spatial queries (room dimensions, lighting conditions, budget constraints) are cleanly validated using standard WebMCP JSON schemas so any client (ChatGPT, Chrome extension, Claude) can invoke them reliably. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Zero-Hallucination Visual Staging : Proving that WebMCP visual asset bridges allow agents to stage authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 Sub-200ms Latency : Delivering real-time catalog search and room fit calculations across 14,400+ products on Vercel Edge. 
 True 1-Click Checkout Loop : Seamless transition from conversational room design in ChatGPT straight into Shopify checkout. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP bridges the gap between text-only AI reasoning and real-world spatial commerce. By providing agents with structured tools and canonical visual assets, e-commerce stores can offer personal interior design consultations directly inside AI chats. 

 

 What's next for Jennifer WebMCP: Multimodal Agentic Interior Designer 

 
 Mobile LiDAR 3D Room Mesh Extraction : Direct boundary estimation from iPhone LiDAR scans. 
 WebXR Spatial Staging : Streaming interactive 3D GLTF models to Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest agents. 
 Real-Time Fabric & Finish Swapping : Allowing agents to swap velvet, leather, and wood finishes dynamically via WebMCP variant tools.

pitch: Doctors want to use AI. They are not sure how it works within HIPAA. This is a WebMCP enabled site to help them get started with the help of their AI agent and staying HIPAA compliant.
about_excerpt: Doctors want to use AI. They are not sure how it works within HIPAA. This is a WebMCP enabled site to help them get started with the help of their AI agent and staying HIPAA compliant. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP tool invoked Works in Chrome - Ten Tools Discovered WebMCP tool runs - web page changes WebMCP Activated Main Hero Header Running in Codex in app browser Site Tools Ready! Entire site built with ChatGPT Pro and Codex, Deep Research Instructions for Judges #2 The 10 WebMCP Tools Instructions for Judges #3 WebMCP Instructions for Judges #1 Inspiration My main inspiration came from knowing doctors who have no idea how to use AI. I just met with a dentist from NYC who makes $400,000 a year and never heard of Codex. Then when I learned about WebMCP I realized this was the perfect technology to help doctors figure out how to deploy AI in their practices and be assured they're not letting the AI run loose and they stay HIPAA compliant. HIPAA.technology gives a doctor and an AI agent one shared workspace, where the doctor sees everything the agent does and keeps control of everything that matters. What it does A physician or medical-practice leader can: Learn three essential boundaries: minimum necessary data, the vendor path, and human clinical judgment. Compare four realistic healthcare AI workflows. Assess whether a workflow is ready for a bounded synthetic rehearsal. Prepare a 21-day AI adoption mission. Review and personally approve - or refuse - the mission's policy gates. Enter a public practice domain for a website debrief that never touches portals, private pages, or PHI. The AI agent can inspect the workspace, focus lessons, select workflows, assess readiness, stage and revise a mission, deliver a public-site debrief, and update the contextual guide. How I used WebMCP The live webpage registers ten structured JavaScript tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : inspect_adoption_workspace focus_learning_lesson select_clinical_ai_use_case assess_use_case_readiness stage_21_day_adoption_mission revise_adoption_mission prepare_practice_website_review deliver_practice_website_debrief set_contextual_guidance focus_mission_week Without WebMCP, an agent has to guess what your app means from pixels and click targets. With WebMCP, it gets real tools with real schemas - bounded inputs, safety annotations, structured results. No guessing. And when the agent focuses a lesson, assesses a workflow, or stages a mission, the doctor sees the interface change immediately. Same workspace, same screen, both of them. Human authority is engineered - expert in the loop. The most important capability is one I intentionally did not build. The AI cannot: Accept organizational policy. Approve the adoption mission. Launch a live-patient-data workflow. Make clinical or compliance decisions. Enter or request PHI. The agent can inspect, explain, focus, assess, stage, and revise. The doctor keeps every decision that matters. Practice Website Debrief A doctor can enter their public practice domain and the agent looks at the public pages and comes back with: What the practice already does well. What could be clearer or more useful. One safe AI opportunity to explore next. This is educational, not a compliance audit. No patient portals, no credentials, no private pages, no PHI. How I built it HIPAA.technology is a React and TypeScript application I created with ChatGPT and Codex, built with Vinext and Vite, and hosted with ChatGPT Sites on the custom domain lab.hipaa.technology . Each WebMCP tool has: A narrow, descriptive name. An explicit JSON input schema. Additional properties disabled. Bounded and validated inputs. Clear descriptions of its effects and limitations. WebMCP safety annotations. Structured results. A visible shared-interface update when applicable. The healthcare model came from a ChatGPT Deep Research paper, Middleware Encryption for HIPAA-Compliant Use of Frontier LLMs in U.S. Healthcare . Its central lesson is baked into the whole experience: encryption is one layer, but you have to govern the entire information path - minimum necessary data, the exact vendor and feature path, logs, agent capabilities, and a human making the calls. Challenges The HARDEST Problem by far was figuring out that my version of Codex wasn't Web Tool enabled. This took hours and hours to figure out. Codex was no help figuring it out. I finally upgraded tonight after midnight and lo and behold, the tools were there. The other challenge was explaining a brand-new browser technology to doctors who aren't technical. So the site includes a dedicated WebMCP judge guide with plain-language setup instructions, the complete tool directory, implementation evidence, and both ChatGPT and Chrome testing paths. Accomplishments Ten state-aware WebMCP tools. A complete clinician-facing product, not a registration proof of concept. Real browser discovery and execution through document.modelContext . A human authority gate that agents cannot bypass. A synthetic-first 21-day adoption mission. A privacy-bounded public-practice website debrief. A contextual AI guide that follows the doctor through the experience. A research-informed workflow visualization. Deployment through ChatGPT Sites on a custom HIPAA.technology domain. A public MIT-licensed repository. What I learned WebMCP is awesome! I can do sites like this all day with Codex. I can't believe this is even real. :) Also: the best tool surface is the smallest one. Ten tools that each do one clear thing, so the doctor and the agent both always know exactly what's happening. What's next Over the next 21 days, I plan to: Test guided sessions with physicians and practice administrators. Add organization-owned workflow templates and evidence capture. Expand the public-site debrief into a structured readiness intake. Add versioned governance playbooks for approved tools and feature paths. Measure whether each team leaves with one bounded workflow, one accountable owner, and one verifiable next action. title: Qianshou
pitch: Qianshou turns everyday travel requests into clear journeys that people can review while AI agents plan routes, describe locations, and switch alternatives through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Qianshou turns everyday travel requests into clear journeys that people can review while AI agents plan routes, describe locations, and switch alternatives through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates ** Inspiration ** Planning a public-transit journey often begins with an ordinary sentence, not a perfectly structured form. People may say, “I want to go to Taipei Main Station,” “from here to Tamsui,” or simply “where am I?” Traditional websites require users to translate that intention into separate fields and controls. Browser agents face the opposite problem: they must inspect the interface, guess what each control means, and hope that the resulting route still matches what the person sees. Qianshou means “holding hands.” The project explores a more collaborative model: a person expresses an intention naturally, an AI agent performs the structured work through WebMCP, and both continue from the same visible journey on the webpage. The project is motivated by travelers who benefit from clearer and lower-friction journey planning, including older adults and people with visual impairments. The current pilot does not claim that every suggested route is fully accessible. Missing accessibility information remains explicitly unknown. ** What it does ** Qianshou is a WebMCP-powered journey-planning web application for Taipei and New Taipei City. A person can describe a journey in natural language without deciding which fields to fill in. Qianshou interprets the request, resolves the places, plans a public-transit route, and presents the journey as readable, step-by-step guidance. When the request depends on “here” or omits an origin, the page can request a fresh browser location. Ambiguous place names are presented for human confirmation instead of being silently guessed. The page combines several kinds of journey information: Step-by-step walking and public-transit instructions Total travel time, walking time, and transfers Alternative routes that can be selected after the first result Arrival information matched to the route’s first transit leg Short-range destination weather Explicit data-source and coverage limitations Qianshou exposes three task-level WebMCP tools: prepare_accessible_journey interprets a natural journey request and prepares the complete result. describe_current_location obtains a fresh location and describes it in human-readable form. select_journey_alternative switches the current journey to an existing alternative and updates the visible result. The person does not need to tell the agent which tool to use. The tool descriptions provide enough meaning for the agent to select the appropriate action. Most importantly, a WebMCP action updates the same page the person is viewing. The route is not trapped inside an isolated chat response: the person and the agent share one journey state and can continue from the same result. ** How we built it ** Qianshou is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, and native imperative WebMCP. The three tools are registered in the browser using document.modelContext.registerTool . They expose meaningful travel actions rather than individual buttons or form fields. Both the WebMCP tools and the manual interface reuse the same server-side journey services, so agent actions and human actions produce the same visible application state. A loopback-only Codex CLI service converts natural-language requests into a strict structured intent. It runs with an explicit schema, timeout, and concurrency limit, without shell, browser, plugin, or project-write access. Place resolution combines Taiwan transportation data with OpenStreetMap Nominatim. OpenTripPlanner 2.9 calculates journeys using GTFS schedules and OpenStreetMap streets. TDX provides public-transit and arrival information, while Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration supplies short-range destination forecasts. Arrival information is bound to the selected journey’s actual first transit leg using its stop, route, direction, and transport mode. Switching an alternative route therefore also refreshes the related arrival context. The application is deployed on Google Cloud Platform with Docker and Nginx. To operate within a small VM, we reduced the routing graph to the relevant service region and applied explicit container memory limits. ** Challenges we ran into ** Natural language contains important spatial ambiguity. “From here to Tamsui” and “from Tamsui to here” use the same word but require the current location in opposite roles. A destination-only request also needs different handling from a fully specified journey. Place names introduce another challenge. A station, district, landmark, and bus stop can share similar names. Combining duplicate search results without erasing meaningful ambiguity required careful normalization and human confirmation. Public-transit routing also involves trade-offs. The fastest route may require excessive walking, while minimizing transfers may produce an impractical detour. We evaluate total duration, walking burden, and transfers together, while allowing no more than two transfers. Real-world data is incomplete. Public feeds do not always contain enough information about station pathways, elevators, stairs, or vehicle accessibility to justify a complete accessibility guarantee. We therefore distinguish confirmed information from unknown data instead of converting missing fields into a positive claim. Finally, route planning, geocoding, arrival matching, and weather services have different response times and failure modes. The interface needed to preserve a coherent result without fabricating data when an upstream service was unavailable. ** Accomplishments that we're proud of ** Implemented three working, non-trivial native WebMCP tools. Made WebMCP tool calls update the same visible journey used by the human interface. Allowed agents to act from natural user intent without requiring users to name a tool. Combined place resolution, transit planning, arrival matching, alternatives, and weather in one journey operation. Implemented correct semantics for omitted origins, “from here,” “to here,” and “where am I?” Preserved human confirmation when a place remains ambiguous. Kept exact browser coordinates out of the result returned to the agent. Added keyboard navigation, responsive layouts, live regions, reduced-motion support, and itinerary speech. Preserved a complete natural-language interface when WebMCP is unavailable. Reported unavailable or incomplete data honestly instead of generating a convincing but unsupported route. ** What we learned ** Agent-native does not mean agent-only. The strongest experience came from giving the agent structured, task-level actions while preserving a complete interface for the person. WebMCP works best when it communicates domain meaning—such as preparing a journey or switching an alternative—rather than exposing a collection of low-level interface controls. We also learned that tool descriptions are part of the product. They must explain scope, intent, and important boundaries clearly enough for an agent to choose the right action without forcing the user to speak in implementation terms. Finally, route quality depends on data quality as much as routing algorithms. An explicit “unknown” is more responsible and useful than an unsupported accessibility or availability promise. ** What's next for Qianshou ** Conduct moderated usability testing with older travelers and people using screen readers. Expand verified accessibility-data coverage before making stronger accessibility claims. Integrate official operational elevator information where available. Add nearby-place discovery for stations, convenience stores, and accessible toilets. Improve arrival coverage and multimodal route comparison. Continue refining English and Chinese place understanding. Expand beyond Taipei and New Taipei only after the data coverage and operating model have been validated. Drag and drop flow chart builder with built in WebMCP support.

 WebMCP powered flow chart builder 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I was thinking about a practical useful tool that makes someones life a little better with WebMCP and that is when I decided to build this flowchart builder app (EasyFloww). It demonstrate WebMCP capabilities in a practical and visually engaging way so more people can understand it and explore. 

 What it does 

 EasyFloww is a drag and drop flowchart builder, it lets users create diagrams easily and share and editable as well as non editable version with anyone easily. With built in WebMCP support and no vendor lock in, any ai model with tool calling capabilities will be able to create flowchart seamlessly. 

 What makes this app special is that an AI agent and a user can work on the canvas together to create diagrams and collaborate in real time. 

 The data is stored in localstorage and never leaves your system, which tighten the security. 

 How we built it 

 I used AI as a companion to plan and develop the application. React and TypeScript is the technologies along with the npm package xyflow which power this application. 

 The app exposes actions as tools using webmcp. We have built and registered 10 tools.
get_flow_state: returns the current nodes and edges (with type, label, config, position, and connected handles) for the active flow
add_node: adds a new node of a given type, label, and optional position
connect_nodes: connects two nodes by ID, with an optional sourceHandle for decision branches.
move_node: repositions an existing node by ID
update_node_config: updates a node's label/condition/description/borderColor
delete_node: removes a node (and its connected edges)
insert_node_between: splits an existing edge to insert a new node directly between two connected nodes
remove_edge: disconnects two nodes by removing a specific edge
clone_flow: duplicates a flow (active or specified) into a new independent tab
import_flow: creates an entire new flow in one call from a complete node/edge JSON graph, with validation 

 Every tool calls the exact same Zustand store functions that the UI itself uses, addNode, moveNode, addEdge, updateNodeConfig etc. There's no separate path for the AI agent through the code, a tool call and a mouse drag both end up mutating the same store the same way. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was to design the architecture of the project in a way that makes the agent-human collaboration foolproof - meaning a human and an agent editing the same live canvas should never produce corruption, silently divergent data, lost work, or ambiguity about who changed what. 

 The design decisions that highlight the actions an agent is performing in the canvas was another challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The end product came out really well and useful, anyone who is looking for an AI support flowchart builder can use this product. 

 I am proud about the fact that I got a deeper understanding about the latest features of the web and got hands on experience in it. I am really proud of it. 

 What we learned 

 I got a pretty solid understanding about the WebMCP protocol and got really confident in implementing it in my future projects. 

 What's next for EasyFloww 

 Most diagram tools lock you into their own built in AI assistant. If you want AI help, you use their model, in their chat box, on their terms. EasyFlow is here to change that, to provide a better experience for the end user to use the AI models they are comfortable with and to create complex diagrams seamlessly. 

 We want to provide the user at most security and privacy possible so that their data belongs to them and not any servers.

title: Review Gate
pitch: A peer-review workspace where your AI assistant can help you review a confidential manuscript without the manuscript ever leaving your browser.
about_excerpt: A peer-review workspace where your AI assistant can help you review a confidential manuscript without the manuscript ever leaving your browser. Like Comment Story Updates The consent gate: the agent asked for three passages, the reviewer chooses which cross. Registered tools listed on the right. Manuscript open: eight tools exposed. Highlighted sentences are the ones released to the agent; the log records every request The disclosure log, exported for the editor: what each tool requested, what was released, what was withheld, with totals. The reviewer's draft, written in-page and exported as Markdown. Home page where you can upload documents. Inspiration Peer reviewers are bound by confidentiality. ICMJE, Elsevier, COPE and NIH all restrict putting a manuscript under review into an AI service, because doing so transmits a confidential document to a third party. Reviewing is slow, detailed, unpaid work that AI is genuinely good at assisting with and reviewers are told they can't use it. That conflict has no resolution today. Reviewers either break confidentiality quietly, or do without. ReviewGate resolves it architecturally instead of by policy: the manuscript never leaves the browser, and the agent only ever sees what the reviewer explicitly hands it. What it does Open a manuscript in .txt, .md or PDF and it is parsed and stored entirely in your browser's IndexedDB. The page exposes eight WebMCP tools to your agent. Every tool that would return manuscript prose pauses and asks you first, showing exactly which sentences are about to cross, with per-passage checkboxes. You release some, withhold others, or deny outright. Every decision is written to an append-only disclosure log you can export as Markdown for the editor: which tool asked, why, how many passages were requested, released and withheld. "I used AI" stops being a confession and becomes an auditable statement. Why this had to be WebMCP Every other way of giving an agent access to a manuscript involves sending the manuscript somewhere. A server MCP has to transmit it. An API integration has to transmit it. Copy-paste transmits it. WebMCP tools execute in the page , in the reviewer's own session, on data that is already in the browser. The agent operates on a document that never moves. Rebuilt as a server MCP this project doesn't get worse but stops being possible. The architecture is the confidentiality argument. How I built it React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind 4, IndexedDB via idb , and a lazily-imported PDF.js for text extraction. No backend, by necessity rather than convenience. Design decisions worth naming: Consent is the return value, not a notification. execute() is async, so the tool simply doesn't resolve until the human decides. No browser confirmation API is needed which also means nothing breaks as the spec moves. A refusal reads as a refusal. Deny a request and the agent receives an explicit statement: "the reviewer declined to release any text; do not infer anything about the manuscript's content from this refusal." An agent that reads an empty result as absence of evidence would conclude a withheld section was blank. Verified live: it replies "I can't assess it yet: access to the Methods section was declined." Graduated disclosure. check_stats_reporting returns the numeric values reported in a paper without the sentences around them which provides a lower-disclosure path for a common review task. The tool surface follows application state. One tool is registered before a manuscript is open, eight after, one again on close. Standing grants are scoped to the sentence. "Release for session" never silently widens to neighbouring passages, and grants die with the manuscript. The claim is enforced, not promised. The deployed CSP sets connect-src 'none' , so the browser refuses every outbound request the page could make. A live counter in the header shows the count, and it reads zero. Challenges I ran into requestUserInteraction() doesn't exist. Several third-party guides document it; Chrome's shipped imperative API doesn't have it. The whole design rested on a human-in-the-loop pause. It turned out not to be needed at all ,an async execute() already makes the agent wait and owning the dialog means owning what it shows. Registering once is wrong. I checked for document.modelContext at mount. An embedding browser installs the API after first paint, so the check found nothing, registered nothing, and never retried, indistinguishable from the site not supporting WebMCP. It now watches for the API and registers when it appears. The sentence splitter broke on decimals. A naive regex split "p<0.05" into "(p<0" and "05).", showing reviewers meaningless fragments in the consent dialog. Embedded browsers block blob downloads silently. The export appeared to succeed while nothing reached the reviewer. Exports now render on screen with copy and download beside them. Real documents don't look like test fixtures. My heading detection only understood ALL-CAPS headings, so a report using "Chapter 3 : Problem Statement" parsed into six wrong sections with the title page promoted to structure. It now handles numbered, chapter and roman-numeral headings, drops contents-page entries, and filters repeated running headers. What I learned That a permission model is more interesting than a capability. WebMCP's obvious use is letting agents do more; the more interesting question is what it lets you safely refuse . And that the failure modes worth engineering against are semantic, not technical, an agent misreading silence as absence would have been far more damaging here than any crash. What's next Per-section rather than per-sentence grants for long manuscripts, a "what the agent has seen this session" view distinct from the chronological log, and redaction; releasing a sentence with figures or identifiers masked. Honest limitations Claim detection is regex pattern matching, not semantic analysis; the tool descriptions tell the agent so. The network counter is a demo instrument while the real guarantee is the CSP plus having no server to send anything to. No journal endorses this tool; it helps a reviewer comply with policy and documents what happened. Tested with 28 automated checks including a WCAG AA contrast audit, and verified live in both ChatGPT's built-in browser and stock Chrome via the WebMCP origin trial.
