title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ .  1 2 



 
 ActionFlow — Hackathon Submission 

 Inspiration 

 Most AI web applications today stop at giving answers . We wanted to build something that could actually help users accomplish tasks on the web . 

 Our biggest inspiration was the idea that WebMCP should be a first-class part of the product , rather than something added at the end just to say that the project uses MCP. 

 We imagined a system where a user can describe a goal in natural language, and an AI agent can discover the capabilities available through WebMCP, plan the necessary steps, execute them, and keep the user in control of important actions. 

 That led us to ActionFlow : an AI-powered web agent designed around the principle of: 

 
 Tell it what you want accomplished, not which buttons to click. 
 

 

 What it does 

 ActionFlow converts natural-language goals into actionable workflows. 

 A user can give ActionFlow a request such as: 

 
 “Find the best Java development internships for me, compare the opportunities, and prepare the applications for the top matches.” 
 

 ActionFlow then: 

 
 Understands the user's objective. 
 Breaks the objective into smaller tasks. 
 Discovers and selects appropriate WebMCP capabilities. 
 Collects and analyzes information. 
 Compares and ranks results. 
 Builds an execution plan. 
 Requests user approval before consequential actions. 
 Executes approved actions through WebMCP. 
 Verifies the result. 
 Records the complete workflow in an activity log. 
 

 The application also provides a WebMCP Tool Explorer , allowing users and judges to see exactly which capabilities the agent is using. 

 

 How we built it 

 ActionFlow is built as a full-stack application with an AI-agent layer at its center. 

 Frontend 

 We built the interface using: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 Tailwind CSS 
 

 The frontend provides the command center, agent execution view, approval interface, WebMCP tool explorer, and activity history. 

 Backend 

 The backend is designed around: 

 
 Java 
 Spring Boot 
 REST APIs 
 PostgreSQL 
 Real-time agent execution updates 
 

 The backend manages users, tasks, workflows, tool execution, approvals, and activity logs. 

 AI Agent 

 The agent follows a structured workflow: 

 Understand → Plan → Discover → Execute → Observe → Reason → Verify 

 Rather than hard-coding a sequence of UI interactions, the agent can select the appropriate capabilities based on the user's objective. 

 WebMCP 

 WebMCP is the key part of ActionFlow. 

 We expose meaningful capabilities such as: 

 
 search_web 
 extract_information 
 compare_results 
 analyze_requirements 
 create_plan 
 request_approval 
 execute_action 
 verify_result 
 

 This makes WebMCP part of the application's core architecture , rather than a superficial integration. 

 Safety 

 ActionFlow also uses an approval layer. 

 The agent can research and prepare actions autonomously, but potentially consequential actions require explicit user approval. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was deciding where WebMCP actually provides value . 

 It would have been easy to build a conventional web application and expose a few functions as MCP tools. However, that would not demonstrate the real potential of the technology. 

 We therefore had to rethink the architecture around capabilities rather than pages and buttons . 

 Other challenges included: 

 
 Designing useful high-level WebMCP tools. 
 Coordinating multiple tool calls within one workflow. 
 Maintaining state across multi-step tasks. 
 Handling failures and unexpected tool results. 
 Designing approval points without making the experience frustrating. 
 Making the agent's actions understandable to the user. 
 Keeping the architecture flexible enough to add new capabilities later. 
 

 The hardest conceptual challenge was balancing autonomy with control : the agent should be capable of accomplishing meaningful tasks while the user remains in charge of consequential decisions. 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're especially proud that WebMCP isn't simply an additional feature in ActionFlow. 

 It is part of the fundamental interaction model . 

 We created a workflow where: 

 
 Natural language → AI planning → WebMCP capabilities → real actions → verification 
 

 We are also proud of the transparency of the system. 

 Instead of hiding what the AI is doing, ActionFlow exposes the workflow through its activity log and tool explorer. 

 Users can see: 
 Understanding request
 ↓
Planning workflow
 ↓
Discovering WebMCP capabilities
 ↓
Executing tools
 ↓
Analyzing results
 ↓
Requesting approval
 ↓
Executing approved action
 ↓
Verifying result
 
 This makes the system easier to understand, debug, and trust. 

 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an agentic application is very different from building a traditional web application. 

 A traditional application generally follows: 

 
 User → UI → API → Database 
 

 ActionFlow follows a much more dynamic model: 

 
 User → Goal → Agent → Capabilities → Results → Reasoning → Action 
 

 We also learned that tool design matters as much as model intelligence . 

 Giving an agent poorly designed tools can make an otherwise capable agent ineffective. High-level, well-defined capabilities allow the agent to reason about what it can accomplish rather than simply reproduce a predefined workflow. 

 Most importantly, we learned that WebMCP becomes significantly more interesting when it is treated as an interface between an intelligent agent and real web capabilities , rather than merely another API format. 

 

 What's next for ActionFlow 

 ActionFlow is designed to grow into a general-purpose web task orchestration platform . 

 Our next steps include: 

 More WebMCP capabilities 

 Add specialized tools for: 

 
 Research 
 Shopping 
 Travel 
 Education 
 Developer workflows 
 Job and internship discovery 
 Productivity 
 

 Multi-agent workflows 

 Different specialized agents could collaborate: 
 Research Agent
 ↓
Analysis Agent
 ↓
Planning Agent
 ↓
Execution Agent
 ↓
Verification Agent
 
 Personalization 

 ActionFlow could learn user preferences, constraints, and recurring workflows while keeping the user in control of their data.

pitch: AI agents search jobs, score fit, and draft cover letters via WebMCP but humans review it then edit it and authorize every submission. High stakes decisions stay in human hands.

AI agents search jobs, score fit, and draft cover letters via WebMCP but humans review it then edit it and authorize every submission. High stakes decisions stay in human hands.

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Applying for jobs can be exhausting. You can spend hours searching through listings, comparing requirements, figuring out where your skills fit, and writing a different cover letter for every application. 

 AI agents can make a lot of that process much faster. They can search, analyze job descriptions, identify skill gaps, and even write application drafts. But there is one part we didn't want an agent to handle on its own: actually submitting the application . 

 That led us to the idea behind EzApply . 

 We wanted to build something where the agent takes care of the repetitive work, while the candidate stays in control of the decisions that matter. When we came across WebMCP , it felt like a natural fit. Instead of an agent trying to scrape a page or interact with a UI blindly, WebMCP lets the website expose structured tools that an agent can use directly. 

 So we thought: what if applying for jobs felt less like filling out endless forms and more like having an AI co-pilot? 

 That's what EzApply is built around. 

 What it does 

 EzApply is a Job Application Command Center built with WebMCP. 

 The agent can take a job from discovery all the way to a ready-to-submit application, but the candidate always has the final say. 

 We currently expose six WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_jobs — Finds jobs based on keywords, salary requirements, and remote preferences. 
 score_job_fit — Compares the candidate's skills with a job's requirements and calculates a fit percentage. 
 identify_skill_gap — Shows which skills are missing and gives suggestions for improving the candidate's resume. 
 generate_application_draft — Creates a tailored cover letter and sends it to the Approval Queue. 
 save_to_drafts — Saves changes made by the candidate to an AI-generated application. 
 submit_application — Handles the final submission, but only after the candidate explicitly confirms it. 
 

 Human-in-the-Loop Approval 

 This is the part of EzApply we're most proud of. 

 AI can prepare an application, but it doesn't get to decide when it is submitted. 

 Every generated application goes into an Approval Queue . The candidate can read the cover letter, make changes directly, and then approve it. 

 The submit_application tool also checks for candidateConfirmation: true inside its execute() function. This means the safety check isn't only part of the interface. The tool itself refuses to submit an application without explicit confirmation. 

 We wanted this to be a real safety boundary rather than just a button that looks like one. 

 Agent Console 

 We also wanted users to understand what the agent was actually doing. 

 The Agent Console displays WebMCP tool calls as they happen, including timestamps and status information. This makes the agent's actions visible instead of turning the whole process into a black box. 

 The 1-Click Pipeline 

 EzApply also has a one-click workflow that demonstrates how the tools can work together: 

 Search → Score → Identify Skill Gaps → Generate Draft → Human Review 

 The agent handles the tedious parts in sequence, while the candidate takes over when a decision actually matters. 

 How we built it 

 One of our goals was to keep the project simple enough that the WebMCP integration remained the focus. 

 The entire application is contained in a single HTML file of roughly 70KB , with inline CSS and JavaScript and no production dependencies. 

 We register our tools through document.modelContext using WebMCP's registerTool() API and provide proper inputSchema definitions so an agent knows what each tool expects. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_jobs" , 
 description : "Searches available tech jobs by keywords, salary, and remote status." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 query : { 
 type : "string" , 
 description : "Job title or skill keyword" 
 } , 
 minSalary : { 
 type : "number" 
 } , 
 remoteOnly : { 
 type : "boolean" 
 } 
 } , 
 required : [ "query" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const results = jobs . filter ( j = > matchesQuery ( j , input ) ) ; 

 return { 
 success : true , 
 count : results . length , 
 jobs : results
 } ; 
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 We also added a small in-memory modelContext fallback. If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, the app can still be explored normally. When WebMCP is available, the same tools are exposed through the native protocol. 

 For the interface, we went with an aviation-inspired command-center theme. Job cards look like boarding passes, jobs have flight-style codes, and the overall interface is designed to feel like you're managing a journey from discovery to application. 

 The project is deployed on Vercel using Vite as a minimal static setup. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the human approval step right 

 We didn't want the approval step to feel like unnecessary friction. At the same time, we didn't want to hide an important decision behind a single confirmation button. 

 We ended up using an inline-editable application draft so the candidate can make changes without leaving the workflow. The approval card is intentionally prominent, making it clear that this is the point where the human takes control. 

 Making WebMCP visible 

 One challenge with a protocol like WebMCP is that most of the interesting work happens behind the scenes. 

 A user doesn't necessarily know that an agent just called search_jobs or score_job_fit . 

 That's why we built the Agent Console. It turns those normally invisible interactions into something users can actually watch, which also helped us understand and debug the agent workflow while building the project. 

 Keeping everything in one file 

 We deliberately challenged ourselves to keep the application lightweight. 

 Instead of reaching for a framework, component library, or large collection of dependencies, we built the application with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 That made the project easier to deploy and kept the focus on what we were actually trying to demonstrate: WebMCP and human-agent collaboration. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Six working WebMCP tools that can be used together as a complete workflow 
 A 1-click agent pipeline that demonstrates tool orchestration from job search to application draft 
 A genuine human approval boundary for the final submission step 
 The candidateConfirmation check is enforced inside the tool itself, not just in the UI 
 A complete application in roughly 70KB with zero production dependencies 
 A real-time Agent Console that makes agent activity transparent 
 A polished interface that makes an otherwise abstract WebMCP concept easy to understand 
 

 What we learned 

 Building EzApply changed how we think about agents on the web. 

 The biggest lesson was that agents don't always need to control the entire experience. In many cases, the better approach is to give the agent well-defined tools and let the human remain responsible for important decisions. 

 WebMCP made that model much easier to explore. Instead of relying on DOM scraping or trying to interpret screenshots, the website can expose structured tools with clear inputs and outputs. 

 We also learned that human-in-the-loop isn't necessarily a compromise . The approval step actually makes the experience feel safer because the user can see exactly what the AI produced before anything important happens. 

 And because the tools run directly in the browser, we were able to build and deploy the prototype without creating a separate backend just to demonstrate the agent interaction. 

 Most importantly, EzApply showed us a different way of thinking about the web: not just as pages that agents have to figure out, but as experiences that can actively provide agents with useful capabilities. 

 What's next for EzApply — WebMCP Job Command Center 

 EzApply is currently a prototype, but there are several directions we'd like to take it. 

 Real

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. Built With chrome css3 express.js gemini html5 javascript node.js redis server-sent-events upstash vercel webmcp Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Jason Ofua Like Share this project: Updates Jason Ofua started this project — Aug 27, 2026 03:41 AM EDT

 Inspiration 

 We wanted chess to feel like a conversation. Wizard Chess combines the atmosphere of magical chess with an AI agent that can understand and control the board directly.
What it does 

 Wizard Chess is a 3D chess game controlled by voice, touch, mouse, or WebMCP. Players can learn through guided lessons, play with an AI mentor, or battle Stockfish at three difficulty levels. 

 How we built it 

 We used TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, chess.js, and Stockfish. The app exposes 29 WebMCP tools for moves, lessons, coaching, settings, saved games, and replays. Voice and WebMCP use the same game actions as the visible interface. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was keeping mouse, voice, and agent interactions synchronized with one game state. We also had to make the 3D board readable while handling voice timing, legal moves, lessons, matches, and replays. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a complete chess experience where a person and an AI agent share the same board. It includes voice control, coaching, six lessons, Stockfish opponents, ratings, trophies, saved games, and replays. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP works well for chess because the game has exact state and clear actions. Giving the agent structured board data is far more reliable than asking it to understand the position from pixels. 

 What's next for Wizard Chess 

 We want to add adaptive lessons, deeper post-game analysis, a hosted leaderboard, richer piece models, and more cinematic effects. The mentor could then remember recurring mistakes and recommend what to practise next.

title: Suggestibility-WebMCP
pitch: suggestibility.ai as WebMCP tools: your agent reads an artifact, recommends a 3, 5, or 7 reviewer board, select which size, then returns consensus and preserved dissent. The agent advises; you decide.
about_excerpt: suggestibility.ai as WebMCP tools: your agent reads an artifact, recommends a 3, 5, or 7 reviewer board, select which size, then returns consensus and preserved dissent. The agent advises; you decide. Like Comment Story Updates https://app.suggestibility.ai running in Chrome ready for reviews, samples are built into the page for you or use something real if you want bottom half of the main screenshot showing the 5 and 7 review sample prompts to test with and where to enter the tester token About the project Suggestibility.ai is an AI Expert Review Board. Submit an artifact — an architecture decision record, a policy, a design doc — and it convenes a panel of independent model families that returns consensus, preserved dissent, and prioritized recommendations. Boards come in three sizes: 3 reviewers for $15, 5 for $29, 7 for $69. It runs on Cloudflare Workers and D1, and it has real paying customers. None of that was built for this hackathon. What the product already had, before any of this, was a rule: panel size is resolved server-side from the plan attached to the customer's credit. It is not a parameter anyone — human or agent — can pass in. That rule existed for revenue integrity, not for a hackathon. But it turns out to be exactly the right shape for agent-driven commerce: an agent that can both recommend spend and trigger it is an agent you cannot leave alone with your credit card. Inspiration The WebMCP Challenge was a chance to put that rule directly in front of an agent and see if it held. WebMCP's topology — the website is the tool provider, the browsing agent is the consumer — is a natural fit for a product whose whole premise is that the agent gets real capability, minus the one capability that actually matters. So the build became: expose the review board as page-side tools an agent can discover and call, and let the constraint be the point of the submission rather than a footnote. The agent advises; the purchase decides. suggestibility.ai is an AI Expert Review Board. Submit an artifact — an architecture decision record, a policy, a design doc — and it convenes a panel of independent model families that returns consensus, preserved dissent, and prioritized recommendations. Boards come in three sizes: 3 reviewers for $15, 5 for $29, 7 for $69. It runs on Cloudflare Workers and D1, and it has real paying customers. None of that was built for this hackathon. What the product already had, before any of this, was a rule: panel size is resolved server-side from the plan attached to the customer's credit. It is not a parameter anyone — human or agent — can pass in. That rule existed for revenue integrity, not for a hackathon. But it turns out to be exactly the right shape for agent-driven commerce: an agent that can both recommend spend and trigger it is an agent you cannot leave alone with your credit card. The WebMCP Challenge was a chance to put that rule directly in front of an agent and see if it held. WebMCP's topology — the website is the tool provider, the browsing agent is the consumer — is a natural fit for a product whose whole premise is that the agent gets real capability, minus the one capability that actually matters. So the build became: expose the review board as page-side tools an agent can discover and call, and let the constraint be the point of the submission rather than a footnote. The agent advises; the purchase decides. What we learned The most useful surprise arrived on day one. The platform already runs a working JSON-RPC MCP server, the kind where an external client connects in from outside. Almost none of that experience transferred. WebMCP is page-side: the website is the tool provider, the agent is the consumer. Same vocabulary, opposite direction — and building for one taught almost nothing about the other. The rest of what got learned came from watching a guard fail, then watching a second guard fail differently. A leak-check script was written to stop demo tokens from reaching the public repository. It caught something real on its first run: the token input's placeholder text read SUGGJUDGE… , which published the naming scheme for the judging codes and made the live ones guessable on sight. It looked like ordinary UI copy. It was a disclosure. A second guard, checking sample metadata for person names, was written in shell — and silently did nothing. Its role-word exclusion matched anywhere on the line, so | Author | Sana Okafor, Mobile Platform | was suppressed by the word "Mobile" further along, and the script reported success every time it ran. It was rewritten in JavaScript with positional anchoring and given a self-test, which immediately found a second gap (bold metadata went unmatched entirely) and one false positive (team names read as person names). A guard that has not been watched fail is a guess, not a guard. The last lesson was about what counts as a billing surface. An existing demo code granted a subscription tier whose allowance was 25 reviews, and the code had 25 redemptions available — meaning one code was worth up to 625 seven-reviewer boards. Nobody had chosen that number as demo policy; it was just what the tier meant once multiplied out. Fixed with a per-code review cap. How we built it The result is a public, Apache-2.0 WebMCP client. It holds no secrets and no review logic — board composition, reviewer selection, synthesis, and scoring stay in the existing platform service. What lives in this repository is eight tools registered on document.modelContext : list_review_options , recommend_board_size , submit_artifact_for_review , get_review_status , get_review_package , list_sample_artifacts , load_sample_artifact , and explore_dissent . recommend_board_size carries the central constraint directly: it reads an artifact and argues for 3, 5, or 7 reviewers, but the parameter that would let it actually set panel size was never exposed to it. It can only ever be advisory, by construction. explore_dissent exists because preserved dissent is the product's actual differentiator — most review tooling averages disagreement into a single confident answer, and this platform doesn't, so pulling out only the minority positions felt like it deserved a first-class tool rather than a field buried in a larger response. Twelve sample artifacts ship with the client, four at each board size, 33,760 words total, spanning architecture decisions, security architecture, data policy, API design, payments, accessibility, and incident review. Each carries a review package already produced by the real platform, so a board can be read in full — consensus and dissent both — with no account and no wait. Challenges we faced Turnstile runs on the review endpoint when configured, and it is currently unset in production for one specific reason: an agent cannot solve a CAPTCHA. Turning it on would break every agent-driven submission with an unexplained "verification failed." Leaving it off keeps the agent path working — a tradeoff, not a solved problem. Cookies were the other authentication fight. The session cookie is httpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and host-only, which is not something to depend on inside an embedded browser like ChatGPT's, where third-party cookie handling is not guaranteed. The client authenticates with a bearer token instead. Getting there meant consolidating five hand-rolled session lookups scattered across the codebase into a single resolver — four of which had only ever accepted a cookie and would otherwise have quietly rejected a token. Latency turned out to be a design constraint, not an implementation detail. A seven-seat board is seven independent reviews plus a synthesis pass, not one larger prompt — so it takes minutes, not seconds. That is why the sample artifacts ship with their review packages already captured: exploring a board has to be instant even though generating one is not. And honesty had to be made mechanical, not promised. The README states that every sample carries a genuine platform review, nothing staged. A release check enforces that directly: the build fails if any sample is missing a real review package, or if a package's reviewer count contradicts what the catalog advertises for that board size. Accomplishments that we're proud of The constraint held. An agent can read a 25,000-word migration plan, make a genuine case for seven reviewers, and still be unable to spend a dollar on its own conclusion. That is the design working under a real agent rather than in a diagram. The guards caught things a careful reader would not have. One found a disclosure hiding in ordinary-looking UI copy. Another found that a single demo code was worth up to 625 seven-reviewer boards — not because anyone chose that number, but because it was what a subscription tier meant once multiplied by its redemption count. Neither was visible by reading the code. All of this shipped against a production system with paying customers, without breaking it: 173 tests passing, a Cloudflare account g

title: Redline
pitch: Your AI agent reviews an employment contract through tools the page registers in your browser and the blurred document snaps into clarity as you decide each redline.
about_excerpt: Your AI agent reviews an employment contract through tools the page registers in your browser and the blurred document snaps into clarity as you decide each redline. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration You get an offer. The salary is great — and the contract is 22 pages of fine print with a 48-hour signature deadline. About 30% of US workers are bound by non-competes, and most people sign without understanding what they're signing. A lawyer costs $400/hour. The alternative used to be asking an AI "is this enforceable?" and getting a confident essay you then had to reconstruct into something actionable. Redline is for the person who actually has: a document, a deadline, and an AI agent they already use. What it does Paste an employment contract (or open one of three deliberately overreaching samples) and it loads blurred — the way a 22-page contract actually feels. Your AI agent then works inside the page: it reads every clause, flags the risky ones with severity and grounded reasons, and proposes concrete redline language. Each proposal lands as a decision card under the exact sentence it modifies. You decide each one — Keep as-is, or Redline it — and accepted changes roll up into a negotiation email, Current vs Proposed side by side, one click to copy. As the agent assesses each clause, it snaps into clarity — but clarity is computed, not decorative: a clause only clears once it's assessed and every redline on it is decided. Reset a verdict and it re-flags. The blur is the progress bar. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP A contract-review tool needs an agent to see inside the document, clause by clause, and write back into it. That is exactly what WebMCP enables: Redline registers seven tools on document.modelContext — get_sample_contract , get_document_state , extract_clauses , get_clause_text , assess_clause , get_enforceability_context , export_negotiation_email . Two-phase dynamic registration: at boot only a get_sample_contract tool exists; once a document is loaded, the app retires it via WebMCP's signal-based lifecycle and registers the six analysis tools. The tool list always matches what is meaningful right now. Grounded analysis, not vibes: get_enforceability_context hands the agent real data — non-compete enforceability across 20 US states (earnings thresholds, void-by-default rules, notice requirements), training-repayment-agreement traps in 5 states, and heuristic families for NDAs, arbitration, and IP assignment. When Redline says a five-year worldwide non-compete is high-severity in Washington, it quotes RCW 49.62. No API keys, no backend, no scraping. The page is the tool provider and the browser is the whole stack (static assets on Cloudflare Workers). What people and agents can do together now The old pattern: ask an AI, get an essay, copy fragments into a text editor, lose the structure. Here the agent proposes and the human decides — and the boundary is enforced by the data flow itself: agent tools write proposals and assessments into clause threads, but redline verdicts can only come from the UI. What was six screens of copy-paste is now one grounded pass with the human keeping the pen on every change. Because all state is derived (blur, completion, the email draft are computed from assessments and verdicts — never stored as flags), the UI can't claim progress the human didn't actually make. How we built it React 19 + TypeScript (strict), Vite, Cloudflare Workers static assets — no backend, no keys. All tool reads go through a live session ref (tools never read stale React state); writes flow actions → store → UI in one direction. The email composer is deterministic: the page and export_negotiation_email emit byte-identical output. The decision UI (FlagBadge, RedlineCard, ClauseChat) renders proposals inline in the document; a 500ms transition snaps each clause from blurred to clear as decisions land. Challenges we ran into WebMCP's registration lifecycle has no unregister API — tools are retired through abort signals, which shaped our two-phase registration design. Making blur honest took a derived rule: early versions cleared clauses on assessment alone; the shipped version requires every redline on the clause to be decided. Keeping page and tool output identical forced us to make the email composer a pure function both paths call. Live agent testing caught real bugs (duplicate redline proposals on re-assessment, chat auto-expand behavior) that we fixed with a pure redline-planning function and better thread state. What we learned The WebMCP model inverts the usual architecture: the app doesn't call the model, the agent calls the app. Designing tools for another developer (the agent platform) forced us to make state readable, actions explicit, and UI claims derived from data — which made the app better for humans too. What's honest about this demo The samples are drafted overbroad — that's the test. But nothing is scripted: the app ships data and heuristics, not verdicts, and accepts whatever a competent model actually produces through the tools. Different model, different analysis — same structure to hold it. Try it: https://redline.kangyow.workers.dev/ — paste your own contract, or start with "The Offer Letter": a $128k role in Seattle with a five-year, worldwide non-compete. Washington law is not impressed. Now the app says so, with the citation. Not legal advice — a hackathon demo. The document lives in your browser session; only what the tools return reaches your agent. title: AidPath Agent Bridge
pitch: A WebMCP-native support navigator where humans control sensitive facts and agents use structured, auditable tools instead of scraping brittle interfaces.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native support navigator where humans control sensitive facts and agents use structured, auditable tools instead of scraping brittle interfaces.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Rule-heavy support and public-service websites are difficult for both people and browser agents. A person may need to understand many conditions, while a generic agent often has to scrape rendered text, guess what controls mean, and automate fragile clicks. We wanted a safer collaboration model: the human controls the facts, while the agent receives explicit, typed capabilities. 

 What it does 

 AidPath Agent Bridge is a WebMCP-native, privacy-first support navigator. It exposes six structured tools that let an agent discover illustrative support options, analyze a structured case, explain one option, compare alternatives, load a safe demo case into the visible UI, and prepare a next-step checklist. 

 The agent does not decide eligibility. Both the human interface and the WebMCP tools call the same deterministic JavaScript rule engine. Matched and missing conditions remain visible and auditable, and meaningful agent actions are shown in an activity log. 

 Why WebMCP is the right fit 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer intent from DOM structure, scrape result cards, and depend on brittle selectors. With WebMCP, the website publishes stable domain capabilities with JSON Schema contracts. The human can inspect or correct facts while the agent performs structured orchestration. This makes the experience faster, more reliable, and easier to audit. 

 A workflow that previously required repeated reading, copying, clicking, and re-checking can become a collaboration: the person reviews sensitive inputs and final evidence; the agent lists options, evaluates the same deterministic rules, compares alternatives, and prepares actionable next steps. 

 How we built it 

 The application is a standalone HTTPS static web app. It registers six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , uses typed JSON Schemas, and annotates read-only operations with readOnlyHint . A local intent layer helps organize free text, but authoritative conditions remain deterministic. There is no backend, account, or persisted user profile. 

 The app degrades gracefully when WebMCP is unavailable and remains fully usable as a normal website. We also created a visible capability status and agent activity log so the user can understand when structured agent interactions occur. 

 Challenges 

 The key design challenge was avoiding an architecture where the LLM silently becomes the decision-maker. We separated agent orchestration from rule evaluation and made the same deterministic functions serve both the human UI and the WebMCP layer. We also documented the distinction between prior AidPath work and the new WebMCP extension with timestamped commit history. 

 Native WebMCP verification 

 On September 3, 2026, the deployed HTTPS app was tested in Chrome 151 on Windows with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and Chrome relaunched. Chrome's native document.modelContext.getTools() discovered all six tools, and native document.modelContext.executeTool(...) successfully executed all six: 6/6 discovery and 6/6 execution PASS . The student case produced Student Stability Bridge 3/3 as the top deterministic result; Housing Stability Support 2/3 exposed Core documents ready as the missing condition; visible agent activity was recorded in the workbench log. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is most valuable when a site exposes meaningful domain actions rather than simply mirroring buttons. A small set of well-designed tools can replace a large amount of fragile UI automation while preserving human review. 

 What's next 

 This challenge build uses explicitly illustrative programs. A production version would connect to verified official sources, attach source URLs and effective dates to every rule, version rule changes, and require human review before consequential use.

title: Airlock
pitch: A private, in-browser data workbench: your CSV is parsed, queried and summarised entirely inside the tab; the agent calls WebMCP tools and gets only the answers.
about_excerpt: A private, in-browser data workbench: your CSV is parsed, queried and summarised entirely inside the tab; the agent calls WebMCP tools and gets only the answers. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Everyone repeats the same warning — "don't paste your bank statement into a chatbot" — and yet AI is genuinely good at exactly that kind of analysis. The blocker was never capability; it's that every normal path (upload the file, paste the rows, sync to a server) copies your raw records out of your hands before any analysis happens. WebMCP hinted at a different shape entirely: what if the agent could call tools that run inside the page and receive only the answers? I wanted to find out whether a hosted AI could analyse something as sensitive as a year of personal spending — or a payslip — without ever receiving it. What it does Airlock is a private, in-browser data workbench. You load a CSV with date , description , category and amount columns and it's parsed and analysed entirely inside your browser tab. The page registers seven WebMCP tools — describe_dataset , sum_by_category , filter_rows , monthly_trend , find_anomalies , top_expenses , clear_highlights — and an agent (ChatGPT's in-app browser, or Chrome with WebMCP enabled) calls them and gets back only aggregates. Ask "what am I spending most on?" or "is anything unusual?" and it answers with real numbers, while the rows it's reasoning about are highlighted in your own table for you to read. On the bundled synthetic year of spending — 965 transactions across 12 categories — it isolates the four genuinely unusual charges by per-category z-score. Open DevTools during the conversation and the network panel stays empty. How I built it Plain TypeScript and Vite, papaparse for CSV, no backend — a backend would undercut the whole premise. Tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , each reading from a module-level store so handlers never close over stale state. The load-bearing design decision is privacy mode : it ships on by default, so the row-returning tools answer with counts, totals and category names instead of row contents, describe_dataset even withholds the file name, and only the human can lower the gate — no tool is registered to change it, because a consent gate the agent can open by itself isn't one. It also re-arms to on every time a new file is loaded, so a fresh, more sensitive file never inherits a previous "off." Challenges I ran into The sharpest one was a flaw in my own premise, caught mid-build: "the file stays in the tab" only rules out an upload — anything a tool returns reaches the model anyway. That redesigned the entire project around drawing the privacy boundary at the answer , not the file. Others: proving it to a real external agent rather than self-invocation, which I did by driving the live tools through Chrome's experimental WebMCP CDP domain, the same path a real MCP client takes; a WebMCP quirk where a thrown error reaches the agent as a generic failure, so I return errors as values to keep the recovery hints; and a consent footgun where turning privacy off then loading a new file left it exposed — fixed by the re-arm-on-load behaviour above. What I learned WebMCP's real novelty isn't "tools on a web page" — it's that computation happens where the data lives , which is what makes it possible to keep the raw data and still get the analysis. I also learned that privacy is about control, not lockout : a default-safe, human-controlled, reversible gate is a far better model than all-or-nothing. And that a WebMCP project is only truly proven when an external agent drives it — so the boundary is enforced in the tool layer and unit-tested directly (27 tests), not just asserted in the UI. What's next for Airlock Tightening the consent model further: auto-reverting privacy after a single disclosed answer, scoping disclosure to only the highlighted rows, and a k-anonymity guard on the aggregate tools to close query-composition reconstruction by an adversarial agent. And input breadth — PDF and image ingestion via pdf.js and in-browser WASM OCR, kept strictly client-side so the guarantee that nothing leaves the tab still holds. title: ToolBraid
pitch: A browser-native WebMCP control plane that lets AI agents use live web tools while humans retain exact authority over every mutation.
about_excerpt: A browser-native WebMCP control plane that lets AI agents use live web tools while humans retain exact authority over every mutation. Like Comment Story Updates Production Recovery complete: live evidence, two approved mutations, receipts, and sealed audit. Native multi-origin WebMCP topology across mission control and six isolated providers. ToolBraid Universal Chrome side panel: page binding, missions, approvals, evidence, and handoffs. Human authority boundary: exact approvals, drift checks, replay protection, and fail-closed dispatch. Why I built ToolBraid I am building ToolBraid alone. I am not employed in tech, I do not have a team behind me, and this is a self-funded project I started from zero for the WebMCP Challenge. The name comes from the idea itself: braid tools from different websites into one mission instead of treating every page like a separate automation. The problem that pushed me to build it was simple. An AI agent can read a page or move a mouse, but it still has to guess what a button means, what data an action needs, and whether a click actually succeeded. That is fragile. WebMCP gives websites a way to expose real named tools with structured inputs and results. ToolBraid sits above those tools and makes them usable across several sites without giving the agent permission to approve its own actions. What it does A person starts with one objective. ToolBraid discovers the available WebMCP tools, keeps the provider and origin attached to each one, rejects suspicious metadata, and maps different provider contracts into a common execution plan. Safe reads can run first so the agent can collect evidence. Anything that changes an external system stops for a separate human approval showing the exact site, tool, arguments, expected effect, and expiry. The public demo uses a production-recovery mission because I wanted a scenario where the safety model actually matters. It discovers nine tools from six isolated provider origins and turns them into seven usable capabilities. It reads real GitHub and Vercel sandbox state, finds the safest recovery path, then asks for two independent approvals: one for the rollback and one for the customer update. If approved, it rolls back only the disposable ToolBraid recovery lab and adds a real comment to one allowlisted GitHub incident issue. It does not touch a customer or business production system. How it works The part I care about most is the authority boundary. Before dispatch, ToolBraid checks the live registry again and verifies the origin, schema, arguments, effect, page binding, expiry, and one-time nonce. If the page, tool, target, or approval has drifted, execution stops. A generic browser action only receives a dispatch receipt. ToolBraid claims verified success only when a trusted adapter can observe the expected postcondition on the exact bound page. The retained run is then sealed with a local append-only SHA-256 audit chain. I also did not want ToolBraid to work only on websites that already support native WebMCP. The Universal Chrome extension can build a bounded local tool surface from normal DOM and ARIA evidence. Those tools are clearly marked as generated by ToolBraid, so they are never confused with tools supplied by the website. The current verified packs cover GitHub, Vercel, and X actions, and supported mutations use browser-observed postconditions. The extension also carries missions across pages, captures bounded screenshot, video, audio, and caption evidence, and provides secure handoffs when the human must log in, complete 2FA, or handle a CAPTCHA. The local Codex/MCP bridge was another important part for me. It lets an agent read the tools bound to the active Chrome page and prepare an exact action. It still cannot create approval or silently dispatch a mutation. That decision stays in the ToolBraid side panel with the person using the browser. The hardest part One of the hardest parts was proving that an action was still the same action the person approved. Navigation, SPA updates, changed schemas, replayed nonces, stale screenshots, ambiguous tab ownership, and worker restarts can all create subtle security problems. I spent a lot of time testing those failure paths instead of only making the happy-path demo look good. The repository includes deterministic tests, real Chrome E2E gates, native WebMCP validation, and a compatibility audit covering 500 public sites with honest pass, partial, and blocked results. How I built it with AI I used OpenAI ChatGPT Sol and Codex heavily as engineering partners. That is part of the project story, not something I want to hide. I set the product direction, chose the security boundaries, reviewed the interface, rejected demos that felt fake, tested the extension on real sites, and kept deciding what had to change. AI helped me implement, debug, test, document, and iterate much faster than I could have done alone, but the idea, decisions, ownership, and final responsibility are mine. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP is not only about replacing mouse clicks with structured tools. A useful agent system also needs provenance, cancellation, drift detection, honest receipts, visible state, and a clear point where the human remains in charge. As a non-tech builder, learning enough about JavaScript, Chrome MV3, cross-origin browser security, native messaging, Vercel deployments, and adversarial testing to bring this together has been a significant personal achievement. What's next Next I want to expand the verified site packs, publish the extension through the Chrome Web Store, make capability packs easier for other people to build, and explore externally anchored audit seals. video_transcript_excerpt: The web can act. Authority should stay human. This is two braid running inside the real local mock-up while Chrome displays the production address. Nothing has been deployed for this preview. The live workspace shows the actual bridge path from codex through MCP and the native host into the extension on browser surface. The agent can request tools, but it cannot mint authority. In the living braid, the mission discovers tools from exact origins, normalizes provider schemas, and carries read-only evidence through separate routes. Every moving packet corresponds to an event in the mock-up's own timeline. The evidence workspace inspects structured reads, visible page metadata, media categories, provenance, confidence, and retention. A real local analysis completes without sending credentials or raw page content anywhere. At the first external effect, the replay stops. Two independent envelopes expose origin, native tool, canonical arguments, risk, target, page fingerprint, recovery path, expiry, and one-time nonce. The human reviews and approves each effect separately. Neither approval can authorize the other. Only after both approvals does execution continue. The redeploy and publication routes move independently, return provider native post conditions, and enter the audit workspaces as separate receipts. A second mission demonstrates compatible read-only fallback. The primary health probe degrades. The replacement preserves the same meaning, and the chain closes with zero external effects. The security mission attacks the same boundary three ways. Instruction-like metadata is quarantined. A changed origin invalidates the page binding. A consumed nonce is rejected on replay. Each challenge ends before provider dispatch, and each rejection becomes auditable evidence. Tor braid gives agents universal discovery. People exact authority, and judges a causal record they can inspect. One mission across the web with the final say always visible.

title: Cadding
pitch: Cadding makes CAD as easy as describing what you want. Create, edit, and export 3D-printable parts with AI, directly in your browser.
about_excerpt: Cadding makes CAD as easy as describing what you want. Create, edit, and export 3D-printable parts with AI, directly in your browser. Like Comment Story Updates Wheel Iphone Cover WebMCP in action Inspiration Cadding was built to make real CAD work faster and more accessible for people who want to design real, 3D-printable objects without having to master complex traditional CAD software. Our goal is not simply to generate 3D meshes from text. Cadding is a browser-based CAD environment where users can create and modify precise, editable geometry, work with multiple parts, and prepare designs that can actually be manufactured and 3D printed. For the WebMCP Challenge, we wanted to take this one step further: make the same CAD environment accessible to external AI agents such as Codex . What we built For the challenge, we connected Cadding's CAD system to WebMCP and exposed 35 structured CAD tools to external agents. These tools give an agent access to a large part of the real Cadding modelling workflow. An agent can: Inspect the complete live CAD scene and understand existing parts Read exact dimensions, parameters, faces, edges and vertices Create primitives and profile-based geometry using extrusions, revolves, sweeps and lofts Change dimensions, positions, rotations and other editable parameters Add holes, fillets, shells and other features Perform boolean operations between parts Create linear and circular patterns Edit topology Align, assemble and mate multiple components Add mechanical connectors and joints Work directly with the same editable CAD scene that the user sees A typical agent workflow can look like: $$ \texttt{cad.get_scene} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.inspect_part} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.get_faces} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.add_profile_shape} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.edit_part} \rightarrow \texttt{cad.fillet_edges} $$ This is important because the agent is not generating an isolated mesh, and it is not trying to control Cadding by guessing where to click. Through WebMCP, the agent operates the actual modelling system using structured CAD operations. Every operation happens inside the live Cadding project, so the human and the AI agent are working on the same editable model . How we built it One of the most important parts of Cadding is the Cadding API . We originally developed this API to give our own AI agent a simple and reliable way to interact with the CAD editor. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that architecture so external agents could use the same modelling capabilities. Instead of building a small set of WebMCP-specific demo commands, we connected WebMCP directly to Cadding's canonical CAD API. The architecture is: $$ \text{External Agent} \rightarrow \text{WebMCP} \rightarrow \text{Cadding API} \rightarrow \text{CAD Engine} \rightarrow \text{Live Editable Scene} $$ This means the WebMCP integration is not a separate prototype sitting next to Cadding. It is an interface into the real CAD system . An external agent can first understand what exists: $$ \texttt{cad.get_scene} + \texttt{cad.inspect_part} + \texttt{cad.get_parameters} $$ and then act on that information using operations such as: $$ \texttt{cad.add_shape}, \quad \texttt{cad.add_hole}, \quad \texttt{cad.boolean_parts}, \quad \texttt{cad.mate_parts} $$ This allows agents to chain multiple operations together to build and modify much more complex objects. Biggest challenge The biggest challenge while building both the Cadding AI agent and the WebMCP integration was making every CAD step extremely easy for an AI model to understand and execute correctly. CAD becomes complex very quickly. An agent needs to reason about dimensions, coordinate systems, part relationships, faces, edges, transformations, feature order, boolean operations, assemblies and the constantly changing state of the model. In simple terms: $$ \text{Reliable AI CAD} \text{Clear Tools} + \text{Precise Geometry Context} + \text{Predictable Execution} $$ Because of this, we spent a significant amount of time improving the Cadding API itself . Our goal was to hide as much unnecessary CAD-engine complexity as possible and turn modelling actions into clear, predictable and structured operations. Instead of expecting an AI model to understand the internal implementation of a CAD engine, we expose actions that map directly to the modelling intent: Create a part Inspect its dimensions Get its faces or edges Add a hole to a specific face Resize an existing body Round selected edges Subtract one body from another Pattern a component Align two parts Mate two faces together We also worked extensively on stable identifiers, constrained parameters, clear tool descriptions, validation and useful execution feedback. This work was critical for making both Cadding's own AI agent and external WebMCP agents more reliable. What we learned One of our biggest learnings was that giving an AI model access to tools is not enough . The way those tools are designed has a huge impact on how capable the agent becomes. We found that: $$ \text{Agent Quality} \propto \text{Quality of the Tool Interface} $$ Complex software like CAD contains a large amount of implicit state and domain knowledge. If the interface presented to the AI is ambiguous, the agent quickly becomes unreliable. By spending months making the Cadding API easier for AI models to reason about, we were able to turn increasingly complex CAD workflows into structured actions that agents can understand and combine. WebMCP allowed us to take that same agent-friendly CAD interface and make it accessible to external agents. The result is a shared CAD workspace where humans and AI agents can work together on the same real, editable and 3D-printable models .  What it is 

 HoldSlot is a booking desk for interview / clinic-style slots. A person and an in-browser agent share the same screen. 

 The agent can search open slots and place a hold . The hold is visible on the board with a timer. Confirm is a human-only button. There is no confirm tool. The agent cannot complete a booking.

Repo: https://github.com/devtechedge/holdslot 
Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AnjYWBRFELY 

 Why WebMCP 

 Agents are bad at calendars. They click the wrong cell, double-book, or submit while the person looks away. 

 WebMCP lets the page own the tools: 

 
 search_slots — open slots by day and duration 
 hold_slot — hold for 3 minutes (does not book) 
 list_holds — current holds and time left 
 release_hold — drop a hold 
 get_board — full board snapshot 
 request_confirm — ask the human to confirm ( does not confirm ) 
 

 The UI updates when a tool runs. The person always sees the hold, the timer, and the confirm step. 

 What people and agents do together 

 
 Agent: search and hold while you watch 
 You: reject a bad hold, or press Confirm booking 
 Both: same URL, same state

 Static HTML / CSS / JS on Vercel. document.modelContext.registerTool(...) on load. In-memory slots. Works in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing .

 Page-owned tools beat “agent, please click the button.” The useful part of WebMCP is a shared, visible contract: the agent can hold, the human still owns the commitment.

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation.
