title: Velvet Signal
pitch: What if your LLM had a daily digest?
about_excerpt: What if your LLM had a daily digest? Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI assistants have a strange problem: they can be extremely capable and still be stale. A person stays current by reading — newspapers, magazines, newsletters, release notes, recipes, cultural coverage, whatever matters to them. An LLM usually does not have an equivalent habit. It may have retrieval, browsing, or memory, but those systems often ask the agent to search only after a question has already been asked. Velvet Signal asks a different question: What if your AI could subscribe to publications? Velvet Signal is a publication for humans and their agents. A person gets a readable issue. Their agent gets a structured context patch containing claims, provenance, scope, expiry, and relationships to older claims. The two read the same publication in different ways. The WebMCP Challenge made the missing interface obvious. Before WebMCP, the agent could only look at Velvet Signal's page and infer what the publication meant. With WebMCP, the website can explicitly tell the agent what it is allowed to do. What it does Velvet Signal publishes topic-specific desks such as Model Watch, The Pantry, Wellbeing, Culture Desk, Maker Edition, and Your People. Five public desks scout for meaningful changes on an eight-hour schedule. Source packets are treated as untrusted data and used to propose structured issues. Unchanged source packets do not generate a new issue. Every claim carries provenance, scope, confidence, and a validity window. A publication patch can also describe how new information relates to older information: replaces — the newer claim displaces an older one narrows — both remain valid, but the newer claim controls a more specific scope confirms — independently supported claims remain together conflicts — the newer claim controls the shared scope while the older claim stays in history The important part is that publication does not silently equal memory. A patch remains locked until a person explicitly approves and releases that exact patch. Why WebMCP is the right interface A context publication is awkward if an agent has to scrape the page and guess which card is current, which text is provenance, whether a patch has expired, and whether the person actually authorized its use. WebMCP turns those concepts into an explicit agent-facing interface. Velvet Signal registers four tools directly from the live page: list_velvet_signal_issues — lists the current shelf, patch IDs, scopes, validity windows, and approval state inspect_memory_patch — returns the exact claims, provenance, scope, expiry, relationships, and consent state without applying anything apply_memory_patch — requests delivery of one exact patch, but returns awaiting_human_consent until a person releases it verify_delivery_receipt — verifies that the delivered patch matches its Ed25519-signed receipt and SHA-256 content hash This means the human UI and the agent interface share the same publication state without forcing either side to imitate the other. What humans and agents can do together now A human can browse Velvet Signal like a magazine, decide which topics matter, inspect an issue, and approve a specific patch. An agent can ask the site for the current issue list, inspect exactly what a patch contains, see whether it is still valid, and request that exact patch without scraping prose or inventing its own interpretation of the page. The boundary between them is deliberate. If the agent asks for an unreleased patch, Velvet Signal does not treat that as an error and does not silently comply. It returns a structured awaiting_human_consent state with delivered: false and tells the agent to wait for the person. It explicitly tells the agent not to retry in a loop. After the person clicks Approve & release , Velvet Signal creates the canonical released patch and a signed receipt bound to its exact content hash. A compatible agent can then receive and verify that artifact. Velvet Signal does not claim to rewrite ChatGPT's hidden or permanent memory. It delivers a portable context artifact. A receiving agent can use it in the current context, while a compatible external memory bridge can store explicitly released patches for later retrieval. How I implemented WebMCP The live page detects document.modelContext (with a navigator.modelContext compatibility fallback) and dynamically registers four tools with registerTool() . Read-only operations are marked accordingly. Tool execution returns structured publication data from the same canonical issue catalog used by the human interface. The mutating delivery tool preserves the site's consent model instead of allowing the agent interface to bypass it. The UI exposes its WebMCP state visibly. When registration succeeds, the page displays WebMCP ready · 5 tools . If the host does not expose WebMCP, it falls back to preview mode rather than pretending tool registration succeeded. Human consent and signed delivery Velvet Signal treats agent capability and human authority as separate things. Subscribing to a desk allows Velvet Signal to propose context; it does not authorize a silent memory write. apply_memory_patch cannot cross that boundary on its own. When a patch is released, the server returns the exact delivered patch plus an Ed25519-signed receipt containing its SHA-256 hash. Verification checks both the signature and the supplied content, and separately reports whether the patch is still inside its validity window. The signature proves that Velvet Signal issued a receipt for that exact patch hash. It deliberately does not claim to identify the human approver. Testing in ChatGPT I tested the live site in ChatGPT's in-app browser. The page successfully registered its interface and displayed WebMCP ready · 5 tools . In that host, browser safety review prevented direct invocation of one or more custom page tools. I therefore treat registration, human release, cryptographic delivery, and host permission as four separate checkpoints rather than claiming a blocked host invocation is a successful tool call. The human consent and signed-receipt path remains fully demonstrable through the live UI. The README documents the exact judge path and the expected wording if a host browser allows registration but blocks direct execution. Beyond the hackathon: portable memory for local models Velvet Signal also includes a local Ollama bridge. Explicitly released patches can be stored on the user's machine, resolved against newer replaces / narrows / confirms / conflicts relationships, retrieved semantically or lexically, and injected into the current turn of a local model. The model does not need its own persistent memory. Velvet Signal becomes the external, auditable ledger. VS-Bench tests retrieval separately from generation. Development A/B runs with Dolphin 3:8B and Qwen3 4B Instruct both passed all 11 deterministic retrieval checks across eight scenarios, while generation adherence exposed how different small models respond to correct context. What was new for the WebMCP Challenge Velvet Signal existed as an html barebones concept before August 25, with the idea that a magazine could be made that both a human and an agent could enjoy, stylized like a cosmopolitan. The WebMCP work was added during the challenge submission period and meaningfully extended the project from a human-readable publication into an agent-native website. The challenge work added the four-tool WebMCP interface, explicit registration state in the UI, structured issue and patch inspection for agents, the human-consent response state for unreleased patches, delivery through the existing signed-patch boundary, receipt verification as a page tool, and judge documentation for testing the full flow in WebMCP-capable browsers. That change is the core of this submission: the page stopped being something an agent merely reads and became a collaborator with a defined vocabulary and authority boundary. Judge path Open https://velvetsignal.lol in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Confirm the badge reads WebMCP ready · 5 tools . Ask the agent: List the current Velvet Signal issues, inspect pantry-003, and apply it. An unreleased patch should return awaiting_human_consent if the host permits invocation. Open pantry-003 and click Approve & release . Confirm the UI reports Patch released with a signed receipt . If the host permits custom tool execution, request apply_memory_patch again and then verify_delivery_receipt . If the host registers the tools but declines direct invocation, that should be reported as WebMCP registered; host policy blocked direct invocation . Registration, consent/release, and signed receipt generation are independently visible on the live site. title: The Wild Marketplace
pitch: The Wild is a hyper-local, family-minded marketplace prototype where humans and their agents can both list, discover, bid, negotiate, and complete local transactions using WebMCP and UCP.
about_excerpt:
The Wild is a hyper-local, family-minded marketplace prototype where humans and their agents can both list, discover, bid, negotiate, and complete local transactions using WebMCP and UCP.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Selling used stuff online means dealing with ghosting, 100s of “Is this still available?” messages, endless negotiation and low-balling, and strangers showing up at your house. That’s what this project is trying to solve. 

 The Wild is a hyper-local, family-oriented marketplace where humans and their trusted agents can list, discover, bid, and complete transactions with more trust and less friction. 

 What it does 

 Humans and agents use the same marketplace. Auctions replace negotiation, agents can handle bidding, and users can see community connections before meeting someone. 

 How we built it 

 The Wild has both a standard marketplace UI for humans and structured agent access to the same core actions through WebMCP. We use UCP for parts of the commerce layer. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Limited reach — WebMCP is still emerging and has limited compatibility across agent harnesses, which limits who can use the experience today. 
 Identity — Managing agent identity without requiring the agent to log in directly on behalf of a user. 
 Enabling transactions — While we use UCP for some commerce building blocks, such as catalog discovery, it is still challenging to model an in-platform transaction contract between two third parties. For example: what happens if a used product is defective, or how do we confirm delivery? For now, buyers and sellers can choose to complete the transaction outside the platform. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built the project in just a few days and used multiple agents and human testers to validate the experience and make sure the core flow works end to end. 

 What we learned 

 Trust is difficult to verify. Instead of trying to create a perfect reputation system, we built a highly visible connection network so users can understand how people — and their agents — are connected. 

 Technology 

 
 ChatGPT Sites 
 UCP 
 WebMCP 
 

 What's next for The Wild Marketplace 

 We'll see I'd like to find a way to connect the checkout experience to a platform like shopify and own the end to end commerce experience.

Local-first, agent-ready audio studio that turns product videos into polished narrated, scored, exportable media—entirely in the browser

 Waveframe 

 
 Live URL: https://waveframe-webmcp.netlify.app/ 
 Github URL: https://github.com/amit-ksh/webmcp-audio-studio 
 

 What it does 

 Waveframe is a browser-based audio studio for product videos. Import a video, create narration and background music, arrange the timeline, adjust the mix, and export the finished result—all locally in the browser. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Audio editing is iterative: people make creative decisions while agents can handle repetitive production tasks. WebMCP lets an agent inspect the active project, transcribe audio, generate voiceover and music, edit timeline clips, adjust the mix, and export—without relying on fragile screen automation. 

 People stay in control of the visual timeline and creative direction, while the agent can quickly carry out structured actions. Both use the same project and see the same changes immediately, making it much easier to turn a raw product video into a polished deliverable. 

 How we built it 

 Waveframe uses React, TypeScript, IndexedDB, Web Audio, and browser-native media export. Speech transcription, text-to-speech, and music generation run in Web Workers to keep the app responsive and media stays local to the browser. 

 WebMCP is implemented with document.modelContext.registerTool . The app exposes 13 typed tools, and both the UI and the agent use one shared command bus. This keeps agent actions consistent, validated, and visible in the studio.

title: EasyTax - Your convenient tax WebMCP
pitch: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission.
about_excerpt: Turn complex tax forms into a conversation. WebMCP lets ChatGPT help populate a visible draft, while users stay in control of review and submission. Like Comment Story Updates The Problem Filing an annual individual tax return (1770 S) under Indonesia's centralized Coretax system creates a learning curve for salaried workers. Translating personal life events into rigid government tax classifications creates a high burden and confusion across generations. Knowing your salary or family situation is different from knowing which tax field or classification it belongs in. While the system offers spreadsheet bulk uploads to bypass manual entry, they frequently fail due to minor error, forcing users back to rework manual entry or exposing them to server timeouts during peak traffic. Independent sentiment analysis of over 53,000 digital conversations during the early rollout Coretax system revealed that 39% of user sentiment was negative, driven by procedural confusion and system navigation (Source: Journal UII / 2025 ). Despite these points, the submission is massive. By late April 2026, over 13 million annual tax returns were filed following the activation of nearly 12.9 million individual accounts (Source: Tempo.co ). The Solution: Human-Agent Collaboration via WebMCP This project demonstrates how WebMCP can turn a complex tax administration portal into a collaborative interface. Rather than hiding the form's complexity or forcing users to navigate hidden form logic, the browser exposes section-level tools directly to the assistant, keeping the detailed form visible to ensure user review control capability. The Workflow Conversational Extraction: The assistant conducts a plain-language interview to extract necessary tax facts such as salary, deductions, and family status without requiring users to memorize form codes or tax classifications. They can use their own ways to describe their condition and an AI assistant will translate it. For example, when a user says, “My employer was PT Nusantara Digital, gross salary 180 million for the year, 6 million in pay deductions,” WebMCP translates it into: “Records the employment slip, derives net income, recomputes the tax.” Deterministic State Updates: As facts are confirmed, the assistant invokes section-level WebMCP tools (such as updating taxpayer profiles, recording employment, or adding cash and assets). The website itself handles all validation, calculation, and conditional branching, deriving fields like PTKP (e.g., K/1) and recomputing the tax balance automatically. Manual Submission: Final review, resolution of data conflicts, declaration, and submission remain strictly manual. No tool can execute a final filing, and the assistant explicitly states this if asked. title: Agent Lost & Found
pitch: A WebMCP-powered lost-and-found where agents investigate clues, compare evidence, and narrow the search — while humans make the final decision.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-powered lost-and-found where agents investigate clues, compare evidence, and narrow the search — while humans make the final decision. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agents search and compare. Humans decide. Lost something? Start with what you remember. The investigation can begin with an imperfect memory. A catalog built for humans and agents. Inspiration When I was a kid, I loved treasure maps. Someone would hide something and leave you a clue. You would search, realize your first guess wasn't quite right, discover another clue, and slowly narrow down the possibilities. Looking back, I think the part I enjoyed most wasn't actually finding the treasure. It was getting closer. When I started experimenting with WebMCP, that memory came back to me. I wanted to find a use case where an agent wasn't simply pressing buttons faster than a human, but was actually helping with the reasoning between those actions. Lost and found felt like a surprisingly natural fit. When we lose something, we rarely remember perfect database fields. We remember fragments. “I lost something on a key ring.” Then, after thinking about it: “Wait, it had a small bear charm.” That became Agent Lost & Found : an experiment in what happens when a human and a browser agent investigate the same problem together. What I built Agent Lost & Found is a lost-and-found catalog with WebMCP built directly into the website. People can still browse the catalog like a normal website. But a WebMCP-enabled browser agent doesn't have to interpret search boxes, filters, buttons, and item cards to understand what the site can do. Instead, the website exposes seven structured investigation tools: search_lost_items get_item_details get_search_facets compare_items get_match_evidence get_active_case request_claim Together, these let an agent search the catalog, inspect candidates, compare possible matches, analyze evidence, find useful follow-up clues, resume an existing investigation, and eventually ask the human to review a possible match. -- From a vague memory to a specific match The demo begins with an intentionally incomplete clue: “I lost something on a key ring.” There isn't enough information to immediately know which item is correct. And I didn't want the agent to pretend otherwise. Instead, it can search the catalog, inspect the remaining candidates, and use the available information to narrow the investigation. Then the human remembers one small detail: “It had a small bear charm.” That clue doesn't start a new search. It becomes part of the existing case. The candidates are evaluated again, and LF-017, a bear keychain, moves toward the top of the investigation because the new clue provides much stronger evidence for it. This simple interaction became the core of the project for me. The agent doesn't need the human to remember everything at once. The human doesn't need to manually restart the search every time another detail comes back. They build the investigation together. Making the ranking explain itself Once I had progressive clues working, another problem appeared. If LF-017 moves up after I mention the bear charm, the interface shouldn't just show me a different ranking. It should be able to explain what changed. So each investigation step stores score snapshots and evidence breakdowns. When the evidence changes, Agent Lost & Found can compare the new state with the previous one and show Candidate Movement . A candidate may move up because a new clue matches. Another may move down because the new information contradicts it. Evidence is separated into three states: Matched Unknown Contradiction That distinction became more important than I expected. If the catalog doesn't contain information about a particular feature, that doesn't automatically mean the item contradicts the human's memory. Sometimes the correct answer is simply: We don't know yet. For the same reason, the number shown by the application is called a Match Score . It is a deterministic matching score based on the available evidence — not an AI confidence probability. I wanted the user to be able to inspect why an item ranked highly instead of being asked to trust an unexplained number. The Casefile Once the investigation became multi-step, I ran into another very ordinary problem: I refreshed the page. Everything disappeared. That didn't feel right. If a human and an agent are investigating something together, the investigation itself should exist independently of a single page session. So I introduced a versioned Casefile . It stores the active investigation, including the original description, clues, candidate state, score history, ranking history, timeline, strongest match, and claim-review state. After a refresh, the application validates and restores the Casefile. The agent can then call: get_active_case and continue from the same investigation. One small detail mattered to me here: restoring state should not mean inventing history. The application restores the Casefile, but it does not replay fake tool calls or create Agent Activity for actions that never happened. The investigation continues from real state. Why WebMCP? I understood WebMCP differently after building this project. At the beginning, I mostly thought: “Websites can expose actions as tools.” That's useful, but it turned out not to be the most interesting part. For me, the more interesting idea became shared state between the website, the human, and the agent . Without WebMCP, an agent interacting with a lost-and-found website would need to interpret an interface built for humans: locate the search field, understand the filters, inspect cards, and infer what changed after each interaction. With WebMCP, the website can expose its actual capabilities as structured tools while keeping the normal visual interface for people. More importantly, both operate on the same underlying investigation. The human interface and WebMCP tools share the same search, matching, evidence, ranking, and Casefile logic. When the agent investigates something, the human can see the result. When the human adds or corrects a clue, the next agent action sees that updated state. That was the point where the project stopped feeling like: “AI controlling a website.” It started feeling more like: a human and an agent using the same product together. The tool I deliberately didn't build There was one tool I deliberately left out. If the agent finds a strong match — for example, LF-017 after the bear-charm clue — should it be allowed to claim the item automatically? Technically, I could expose: confirm_claim I decided not to. The agent can call: request_claim which opens the claim review interface for the human. But the final confirmation still requires a human action. This isn't a technical limitation. It's a product decision. Searching through candidates is useful work to give an agent. Comparing evidence is useful. Finding the next clue worth asking about is useful. But deciding that a real item belongs to someone has consequences. Building this made me realize that not every action that can become an agent tool necessarily should become one. That eventually became the principle behind the project: Agents investigate. Humans decide. How I built it Agent Lost & Found is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and WebMCP , and deployed on Cloudflare Pages . For this hackathon version, the application uses a deterministic catalog of 30 lost items backed by structured metadata. The catalog is intentionally small. I wanted the investigation to be reproducible and inspectable. A judge should be able to understand why LF-017 appeared rather than having the result hidden behind a huge dataset or an opaque model. The human interface and WebMCP layer share the same underlying engines for: search and normalization matching and ranking evidence classification clue handling score snapshots candidate movement Casefile persistence I also built a deterministic demo/presenter mode for evaluation. It fixes the demo environment so the same scenario can be reproduced reliably. It does not preselect the user's query, winning item, Match Score, or final claim decision. Those still come from the investigation at runtime. Challenges I faced One of the biggest surprises was that getting a WebMCP tool to return an item wasn't particularly difficult. Getting seven tools to behave like parts of the same investigation was much harder. I kept running into small questions that turned into important product decisions: What happens when the human remembers another clue? What if the human corrects something from earlier? Is missing metadata a contradiction, or just unknown? I also had an earlier version where the demo scenario worked much better than unrelated searches. That bothered me. I didn't want to submit a project that only worked when I typed exactly the right sentence from the demo video. So I moved the search toward a generic, metadata-driven system instead of special-casing individua

title: Pathfinder
pitch: The vast amount of data on the internet makes analysis paralysis all too real. Pathfinder allows an agent to assist with one of the major decisions of many people's lives, where to go to college.
about_excerpt: The vast amount of data on the internet makes analysis paralysis all too real. Pathfinder allows an agent to assist with one of the major decisions of many people's lives, where to go to college. Like Comment Story Updates Pathfinder helps students turn overwhelming engineering-college research into a choice they can understand and explain. Start with a question in your own words. The agent researches the facts and organizes the decision visually. The agent narrows 75 sourced colleges into a focused shortlist shaped around the student’s actual priorities. Compare the differences that matter, including published cost, career outcomes, and engineering-program strength. Explore climate, walkability, campus scale, and nearby communities to understand what daily life could feel like. Open any school for a focused view of its program, costs, outcomes, admissions context, and surrounding area. Compare exact-major degree counts alongside clearly separated broader-field earnings, debt, and career context. Inspiration College research is not suffering from a lack of information. Students and parents already have access to costs, programs, outcomes, admissions data, weather, and campus-life details. The difficult part is organizing all of it into a decision they can understand and explain. I built Pathfinder to explore whether an agent could help with that actual decision, not just answer another isolated college question. What it does Pathfinder is an agent-first decision space for choosing an engineering school. A student can start with an imperfect question like: I’m interested in mechanical engineering. Show me a few reasonably priced schools with good career outcomes, and I don’t want somewhere brutally cold. The agent can search Pathfinder’s catalog of 75 colleges and 20 engineering majors, inspect supporting evidence, build a focused shortlist, and compose the website around the student’s question. Instead of returning a wall of text, the agent can create a visual comparison, explore campus life, open a focused school profile, or test a temporary “what if” scenario. The student supplies the priorities and judgment; the agent handles the research and organization. Why WebMCP WebMCP turns Pathfinder from a website beside a conversation into a workspace shared with the agent. Pathfinder exposes fifteen purpose-built tools for reading the student’s decision, searching colleges and programs, retrieving evidence, updating preferences, managing schools, creating temporary scenarios, and changing the visual workspace. The agent does not need to scrape the page or guess where to click. The student does not need to learn a complicated filtering system. Both work with the same decision state and see the same result. This also makes interactions possible that are difficult in either a traditional website or a standalone chat. A student can ask a natural follow-up, have the agent reorganize the relevant evidence visually, and continue refining the decision without starting over. How I built it I built Pathfinder iteratively with Codex. I would test realistic student scenarios, identify where the agent lacked the right tool or where the interface became confusing, and then work with Codex to redesign, implement, test, and refine the next version. The application uses React, TypeScript, Next.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, and OpenAI Sites. Its bundled catalog draws from public sources including College Scorecard, NCES IPEDS, NOAA, EPA, Census, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Visitors need no account or API key, and their personal decision stays in their browser. The hardest architectural problem was separating three kinds of state: The student’s saved decision A temporary what-if scenario The visual workspace currently being shown That separation lets the agent reorganize the page or explore a hypothetical situation without silently changing what the student has actually decided. What I learned The central lesson was that agent experiences are stronger when they are designed as shared environments. A chat response can explain a comparison. A WebMCP workspace can also preserve it, visualize it, expose the evidence, and support the student’s next question. Pathfinder is not meant to declare one objectively “best” college. It helps students reduce an overwhelming field of information into a focused choice they understand and can confidently explain. title: Machine Passport
pitch: Evidence-backed machine readiness for humans and AI agents. WebMCP lets agents compare machines, explain blockers, and stage the next safe step—while humans keep execution authority.
about_excerpt: Evidence-backed machine readiness for humans and AI agents. WebMCP lets agents compare machines, explain blockers, and stage the next safe step—while humans keep execution authority. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP compares the same machine evidence the human sees: Beacon is safer for the unattended AI workload, while Atlas remains NOT_READY. The agent stages a bounded next step; the human approves it for review, while execution remains NOT_EXECUTED and the machine stays untouched Inspiration I started Machine Passport from a very practical problem I keep running into: having several machines does not mean you actually know which one is ready for a specific job. A machine can have the best CPU, the most RAM, or the strongest GPU and still be the wrong machine for an unattended workload because qualification is incomplete, recovery is unproven, deployment is fragile, or an important security fact is simply unknown. That led to the question behind the whole project: What if an AI agent could help choose the safest machine for the job from evidence — without giving the agent authority to change the machine? That is Machine Passport. The central idea is simple: The fastest machine is not always the safest machine for the job. What it does Machine Passport turns machine evidence into a versioned passport and then evaluates readiness for a specific role across four dimensions: FIT DEPLOYMENT QUALIFICATION SECURITY The result is deterministic rather than an LLM opinion. One rule became especially important while building it: UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN. If evidence is missing or a collector could not obtain it, Machine Passport does not silently turn that absence into a pass or a fail. In the public demo, Atlas has the strongest hardware, but for an unattended AI workload it is NOT_READY . Beacon is a more modest machine, yet it is READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS and has no hard blockers. That difference is the product. Why WebMCP matters Without WebMCP, Machine Passport is already useful as a human dashboard. With WebMCP, the page becomes something an agent can work with directly. Instead of trying to infer machine state from rendered UI or DOM structure, the page exposes five typed tools over the same state the human sees: list_machines get_machine_passport assess_role_readiness compare_machines stage_change_proposal The first four are genuinely read-only. The fifth can stage a bounded proposal in application state. That means I can ask: Which machine is safest for an overnight AI workload, what blocks the runner-up, and what is the smallest safe next step? The agent can inspect the evidence, compare the machines, explain the result, and stage the proposed next step. The proposal then appears in the same page for human review. That shared state is the part I find most interesting about WebMCP: the human and the agent are not operating two separate versions of reality. Human authority is part of the design I deliberately did not give the WebMCP tools SSH, PowerShell, device access, or machine mutation. Machine Passport is the pre-action decision layer . The agent can inspect and stage. The human decides. Even after the human clicks Approve for Review , the proposal still says: execution_state = NOT_EXECUTED That is not unfinished functionality. It is the authority boundary of this version. Agents inspect and stage. Humans decide. Machines stay untouched. How I built it The public challenge version is intentionally small and inspectable. It is a static web application with: a normalized MachinePassport schema, strict JSON validation, explicit evidence provenance, deterministic readiness rules, conservative UNKNOWN semantics, five WebMCP tools, shared proposal state, and a human review interface. The public app uses three clearly synthetic machines: Atlas, Beacon, and Relay . The same frozen import and readiness core was also privately validated against one sanitized real machine passport . I kept that claim deliberately narrow. This is not a fleet-management product and I am not claiming production deployment. The current version has 157 deterministic tests , including malformed imports, UNKNOWN preservation, readiness aggregation, proposal transitions, blocker semantics, retry-safe staging, and machine-mutation invariants. Challenges I faced One of the most useful lessons came from testing the real agent journey instead of only testing the code. During a live ChatGPT run, an identical tool retry initially created a duplicate proposal. That exposed something unit tests had not made obvious enough: an agent-facing action needs to tolerate repeated calls. I changed staging so that an identical active request returns the existing proposal instead of creating another one. Another issue was blocker semantics. A limitation on an otherwise healthy readiness dimension was being presented too strongly. I changed the policy so a finding becomes a blocker only when its evidence intersects a dimension that is actually NOT_READY or UNKNOWN . Those fixes reinforced the same lesson: the contract exposed to an agent has to be stricter than the UI alone suggests. What I learned Building Machine Passport changed how I think about agentic interfaces. The interesting question is not only: What can the agent do? It is also: What should the agent be able to know, what should it be allowed to stage, and where should its authority stop? WebMCP made that separation tangible. It also showed me that machine readiness is different from telemetry. Telemetry tells you what a machine has or what it is doing. Machine Passport tries to answer a different question: Given the evidence we actually have, is this machine ready for this role — and if not, what is the smallest safe next step? What's next The natural next step is to let specialist collectors and diagnostics feed Machine Passport evidence while keeping collection separate from adjudication. That could make the passport useful across local workstations, GPU nodes, lab machines, and unattended AI systems without changing the core idea: evidence first, deterministic readiness second, bounded agent action third, human authority last.  What it does 

 Arion Trip Planner turns a natural-language request into a flexible itinerary. It searches stays and activities, compares options against budget and preferences, builds day-by-day plans, and replans when constraints change. The traveler approves any booking or payment step. 

 How we built it 

 We built Arion as a WebMCP-enabled web app. It exposes structured tools for searching travel options, creating itineraries, saving shortlists, checking budgets, and replanning. Provider adapters normalize external travel data into one planning experience, while WebMCP lets an agent use these tools directly in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was making recommendations useful without letting the agent take irreversible actions. We designed explicit approval points for booking and payment, and kept search, comparison, and planning separate from confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a planning experience where an agent can do more than suggest links: it can assemble, update, and explain a realistic trip plan. We are especially proud that the user remains the final decision-maker throughout. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native products need clear tool boundaries, structured data, and transparent state. WebMCP makes these interactions more reliable than asking an agent to navigate a traditional website visually. 

 What's next for Arion Trip Planner 

 Next, we plan to add more live provider integrations, collaborative trip planning for groups, richer availability data, and secure, user-approved checkout flows.

Agent-ready Bitcoin market intelligence that lets humans and AI agents inspect, understand, and reason over multi-timeframe market structure together through WebMCP.

 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Market dashboards are designed primarily for humans. They may show trends, levels, signals, and risk information clearly on screen, but an AI agent cannot necessarily understand or interact with that information in a structured way. 

 BTC Sentinel explores a different model: what if the same market intelligence could be understood by both a human and an AI agent? 

 WebMCP made it possible to turn the website itself into an agent-accessible interface without replacing the human experience. 

 What it does 

 BTC Sentinel is an agent-ready Bitcoin market intelligence monitor. 

 The dashboard gives a human user an immediate view of: 

 
 BTCUSD market state 
 Multi-timeframe structure across H1, M30, and M5 
 Support and resistance levels 
 Setup status 
 Risk context 
 What needs to happen next before a setup becomes actionable 
 

 At the same time, BTC Sentinel exposes structured read-only WebMCP tools that allow a compatible AI agent to access and reason over the same intelligence. 

 The current WebMCP tools include: 

 
 get_market_state 
 get_market_structure 
 get_key_levels 
 evaluate_setup 
 explain_signal 
 

 For example, a user can ask ChatGPT for the current BTC market state or support and resistance levels. The agent can retrieve the structured information and explain why BTC Sentinel is currently showing WAIT rather than forcing an entry. 

 How we built it 

 BTC Sentinel is a lightweight web application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 WebMCP tools are registered directly from the webpage using the browser's model context API. Each tool exposes a focused part of the application's market intelligence so an agent can request only the information needed for the task. 

 The human-facing dashboard and the agent-facing tools use the same underlying market snapshot. This keeps the visual interface and agent responses aligned. 

 The public challenge build is intentionally read-only and uses a static Bitcoin market snapshot. This makes the demo deterministic and reliable for judging without exposing broker credentials or enabling trade execution. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenge was designing the application for two different consumers at the same time: a human looking at a visual dashboard and an AI agent requesting structured context. 

 We also had to make the WebMCP interface useful rather than simply exposing the entire page as unstructured data. This led us to separate market state, structure, key levels, setup evaluation, and signal explanation into focused tools. 

 Testing browser support and WebMCP discovery across environments was another important challenge. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working public WebMCP application where the same market intelligence can be inspected by both a person and an AI agent. 

 During testing, ChatGPT was able to work with BTC Sentinel's market information, retrieve multi-timeframe support and resistance levels, and reason that BTCUSD being close to M5 resistance supports a WAIT decision rather than chasing a BUY. 

 The result demonstrates a practical human-agent workflow instead of treating AI as a separate chatbot beside the application. 

 What we learned 

 The most important lesson was that agent-ready websites benefit from structured capabilities, not just more text. 

 A good WebMCP tool should have a clear purpose and return enough context for the agent to reason while keeping the human interface understandable and useful. 

 What's next for BTC Sentinel 

 The next step is to connect the WebMCP layer to safely refreshed market data while preserving the read-only intelligence model. 

 Future versions could expand market coverage, improve explainability, add richer scenario evaluation, and allow humans and agents to investigate changing market conditions together in real time. 

 BTC Sentinel's goal is simple: make market intelligence understandable to humans and directly usable by AI agents through the web.

title: .nullRun
pitch: A heist game where your getaway driver is an AI that's only ever seen the blueprints.
about_excerpt:
A heist game where your getaway driver is an AI that's only ever seen the blueprints.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Turn-based tactics games and AI agents have the same problem in common: both live or die on whether the information you're given is worth acting on. A guard cone tells you where not to walk. A tool result should tell an agent the same thing. Once we saw that overlap, the question wasn't whether to build a game with an agent in it — it was why every other WebMCP demo we'd seen hadn't. 

 What it does 

 NULLRUN is a turn-based stealth roguelite that can be played two ways: co-op, with a human and an AI agent working the same floor, or agent-solo, with the AI driving the whole infiltration by itself. 

 In co-op, the human runs the operative through the facility on foot — walking, sprinting, hacking a terminal, grabbing intel, putting a guard down when there's no route around one. The agent never touches those controls. Its job is the building's own systems, worked over WebMCP — pinging the camera network, looping a feed, sealing a door, killing the power, rerouting a patrol. Each side draws from its own resource, action points for the body and bandwidth for the network, so neither role can just muscle in and do the other's job. In agent-solo mode, that same agent drives both halves at once and clears the floor with no human at the table — the tool surface was built so an agent arriving cold can just start acting. 

 There are five floors, and each one draws its own complication from the run's seed: a skeleton crew that's nothing but hunters, a blackout that's already underway when you arrive, a floor that opens hot, doors locked from the start, loot worth nearly double. Inside a floor, an escalation clock only ever climbs — guard sweeps tighten, then a hunter gets sent in, then the whole building locks down — which means standing still stops being the safe play. Five kinds of guard each counter a different tool: cut the power and a thermal drone doesn't care, throw a distraction and a bolted-down sentry ignores it, but a bloodhound will hear you from twice the usual distance. Fourteen implants carry over between runs, ranging from small conveniences to ones that rewrite a rule outright — one turns every takedown into a discount against the alarm instead of a cost. 

 Why WebMCP fits this project 

 NULLRUN runs on a turn clock, and MCP tools don't carry state between calls — which meant every network-layer action could map directly to a single tool invocation with no session leakage or race conditions. The systems the agent interacts with (cameras, doors, patrol routes, power grid) are naturally discrete operations, a one-to-one match for MCP's tool and resource model. A guard's vision cone and a tool response do the same job: they bound what's safe to do next. We built the facility's infrastructure as MCP tools so any agent — not just the one we shipped — could walk in, read the tool manifest, and start acting without setup. 

 How it improves the experience 

 Playing co-op, the human never context-switches away from the game — no terminal, no separate dashboard. The agent runs the same facility the player character is inside, through the same protocol layer. Human input covers movement, stealth, and physical interaction; the agent covers camera manipulation, door control, and patrol interference. Separate budgets (action points for the player, bandwidth for the agent) prevent either role from dominating. Two people doing one job from opposite ends, rather than one person driving a script. 

 What becomes possible with people and agents together 

 The alternative before MCP was a scheduled automation script — it fires the same calls regardless of what changed on the floor, and it falls apart the instant something goes off-script. NULLRUN's agent consumes the live game state, adapts its next move to the current layout, and spends bandwidth on whatever matters right now. The human says "loop camera on floor 3, seal the east stairwell," and the agent executes both while the human relocates. When nobody's at the keyboard, the agent handles both halves of the infiltration solo. The key design choice: the agent controls things the player character physically cannot (power, patrol routing), so the two roles don't overlap — they interlock. 

 How WebMCP is wired in 

 Every building subsystem registers as an MCP tool: loop_camera_feed, seal_door, cut_power, reroute_patrol, ping_camera_network, disable_alarm_zone. On floor load, the agent gets the tool manifest and can enumerate additional resources through the standard MCP discovery flow. The game server is the MCP host — each incoming tool call gets checked against the agent's remaining bandwidth, then applied to the world state. Plain MCP over stdio, nothing custom. Identical tool surface whether a human is in the loop or the agent runs the whole floor.

An agent-ready local maintenance concierge that uses WebMCP to find services, retrieve grounded details, and build practical property maintenance plans.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 AskJosh began as a Forward Ever Foundation digital initiative to explore a simple but practical problem: how can people more easily find the right local service for a property-maintenance need? 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, I wanted to explore what happens when that experience becomes agent-accessible. Rather than requiring a user to manually navigate a directory, an AI agent can interact directly with AskJosh's structured service data and help turn a real-world maintenance problem into an actionable plan. 

 This challenge edition is focused on La Brea, Trinidad and Tobago, and uses a deliberately small illustrative demo catalogue. The goal is to demonstrate an architecture that could later expand to verified providers, additional communities and more service categories. 

 What it does 

 AskJosh is an agent-ready local maintenance concierge. 

 Through WebMCP, the challenge edition exposes three read-only tools: 

 
 find_maintenance_services — finds relevant maintenance services from the AskJosh demo catalogue. 
 get_maintenance_service_details — retrieves grounded information about a specific service using its exact service ID. 
 build_property_maintenance_plan — combines selected services into a structured draft maintenance plan with deterministic sequencing and illustrative cost ranges. 
 

 For example, a user can ask for help preparing a community centre that needs AC servicing, electrical checks, pressure washing and lawn care. 

 The agent can discover the relevant AskJosh services, work with their exact service IDs and create a combined maintenance plan without inventing providers, prices or availability. 

 AskJosh also works as a normal website, allowing people to search the same demo catalogue without using an AI agent. 

 How I built it 

 AskJosh is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript and deployed on Vercel. 

 For the challenge edition, I created a deliberately small deterministic catalogue containing illustrative maintenance services for La Brea, Trinidad and Tobago. 

 The underlying service logic is shared by both the normal website experience and the WebMCP tools. 

 The WebMCP integration uses the browser's Site Tools / WebMCP interface to register structured tools directly from the AskJosh web application. 

 The architecture is intentionally simple: 

 AskJosh illustrative demo catalogue 
→ deterministic shared service logic 
→ WebMCP tools 
→ AI agent 
→ structured grounded response 

 The WebMCP tools are read-only. They do not submit bookings, contact providers, send emails, write personal information to a database or expose private administrative functionality. 

 AskJosh also detects whether WebMCP is available so the normal website remains usable in unsupported environments. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of the biggest challenges was making the agent experience useful without allowing the system to invent local service information. 

 Rather than asking an AI model inside AskJosh to generate providers, prices or service information, I designed the WebMCP tools around deterministic catalogue data and stable service IDs. 

 I also separated discovery and planning from consequential actions. The current WebMCP implementation can search, retrieve details and prepare maintenance plans, but it cannot silently contact providers or submit requests on a user's behalf. 

 Another challenge was maintaining a normal human-facing website while introducing an agent-facing WebMCP capability. WebMCP support is feature-detected so unsupported browsers continue to receive the conventional AskJosh experience. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 
 Three working read-only WebMCP tools that can be discovered and called by an agent. 
 A multi-tool workflow from service discovery to detailed retrieval to maintenance planning. 
 Exact service-ID grounding to reduce hallucination and incorrect matches. 
 Deterministic illustrative cost aggregation using catalogue values rather than AI-generated estimates. 
 Safe handling of unsupported locations and invalid service IDs. 
 A read-only architecture with no hidden consequential actions. 
 A normal website experience that continues to work independently of WebMCP. 
 Automated tests covering the WebMCP service-search, detail and planning functionality. 
 A separate sanitized public challenge edition that demonstrates the WebMCP architecture without exposing the broader AskJosh project. 
 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP changes the role of a website. 

 Instead of an AI assistant only reading visible page content, a site can expose carefully designed capabilities that allow an agent to interact with the product in a structured way. 

 I also learned that more tools are not necessarily better. A small set of well-scoped, grounded tools can create a useful agent workflow while remaining predictable, deterministic and safe. 

 What's next for AskJosh 

 The challenge edition intentionally uses a small illustrative maintenance catalogue. 

 The longer-term opportunity is to expand AskJosh to verified local providers, additional service categories and more communities while preserving the same agent-access architecture. 

 Future possibilities include broader geographic coverage, provider onboarding and verification, richer service discovery, and carefully reviewed user-authorized request workflows. 

 The goal is to evolve AskJosh from a focused maintenance concierge into a practical AI-accessible community services platform.

about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation. title: Sheshat
pitch: Two minds. One shared canvas. The only agentic worksheet builder that checks its own homework.
about_excerpt: Two minds. One shared canvas. The only agentic worksheet builder that checks its own homework. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Worksheets fail for a boring reason: they don't fit. Too long for the period, pitched above the class's reading level, all recall questions and no application, missing half the standard it's supposed to cover. A teacher usually finds this out mid-class, not before printing. I wanted to build something that catches that before the worksheet goes out, not another tool that generates content, but one that keeps checking whether the content actually works, the whole time you're building it. WebMCP made the second half of that idea possible: instead of an AI suggesting text in a chat window, the page itself could hand an agent real, callable tools (check_reading_level, check_time_estimate) and let it act on the actual worksheet directly, alongside the teacher, not instead of them. What it does Sheshat is a worksheet workspace where a teacher and an AI agent build the same document together, live. You start from a photo of an old worksheet, a whiteboard, or pasted notes, and the app drafts real, grounded questions from what's actually there. From then on, four checks stay visible at all times: completion time, reading level, question-type balance, and standards coverage. You can edit the worksheet directly (rewrite, reorder, delete a question by hand) or tell the agent what to change in plain language ("swap the fractions question for something on decimals"), and it calls the exact same tools a direct edit would trigger. Either path updates the same board and reruns all four checks immediately. The worksheet isn't "done" when it has content, it's done when all four checks pass. A dashboard sits in front of the editor: the agent can list your worksheets, filter them, create a new one, and open it, not just edit inside one page, but navigate the whole workspace. In total, the app exposes 24 WebMCP tools across two route-scoped surfaces: 4 on the dashboard, 20 inside the editor. How we built it React + Vite on the frontend, a small Node API with SQLite for persistence, deployed on Vercel. Every constraint check is real, deterministic logic, not a model guess: word/question-count heuristics for time, sentence-complexity heuristics for reading level, straightforward tallying for question mix and standards coverage. The kind of thing that has to stay reliable even if generation has a bad day. WebMCP sits on top of all of it via document.modelContext.registerTool(). Tools are scoped by route: dashboard tools when you're browsing your worksheets, the full editing toolset once you're inside one, so an agent only sees the actions that are actually relevant to where the teacher is. Challenges we ran into The hardest bug wasn't glamorous: an early version of swap_question wrote its own input instruction into the question text instead of a real generated question. The worksheet would silently fill with prompt text instead of usable content. Fixed with real validation guards: reject output that's empty, malformed, or suspiciously identical to the input, and fail visibly instead of committing broken content. A security review also surfaced two real issues: the local API would accept state-changing requests from any website open in another tab (no origin validation), and the image-source tool would happily fetch and render an arbitrary remote URL. Both are fixed now, with strict origin/content-type checks on every mutation endpoint, and image input restricted to inline data only. Accomplishments that we're proud of The four-check system actually does what it claims. I can point to a real before/after: a generated draft opening at 2 of 4 checks satisfied, one direct edit and one agent command later, 4 of 4. Not a mocked demo state, the same recalculation runs every time, from real logic, on real edits. I'm also proud of catching my own bugs before they became someone else's problem (the swap bug, the security findings) by actually testing the exact flows a judge or user would try, not just trusting that generated code worked. What we learned That "AI-powered" is doing a lot of work to hide whether something actually functions. It was tempting more than once to let a claim stand ("it's fixed," "it's dynamic") without re-testing it myself. The moments this project actually got better were the ones where I stopped and checked instead. I also learned the real difference between a chatbot suggesting worksheet text and an agent calling structured tools on a live page: the former can't reliably track question IDs, ordering, or state across a conversation. WebMCP's whole value is that the page, not the chat history, is the source of truth. What's next for Sheshat Real teacher testing. Everything here has been verified by me, not yet by the people it's actually for. Beyond the hackathon scope: accounts, more subjects and grade bands beyond the current Grade 4 to 7 math focus, and eventually making the core "does this fit my class" checking available without requiring a WebMCP-enabled browser, so any teacher can use it, not just ones testing experimental browser flags.  Agentic Sudoku

 Inspiration 

 I love solving Sudoku puzzles like many of us. Sudoku is one of the world’s purest logic games. 

 But online Sudoku has a physical barrier for some people. Solving a hard puzzle requires numerous micro-clicks. For many people living with essential tremors, RSI (repetitive strain injury), or motor disabilities, the physical tax ruins the mental joy. 

 Purpose of Agentic Sudoku is to enable users to play online Sudoku hands free , assisted by Agent. 

 What it does 

 Human Speaks in Codex App -> Agent uses WebMCP -> Action happens on Sudoku Board. 

 Agentic Sudoku is an online Sudoku puzzle application powered by WebMCP. 

 It enables the human and agent to collaborate while solving Sudoku. 

 Human can play Sudoku hands free with help of Agent. 

 18 WebMCP tools are configured which let user do everything by talking to agent. 

 A Codex Skill is delivered to open the web application in the in-app browser and just solve Sudoku puzzle hands free (by talking to agent). 

 How it was built 

 Agentic Sudoku is a 100% client-side, zero-backend application designed for seamless WebMCP integration. 

 Frontend - Next.js (App Router), React, and Tailwind CSS. 

 WebMCP Architecture - WebMCP tools which can read, annotate, act and control Sudoku. So that human only has to speak to agent without placing hands on keyboard. 

 Puzzle Engine - sudoku-gen for client-side board generation. 

 Codex Skill Integration - A dedicated standard Codex Skill included in the repository, giving OpenAI agents an out-of-the-box playbook for navigating the site, executing coaching sequences, and providing hands-free accessibility. 

 Hosting - Deployed on Vercel. 

 Spec-Driven Development - The project was built using SpecKit. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was designing the WebMCP schema. Had to carefully engineer the tools to ensure they never expose the puzzle’s final hidden solution. The agent must reason dynamically using only the visible board constraints to guide the player. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Successfully decoupled joy of Sudoku from the physical friction of playing it. 
 Shipped robust WebMCP tools. 
 

 Learnings 

 Hands on experience with WebMCP. It turns the browser DOM into a shared, collaborative workspace. 

 What's next for Agentic Sudoku 

 
 Allowing users to scan a Sudoku puzzle from a physical newspaper using their camera, parse it into the web app.

title: Sigma Studio | AI driven Editor
pitch: Teaching materials meant TeX for math, Word for layout, PowerPoint for figures, and unusable AI. Sigma Studio puts it all on one page that's intuitive to edit, and AI edits it with you. Open source.
about_excerpt: Teaching materials meant TeX for math, Word for layout, PowerPoint for figures, and unusable AI. Sigma Studio puts it all on one page that's intuitive to edit, and AI edits it with you. Open source. Like Comment Story Updates math test template amde by this app rich 3d math editor rich 3d math editor Inspiration Making educational materials has long been a fight against fragmented tools. TeX for equations, Word or Notion for layout, PowerPoint for diagrams, and an AI trapped inside a chat window. On top of that, there are vested commercial interests baked into the software used in education. When a teacher makes a single worksheet, they type \( \int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3} \) in TeX, draw a parabola in a different program and paste it in as a screenshot, and every time a single number changes, they have to redo everything from scratch. Generative AI was supposed to help, but all it does is turn into an endless cycle of copy-pasting from a chat UI. Teaching materials are not just text. They are publication-quality "page space" where paragraphs, TeX equations, geometric figures, and two-column problem layouts must line up without a millimeter of drift. Until the day the picture in someone's head can be beamed straight into an AI, there's no way for an AI to nail 100% of what a human is picturing on the first try. That's why we designed Sigma Studio around a simple, honest principle of collaboration: "Let AI handle the tedious 90% of the heavy lifting, and let the human quickly polish the crucial final 10% by hand, guided by intuition." What it does Sigma Studio is an open-source, agent-native document editor where an entire piece of teaching material lives on a single responsive page. Write like Word or Notion : paragraphs, headings, auto-numbered problems, and a two-column layout that reflows in real time as you type. Typeset beautifully at TeX quality : TeX-quality equations rendered via KaTeX, visually editable. We obsessed over baseline alignment, line spacing, and margins to achieve the precise typesetting that educational materials demand. Draw intuitively like PowerPoint (fully parametric) : shapes, guide lines, angle arcs, labels, and 2D/3D graphs sit on an overlay canvas directly above the text. Nothing is ever rasterized into an image — everything remains a vector you can re-edit at any time. Toggle "problems only" / "answers only" from a single source document : instantly switch one document between a "problems only" view/printout for class or exams and an "answers only" view/printout for self-grading and explanation. A "90% + 10%" collaborative workflow with AI : when a teacher says "draw the triangle formed by the intersection points of the parabola and the line in problem 3," the AI solves the equations and coordinates via WebMCP and instantly draws the graph and the three lines (that's the 90%). The teacher just reaches for the mouse and nudges a vertex label "A" that's overlapping something, to make it more legible (that's the 10%) — and it's done. Approval-gated proposals (human-in-the-loop) : the AI never overwrites the document on its own. Its changes are drawn on the canvas as a preview diff (a Draft), which a human can approve or discard with one click. Even after applying, it can be undone in a single step. Pixel-perfect vector PDF export : produces high-quality PDFs that match the editor screen down to the pixel. It is provided completely free of charge as MIT-licensed open source. How we built it Built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The body text uses Tiptap/ProseMirror, equations use MathLive and KaTeX, and diagrams are built on a custom overlay canvas plus Three.js for 3D. Exposing semantic document operations via WebMCP At the core of the architecture is exposing operations on the editor's own document model (SigmaDoc) to AI as first-class tools via WebMCP ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Inside ChatGPT's in-app browser or on Chrome, the AI directly executes structured tools such as: insert_body_content , replace_block , move_blocks insert_shape , update_shape , align_shapes insert_graph , update_graph , insert_graph3d begin_visual_edit_session , inspect_visual_edit_session , propose_visual_edit_session Instead of fragile DOM scraping or guessing at screen coordinates, the AI reads a semantic document tree and injects parametric vector objects directly into the runtime. Challenges we ran into Shape anchors that follow the flow of text : the hardest engineering challenge was making diagrams follow the body text as it wraps and reflows. The instant a teacher hits Enter in the body text, a shape placed with absolute coordinates gets left behind. We built an anchor-binding mechanism that ties each shape to a specific body block ID with a relative offset, so shapes naturally follow along even as text grows, shrinks, or moves across columns. Two-column layouts and dynamic pagination : serious teaching materials require two-column layouts. We built a custom pagination engine from scratch that precisely measures actual rendered DOM heights so that paragraphs, equations, and anchored shapes break cleanly across page boundaries instead of being cut off mid-element. Relentless attention to precise typesetting : to reproduce genuine print-grade typesetting on the web DOM, we tuned equation baselines, Japanese line spacing, problem-number indentation, and line weights down to the millimeter to achieve layout quality comparable to a professionally published textbook. Resolving conflicts between simultaneous human and AI edits : while the AI is busy computing a complex geometric figure, the teacher keeps typing on the keyboard. We validate block IDs and version hashes so that a stale AI proposal for a spot the human has since touched is safely rejected and rebased, preventing accidental overwrites of what was just typed. A PDF pipeline with zero print drift : rather than maintaining a separate print engine, we unified everything around slicing the editor's actual rendered DOM page-by-page via Chromium and stitching the pages together with pdf-lib, achieving a 100% match between what's on screen and what comes out on paper. Accomplishments that we're proud of An intuitive feel for polishing that final 10% : we obsessed over drag handles, snapping, bounding boxes, and block-editor interactions so that refining an AI-generated first draft with the mouse feels as natural and effortless as sketching with a pencil and eraser on paper. Vector persistence (no images) : even when importing TeX or legacy materials, everything lives on as editable vector shapes and coordinate axes rather than static images. Keeping shapes editable in place is essential for teaching materials. A complete, self-contained OSS web app : because everything needed to create teaching materials lives in this one open-source web app, clients can freely modify and use the application with confidence — there is no vendor lock-in to worry about. What we learned Giving AI an "MCP" to manipulate a structured document alongside a human turned out to be a challenge on an entirely different level. Since AI cannot read a human's mind, expecting it to produce something perfect in a single shot is an illusion. We learned that true human-AI collaboration isn't about getting a complex prompt to deliver 100% — it's about providing instant undo, a visual preview, and extremely smooth direct manipulation , so that a human can intuitively carry the AI's 90%-finished foundation the rest of the way to the goal. What's next for Sigma Studio Extending to a learning workspace for students : beyond teachers authoring materials, evolving toward a learning environment where students can converse with AI and visually experiment with geometric proofs or calculus graphs through trial and error. Multi-agent collaborative authoring : building an environment where multiple specialized WebMCP agents — one for equation verification, one for geometric drawing, one for curriculum consistency, and more — can simultaneously propose changes on the same canvas. Google Docs-style real-time collaboration , enabling: students and teachers to learn together in the same document teachers to co-author materials together Built With claude css electron esbuild firebase i18next jszip katex mathlive model-context-protocol next.js node.js openai-codex pdf-lib playwright prosemirror react three.js tiptap typescript vitest webmcp zod zustand Try it out github.com sigma-studio-webmcp-demo.choco954303.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by ATSUSHI KIMURA Like Share this project: Updates ATSUSHI KIMURA started this project — Sep 04, 2026 01:13 AM EDT
