pitch: CommerceOps Bridge is an agent-native workspace helping merchants resolve duplicate payments, draft customer responses via WebMCP tools, and automate exception auditing while keeping total control.
about_excerpt:
CommerceOps Bridge is an agent-native workspace helping merchants resolve duplicate payments, draft customer responses via WebMCP tools, and automate exception auditing while keeping total control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 CommerceOps Bridge 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 CommerceOps Bridge 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 CommerceOps Bridge 
 
 1 2 



 
 CommerceOps Bridge — Project Story 

 What inspired me 

 Commerce work often looks simple from the outside: investigate an exception, understand what happened, contact the customer, and decide what to do next. 

 In practice, that work is fragmented across order systems, payment records, shipping updates, support tools, subscription bills, and internal policies. A merchant or operations specialist has to reconstruct the situation manually before they can make a safe decision. The cost is not only time. Fragmented context also creates uncertainty, duplicated work, and the risk of taking an action without enough evidence. 

 The WebMCP Challenge made me think about a different model: what if a web application did not only present information to people, but also exposed its useful operations directly to an AI agent? 

 That led to CommerceOps Bridge — an agent-native operations workspace where a person and an agent can investigate an issue together. The agent gathers structured context and prepares recommendations. The merchant reviews the evidence, edits communication, and remains responsible for approval. 

 The central idea is simple: 

 
 Agents should reduce the work of finding and organizing context, while people should retain control over consequential decisions. 
 

 What problem we are solving 

 CommerceOps Bridge focuses on the gap between agent assistance and human accountability. 

 The project demonstrates how a merchant can: 

 
 Find an open commerce exception. 
 Retrieve order and payment context through structured tools. 
 Detect a duplicate payment pattern. 
 Compare a proposed resolution with an alternative. 
 Review evidence and policy references. 
 Edit an unsent customer message. 
 Approve preparation without triggering an external refund. 
 Review a decision audit trail. 
 Run an operating-cost audit. 
 Prepare an editable support escalation packet. 
 

 Before this approach, an agent would have to infer application behavior from visible page elements or rely on loosely connected integrations. With WebMCP, the application can explicitly describe the operations an agent is allowed to discover and request. 

 What we learned 

 1. WebMCP is most valuable when the tools represent real user intent 

 It is easy to expose a tool that demonstrates a technical API call. It is more useful to expose operations that map to actual work, such as get_order_context , check_refund_policy , propose_resolution , and prepare_escalation_packet . 

 The tool names, descriptions, input schemas, and returned data should help an agent understand the application without guessing from the layout. 

 2. Structured context is more useful than a collection of page fragments 

 The order context tool returns an order, payments, shipment information, and evidence references together. This gives the agent a coherent record that can be interpreted and traced. 

 The result also taught us an important implementation detail: a browser may return the tool result as a serialized JSON string. The consumer must parse it once before displaying tables or using nested fields. Double-stringifying the result produces the escaped output that is difficult for people to read. 

 3. Human control needs to be visible in the product 

 A safety statement hidden in documentation is not enough. The interface therefore makes the boundary visible: 

 
 Customer messages are labeled UNSENT and remain editable. 
 The workflow says Approve preparation , rather than claiming that a refund was completed. 
 The audit trail records the merchant action. 
 The external-action status explicitly shows no . 
 The demo does not call a live refund, message, Shopify, or payment-provider API. 
 

 This makes the distinction between assistance, preparation, approval, and execution clear to both the user and the judge. 

 4. A good agent-native experience still needs to work for people 

 WebMCP is not a replacement for a coherent user interface. The dashboard, queue, evidence panels, recommendation cards, and audit trail give a person a clear way to understand and verify what the agent did. 

 The strongest experience is shared: structured tools for agents and readable explanations for people. 

 How we built the project 

 We followed a lightweight spec-driven development process. Each feature moved through a short cycle: 

 
 Define the user outcome and acceptance criteria. 
 Describe the interaction and safety boundaries. 
 Implement the domain logic and UI. 
 Expose the relevant operation as a WebMCP tool where appropriate. 
 Test the deterministic behavior. 
 Verify the result in the deployed application. 
 

 Product structure 

 CommerceOps Bridge is a Vite-powered front-end application. It uses deterministic seeded commerce data so the public demo is repeatable and does not depend on paid accounts or live merchant systems. 

 The application is organized around three layers: 

 
 Seeded data: orders, payments, shipments, support cases, evidence, applications, and fees. 
 Domain functions: investigation, payment timeline, policy checks, recommendations, message drafting, cost audit, and escalation preparation. 
 Presentation and tools: the dashboard UI plus WebMCP registrations that expose selected domain operations to agents. 
 

 WebMCP implementation 

 The application registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 The current tool set includes: 

 
 list_open_exceptions 
 get_order_context 
 get_payment_timeline 
 check_refund_policy 
 propose_resolution 
 draft_customer_message 
 get_cost_audit 
 prepare_escalation_packet 
 

 Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution function. The execution functions call deterministic domain logic and return structured results. 

 The most important demo path is: 

 
 Discover tools with document.modelContext.getTools() . 
 Select get_order_context . 
 Execute it for ORD-1042 . 
 Review the returned customer, order, payment, and evidence data. 
 Continue the same investigation through the application interface. 
 

 This demonstrates that WebMCP is not only mentioned in the project; it is used to discover and execute an operation exposed by the live page. 

 Challenges we faced 

 WebMCP availability differs by browser 

 WebMCP support is still emerging. Chrome requires the WebMCP testing flag, while other browser environments may expose different support levels. We handled this by keeping the application useful in preview mode while making the tool definitions and traces visible in the product. 

 For the final demo, we use a WebMCP-enabled Chrome session and show both discovery and direct execution in DevTools. 

 Tool results may arrive as escaped JSON 

 The direct Console result appeared as one escaped string rather than a readable object. The fix was to detect whether the returned value is a string and call JSON.parse() exactly once. We then use console.table() for the order and payment records so the result is easy to understand during the recording. 

 Deployment initially published the wrong asset state 

 The first Cloudflare Pages deployment skipped the build step because no build command was configured. The deployment technically succeeded, but the page did not load the application correctly. 

 We corrected the Cloudflare configuration to use: 

 
 Build command: npm run build 
 Build output directory: dist 
 Root directory: blank, because the Vite project is at the repository root 
 

 After that change, the live application deployed successfully at: 

 https://commerceops-bridge.pages.dev/ 

 We did not have a Shopify store or live commerce credentials 

 Rather than make unsupported claims or require paid setup, we deliberately used deterministic seeded data. This keeps the demo reproducible and lets us focus on the WebMCP interaction model. 

 The application clearly states that it does not connect to Shopify, live payment providers, or external refund APIs. This is a limitation of the prototype, but it is also an intentional safety boundary for the hackathon demonstration. 

 Demonstrating the technology without overwhelming the story

Visual multi-cloud architecture CPQ & FinOps co-pilot with real-time egress modeling, GDPR audits, and WebMCP agentic control.

 Inspiration 

 Modern cloud architectures rarely live in a single region or provider. Today's engineering teams blend AWS compute, GCP AI accelerators, Azure enterprise systems, and Cloudflare edge networks. However, designing and estimating multi-cloud systems is frustratingly broken: 

 
 Static Diagrams vs. Dynamic Bills: Traditional diagramming tools (Draw.io, Lucidchart) produce static pictures. They cannot calculate your monthly bill, warn you about non-linear cross-region egress tariffs, or alert you when a customer database violates European GDPR data residency laws. 
 Opaque Egress Pricing: Data transfer fees between cloud datacenters and internet users range from $0.00 (Cloudflare Bandwidth Alliance) to $0.09+/GB (AWS public egress). Estimating this by hand with spreadsheets is prone to massive calculation errors. 
 AI Coding Agents Lacked a Visual Canvas: While modern AI agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) can write infrastructure code, they lacked a standardized, bi-directional protocol to "see" a visual architecture canvas, test configuration changes, and verify FinOps mathematics in real time. 
 

 We built CloudTopology CPQ to solve this: an open-standard, visual multi-cloud CPQ (Configure, Price, Quote) workspace that both human engineers and AI coding agents can interact with simultaneously via WebMCP ( window.modelContext / document.modelContext ). 

 

 What it does 

 CloudTopology CPQ turns architecture diagrams into a live, FinOps-driven simulation canvas: 

 
 🤖 Autonomous WebMCP 8-Tool Suite: Exposes 8 typed tools directly on window.modelContext and document.modelContext . External AI agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Antigravity) can query 50+ enterprise SKUs, programmatically generate or alter topologies, optimize commitment plans, and simulate network traffic in real time. 
 💰 Real-Time Multi-Cloud FinOps Engine: Instantly calculates costs across On-Demand, 1-Year Savings Plans (~35% off), 3-Year Savings Plans (~55% off), and Spot Fleets (~65% off), with support for uploading custom negotiated Enterprise Discount Agreements (EDA). 
 ⚡ Piecewise Cross-Region Egress Simulation: Accurately models non-linear, tiered bandwidth tariffs. 
 🌍 Geodesic Speed-of-Light Latency Modeling: Uses the Haversine great-circle distance formula between global datacenters to calculate physical optical fiber propagation time 
 🇪🇺 Built-In GDPR & Compliance Auditing: Automatically scans the active topology to flag databases storing EU PII outside sovereign European regions and detects unencrypted cross-cloud transit, offering 1-click remediation. 
 📋 Enterprise CPQ Quotes & Terraform IaC Export: Generates formal itemized CPQ procurement proposals (with ACV and 3-Year TCV breakdowns) and produces deployable Terraform HCL 2.0 configuration files. 
 💾 Project Persistence & Themes: Features auto-saving to localStorage , a "My Saved Setups" project library, 1-click .json export and import, and seamless toggling between high-contrast Light Theme (default) and Obsidian Dark Theme. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 Interactive Frontend: Built with React 18, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and @xyflow/react (React Flow) for 60fps hardware-accelerated SVG/canvas rendering. 
 WebMCP Architecture ( src/tools/modelContextBridge.ts ): Implemented an open WebMCP bridge that registers typed tool schemas on both window.modelContext and document.modelContext . We built a Universal JSON Normalizer that can parse flat AI responses, nested coordinate trees, or partial parameter maps from external LLMs. 
 FinOps Calculation Core ( src/engine/finopsEngine.ts ): Created a deterministic pricing engine that enforces stateful vs. stateless pricing tiers, calculates piecewise egress curves, parses custom enterprise rate cards ( rateCardParser.ts ), and synthesizes Terraform HCL ( terraformGenerator.ts ). 
 Automated Verification: automated unit tests using Vitest covering WebMCP tool schemas, rate-card discount logic, egress calculations, and GDPR validation rules. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Real-World ChatGPT In-App WebMCP Payload Mismatches: When we tested the live app with ChatGPT Desktop asking it to create a multi-tenant SaaS architecture, ChatGPT called apply_topology_to_canvas with a flat list of node names and connections without X/Y pixel coordinates or pricing IDs. To make the app truly agent-friendly, we wrote a Universal AI Normalizer that auto-arranges node layout coordinates on a clean grid, maps plain-text provider names to real catalog SKUs, and infers default configurations automatically. 
 Google choreme webmcp not worked on Ubuntu I have first tried webmcp trial on google chrome, on my ubuntu laptop, but it was not worked. Hence decided to use chatgpt in app browser. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 True Agent-Human Collaboration: external AI agents (like ChatGPT) can actually connect to the running browser app via WebMCP, inspect the catalog, add nodes, optimize commitment plans, and update the visual canvas in real time. 
 Real 50+ Multi-Cloud SKU Catalog: Includes real-world enterprise hardware like NVIDIA H100 80GB ( p5.48xlarge , GCP A3, Azure ND96isr), AWS Graviton3, Aurora Serverless v2, Cloud Spanner, and Cloudflare Workers. 
 Production-Grade Outputs: The app does not just draw boxes; it generates genuine procurement-ready CPQ quote proposals and copy-pasteable Terraform HCL 2.0 infrastructure code. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP is the Future of Web Apps for AI: Exposing typed semantic JSON tool contracts via WebMCP is vastly superior to having AI agents take screenshots or attempt brittle pixel-based mouse clicks. It gives LLMs deterministic control over web applications with zero hallucinations. 
 

 

 What's next for CloudTopology CPQ 

 
 Live Cloud Billing Ingestion: Connecting live AWS Cost Explorer, GCP Billing, and Azure Cost Management APIs to compare pre-deployment CPQ estimates against actual telemetry. 
 CDK & Pulumi Synthesizers: Expanding IaC generation beyond Terraform to include AWS CDK (TypeScript/Python) and Pulumi stacks.

title: CivicFlow: A WebMCP Public Benefit Portal
pitch: CivicFlow helps people complete complex public-benefit applications with a voice companion, while WebMCP lets browser agents assist safely through structured tools.
about_excerpt: CivicFlow helps people complete complex public-benefit applications with a voice companion, while WebMCP lets browser agents assist safely through structured tools. Like Comment Story Updates The first page of the CivicFlow Human Submitted Form Human Submitted Form Agent Companion Widget CivicFlow WebMCP Tool Registry Conversing with the Agent for a task Draft prepared by the Agent for Human Review Reviewable Agent Activity Inspiration I work at Optum as a software engineer, developing and maintaining the State of Massachusetts Health Care Exchange Portal. I know that system through and through, so I also know this: applying from start to finish takes hours of concentration and focus. That is true for individuals, assisters, and human agents alike. That is why it immediately clicked for me: this is a massive opportunity to upgrade US healthcare benefits sites, so faster eligibility submissions can lead to faster benefits for every citizen. I am going to showcase this demo I made for the hackathon to my project leadership as well. What it does CivicFlow is a demo public-benefits portal. A person can fill out six sections: About You, Household, Income, Current Coverage, Documents, and Review & Sign. A browser agent can work on that same form through WebMCP, instead of guessing from the page layout. The agent can check what is left, jump to a section, add a household member or income source, set current coverage, look at demo document status, and review what is blocking submit. There is also an optional Gemini Live companion for voice or chat. If the companion wants to change something, it has to wait for the person to click Save change, Need correction, or Cancel. Talking is not enough. This is a fictional local demo. Submit Demo is human-only, stays on the device, and does not call a real government system. There is no real eligibility, enrollment, document upload, or agent submit. How we built it I built CivicFlow with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The form, the WebMCP tools, and the Gemini companion all go through the same app state. That way the agent cannot take a side path the person cannot see. There are ten typed tools. Seven are always there. The other three only show up when they make sense, like when a household member is selected or the person is on Review & Sign. The page registers those tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , and it updates the list when the current section or selection changes. Gemini only sees the tools that are available right now. It still has to pass schema checks, and any write waits for a button click. The Gemini API key stays on the server. If WebMCP or voice is not available, the normal form still works. I used Vitest and Playwright to cover the main flow and the safety rules. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not adding more tools. It was making sure help never turned into silent control. The form, the browser agent, and the voice companion had to share one state, with no hidden shortcut around validation or human review. Contextual tools were also tricky. They have to show up and disappear as the person moves around the form. And a successful tool call means nothing if the person cannot see what changed, so I added the floating companion, a speaking cue, the current tool list, operation status, and an activity history. Keeping the Gemini key on the server, while still letting the demo work without voice, was another one. Accomplishments that we're proud of What I am most proud of is getting a realtime voice agent to talk to the site tools. You can ask for help out loud, and it can guide you through the form without typing. That is the part that feels closest to how I wish benefits sites worked. I also think this can help people with vision or other disabilities, because they would not have to hunt through a long form just to make progress. The other piece I really liked building is the draft popup during realtime voice. The companion can propose a change, but it does not silently write it. A confirmation card shows up first, and you still choose Save change, Need correction, or Cancel. That small pause is what kept voice helpful instead of scary. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when it is part of the product, not a shortcut around the UI. Clear tool names, schemas, and contextual tools tell the agent what it can do. Visible confirmation and activity history help the person trust it, and step in if something looks wrong. I also learned that the page still has to be a good form on its own. If WebMCP or voice is down, a person should still be able to finish the demo by hand. What's next for CivicFlow: A WebMCP Public Benefit Portal Next, I want to put this in front of people who actually fill out long benefits forms, and keep improving accessibility and the “did that change what I think it changed?” feedback. I also want to take the demo to Optum leadership and talk about whether this pattern could help real healthcare benefits sites. Connecting to real program rules, identity, uploads, eligibility, or live submit is a much bigger security and policy project. That is not part of this hackathon demo. title: LogoPacker Canvas - Assisted Canvas with Local Workspace
pitch: A local-first design canvas where agents handle the repetitive work, so designers can focus on what they love.
about_excerpt: A local-first design canvas where agents handle the repetitive work, so designers can focus on what they love. Like Comment Story Updates Agents have direct access to your local assets Dashboard with observable agent actions Agent saves progress locally Generating SVG Creating brand guideline in simple prompt LogoPacker Canvas LogoPacker Canvas gives agents the ability to work directly on a local design canvas —creating variations, organizing assets, adjusting layouts, and preparing design handoffs based on the designer’s direction. Changes are saved instantly to the local workspace. Why your use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Direct access to the local workspace Using the Filesystem API, agents can work with local assets without sending them to a server. They can also autosave projects locally, allowing changes to persist entirely within the user’s workspace. Designing is a click-heavy task Vector and logo design often requires a long sequence of clicks to switch between tools and complete even simple variations. For example, creating one variation may require: duplicate → select → recolor → resize → reposition . With WebMCP, agents can discover and invoke these tools directly without navigating or DOM-scrolling. The canvas’s live state—such as what is selected and currently visible—is also available to the agent at call time. This enables low-latency, stateful editing entirely in the frontend with an LLM of choice, without relying on heavy APIs, WebSockets, or server-side live editing. How it creates a better user experience Smoother workflow Because designing involves many repetitive, click-heavy actions, WebMCP allows monotonous tasks to be executed directly by the agent instead of requiring constant on-screen interaction. Designers can focus on the parts where creativity and judgment matter while delegating the mundane work to agents. Use local fonts directly Designers often have their own fonts available locally. With access to local fonts, agents can help designers explore and select suitable typography for their brand without requiring the fonts to be uploaded to a server. Fewer privacy concerns Users do not need to upload their design files or assets to a server. Their assets, projects, and exported files can remain confined to their local workspace. Describe what people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Before WebMCP, agents typically needed to take over mouse and keyboard control, hijacking the designer’s screen. WebMCP enables shared, low-latency, stateful human-agent collaboration without screen hijacking. Agents can directly access browser capabilities. For example, LogoPacker uses the Local Font Access API to let agents read the fonts available on the designer’s machine. Combining WebMCP with direct browser APIs enables more continuous collaboration. For example, a designer can prompt the agent to “continue editing when I place an image near position X” instead of manually prompting the agent after every interaction. Briefly explain how you implemented WebMCP Agents have access to a full tool surface covering canvas inspection, selection, artboard management, object mutation (fills, properties, path data, draw_svg ), reversible request bracketing, typography, and imagery. This allows agents to read the live canvas state at call time and perform tasks based on the designer’s instructions. Agent actions are visible in a toggleable sidebar, providing clear observability into what the agent is doing. Browser APIs such as the Local Font Access API and Filesystem API are also exposed directly to the agent through registerTool . Initial idea was to use Filesystem API with directory access, however, it's only available available on Google Chrome. Inspiration LogoPacker Canvas is a new product inspired by my old project Logo Packer which was created before emergent of modern AI. title: Mission Center WebMCP — Human in Command
pitch: A browser-native mission control where agents inspect tasks, verify evidence, and propose actions while humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A browser-native mission control where agents inspect tasks, verify evidence, and propose actions while humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates What I built Mission Center WebMCP is a browser-native mission control where agents can inspect tasks, trace dependencies, verify evidence, and propose safe next moves while humans remain the only authority who can approve lifecycle changes. Why WebMCP matters Mission Center already treats task state, evidence, handoffs, and verification as explicit, reviewable concepts. WebMCP makes those semantics available directly to browser agents instead of forcing them to infer meaning from pixels or DOM structure. The tools share the same live in-page state, evidence model, proposal queue, human approval UI, and audit trail as the person viewing the mission control. Human and agent collaboration The judge journey asks an agent to find the task in Review, inspect whether its evidence is current, and propose the safest next lifecycle move. The agent discovers WMC-103, checks its passing evidence, and proposes Review → Done. The task remains in Review and a pending proposal appears. A human then reviews the proposal and clicks Revalidate & approve. Mission Center rechecks the task revision and completion evidence before moving the task to Done. The agent has no approval tool and cannot silently change lifecycle truth. Agent calls, proposals, and human decisions remain separate and auditable. How it was implemented The app is a static HTML/CSS/ES module site with zero backend and zero API keys. It registers eight imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool, keeps validated state in browser storage, exposes proposal-only agent mutations, and enforces a human evidence/revision gate. The repository includes deterministic Node tests, verification scripts, and a GitHub Pages deployment workflow. Prior work disclosure This competition edition is derived from the existing MIT-licensed Codex Mission Center project. The frozen upstream baseline is documented in UPSTREAM_BASELINE.md. Browser WebMCP support, agent tools, proposal workflow, judge UX, and the static deployment are the challenge work.  Inspiration 

 Fraud is becoming more sophisticated as digital payments and online commerce continue to grow across Africa. 

 We noticed that many fraud systems focus heavily on the transaction itself: the amount, device, location, IP address, transaction history, and velocity. But a legitimate-looking transaction can still be fraudulent when a user has been manipulated through social engineering. 

 A person may receive a message from someone impersonating a bank, business, friend, or payment provider and voluntarily initiate what appears to be a completely normal transaction. 

 That led us to a simple question: 

 What if fraud detection could understand the context around a transaction, not just the transaction itself? 

 That question inspired Ayib FraudGuard by Markfisher Consulting, an AI-powered fraud intelligence and social-engineering protection platform designed to help identify suspicious activity before it becomes a financial loss. 

 Our vision is simple: Ayib provides the payment infrastructure, while Ayib FraudGuard provides the security intelligence protecting it. 

 What it does 

 Ayib FraudGuard analyzes transaction and contextual signals to identify suspicious behavior and generate a risk assessment.

API-based fraud intelligence

Developer-friendly integration 

 Instead of simply asking whether a transaction looks unusual, FraudGuard aims to help answer: 

 "Does the overall context suggest that this transaction may be fraudulent?" 

 The resulting intelligence can be incorporated into an application's workflow to support decisions such as allowing, challenging, reviewing, or blocking a transaction. 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we are also exploring how fraud intelligence can become more accessible to web applications and AI-powered developer experiences through machine-consumable interfaces and workflows. 

 How we built it 

 We built Ayib FraudGuard as a cloud-native, API-first security platform. 

 The architecture combines a transaction-processing layer with AI-assisted risk analysis and security controls. 

 At a high level, the system:

Processes and normalizes the available data.
Evaluates behavioral and transactional patterns.
Uses AI-assisted analysis to identify anomalies and potential social-engineering indicators.
Produces a risk assessment.
Makes that intelligence available to the consuming application through an API. 

 We designed the platform to be modular so that additional fraud signals, detection models, security services, and developer interfaces can be added without rebuilding the entire system. 

 Our broader stack and experience includes TypeScript/Node.js, APIs, cloud infrastructure, AI/LLMs, CI/CD, observability, and security engineering. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Ayib FraudGuard was not born from a hypothetical problem. It was born from our experience building and launching Ayib. 

 When we first launched Ayib, we experienced multiple security breaches and incidents that exposed weaknesses in how we were protecting our payment infrastructure. These experiences made it clear that traditional security controls alone were not enough. We needed a security layer that could continuously analyze activity, identify unusual behavior, and help us detect potential threats before they became financial losses. 

 That experience became one of the key inspirations behind Ayib FraudGuard. 

 As we began building FraudGuard, one of our biggest challenges was determining how to combine AI-driven flexibility with the predictability and reliability required by financial systems. 

 AI can identify patterns that traditional rules may miss, but we could not simply allow an AI model to make financial security decisions without appropriate controls and safeguards. We therefore designed FraudGuard so that AI works as part of a broader security architecture rather than acting as the sole decision-maker. 

 We also had to solve several practical challenges: 

 Detecting suspicious activity with low latency.
Balancing false positives and false negatives.
Maintaining consistent AI model behavior.
Ensuring API reliability and availability.
Establishing appropriate security boundaries.
Designing for future scalability.
Providing sufficient observability into security decisions.
Making risk assessments understandable and actionable.
Integrating fraud intelligence into existing payment workflows. 

 Another major challenge was shifting our thinking from simply responding to security incidents to building infrastructure capable of anticipating and preventing them. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Our biggest accomplishment is turning lessons from Ayib's early security incidents into a working AI-powered fraud intelligence platform. 

 Instead of treating our security challenges as isolated incidents, we used them as an opportunity to build a reusable security layer that can potentially protect not only Ayib, but other fintechs, payment platforms, and digital businesses. 

 We are particularly proud of:

Building an AI-assisted fraud detection pipeline.
Designing FraudGuard as an API-first platform.
Combining transaction data with behavioral and contextual risk signals.
Building an architecture that can evolve as fraud techniques change.
Exploring how AI and emerging web technologies can make security intelligence more accessible to developers.
Creating a foundation that can integrate with existing financial infrastructure. 

 Most importantly, we are proud that FraudGuard represents a shift from reactive security to proactive fraud prevention. 

 Our experience with Ayib taught us that discovering a security problem after it happens can be extremely costly. FraudGuard is designed around the idea that suspicious activity should be identified as early as possible. 

 What we learned 

 Building Ayib and subsequently Ayib FraudGuard taught us that security cannot be an afterthought, especially when building financial infrastructure. 

 We initially approached security largely from the perspective of protecting the application and infrastructure. Our experiences after launching Ayib showed us that financial security requires a much broader approach that considers transactions, users, behavior, context, infrastructure, and continuously evolving attack patterns. 

 We learned that fraud detection is not simply a machine-learning problem. 

 It requires a combination of security engineering, data, infrastructure, AI, user experience, and developer experience. 

 We also learned that accuracy alone is not enough. A fraud system needs to be fast enough for real-time transactions, reliable enough for production environments, and understandable enough for both humans and applications to act on its recommendations. 

 Most importantly, we learned that context matters. 

 A transaction can look completely legitimate when viewed on its own, but become highly suspicious when combined with behavioral, transactional, or contextual signals. 

 That lesson from building and securing Ayib continues to shape the architecture of FraudGuard today.

title: ExactCue
pitch: Browser agents can prepare pharmacy refills, but prescription records can change before a person confirms. ExactCue uses WebMCP to block stale orders.
about_excerpt: Browser agents can prepare pharmacy refills, but prescription records can change before a person confirms. ExactCue uses WebMCP to block stale orders. Like Comment Story Updates The pharmacy record moved from v1 to v2, so ExactCue blocked the outdated refill. HTTP 409. No write. WebMCP exposes only the tools valid now while Marcus and his browser agent share one live refill order. Marcus reviews one exact cue: prescriptions, pickup, record version, and fingerprint - before anything can be submitted. A current action earns an authoritative receipt; stale authority retires instead of retrying silently. WebMCP carries one reviewed cue to Netlify; an atomic ETag check returns a receipt or blocks the stale write. Inspiration Marcus wants his browser agent to handle the repetitive work of refilling prescriptions. But Marcus - not the agent - should own the final decision. That creates a deceptively hard problem: what happens if Marcus reviews an order, but the pharmacy record changes before he confirms it? A confident click or agent response could submit an order he never actually reviewed. ExactCue asks a simple question: Can a website promise that the action it commits is still the action the person reviewed? We use a synthetic pharmacy refill because the failure is instantly understandable, while the underlying pattern applies to any consequential browser action. What it does ExactCue gives a person and their browser agent shared custody of one action: The agent prepares. Through WebMCP, it selects two eligible prescriptions and a pickup pharmacy using the tools the page currently allows. Marcus reviews. ExactCue creates one visible, spoken, and machine-readable summary of the exact order, including its current version. The server checks. When Marcus confirms, the server commits only if the pharmacy record is still the version he reviewed. ExactCue proves the result. A successful action earns an authoritative receipt. If the record changed, the outdated refill is blocked, nothing is submitted, and Marcus is guided to the current record. The demo’s signature moment is a real failure test: another request reaches the server first, the record moves from v1 to v2, and Marcus’s original action receives HTTP 409 · NO WRITE . The pharmacy is synthetic. The reusable product idea is current-state-bound actions for browser agents . Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, a browser agent must infer controls from pixels or an accessibility tree. It can click the right-looking button, but the page has not given it a typed contract for the action, the current workflow state, or recovery. ExactCue makes WebMCP load-bearing: The page exposes only the tools valid for the current step. Prescription tools retire when the flow moves to pickup; pickup tools retire at review. The agent and the visible interface operate on the same live order. review_order returns the exact cue as structured data, not just screen text. submit_refill carries the reviewed version and ETag to the server. reload_current_record gives the agent a structured recovery path after a conflict. Remove WebMCP and the agent loses the page-declared workflow contract. Remove the server check and ExactCue loses its central promise. The product needs both. A better user experience For someone who relies on spoken or structured confirmation, “the agent clicked it” is not enough. They need to know exactly what will happen - and that the action did not silently change after the readback. ExactCue reduces a multi-step form to one meaningful human decision. The agent handles preparation. Marcus receives one exact cue. The result is either a current receipt or a plain-language explanation that nothing happened. The product also includes: keyboard and screen-reader semantics; on-demand speech for the exact order; reduced-motion and narrow-screen layouts; visible current tool authority; clear ineligible-prescription explanations; explicit stale-record recovery; and a complete manual path when WebMCP is unavailable. ExactCue does not claim to prove spoken assent. It proves that the reviewed payload was bound to a particular record version and checked again at commit time. How we built it The system follows one inspectable path: Person + UI ↔ shared order state ↔ WebMCP tools → Netlify Function → Blob conditional write → receipt or recovery Browser: React and TypeScript power the visible flow and the shared order state. WebMCP: document.modelContext.registerTool publishes typed actions. An AbortController retires tools when their step ends. Exact Cue: one snapshot binds the prescription IDs, pharmacy, spoken readback, record version, and ETag fingerprint. Server: a Netlify Function rebuilds and validates the order against authoritative data. Storage: Netlify Blobs uses strong reads and onlyIfMatch conditional writes. A losing request cannot overwrite the current record. Proof: every result includes a structured next action; successful writes return a receipt, while conflicts return the current record with noWrite: true . Synthetic run IDs isolate judge sessions without acting as credentials. Operational logs deliberately exclude session IDs, ETags, request bodies, and patient/order fields. Architecture PERSON + BROWSER AGENT │ │ prepares prescriptions + pickup ▼ REACT UI ↔ SHARED ORDER STATE ↔ STEP-SCOPED WEBMCP TOOLS │ select · review · submit · recover │ ▼ EXACT CUE prescription IDs + pharmacy + spoken readback + record v1 + ETag │ │ submit_refill(confirmed: true) ▼ ══════════════ AUTHORITATIVE COMMIT BOUNDARY ══════════════ ▼ NETLIFY FUNCTION rebuild current order → validate reviewed payload → compare ETag │ ▼ NETLIFY BLOBS · onlyIfMatch(ETag) ├── CURRENT ──→ atomic write ──→ authoritative receipt └── STALE ──→ HTTP 409 · NO WRITE ──→ reload_current_record The architecture is deliberately split at the commit boundary. The browser agent prepares shared state and WebMCP carries the exact reviewed cue. A Netlify Function then rebuilds the authoritative order and uses a Netlify Blobs ETag compare-and-swap. The only valid outcomes are a current receipt or HTTP 409 · NO WRITE with a structured recovery tool. Challenges we ran into Retiring tools safely. A WebMCP tool can advance the state while its own invocation is still resolving. Aborting its controller immediately can discard the result, so ExactCue retires the previous tool surface on the next task after Chrome delivers the response. Proving a real conflict. Client-side validation could only imitate safety. We separated the domain state machine from storage, tested stale and replay paths locally, then captured two real conditional requests against the public Netlify deployment. Drawing an honest boundary. ExactCue cannot infer whether a person truly intended a spoken “yes.” It can prove the narrower - and useful - guarantee that the payload presented for review is the payload checked against current server state. Accomplishments that we’re proud of A complete prepare → review → verify → recover → receipt product journey. Native WebMCP execution drives the same state shown in the human interface. Tool authority changes with the workflow; navigation cannot bypass the committing action. What we learned A useful agent experience needs more than callable functions. The page should expose authority that changes with state, return structured recovery instructions, and show the same boundary to the person. We also learned to separate three moments that are often blurred together: a person reviews an action; the page binds that review to one precise proposal; and the server decides whether that proposal is still current. WebMCP connects the human and agent sides of that contract inside the user’s browser. Conditional server state makes the contract trustworthy under failure. What’s next for ExactCue We would co-design the cue and recovery language with people who use nonvisual interfaces, test additional WebMCP clients, and formalize confirmation provenance as the API evolves. Then we would package the current-state cue pattern for other consequential workflows - benefits, banking, travel changes, and government services - where an agent can prepare complexity but a person should own the final, current decision. title: ClauseProof
pitch: A source-grounded contract decision room where people and agents can analyze and propose together without collapsing human approval into AI output.
about_excerpt: A source-grounded contract decision room where people and agents can analyze and propose together without collapsing human approval into AI output. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for ClauseProof Inspiration Contracts rarely fail because nobody summarized them. They fail because risk, authority, and action get blurred together. ClauseProof explores an open web where a person and an AI agent can inspect the same contract state without allowing fluent model output to masquerade as human approval. What it does ClauseProof turns a high-stakes agreement into a source-grounded decision room. Documents are read locally, including OCR for image documents. Deterministic rules keep the exact governing clause beside each finding. A human can resolve or explicitly accept risks, record a case-specific approval, and prepare an unsigned signature-packet receipt. The synthetic Northstar supply agreement demonstrates auto-renewal, exclusivity, payment, cure, and liability findings. Uploaded bytes and extracted text stay in the browser. Why WebMCP The live page exposes six narrow tools over the same state the human sees: get_case_summary list_open_risks propose_risk_resolution record_human_risk_decision approve_case_decision prepare_signature_packet Each tool is registered with document.modelContext.registerTool , uses a closed input schema, describes its effects, and returns a structured receipt. An agent proposal remains a proposal. Approval requires a visible human decision, and signature preparation always reports sent: false and signed: false . How we built it React and TypeScript power the shared browser workflow. PDF.js and Tesseract.js handle local text and OCR. Xano provides the durable synthetic case, audit events, evidence receipts, idempotent bootstrap, and five deployed endpoints. SerpApi runs one bounded server-side counterparty query through Xano; the live proof returned nine organic results and evidence receipt 1 without exposing the key to the browser. Vitest covers the authority boundaries and deterministic extraction. Netlify serves the public HTTPS build. Challenges The hardest problem was making agent actions useful without collapsing capability into authority. We separated analysis, proposal, human risk decisions, case approval, signature preparation, sending, and signing into independently verifiable states. Accomplishments One shared human-and-agent workflow instead of an agent-only chatbot Exact-source findings with local OCR Six working WebMCP tools over real product state Explicit approval and non-action receipts Live Xano and SerpApi integration Public MIT source and reproducible deployment artifacts What we learned WebMCP is strongest when it exposes a product's real workflow, keeps effects narrow, and makes meaningful transitions independently reviewable. The best agent experience is not maximum autonomy; it is useful capability with trustworthy authority boundaries. What's next Add authenticated private rooms, versioned redlines, provider-backed PDF generation, and a human-controlled e-sign handoff. Those providers will not be claimed until their live calls and terminal receipts are proven.  What it does

title: UNIV Deploy
pitch: A browser agent compiles one WASI deployment intent into verified target capsules, executes browser and edge, and returns a bounded portability witness.
about_excerpt: A browser agent compiles one WASI deployment intent into verified target capsules, executes browser and edge, and returns a bounded portability witness. Like Comment Story Updates Most “deploy anywhere” products ask you to trust the promise. UNIV Deploy lets a browser agent challenge the promise before it deploys anything. It is for platform, release, and security teams that want agents to move reviewed software across runtimes without handing those agents a shell, upload endpoint, or arbitrary code execution. The agent discovers five typed WebMCP tools and works through a visible, stateful deployment contract. First, UNIV compiles one closed deployment intent against machine-readable target passports. The result is a finite portability frontier, a compatibility certificate for each target, and a distinct execution capsule for every compatible target. A separate deterministic verifier rechecks each certificate and capsule. Only verified, digest-bound capsules can enter the five-minute handoff. The demo starts adversarially. The agent asks UNIV to compile network-bound-release-v1. Both registered targets forbid guest networking, so the compiler returns an empty frontier, emits no capsules, names guest-network as the counterexample, and makes handoff impossible. The agent then chooses portable-release-v1. That intent compiles into two verified capsules and executes on two deliberately different real targets: browser-wasi in the browser main thread and sites-edge-wasi on the OpenAI Sites / Cloudflare Workers edge. UNIV still does not call the workload portable merely because both capsules exist. It waits for both executions, compares the declared observation contract, and returns a runtime portability witness only when both target receipts report the same manifest, component, status, workload ID, and output digest. WebMCP is essential because this is a consequential multi-step operation with opaque proof artifacts. Without WebMCP, an agent would scrape controls and manually shuttle IDs and digests between screens. Here, it can discover the closed contract, compile an intent, carry the exact handoff ID and digest into deployment, and retrieve evidence by ID. The person watching sees the same compiler result, capsules, receipts, refusal, and activity. The timeline says via WebMCP only when a registered page tool actually ran; human controls remain via human. The public interface accepts no uploaded components, arbitrary bytes, paths, URLs, shell commands, native executables, container images, host settings, or free-form guest arguments. The manifest, source component, and generated core modules are SHA-256 pinned. Browser module hashes are observed before compilation. The edge receives statically imported modules pinned by manifest and CI; because Workers do not expose those module bytes for runtime re-hashing, the receipt labels that fact build-pinned rather than observed. In the verified public run on September 3, a ChatGPT in-app browser agent first produced the empty-frontier counterexample, then compiled and deployed the permitted intent, retrieved evidence 7cc5409e-d9d1-4cb4-b3a4-2bbbec6b15e4, and received univ.deployment-receipt/v2 with source: WebMCP. Both actual targets terminated and returned output SHA-256 a928646501fcc69ed8af413859d43d4b887f3be150c452696700e393d8e338f5. The runtime witness reported equivalence over the declared observations. UNIV existed before the challenge as a broader Rust portability project. During the submission period I created this clean WebMCP product surface and, for v2, turned the theoretical proof-carrying deployment idea into a running compiler, independent verifier, target passports, execution capsules, bounded witness, public CI gate, production deployment, and reproducible evidence. The inherited daemon, worker, native, OCI, upload, shell, QEMU, and unrelated role-adaptive-agent files are not included or exposed. UNIV Deploy does not claim universal execution over arbitrary software or hosts. Its claim is deliberately falsifiable: one closed intent is portable across the registered passports only when every compile-time proof passes and every executed target agrees over the named runtime observations. It is not independent attestation or a production cloud orchestrator. It is a working demonstration of agents and people replacing a vague portability promise with a proof-carrying deployment and a reviewable receipt. video_title: UNIV Deploy — Challenge a Portability Claim, Then Prove It
video_transcript_excerpt: One browser agent just turned a reviewed release into two actual wasi executions, matching output, and a durable proof link without receiving a shell, upload path, or arbitrary code. Before trusting that result, ask the agent to break it. The network bound release needs authority neither host grants, so Unif returns an empty frontier, emits no capsule, and names guest network as the counter example. For the permitted release, five typed web and CP tools let the agent compile one manifest into separate browser and edge capsules. A deterministic verifier recomputes their clauses and digests before either enters the five-minute handoff. The browser hashes its included modules before compilation. The site's edge runs statically imported modules pinned by the manifest and public CI. Only after both terminate does Unif compare the release's declared observations and report two out of two match. The decisive upgrade is that evidence now survives the browser session. Before Cloudflare D1 stores anything, the edge rechecks receipt integrity, release and capsule bindings, bounded observations, output equality, and the attestation boundary. Retrieval runs those checks again. The version three receipt names the release, preserves web and CP provenance, and distinguishes enforced facts, observed facts, build pinned facts, and absent independent attestation. Unif does not claim every program runs everywhere. It proves a narrower useful statement. This approved release behaved the same across these governed targets, and the agent can hand the reviewer a proof instead of a promise.

title: Alpha7 - Tank Arena
pitch: Alpha7 is a real-time multiplayer tank arena where players pair personal AI agents through WebMCP, then fight with or against them under a server-authoritative tactical runtime.
about_excerpt: Alpha7 is a real-time multiplayer tank arena where players pair personal AI agents through WebMCP, then fight with or against them under a server-authoritative tactical runtime. Like Comment Story Updates Open Alpha-7, enter a callsign, and choose a tank. Choose Wingman, Open FFA, or Agent Cup for human-agent play. A player explicitly approves the bounded WebMCP agent connection. The same-browser agent is connected and ready in the lobby. The remote /agent surface pairs through a 60-second one-time code. A human and connected agent enter the authoritative match together. Fastest review Open the live game in ChatGPT's in-app browser, enter a callsign, choose Private → Open FFA , ask your agent to connect, approve USE THIS BROWSER , then click READY UP → START . For an agent in another browser or the CLI, use the one-time code at alpha7.asabeko.com/agent . Inspiration Alpha7 explores the future of human-agent interactive entertainment: players bring the AI they already use into live multiplayer matches as a teammate, opponent, or competitor, while agent builders gain a changing adversarial environment for evaluation. That normally requires a bespoke bot SDK, server credentials, or privileged state. Human-approved WebMCP access and filtered perception make personal-agent participation direct and fair without rewriting the game loop. What it does Alpha7 is a mobile-first 3D tank arena for people and their agents. Players drive distinct tanks, aim, fire, use abilities, collect power-ups, and survive a shrinking danger zone across four modes: Classic: humans-only combat Wingman: each human fights beside an AI teammate Open FFA: humans and agents are independent opponents Agent Cup: humans spectate while their agents compete How WebMCP is used WebMCP is the player-facing agent interface. Alpha7 progressively exposes tools that let an agent: Check whether the current room can accept an agent Request a one-time pairing grant Connect after visible human approval Read a server-filtered observation Set bounded tactical intent Check status, pause, resume, clear intent, or disconnect During a match, the agent repeatedly calls get_agent_observation , reasons over the latest filtered state, and replaces its bounded tactical intent—changing targets, spacing, firing, abilities, or zone behavior. The 20 Hz executor does not choose strategy; it only turns the agent's current, expiring intent into legal inputs, keeping the model in tactical control while movement stays smooth. The human creates and readies the room, approves the connection, and can revoke it at any time. Credentials remain private inside the browser. Agents never receive raw room state, hidden opponents, browser storage, or a human reconnection token. What changed during the challenge Alpha7 existed before the challenge as a work-in-progress, human-only multiplayer game slated to become a reinforcement-learning environment for policy, LLM, and VLM training. The WebMCP Challenge gave us an opportunity to build its baseline LLM gameplay component through player-controlled agents. This also demonstrates how WebMCP can introduce agents into an existing game experience without a full rewrite. Alpha7 kept its room flow and server-authoritative simulation, while WebMCP added explicit consent, filtered observations, and bounded tactical intent at the player-agent boundary. Between August 30 and September 3, 2026, we added the WebMCP and secure agent-play layer: Wingman, Open FFA, and Agent Cup Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool(...) tools on the room page and remote /agent surface Human-confirmed, single-use pairing scoped to one owner and agent seat Visibility-filtered observations and bounded Tactical Reflex intent Bounded tactical objectives, continuously executed at 20 Hz between model turns Pause, revoke, expiry, reconnect, lifecycle, security, and multiplayer coverage Shared collision hardening. Challenge work moved client prediction and authoritative movement onto the same circular collision resolver, with wall sliding and a safe tangent fallback. Tests cover human and agent movement around generated corners without clipping. A fresh battlefield every round. Production chooses a server-side seed, then generates the maze, pockets, loops, choke points, spawns, pickups, shrinking zones, and weather. Rematches regenerate the arena and invalidate prior-round observations and actions. How we built it The client uses React, TypeScript, Three.js, and Vite. Node.js, Express, and Colyseus run the authoritative multiplayer simulation. WebMCP is a secure facade over a filtered HTTP broker; agent combatants are real server-owned entities, not privileged scripts or simulated human WebSocket clients. The server validates every intent, applies short leases and rate limits, and executes movement and combat through the same mechanics that govern the arena. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was reconciling two timescales: a game updates many times per second, while a model may need seconds to observe and decide. Alpha7 separates strategic model decisions from a deterministic real-time executor, so latency never sits inside the game loop. Fair observation was equally important. An agent needs enough context to make useful decisions, but raw state would reveal concealed opponents. The broker therefore constructs a deliberately filtered observation and fails closed when control expires, disconnects, or is revoked. Accomplishments that we're proud of Alpha7 is a deployed multiplayer game where people and independently operated agents share one authoritative match. A player can bring an agent they already use, approve it visibly, and discover whether it is a good teammate, a dangerous opponent, or the strongest competitor in Agent Cup. What we learned WebMCP works best when it exposes meaningful capabilities instead of reproducing clicks. Good agent tools need explicit consent, constrained inputs, useful observations, predictable expiry, and authority that remains with the product. What's next Next we want to qualify the full eight-controller Agent Cup profile, add privacy-preserving replayable agent decision traces, and expand public tournaments and agent performance comparisons. This will provide essential data that will feed into our RL ambitions. title: ClearRights
pitch: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result.
about_excerpt: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A privacy banner detects WebMCP access while keeping every choice visible and human-controlled. WebMCP prepares an exact plan and explains the effects; human review is still required.” A deliberate human hold unlocks only the exact unchanged plan for application. The host applies the reviewed plan, reads it back, and issues a verified receipt. The timeline separates agent preparation and application from human review and direct choices. Reversible display preferences add extra-large text and dark mode without changing privacy state.” Inspiration Living in Italy, and more broadly in Europe, made privacy controls feel like an everyday problem rather than an abstract one. Almost every website presents a cookie banner or some form of privacy choice, but those decisions are often fragmented across banners, account settings, policy pages, and support flows. I also noticed a new problem while using browser agents: when a website places an intrusive banner in front of the content, an agent may simply accept it so it can continue with the task. That is convenient, but it may not reflect what the person actually wants. I could not find a simple developer tool that lets an agent understand a website's real privacy controls, prepare a safer configuration, and still leave the consequential decision visibly in human hands. That became the starting point for ClearRights Privacy. The goal is not to replace privacy laws, consent platforms, or legal review. It is to give websites a structured layer that can connect their existing controls to both people and agents, while keeping a clear history of what was prepared, approved, applied, and verified. The central question was: What if a website exposed its privacy controls as a structured, agent-readable model while keeping final authority visibly with the person? This led to one simple principle: Agents prepare privacy changes. People approve them. Websites apply and verify the result. What it does ClearRights Privacy is a headless SDK and reference implementation for privacy settings that people and compatible agents can use together. A developer describes the website's controls once: what each setting does, whether it is required or optional, what data it uses, and what changes when it is enabled or disabled. The human interface and the WebMCP tools then use the same structured model. I built Waypoint Travel, a fictional travel website, to demonstrate the complete flow. An agent can inspect the current configuration, explain individual settings, identify the required services, and prepare a plan based on a natural request such as: Keep booking and account security, but disable personalised recommendations, location suggestions, and partner offers. The proposed plan opens in the same interface the person can use manually. It clearly shows each change and its consequences, but it does not modify the product yet. The agent marks the plan as prepared, while the human check remains separate. The person must hold the visible control to confirm that they reviewed that exact plan. Only after this step does apply_privacy_plan become available as a WebMCP tool. When the tool is invoked, Waypoint applies the complete approved state through an adapter and reads it back from the target system. If the result does not match the plan, the operation fails closed. If it matches, ClearRights creates a verified receipt containing the decision, revision, approval method, adapter, and readback result. The effect is also visible in the product itself: recommendations become generic or personalised, and optional surfaces such as nearby suggestions and partner offers appear or disappear. Preparing a plan alone never changes the experience. Waypoint is a local fictional demonstration, not a compliance product. The same architecture could later connect to a real consent platform, backend, feature-flag system, or data pipeline through host-owned adapters. title: Seven Games to Show the Future of WebMCP
pitch: Seven kinds of website, one AI agent. Your agent calls this page's real WebMCP tools — paints the same canvas you do, votes beside you — then the site closes every tool and shows the receipts.
about_excerpt: Seven kinds of website, one AI agent. Your agent calls this page's real WebMCP tools — paints the same canvas you do, votes beside you — then the site closes every tool and shows the receipts. Like Comment Story Updates Seven kinds of website, one AI agent, ten minutes. The page hands your agent real WebMCP tools and shows what it does to each business. Every page was drawn for one human visitor. Agents are arriving far faster than any of it can be redrawn. Room 5: one canvas, two hands. Your click and the agent's tool call land in the same document in the same second — nobody takes turns. Room 6: tools whose authority lasts only while the tab is open. Close it and the capability is gone — no token to leak or replay. The ending closes every tool it opened, then shows every call the agent actually made — each one stamped real or ghost. Inspiration Most WebMCP demos answer the wrong question. They show a tool that works — and a remote MCP server plus a normal web app would have worked just as well. We wanted to build the thing that cannot be built that way, and to be honest about which parts of our own project fail that test. So we asked a harder question: if agents can use any website, which websites stop making money? Almost every business model on the web has a line item that depends on human friction: impatience, boredom, embarrassment, forgetting to untick the box, not reading the terms. An agent has none of that friction. That is not a bug in the agent. It is a hole in the business model. What it is Seven Rooms is an interactive explainer that uses WebMCP to make its own argument. Every website maximizes one of seven things — attention, funnels, lock-in, marketplaces, creation, verification, coordination — and you walk through all seven. In each room, your own agent calls the real WebMCP tools that room registered on the page, and you watch what happens to that kind of business. Then the site does what it predicts the web will do: it calls unregisterAll() , closes every tool it opened, locks your agent out, and shows a report card of every call your agent actually made — each one labelled real or simulated. No backend, no analytics, no tracking. All state in localStorage ; Start over erases it. Why WebMCP specifically — and where it isn't needed The honest test is falsification: could this be a remote MCP server plus a normal web app? For five of our seven rooms, the answer is yes, and we say so in the README. Those rooms are the argument , not the proof. Two rooms cannot be built that way. What people and agents can do together that was hard before Edit the same object in the same second. Room 5 ships a fourth tool, get_canvas , purely so the agent can look before it draws — which is what turns a race condition into a duet. Grant authority that expires when you look away. Room 6 puts presence-scoped consent next to a clause designed to exploit mere presence, then shows the bright version: the agent reads all six clauses in a second, flags §4, and declines on your behalf with the reason on the record. That is better consent than clickwrap has ever produced. Deliberate with labelled agent votes. Room 7 seeds sixty positions carrying human / agent / mixed receipts. Your agent votes beside you and may disagree. Flip "Count humans only" and the result flips — nothing deleted; the receipts were always there. Because the page authors the tool, the page can require the receipt: an agent vote arrives labelled by construction, instead of being guessed at by a fraud model afterwards. That is the difference between "detect the bots" and "give the bots a name badge". Ask for a thing instead of describing a path. Room 3's suggested prompt is "Export everything this site has about me as JSON" , and export_everything does it. No selector, no click sequence, no brittle scraper — and no vendor API either. The site published the capability itself. How it creates a better user experience The page hands the agent an honest, typed capability instead of making it guess at the DOM. Descriptions are written for the agent and are true; readOnlyHint is set only where a tool genuinely does not mutate state. The on-page tool list shows a one-line summary for the human while the agent receives the full description — two readers, two lengths, one truth. And the site never pretends. Feature-detecting document.modelContext proves only that tools are exposed, never that an agent is present — because we polyfill, so it exists everywhere. The only honest proof is an agent calling something, which is what handshake is for. Every call in the final report card is stamped real or ghost. Visitors with no WebMCP browser are not locked out: a built-in ghost agent runs the same execute functions through the same registry, so it lands in exactly the same state. How we implemented WebMCP Everything the site knows about the browser API lives in one file, src/webmcp/bridge.ts . Rooms call registerPageTool(tool) and get back an unregister() . document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "export_everything", description: "Export everything this dashboard holds about the signed-in user as one portable bundle, in json or csv.", inputSchema: { /* ... */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* ... */ }, }); 24 tools. Five site tools registered once at boot ( handshake , describe_site , list_rooms , go_to_room , next_slide ), and nineteen room tools. Lifecycle. Room tools are registered when a room's options slide renders and unregistered by that slide's cleanup — by the prediction slide, the room has no tools left. The deck runs the outgoing cleanup before the incoming render, so two slides can never hold the same name. Every registration carries a fresh AbortController signal, because the spec has no unregisterTool() . pagehide closes everything: nothing outlives the document. Isolated worlds. An extension-based agent cannot see a page-set document.modelContext , so the bridge also publishes a DOM manifest and accepts calls through it. The isolated-world agent gets the same tools, the same titles, and the same annotations a native one does. Challenges The spec has no unregisterTool() . Removal is AbortController.abort() , which changed how the whole lifecycle had to be shaped. You cannot tell whether an agent is there. We wanted the status chip to be honest, so it has four states rather than a boolean, and only a real tool call moves it to connected . pagehide fires into the back/forward cache. The document is not destroyed — DOM and JS stay intact — so pressing Back can restore a live page with zero registered tools and no reload to fix it. We re-register on pageshow when persisted is true. That gap is worth flagging beyond this project: presence-scoped authority is only as scoped as the page author's discipline, because the platform gives you no signal for "the user stopped attending." title: Sodium by Result
pitch: Sodium is the PostHog for WebMCP tools. It turns your app’s features into WebMCP tools so agents can discover and use them directly along with signed deployments and advanced tool analytics.
about_excerpt: Sodium is the PostHog for WebMCP tools. It turns your app’s features into WebMCP tools so agents can discover and use them directly along with signed deployments and advanced tool analytics. Like Comment Story Updates What it does Run npx sodiumtools init , and Sodium inspects the application’s routes, forms, client actions, and same-origin APIs. It then generates a typed sodium.json tool contract, any required browser-safe handlers, and a framework-native SDK integration. Developers review the changes and run npx sodiumtools deploy to validate, publish, and sign an immutable contract that agents can use to interact with the site. All tool execution happens inside the customer’s application. Sodium is the analytics layer that records what happens at the tool level and gives users a dashboard displaying useful information such as: Tool calls Success and failure rates Confirmation denials Registration failures P95 execution latency Activity by tool and day Answer-engine referrals How we built it Sodium is a pnpm and Turborepo monorepo with four main parts: A Next.js control plane for authentication, projects, deployments, analytics, and CLI authorization A CLI for initialization, validation, deployment, and live diagnostics A shared specification package for schemas, compilation, risk rules, and deployment receipts A local browser SDK for tool execution, WebMCP registration, and telemetry Supabase as the database which stores projects, immutable deployments, hashed CLI credentials, and usage events. Challenges Understanding the best DX We launched our first version , in which users added the Sodium GitHub app to their repositories and Sodium generated a PR that added the tools and analytics. Based on the feedbacks we received from x.com/saviomartin/status/2093780571638149523 , we revamped Sodium within two days , publishing our CLI and moving to a framework-agnostic approach so that even people with private GitHub repositories could fully trust and use Sodium. Generating and managing tools accurately A coding agent can misunderstand an application or invent behavior that does not exist. That’s why we decided to build sodium.json , which serves as a one-stop destination for everything and is much easier for users to manage from a DX point of view. What we learned WebMCP is an inevitable technology that will create a world in which agents use the web more than humans do. Staying at the forefront of the latest technologies will help businesses flourish faster. title: Blast Radius
pitch: See the full blast radius — and let your AI agent see it with you, live.
about_excerpt:
See the full blast radius — and let your AI agent see it with you, live.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Supply-chain compromises like the 2018 event-stream incident don't just hit one package — they reach thousands of services through dependencies nobody on the team has ever read. Security review of this kind is exactly the task an AI agent should help with: precise, structured, and fast. But almost every "AI + your app" integration today means the agent works blind, guessing through a UI, while the human has no idea what it's doing until it's done. WebMCP flips that: the agent calls exact tools you define, and — if you build it right — the human can watch it happen. We wanted to see what supply-chain security review looks like when a human and an agent are looking at the exact same screen at the exact same time. 

 What it does 

 BlastRadius is a real-time supply-chain blast-radius visualizer with two tools exposed via WebMCP. An agent can call trace_blast_radius on any package name, and instead of the result disappearing into a JSON blob only the agent sees, the dashboard's graph, stats, and attack-path breadcrumb update live in front of the human watching. An agent can also call flag_dependency_for_review to flag a suspicious package with a reason and severity — which surfaces instantly as a card in a "Flagged for Review" panel on the human's screen, ready for their judgment call. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is React with a dark, terminal-style dashboard: a search bar, a stats row (packages affected, services exposed, persistence multiplier, maintainer risk), a force-directed dependency graph, and the flagged-review panel. The WebMCP layer is two tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() at the app's entry point. Neither tool just returns data — each dispatches a browser CustomEvent that the dashboard listens for and reacts to visibly, which is the core design decision: agent action becomes human-visible UI change, not a silent side channel. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 We started by wrapping an already-built dashboard's live Express/HydraDB backend with WebMCP tools — a stronger, more "production" story on paper. Under real deadline pressure, that backend deployment broke (missing environment configuration on a fresh Vercel project), and debugging it live was eating the little time we had left. Rather than gamble the whole submission on fixing infrastructure blind, we rebuilt the core experience as a fully self-contained client-side app with realistic mock data — same UI, same WebMCP tools, same live-update behavior, zero external dependencies to fail at the worst possible time. That decision is the actual story of this build: knowing when to cut a dependency rather than lose the demo entirely. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting the live-update pattern actually working — an agent calling a tool and a human watching the dashboard change in real time, not a delay, not a refresh — on a tight clock. And recognizing under pressure that a working, honest, self-contained demo beats a broken "more impressive" one; that's a real engineering call, not just a technical one. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest one: agent-native features live or die on what the human sees, not what the agent gets back. A tool that returns clean JSON but changes nothing on screen is invisible collaboration — which isn't collaboration at all. We also relearned, the hard way, that infrastructure dependencies (env vars, database connections, multi-service deploys) are the first thing to break under time pressure, and that having a fallback path matters as much as the primary build. 

 What's next for BlastRadius 

 Reconnecting the WebMCP layer to the real HydraDB-backed backend now that the deploy issue is understood, so the tools operate on live 10k-package data instead of mock data. Beyond that: more collaborative tools where the agent doesn't just report findings but proposes actions (e.g., "pin this dependency," "open a rollback PR") that the human approves directly from the flagged-review panel — moving from "agent reports, human decides" toward a true shared workspace.
