title: Marinela AI Concierge
pitch: WebMCP lets compatible browser agents match clients to current salon services and prices, check live availability, and open a prefilled review while booking confirmation remains human.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets compatible browser agents match clients to current salon services and prices, check live availability, and open a prefilled review while booking confirmation remains human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Marinela Hair Design is an operating hair salon in Solin, Croatia. Its production website already had protected booking, public pricing, dashboard-managed services, and calendar connections. For the challenge, we added a WebMCP layer that lets a compatible browser agent turn a natural-language request into structured, current salon data—without handling personal information or final booking confirmation. What it does Marinela AI Concierge exposes five focused WebMCP tools directly from the public salon website: get_salon_information returns public salon details, staff, and opening hours. find_bookable_services searches the active service catalog. search_price_list searches current public price-list rows. check_appointment_availability checks live availability for a service, stylist, and up to seven dates. prepare_booking_for_confirmation rechecks one selected time and opens the salon's first-party booking page with the service, stylist, date, and time preselected. The first four tools are read-only. The fifth performs only visible page navigation: it cannot reserve, create, or confirm an appointment. The client must review the summary, enter personal details, acknowledge the privacy notice, complete Cloudflare Turnstile, and click the final confirmation button. No WebMCP tool can cancel or reschedule bookings, look up customers, or access salon administration. The system also keeps two different price concepts honest: the matched bookable Balayage color service remains price on request , while the separate public price list provides current €100–€200 Balayage variants as context rather than a guaranteed quote. How we built it The production application uses TypeScript, React, Next.js, Vite/Vinext, and Cloudflare infrastructure. Native imperative WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a constrained JSON input schema with additionalProperties: false , followed by runtime shape and value validation. Tools are registered only on approved public routes and are removed during navigation or component unmount. Same-origin, rate-limited, no-store routes expose a sanitized salon catalog and availability results. Availability is checked against salon hours, existing booking claims, and the selected stylist's connected Google Calendar. A verification failure is returned as an error and is never represented as a fully booked day. The booking handoff rechecks the selected slot, passes only non-personal selections to the first-party booking page, and never calls the booking-creation endpoint. If the client later submits the visible form, the existing server validates the slot again. The public repository contains sanitized production source, setup and security documentation, an MIT license for code, a separate brand-asset notice, and a GitHub Actions workflow. The latest public workflow is green and the release suite passes all 35 tests. Challenge scope The salon website, visual identity, staff dashboard, Google Calendar integration, public price list, and conventional protected booking flow existed before the challenge. During the submission period, the project was meaningfully extended with five WebMCP tools, the live Concierge catalog, agent-prepared booking review, a dedicated /concierge experience, explicit privacy boundaries, fail-closed safety controls, documentation, and regression tests. Challenges The main challenge was making agent capabilities useful without exposing private customer or administrative data. We also had to preserve honest distinctions between a bookable service and an informational price row, a currently unavailable time and a verification failure, and a prepared review and an actual booking. Accomplishments Shipped five focused WebMCP tools on a live production salon website. Connected service discovery, public price context, and live availability in one agent-ready flow. Kept appointment creation and every personal-information field outside the WebMCP tool surface. Added strict schemas, runtime validation, same-origin checks, rate limits, and fail-closed behavior. Published reproducible public source with automated quality gates and 35 passing tests. What we learned Effective WebMCP design is not only about exposing functions. Tool scope, failure semantics, data provenance, and the boundary between assistance and consequential action are equally important. A visible human-confirmation step can be a product advantage: the agent reduces discovery work while the client retains control over identity, consent, and the final transaction. What's next Next steps include testing with additional WebMCP-capable clients, refining tool descriptions from real salon scenarios, and adapting the same human-confirmed pattern to other appointment-based small businesses without expanding write authority. title: The Pass
pitch: A governed WebMCP diagnostic-to-approval workflow where agents prepare work and humans retain final authority.
about_excerpt: A governed WebMCP diagnostic-to-approval workflow where agents prepare work and humans retain final authority. Like Comment Story Updates The Pass is a narrow, working proof of agent-ready operations software: a diagnostic-to-approval workflow where people and AI agents operate on the same business state, while the final authority decision remains human-only. Small operations teams can review a synthetic client diagnostic, inspect findings, create a task, assign an owner, check its approval gate, and prepare it for human approval. The human operator then resolves the task in the Approval Queue. This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the application exposes explicit, typed capabilities instead of asking an agent to infer meaning from buttons or DOM structure. WebMCP creates a better experience by making the workflow legible and dependable to both participants. The six registered tools are get_client_context, get_diagnostic, create_task, assign_owner, check_gate, and prepare_for_approval. Their inputs and outputs are explicit; writes are atomic and idempotent; and the human-only approval boundary is structural: there is intentionally no approve or reject tool. People and agents can collaborate on the same workflow without duplicating state or granting unrestricted application control. An agent can do the useful preparation work and leave a clear, auditable item waiting for a person with authority. That separation was difficult to guarantee with selector-based browser automation. The app is a static React/TypeScript/Vite deployment on Cloudflare Workers. Dexie-backed IndexedDB is the single state authority, and the human UI plus WebMCP tools call the same mutation functions. The live synthetic demonstration is Ember & Oak Hospitality Group at https://ffc-the-pass.ldr-3cd.workers.dev . The public source repository is https://github.com/ldr-Fulcrum/ffc-the-pass and includes an MIT license. To test: open the live URL in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome 149+ with WebMCP testing enabled. Discover the six tools, then review the Ember & Oak Midtown diagnostic (EO-OKC-01), create a task from a finding, assign an owner, check the gate, and prepare it for approval. Confirm that the task appears in the human Approval Queue. Approval and rejection are manual UI actions only. All displayed business data is synthetic and for demonstration/testing. title: Concord — an agent that cannot overpromise
pitch: WebMCP tells an agent what a site can do. Nothing tells it what a site can take back. Concord is that missing layer: it computes what it can honestly promise across sites before contacting any.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tells an agent what a site can do. Nothing tells it what a site can take back. Concord is that missing layer: it computes what it can honestly promise across sites before contacting any. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent books your flight on one site and your hotel on another. Halfway through, the hotel fails. Ask what happens next and no part of the web can answer. inputSchema describes a tool's shape . readOnlyHint describes whether it has an effect . Nothing anywhere describes whether that effect can be reversed — which is the one fact an agent needs to plan across sites rather than to act and hope. So today that gap is filled by a marketplace: an intermediary both businesses have a contract with, which is why one sits between almost every pair of businesses an agent might transact with, taking 15–30% to stand there. The tax is not for the booking. It is for the guarantee. The failure mode of agentic commerce is not the booking going wrong. It is the agent telling you it went fine. What it does Concord is a convention over WebMCP by which any site declares its commitment surface — one of three rungs: Rung Meaning Example reservable hold it, release it, nothing happened an airline seat compensable undoable, but it leaves a mark a hotel charge and refund irreversible it cannot be taken back a government fee …and an in-browser coordinator that computes the strongest honest guarantee across several such sites before contacting any of them — then refuses when the honest answer is that atomicity is not available at any price. Three things to try on the live URL, in ninety seconds: Ask for a flight, a hotel and the visa fee. The agent reads back what it can promise, which step is the point of no return, and which charge becomes briefly real before being reversed. Only then does a Go ahead button exist. Ask for a flight, the visa fee and the entry permit — two things nobody can take back. It says it cannot do that as one commitment, and that nothing has been contacted. There is no button on that answer. Kill the coordinator mid-commitment. Reload. It asks every vendor what actually happened and puts back what can be put back. Why WebMCP, specifically This needs exactly the thing WebMCP uniquely provides and nothing else does: two mutually distrusting origins' authenticated, typed capabilities present in one execution context, under the user's authority, with consent enforced on both sides by the browser. That is not scraping and it is not an API partnership. A participant grants with registerTool 's exposedTo . The embedder grants with allow="tools" . The coordinator must ask by name with getTools({ fromOrigins }) . Three separate grants, none forgeable by any party, and none requiring the participants to have heard of each other. No server anywhere is in the commitment path. How WebMCP is implemented The permission model is registerTool itself. This is the idea the whole project rests on: concord_commit does not exist until a person accepts the exact guarantee they were shown. Not disabled. Not registered. Four read-only tools at boot. concord_explain_guarantee appears once something is proposed. Explaining is not consent, so the surface does not change when the agent reads the guarantee out. A human clicks Accept on the page — registerTool puts concord_commit on the surface. The commitment begins — an AbortController takes it away again, so a second call arriving mid-flight finds nothing to call. toolchange fires on every one of those transitions, and you can watch it in the tool inspector. There is no tool that grants that permission, and there will not be one. An agent has every door; none of them opens this one. The rest of the surface actually used: exposedTo — each participant exposes its tools only to the coordinator's origin, so cross-origin consent is explicit on the participant's side. allow="tools" + Permissions-Policy: tools=(self "…") — the embedder's half of the same consent, verified on every deployed origin. Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 — required for cross-document tool access; without it getTools() returns empty with no error . getTools({ fromOrigins }) — discovery, opt-in on both sides, asked one origin at a time. executeTool(tool, jsonString) — arguments as a JSON string, per Chrome's imperative API. annotations.readOnlyHint — used honestly: true on the two tools that perform nothing, and on nothing that acts. AbortSignal — a deadline on every call, enforced by the coordinator too, which does not assume a participant honours cancellation. modelContext.requestUserInteraction — feature-detected. Chrome 151 does not implement it, so we measure that and use it wherever it exists: a second door onto the same accept, deliberately not a lock. A test hands it a host that approves every request and requires the surface to stay exactly as it was. If asking for attention could produce consent, the central claim would be false. And it fills a gap in the standard rather than decorating it. SPEC §19 proposes the missing annotation upstream: annotations: { readOnlyHint: false, commitment: 'reservable' | 'compensable' | 'irreversible', reverses: 'release_seat', ttlSeconds: 900, } The receipt Every commitment produces an RFC 6962 Merkle receipt in which every statement is signed by the counterparty that made it , with per-vendor ECDSA P-256 keys resolved from each vendor's own origin over TLS — never from a map the coordinator writes. The outcome is derived from the statements, never read off the receipt , because that field is the one thing no vendor signs. Check one on an origin we do not run, or with npx concord-verify receipt.json , and nothing of ours executes. How we built it, and what broke Zero dependencies, on purpose. Node's own test runner, a ~100-line property-testing kit, and Chrome. An audit found the receipt was forgeable. Seven of fourteen forgeries verified clean: a coordinator could delete a charge, relabel the outcome "Committed", and the receipt passed, because verifyReceipt gated its strictness on a string nobody signed. Fixed by deriving the outcome from the entries and by provable silence — a vendor that did nothing signs that it did nothing, so an absence is distinguishable from a deletion. You can fire all fourteen at our own verifier from the live site. Running on the real API found two defects a polyfill can never surface. The coordinator was not delegating tools to the origins it embeds, so every participant registered and none was discoverable. And Chrome returns inputSchema as a JSON string where the polyfill returns an object. Both worked flawlessly under the shim — which is the argument for never trusting one. getTools({ fromOrigins }) rejects for the whole call when any one origin is unreachable. One dead site produced "0 of 6 answered" and a failure screen with five participants healthy. Discovery now asks one origin at a time. What we learned That a sampled mutation score is not a score. We reported 92%. It came from 60 mutants taken every-Nth from a list sorted by file and by operator — a stratified sample of a sorted population. Running all 116 gave 87% . Closing what that exposed took it to 97% (112/116) , and the four survivors are documented as equivalent with the reasoning attached, not hidden. That a property test which cannot fail passes loudest. Our first reference-model test registered the commit tool in 1% of the states it checked, and its unwind-ordering property was vacuous in 95% of runs because the fixture had one participant of each rung — so reversing and not reversing produced identical output. Mutation testing found it. Every property now asserts how much of the interesting space it reached and fails rather than going green faster. That the measuring instrument needs measuring too. Our mutation runner's timeout killed the npm wrapper but not the test process beneath it; two orphans took throughput from ten mutants a minute to ten every three — and a loaded machine turns survivors into false kills, silently inflating the score. Challenges Refusing well is harder than committing. Anyone can run a saga. The hard part is computing, from declarations alone and before contact, that no honest promise exists — and then having no button on that answer. Proving a negative in a browser. "The commit tool does not exist yet" is only worth something if you can watch it not exist. So the claim is checked through the same getTools() an agent calls, state by state, against the live deployment. Not overclaiming about our own proof. We ship a formal model — 855 reachable states, 9 safety invariants, breadth-first so a violation reports the shortest trace. spec/Concord.tla is generated from the same declaration the checker executes, so it cannot drift. But TLC has not been run against it, and the README says so in those words rather than letting a .tla file imply a proof nobody ran. What it can't do — said before you ask A vendor can lie about being compensable. One does, on purp
video_title: Concord — an agent that cannot overpromise (WebMCP Challenge)
video_transcript_excerpt: Every website tells an agent what it can do. Nothing tells it what it can take back. This is Concord. Before it contacts anybody, it works out what it can honestly promise across sites that have never heard of each other. A flight that can be canceled, a hotel that can be refunded, and a visa fee that cannot be taken back. So that one goes last. Here is how that is enforced. Not a prompt and not a check inside a tool. This panel is the live output of get tools. Five read-only tools. The commit tool is not disabled. It is not registered. The agent has proposed and read the guarantee out, and it still has no way to commit because explaining is not consent. Now I accept and register tool puts the commit tool on the surface. No tool does that. A person clicked, and the moment the commitment starts, an abort controller takes it away again. Ask for two things nobody can undo and it refuses. Nothing was contacted, there is no button and no commit tool. A refused plan never produces one. Every statement in the receipt is signed by the counterparty, not by us. These are 14 real receipts, each edited the way a coordinator with a motive would. Seven of them verified clean until an audit found it. The outcome is derived from the statements now, and you can fire these yourself. And here is one on a different origin, which has no tools and no coordinator. It fetched each key from that vendor's own site. The coordinator that produced this receipt was never asked anything. A permission model made of register tool and abort controller, and an agent that cannot over promise because the words for it do not exist.

title: Waggle WebMCP
pitch: Shared project memory for ChatGPT. Agents recall context and propose corrections; humans approve the exact truth that becomes authoritative, with provenance and lineage preserved.
about_excerpt: Shared project memory for ChatGPT. Agents recall context and propose corrections; humans approve the exact truth that becomes authoritative, with provenance and lineage preserved. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Waggle WebMCP site tools waggle approved change Waggle Graph Studio Inspiration AI agents are getting better at remembering things across sessions, but persistent memory creates a new problem: who decides what the agent is allowed to remember as truth? Most memory systems focus on retrieval—store information, search it later, and return the most relevant result. But project memory is not just a collection of facts. Decisions change. Requirements conflict. Old assumptions become invalid. And if an agent can silently rewrite its own memory, the same system is both suggesting and deciding what becomes authoritative. I wanted a different model: Agents can propose. Humans decide. That became the core idea behind Waggle WebMCP : a shared project-memory workspace where ChatGPT and humans operate on the same governed memory, but humans retain control over what becomes authoritative. Waggle already existed as a local-first persistent memory engine with graph-backed retrieval, provenance, SQLite storage, optional Neo4j support, and an MCP interface. For the WebMCP Challenge, we extended that foundation into a new browser-native human + agent collaboration experience. What it does Waggle WebMCP gives ChatGPT direct semantic access to the memory visible in the Waggle Workspace. Instead of forcing the model to inspect cards, scrape the DOM, or navigate a dashboard, the page exposes four purpose-built WebMCP tools: get_project_brief — gives ChatGPT a structured summary of the project's current authoritative state. recall_memory — retrieves current authoritative memories while excluding superseded or expired information. propose_memory_change — lets the agent suggest a correction without modifying authoritative memory. apply_approved_memory_change — applies only a proposal that has already been explicitly approved by a human. The important part is the boundary between the last two operations. An agent can say: “This storage decision conflicts with the local-first requirement. I recommend changing it.” But the change remains a proposal . A human can then reject it, approve it, or edit the exact wording before approval. Once approved, the content is frozen. When ChatGPT later calls apply_approved_memory_change , it provides only the proposal ID—it cannot substitute different text or bypass the review step. The resulting flow is: Agent recalls memory ↓ Agent proposes a correction ↓ Human edits / approves ↓ ChatGPT applies the approved proposal ↓ Previous memory is superseded ↓ New human-approved memory becomes authoritative ↓ ChatGPT immediately recalls the corrected truth Every change preserves provenance and an updates relationship between the previous and new memory. The user experience The main Workspace is designed for humans rather than as a raw graph viewer. It shows: Current Context Key Decisions Recent Memories Pending Human Review a live Memory Map an auditable Activity timeline For deeper inspection, Graph Studio shows the actual underlying nodes and edges, including supersession lineage. I also built a six-step Guided Demo specifically around real WebMCP events. It does not use fake “Next” buttons. The guide advances only when the matching action really occurs: ChatGPT calls get_project_brief ChatGPT calls recall_memory ChatGPT creates a proposal The human edits and approves it ChatGPT applies the approved proposal ChatGPT recalls the newly authoritative memory At the end, the judge can open Graph Studio and inspect the exact lineage that was created. How I built it The challenge implementation keeps Waggle's existing memory engine as the source of truth rather than creating a second WebMCP-specific database. The architecture is roughly: Human ───────────────→ React Workspace │ │ review / inspect ▼ ChatGPT ── WebMCP ──→ Waggle Web API │ Workspace services / \ MemoryGraph Proposal state │ │ └──── approved ────┘ │ ▼ Authoritative memory + provenance The frontend is built with React/Vite , while the existing Waggle backend runs as a Python ASGI application . The WebMCP adapter registers page-level tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . For authoritative recall, we reuse Waggle's scoped graph retrieval instead of implementing a parallel search system. Proposal state is stored separately from normal knowledge so a pending agent suggestion cannot accidentally appear in ordinary memory retrieval. Each proposal records a fingerprint of the memory version it targets. If that memory changes before review or application, the proposal becomes stale rather than overwriting newer information. When an approved proposal is applied: a new authoritative memory is created; the previous memory becomes superseded; an updates edge links the two; proposal and reviewer provenance are preserved; subsequent normal recall returns only the new authority. Building a safe human approval boundary One of the hardest parts was making human approval an actual system property , rather than just a UI convention. A weaker implementation could have let the model call something like: update_memory(memory_id, new_content) and merely asked it to wait for permission. We deliberately did not do that. Instead: propose_memory_change(...) can create workflow state but cannot change authoritative memory. And: apply_approved_memory_change(proposal_id) accepts only an already-approved proposal identifier. There is no new_content parameter at application time. That means the agent cannot alter the text after the human has reviewed it. This separation between proposal authority and write authority became one of the most important lessons from the project. Challenges we faced 1. Avoiding a second memory system Waggle already had graph storage, retrieval, provenance, and validity semantics. It would have been easy to build a simplified WebMCP demo beside it. Instead, we made the Workspace and WebMCP tools operate on the same underlying memory state so the demo represents the actual product architecture. 2. Handling stale proposals safely A proposal may be correct when created but dangerous later if another actor has already changed its target memory. We solved this with version fingerprints and fail-closed stale handling. A stale proposal cannot overwrite a newer authoritative state. 3. Hosting a zero-login judge experience The core Waggle architecture is local-first, but a hackathon judge needs a public URL with no setup. For the challenge deployment, each browser gets an isolated seeded workspace. Sessions are separated using an opaque secure cookie and separate project namespaces, so one judge cannot modify another judge's demo state. The hosted instance uses ephemeral SQLite because it runs on a free deployment tier. It is explicitly a seeded challenge demonstration, not a claim that the hosted deployment itself is local-first. 4. Real ChatGPT browser integration A normal browser test was not enough—we needed the actual ChatGPT Site-tool flow to work. We added a Site-tools preflight to the Workspace and validated the complete sequence in native ChatGPT twice from clean seeded states. All four WebMCP tools were discovered and invoked, the human-approved SQLite decision became authoritative, the previous Neo4j decision was excluded from normal recall, and Graph Studio showed the resulting real updates lineage. 5. Responsive human review The ChatGPT browser has a narrower usable viewport than a normal desktop browser. During testing, the Guided Demo could overlap the human approval controls. We changed the guide layout specifically for the human-review step and added browser regression coverage at the smaller viewport so Edit & Approve remains accessible. What I learned The biggest lesson was that human control should be represented as a capability boundary, not just a prompt instruction . Telling an agent “please ask before changing memory” is weaker than designing the API so it physically cannot apply arbitrary content. We also learned that provenance is much easier to understand when presented at two levels: the Workspace explains what the human needs to decide; Graph Studio explains what actually happened to the underlying memory. And WebMCP turned out to be especially well suited to this kind of interaction because the human and the model can collaborate around the same visible web application while each side has different capabilities. The agent does not need to imitate a human clicking through the interface. It can call semantic tools directly, while the human retains the parts of the workflow that should remain human-controlled. What I'm proud of The final challenge flow is not simulated. A judge can: open Waggle with no account; ask ChatGPT for project context; retrieve the current authoritative decision; ask the agent to propose a correction; personally ed

title: MarkDown Stripper
pitch: MarkDown Stripper uses WebMCP to help people and agents clean documents, detect sensitive data locally, and prepare AI-ready content—with human approval before anything is shared.
about_excerpt: MarkDown Stripper uses WebMCP to help people and agents clean documents, detect sensitive data locally, and prepare AI-ready content—with human approval before anything is shared. Like Comment Story Updates Description Input use cases Inspiration Sharing a document with an AI agent often begins with an unreliable manual process: remove formatting, repair broken structure, extract useful references, look for sensitive information, and decide what is safe to share. Traditional browser automation adds uncertainty because agents must guess which controls to use and how to interpret the page. We built MarkDown Stripper to create a safer, structured handoff between people and agents. WebMCP was a natural fit because it lets the application expose precise capabilities while keeping the person in control of the same visible workspace. What it does MarkDown Stripper is a local-first document preparation workspace. It imports Markdown, TXT, HTML, DOCX, PDF, and image files, then converts them into Plain, Readable, or AI-ready text. It extracts references, identifies unresolved references, performs OCR, and detects potentially sensitive information locally. Through WebMCP, an agent can inspect bounded document state, prepare an AI-ready handoff, run a privacy scan, check readiness, and redact findings that the person selected by ID. Sensitive content reads and export actions remain blocked until the person reviews the document and explicitly approves that exact version. If the document or relevant processing state changes, approval is automatically invalidated. Why this use case strongly fits WebMCP Document handoff is a multi-step, stateful workflow, not a single button click. An agent needs to understand the document’s current state, choose appropriate conversion settings, inspect risks, make controlled changes, and verify whether the result is ready. With conventional browser automation, the agent must infer all of this from labels, coordinates, and changing page layouts. WebMCP gives the agent narrow, typed operations that express the application’s real capabilities and return structured, verifiable results. It allows the agent to act reliably without creating a separate interface or bypassing the person. The result is a genuinely collaborative workflow in which the agent handles repetitive preparation while the human retains authority over sensitive content. How it improves the user experience The user no longer has to manually clean a document, hunt for references, run separate privacy checks, and repeatedly explain the page state to an agent. The agent can prepare the visible document, run local checks, and report exactly what still needs attention. Every mutation remains visible in the normal interface, privacy findings have stable IDs, long results are returned in bounded pages, and the readiness tool provides clear next steps without exposing document text. The approval gate makes the boundary understandable: preparation can be delegated, but content cannot be read, copied, or downloaded by the agent until the person approves the current version. What people and agents can now do together A person can import or paste a document and ask an agent to prepare it for a safe AI handoff. The agent can switch the output to AI-ready context, preserve useful references, open Insights, run the local privacy scan, and explain which findings require review. The person decides which finding IDs should be redacted and can see each resulting change in the editor. After a redaction, the agent can scan the new version and check readiness again. The person then reviews and approves that exact state. Only after approval can the agent retrieve a bounded text segment, list approved assets, copy the output, or initiate a local text download. This review-first collaboration would be fragile and difficult to verify through coordinate-based automation alone. How we implemented WebMCP The application uses React, TypeScript, and Vite, with a Cloudflare Worker serving the production build. The top-level page registers 14 imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These tools share the same live React state and actions as the human interface, so agent actions remain visible and verifiable. Each tool has a narrow JSON Schema plus runtime input validation. Content-bearing responses use bounded, cursor-based pagination and are marked as untrusted content. Successful calls return structured JSON, failures reject, and registration is cancelled through an AbortController when the page unmounts. Sensitive tools require an approval fingerprint tied to the exact document, conversion settings, privacy findings, scan status, warnings, and unresolved references. Any relevant change invalidates that approval. Conversion, OCR, privacy scanning, redaction, and document processing run locally in the browser. Aggregate telemetry contains only allowlisted dimensions and never includes document text. The repository includes automated tests for document processing, WebMCP tools, approval invalidation, pagination and output limits, atomic registration, and Worker behavior. Challenges we ran into One major challenge was giving agents useful access without exposing the entire document automatically. We solved this with bounded, cursor-based reads and a human approval checkpoint tied to the exact document state. We also had to keep agent operations synchronized with the visible interface. Instead of creating a separate automation layer, the WebMCP tools call the same actions used by the React application. Document imports created additional complexity because PDFs, scanned images, DOCX files, and Markdown preserve structure differently. OCR and privacy detection also needed to remain responsive while running entirely in the browser. Finally, changing or redacting a document had to invalidate previous approval reliably. We addressed this with an exact-state fingerprint covering the document, conversion settings, scan status, warnings, and findings. Accomplishments that we are proud of We created a non-trivial set of 14 WebMCP tools that supports a complete workflow rather than wrapping a single button. The application lets people and agents collaborate in one shared workspace while preserving a meaningful human privacy checkpoint. An agent can prepare and evaluate a handoff, but it cannot retrieve or export document content until the person approves the current version. We are also proud that document conversion, OCR, privacy analysis, and redaction happen locally. The project supports several document formats, provides multilingual OCR options, and remains fully usable as a human-facing editor when WebMCP is unavailable. What we learned We learned that agent-native applications need more than tool exposure. Tools need clear boundaries, verifiable state, careful handling of untrusted content, and mutations that remain understandable to the person using the page. We also learned that human approval should be attached to data state rather than represented by a permanent boolean. Approval must expire whenever the content or relevant processing state changes. Most importantly, WebMCP works best when agents and people operate on the same product state instead of using separate interfaces. What is next for MarkDown Stripper Next, we plan to add configurable privacy policies, more document formats, stronger multilingual detection, and clearer explanations for each privacy finding. We also want to introduce reusable handoff profiles for workflows such as research, customer support, legal review, and AI knowledge-base preparation. Longer term, MarkDown Stripper could provide a standard privacy-aware handoff layer for any web application that prepares user-controlled information for agents. title: Tempo
pitch: Tempo is a calendar that organizes your life for you. Tell it what you need to do, and AI can find time in your busy day, plan your schedule, and manage your events through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Tempo is a calendar that organizes your life for you. Tell it what you need to do, and AI can find time in your busy day, plan your schedule, and manage your events through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard Title Page Inspiration As an incoming university student, I found my university's portal surprisingly inconvenient for organizing my class schedule and timetable. Getting that schedule into a calendar I could actually use meant manually organizing and reshuffling everything. Outside of school, I also play sports, make music, and work part-time. Trying to fit studying, classes, work, practices, and everything else into the same week often meant constantly moving things around to find time for what I needed to do. As someone that believes that being organized is a key value to success, I needed to use my calendar more efficiently. I wanted a calendar that could do more than just store events. I wanted to be able to tell it what I needed to accomplish and have it help organize my time for me. That's why I built Tempo , a calendar designed to work with AI agents using WebMCP. What it does Tempo is a calendar designed to work with AI agents through WebMCP . Instead of manually searching through your calendar and rearranging events, you can tell an agent what you want to accomplish. It can understand your existing schedule, find available time, and make changes directly to your calendar. For example: "Find me three one-hour study blocks around my classes this week and add them to my University calendar." Tempo can also manage recurring events, multiple calendars, conflicts, and other everyday calendar tasks. The agent completes the slow task of manually typing events so you can stay organized for efficiently. How I built it Tempo was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS . The calendar takes many pieces from calendarcn made by vmnog. GitHub . Title page and many other assets were made using Figma. I first took pieces from calendarcn to built the calendar itself, including multiple calendar views, recurring events, event management, search, conflict detection, undo/redo, local persistence, and ICS import/export. I then built a WebMCP layer on top of that foundation. Tempo has structured tools through document.modelContext . These tools allow an agent to read calendars and events, find conflicts, create and modify events, manage calendars, and safely perform destructive actions with confirmation. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was figuring out how an AI agent should safely interact with a calendar. Calendar actions can have real consequences, especially when an agent is creating, moving, or deleting events. If Tempo made the process of creating or organizing a calendar longer, it would not be an useful tool. I wanted agents to have meaningful control without allowing actions to happen unpredictably or silently. I also had to design the WebMCP tools around the existing calendar architecture so that agent actions use the same state, history, and conflict-handling systems as actions made through the UI. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that Tempo is more than a calendar with an AI chatbot attached to it. I've personally used it to transfer my university course timetable to other calendars. The agent can actually interact with the calendar through structured WebMCP tools, allowing it to read, reason about, and modify the user's schedule. I'm also proud of how it all came together, from the visuals I spent hours in figma creating, to the calendar functionality itself. This allowed us to demonstrate WebMCP solving a real problem rather than building a purely technical proof of concept. Tempo also highlights how building is the best way to learn new things. What I learned I learned that making an application agent-ready requires more than adding an AI interface. The agent needs clear, well-defined tools that describe what it can actually do. I also learned that AI is most useful when it removes friction from something people already do. Instead of creating another complicated scheduling interface, Tempo lets users describe what they need and gives an agent the tools to help make it happen. The simple but tedious task it streamlines is the key to its effectiveness. One of the biggest unlocks for me was learning how to use Figma along this process. From personal experience at hackathons, sometimes well thought of ideas can loose to simple ones with polished execution. I'm sure Figma will be a tool I will use for many future projects. What's next for Tempo The next step is turning Tempo into a polished product and pushing the agent experience further. I want to refine the visual design, improve the Agent Link experience, build more advanced scheduling workflows, and make voice interaction a core part of the experience. Creating a more effective mobile experience could also allow people to use Tempo on the go. Ultimately, I want Tempo to make organizing your calendar feel less like a chore and more like having an assistant that can actually manage your time easily. title: Runtime Truth
pitch: Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. Runtime Truth detects when a WebMCP action reports success but the authoritative application state says otherwise.
about_excerpt:
Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. Runtime Truth detects when a WebMCP action reports success but the authoritative application state says otherwise.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As AI agents move from reading websites to taking real actions — booking, buying, submitting forms, and changing application state — a new reliability question appears: 

 How do we know the action actually happened? 

 A tool can return SUCCESS , but the authoritative application state may tell a different story. 

 Runtime Truth explores that gap. 

 What it does 

 Runtime Truth exposes a WebMCP tool called reserve_table . 

 In the demo, an agent requests a reservation for two people at 7 PM. 

 The tool reports: 

 SUCCESS — Reservation ID: R-1042 

 But the reservation is deliberately not persisted. 

 Runtime Truth then independently checks the authoritative application state. 

 It finds: 

 RESERVATION NOT FOUND 

 and flags: 

 DIVERGENCE DETECTED 

 The core principle is simple: 

 Don’t trust the tool response. Verify the state. 

 How I built it 

 The project uses WebMCP's imperative API to register a structured website tool that agents can discover and execute. 

 The execution flow is: 

 
 The WebMCP tool performs the requested action. 
 The application receives a declared result. 
 Runtime Truth independently queries the authoritative post-action state. 
 The declared result and observed state are compared. 
 A mismatch is surfaced as execution-state divergence. 
 

 The demo uses deterministic fault injection so the failure can be reproduced consistently. 

 The application is built with Python, Flask, JavaScript, and WebMCP, and deployed on Render. 

 Challenges 

 The most important challenge was separating tool execution from verification . 

 If verification simply trusts the same response that declares success, it cannot detect false-success states. 

 I also had to test WebMCP registration, discovery, and execution independently. The final implementation was verified using Chrome's WebMCP testing support: 

 
 tool registration 
 tool discovery 
 WebMCP tool execution 
 independent post-action state verification 
 

 What I learned 

 A successful tool response is a claim about execution, not necessarily proof of the resulting state. 

 As WebMCP makes websites increasingly agent-native, verification may become especially important for consequential actions such as purchases, reservations, submissions, and workflow changes. 

 I also came across Greg Isenberg's discussion of an "agent mystery shopper" concept for testing whether agents can actually complete important website journeys. 

 Runtime Truth approaches a narrower technical version of that problem: 

 When a tool declares success, did the expected state transition actually occur? 

 I see that discussion as an independent signal that completion verification is becoming relevant as agents perform more real-world actions on the web. 

 What's next 

 Runtime Truth is intentionally small. 

 The next step would be testing the same verification pattern across additional state-changing actions such as purchases, submissions, and asynchronous workflows. 

 For this challenge, the goal is narrower: 

 demonstrate clearly that tool success and state truth are not always the same thing.

title: PixelAid
pitch: PixelAid is a free web app for turning oversized, fake, matted, or messy pixel images into transparent PNGs, stable palettes, and export-ready bundles. From AI all the way to game engines.
about_excerpt:
PixelAid is a free web app for turning oversized, fake, matted, or messy pixel images into transparent PNGs, stable palettes, and export-ready bundles. From AI all the way to game engines.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 I made PixelAid for the part of pixel art cleanup that kept wasting my night. 

 AI image tools can give you a cute sprite in seconds. So can a quick Photoshop pass, a screenshot crop, an old exported sheet, or a tool that says “pixel art” and leaves you with a giant blurry PNG. The image looks fine in a chat window. Then you open it in Aseprite, Unity, Godot, or your own engine and the whole thing falls apart: fake pixels, too many colors, weird transparency, a halo around the edge. 

 PixelAid starts after the image exists. It looks at the file, guesses the grid it was trying to be, cleans the background, reduces accidental colors, preserves useful details, and exports something you can inspect or keep working on. 

 What it does 

 
 Pixel snapping and grid alignment for pixel-perfect images 
 chroma and smart background removal 
 color space recognition and flattening (ai images typically generate > 10,000 unique colors whereas pixel art typically uses 8 - 32 colors. We use CIELAB and other color space algorithms 
 Resize and clustering work. There are a lot of algorithms in here to make the output art deterministic, repeatable, and correct. 
 Frame size detection - PixelAid understands whether your image is a static sprite, a spritesheet, or a framegrid of multiple animations. It also offers sprite animation previews and players so you can apply your pixel art fixes to animations too 
 

 How we built it 

 I have a much longer essay on how it works and the algorithms used internally: https://oscarsanchez.com/essays/ai-pixelart-is-broken/ but essentially the app itself a headless runner with a main algorithm owning the detection and then spreading to different algorithms based on what we need to do. The headless capability allows me to release PixelAid as a cli, a web app, and a desktop app. So you can use it however you want. The source is free and it's also on itch.io 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Detection is hard, getting colors to match is hard, sizing is hard. But colors are definitely the worst - if you ask AI to make an image of a white cloud, there will be 10,000 shades of "white" in that output. It may not seem significant, but if you have a character with red hair, yellow jacket, blue pants, green socks, brown shoes - that's already 5/8 colors you can end up with! 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 The headless app and ability to release in so many ways. Adding webmcp was really simple too! 
 

 What we learned 

 What's next for PixelAid 

 The algorithm can always be better. Image generation itself is not part of pixel aid either, and it can be.

title: Deshi digest
pitch: Deshi Digest is an AI-powered nutrition platform for Bangladeshi food, now enhanced with WebMCP so AI agents can search, compare, analyze, and help plan healthier local meals.
about_excerpt:
Deshi Digest is an AI-powered nutrition platform for Bangladeshi food, now enhanced with WebMCP so AI agents can search, compare, analyze, and help plan healthier local meals.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 plate analyzer 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 front page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 log meal 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 chat bot 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 plate analyzer 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 front page 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 log meal 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 chat bot 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 plate analyzer 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Deshi Digest started from a problem in my own life. 

 Over time, I gained much more weight than I was comfortable with. I wanted to control my eating habits and understand what I was actually consuming every day. 

 So naturally, I tried looking for nutrition apps. 

 But I noticed a problem. 

 Most of them understood foods like pizza, pasta, cereal, sandwiches, or packaged Western products very well, but they were much less useful when my plate contained things like rice, dal, bhorta, khichuri, kacchi biryani, fish curry, paratha, pitha, or several Bangladeshi dishes together . 

 And even when I could find nutritional information, the experience still felt generic. 

 I did not just want an app that told me: 

 "You ate 700 calories." 

 I wanted something that actually understood me, my food, my habits, my goals, and the way people around me eat. 

 That was the beginning of Deshi Digest . 

 My initial thought was simple: 

 What if I could create a personalized AI food companion built around Bangladeshi food? 

 But as I continued building it, that idea became much bigger. 

 

 What Deshi Digest does 

 Deshi Digest is an AI-powered personalized food, nutrition, and lifestyle companion centered around Bangladeshi cuisine . 

 It is designed to follow the complete journey around food: 

 Understand what you eat → track it → get personalized guidance → decide what to cook → find the ingredients → and actually get the food. 

 Personalized food and nutrition 

 Deshi Digest helps users understand Bangladeshi meals instead of forcing them into a food database designed for another culture. 

 The system can help users explore foods, analyze meals, understand nutrition, track their food-related activity, and receive recommendations based on their own situation. 

 I have also been working on fine-tuning AI around Bangladeshi food , so the intelligence behind Deshi Digest can better understand local dishes, ingredients, terminology, and eating habits. 

 AI is therefore not simply a chatbot added on top of the website. 

 It is intended to become the intelligence connecting the entire experience. 

 

 Care Companion 

 Food is only one part of taking care of yourself. 

 That led me to build the Care Companion concept into Deshi Digest. 

 Instead of only showing numbers, the Care Companion is designed to stay alongside the user and help them understand their daily food decisions in a more personal and conversational way. 

 For example, instead of simply warning: 

 "You consumed too many calories today." 

 the companion should understand the context and help the user decide what to do next. 

 A user might say: 

 "I already had kacchi for lunch. What should I eat tonight?" 

 The Care Companion can help adjust the rest of the day's choices rather than treating one meal as a failure. 

 The goal is to make Deshi Digest feel less like a calculator and more like a personal food companion that understands your journey over time. 

 

 Built for students and bachelors too 

 While working on the project, I realized another everyday problem. 

 Students and bachelors often see amazing food online or at restaurants but think: 

 "I can't cook that." 

 or: 

 "That will cost too much." 

 But good-looking and enjoyable food does not always need expensive ingredients. 

 Deshi Digest is designed to help someone say: 

 "I have eggs, potatoes, rice, onions and 200 taka. What can I make?" 

 and receive practical ideas based on what they already have and what they can afford. 

 It can help turn ordinary ingredients into attractive meals while keeping the recipe realistic for someone living alone or on a limited budget. 

 So Deshi Digest is not just about telling people to eat less. 

 It should also help people enjoy food more intelligently. 

 

 From recipe to grocery 

 Then I thought about another problem. 

 Suppose Deshi Digest recommends a meal. 

 The user still has to: 

 
 figure out the ingredients, 
 find a grocery shop, 
 determine where it is, 
 travel there, 
 and then buy everything. 
 

 Why should the experience stop at the recipe? 

 That led to the grocery discovery and route experience . 

 Deshi Digest can help users discover grocery options and find a suitable route to get the ingredients they need. 

 The vision is that after choosing a meal, the experience can continue naturally: 

 Choose meal → see required ingredients → find grocery options → get the route → buy the food or ingredients. 

 And where purchasing is available through the platform, users can continue from discovery directly toward buying what they need. 

 This makes the platform useful not only for deciding what to eat , but also for answering: 

 "How do I actually get it?" 

 

 A complete food journey 

 This is the experience I want Deshi Digest to create. 

 Imagine saying: 

 "I want to cook something special tonight, but I only have 300 taka." 

 Deshi Digest could help: 

 
 understand your preferences 
 consider your recent meals 
 suggest suitable Bangladeshi dishes 
 show affordable alternatives 
 generate a practical recipe 
 identify missing ingredients 
 help locate grocery options 
 guide you to the shop 
 and help you obtain what you need 
 

 Or you could say: 

 "I already ate biryani for lunch. I still want something tasty tonight." 

 Your Care Companion could understand the context and help balance the rest of your day without simply telling you not to eat. 

 For me, this is what personalization should actually mean. 

 

 Why WebMCP? 

 While building all of these capabilities, I realized something else. 

 Why should Deshi Digest only work when someone manually opens the website and clicks through every feature? 

 An AI agent should also be able to understand what Deshi Digest can do. 

 That is why WebMCP fits naturally into the project. 

 With WebMCP, Deshi Digest can expose its useful capabilities directly to AI agents in a structured way. 

 Instead of an agent trying to visually understand buttons and pages, Deshi Digest can effectively tell the agent: 

 "These are the things I can help you with." 

 An agent could potentially use Deshi Digest to: 

 
 search Bangladeshi foods 
 understand local dishes 
 retrieve food and nutrition information 
 compare meals 
 analyze someone's food choices 
 work with the Care Companion 
 generate practical meal ideas 
 plan meals around a user's budget 
 find required ingredients 
 discover grocery options 
 help find routes to grocery shops 
 and assist with the journey from deciding what to eat to actually obtaining the food 
 

 

 Human + AI Agent + Deshi Digest 

 This creates an experience I find especially exciting. 

 Instead of: 

 Human → Website → Click → Click → Search → Result 

 we can move toward: 

 Human → AI Agent → WebMCP → Deshi Digest 

 For example, someone could simply tell their AI agent: 

 "Use Deshi Digest. I ate kacchi today, I don't want to spend more than 250 taka tonight, and I want something easy to cook. Find something suitable and tell me where I can get the ingredients." 

 The agent could use Deshi Digest's specialized capabilities to help complete that entire task. 

 The user does not need to know which page contains which feature. 

 They simply express an intention. 

 That is what makes WebMCP particularly interesting to me. 

 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges has been understanding Bangladeshi food itself. 

 Our food is incredibly diverse. 

 The same dish can have very different nutritional values depending on: 

 
 ingredients 
 portion sizes 
 cooking oil 
 preparation method 
 restaurant 
 household 
 and region 
 

 A Bangladeshi plate may also contain rice, meat, dal, vegetables, bhorta, curry, and several other items together. 

 Teaching AI to understand that is much more

title: Redini-Atelier
pitch: A WebMCP design studio where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets you can preview, amend and undo before the canvas changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP design studio where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets you can preview, amend and undo before the canvas changes. Like Comment Story Updates How it works—agent intent→one editable ChangeSet→human negotiates→receipt & history. Atelier is the product Redini is the transaction layer Inspiration Most AI agent demos mutate your app silently. You ask for a change, it happens, you hope it was right. Approval dialogs are binary — yes or no — while real design work is never binary. I wanted the opposite: what if every agent action arrived as a set of related, negotiable changes you can actually see together? A title, a background, a logo position — proposed at once, previewed as one coherent poster, edited one by one. That question became Atelier, powered by Redini . ## What it does Atelier is a WebMCP design editor where agent actions arrive as editable ChangeSets instead of silent mutations. ONE agent intent → ONE WebMCP call (design_update) → ONE ChangeSet → derived preview → amend / skip → atomic commit → receipt → Undo ↔ Redo One call can propose 3 or 6 operations at once. Before anything touches the live canvas you can preview the full result, amend any parameter with typed controls, skip any operation, and commit only the accepted subset. The receipt preserves the distance between what the agent intended and what you authorized: INTENDED / AMENDED BY YOU / SKIPPED BY YOU / APPLIED — STATE v0 → v2 Redini is the small, app-agnostic transaction layer underneath. Every commit, undo and redo advances the version — \( v_{n+1} > v_n \) — so a proposal that was staged on an old state becomes stale instead of being silently applied elsewhere. Live: https://redini-atelier.netlify.app — Try ?clean=1 for the focused agent path. ## How we built it Stack: TypeScript + Vite, native DOM/CSS, Netlify static hosting. No framework, no snapshots — forward operations + compensating inverses only. WebMCP: We use the native surface — document.modelContext.registerTool() , getTools() , executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args)) . The public app exposes 5 focused tools: design_update , list_templates , get_current_design , filter_templates , get_vendor_content . design_update stays pending while you negotiate and resolves with a concise result like {"status":"committed","appliedCount":2} . Undo/Redo are intentionally human-side only. Verified like a product: 104 tests, tsc --noEmit clean, production builds, and a real Chrome 149+ E2E that drives the true executeTool path — including PREVIEW — not applied yet , amend, skip, Commit N changes , receipt, Undo, Redo, keyboard ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z , and stale proposals. Deployed with explicit Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) so the experimental browser gate is unambiguous. ## Challenges we ran into WebMCP is still experimental. executeTool expects the tool object + JSON string , Chrome needs --enable-features=WebMCP , and documents must be origin-keyed or registerTool must reject with SecurityError . We found all three with a real Puppeteer spike on Chrome 149. Product challenges were harder: Preview without double-render: simulate() already gave the right derived state, but we rendered it as a translucent overlay on top of the committed poster. Fix: hide the committed canvas while previewing. Honest atomicity: if runtime.apply() mutates then throws without returning an inverse, the world may be partially changed. Redini never claims “nothing happened” in that case — it surfaces stateUncertain instead. Derived bounds: move {x:640,y:400} passes a per-field check but puts the logo fully outside the 640×400 canvas. Bounds are now validated on the sequential derived logo state and re-validated at commit. ## Accomplishments that we're proud of A complete, demo-ready loop that holds together under verification: agent proposes 6 changes in one call → you amend one, skip one, commit 2 of 6 → receipt → Undo → Redo → provenance shows Agent proposed vs You staged Template "..." , all with 0 console errors . We are proud of the small things judges can falsify: the badge names the proposal that owns the preview, Commit is disabled at 0 ops, templates are real <button> s, and the 104-test suite includes the exact repros from our external audits. And it works inside the real ChatGPT in-app browser — our final smoke was there, on the Netlify URL, with frame-ancestors allowlisted for it. ## What we learned A transaction layer does not need snapshots. Set-semantics + idempotent inverses are enough, and the hardest part is not the algorithm but making the UI tell the truth. We also learned to keep the agent surface small — 5 tools and one negotiable ChangeSet are more legible than a toolbox of approvals. Built solo for my first hackathon, it was also a crash course in reading specs before building. ## What's next for Redini-Atelier Redini stays a small, reusable guard. Next we want to make it a tiny npm module with a cleaner validate(op, priorOps?) contract, add opt-in persistence for history, and try the same pattern on other domains — dashboards, forms, planning tools — where one agent intent naturally touches several related fields. Code is MIT at https://github.com/cioffiAI/redini-atelier — v1.0.0-challenge is frozen, main stays open. about_excerpt: Plan, preview, and pack with AI. Just tell ChatGPT what you're bringing, and through WebMCP it automatically generates a physically optimized 3D packing plan broken down by layers and order to pack. Like Comment Story Updates Labled Layers Packed, labeled Empty Closed Duffel bag Backpack Inspiration I always procrastinate packing until the very last minute, then struggle to find what belongs where even if I already have a packing list in mind. After I guess where everything should go and then rearrange my suitcase a dozen times, I finally come to find that it doesn't fit. With AI becoming good at understanding what we need through context and chatlogs, I wanted to create a tool for ChatGPT to express a simple request into something physical and visual that we could actually use. What it does Paqly turns any packing list into a 3D packing plan that you can breakdown into clearly labeled layers. Instead of organizing and planning what to put and where, you can simply tell ChatGPT what you want to bring or even just ask ChatGPT to create a list for you. ChatGPT would then communicate with Paqly directly through WebMCP and create a 3D visual based on the specified suitcase and items. With Paqly, you are able to see where each item should go, which layer it belongs in, the order in which each item should be packed, how much of the suitcase is filled and whether the packing list actually fits. How I built it The core of Paqly is a WebMCP integration that exposes packing functionality directly to AI agents. Rather than requiring an agent to navigate the website like a human and click through forms, Paqly exposes structured tools that allow ChatGPT to send packing information directly to the application. From there, the packing system takes the item dimensions and suitcase constraints, determines an arrangement, groups the result into packing layers, validates the placement, and passes that result into the interactive 3D visualisation. A lot of the work also went into making the output understandable. A mathematically valid arrangement is not very useful if a person cannot tell what they are looking at, so the 3D view includes item labels, separated layers, a re-playable packing order and an interactive suitcase view. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the packing plan physically believable rather than just visually impressive. Early versions could technically place objects inside the scene while still producing obviously bad results: items could overlap, float, extend outside the suitcase or leave large amounts of wasted space. This meant I had to treat validation separately from visual rendering and continuously check that the generated arrangement actually made sense. Another challenge was the WebMCP integration itself. I wanted the AI to interact with Paqly through structured WebMCP tools rather than simply using browser automation to click around the interface. Finally, 3D packing is much harder than displaying a normal list. Different objects have different dimensions, orientations and levels of compressibility, while the final result still needs to be simple enough for someone to reproduce with a real suitcase. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Paqly goes beyond giving packing advice. You can describe what you are trying to pack like thinking aloud and get back an actual spatial plan showing where everything should go, and the combination of AI, WebMCP and interactive 3D makes the result easier to obtain and follow. I'm also proud of how much the physical packing and visualisation improved throughout development. What started as basic object placement became a layered system with packing order, fit validation and a much clearer 3D representation of the suitcase. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving AI tools is much more interesting than simply putting an AI chatbot inside a website. WebMCP lets the AI interact with the actual functionality of Paqly. The AI handles the vibes, while Paqly handles the specialised packing logic and visualisation. I also learned how quickly a 3D system can look correct while being physically wrong. Building this forced me to think much more carefully about constraints, validation and the difference between generating something that looks good and generating something that actually works. What's next for Paqly The next step is making Paqly understand more about the real world. I want it to support a much larger library of real items, better modelling of soft and compressible objects, different suitcase types and more advanced physical optimisation to better simulate a real packing environment. I want it to be able to mathematically find not just the optimal placement for each item, but the optimal fold, the optimal angle, and other features that make a paq perfect. pitch: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time.
about_excerpt: Design tomorrow’s living spaces, one room and invention at a time. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Design future living spaces through natural conversation. A user-created future floor plan, edited through WebMCP. Export the current floor plan exactly as it appears. Inspect, propose, validate, and apply floor-plan changes. Inspiration When I first used a computer as a child, there was something I wanted even more than a game: software that would let me design my own floor plans. I dreamed of moving walls, expanding rooms, and placing devices that did not yet exist—as naturally as drawing ideas on paper. Today, many floor-planning tools are available. However, I wondered whether designing a home could become more accessible and imaginative if people could simply describe what they wanted instead of learning specialized controls. That idea inspired me to build HABITAT//NULL, a future floor-plan simulator powered by WebMCP. What It Does HABITAT//NULL is a floor-plan simulator where users and AI collaboratively imagine future living spaces. Users can describe changes in natural language, such as: “Make the kitchen larger.” “Split this room at a 60/40 ratio.” “Turn this area into a parking space.” Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the current floor plan, propose a change, validate it, and apply it to the design. The project is not limited to conventional furniture. It is also designed to let users invent and place their own futuristic tools, devices, and living systems. Completed floor plans can be saved as PNG or PDF files exactly as they appear on the screen. Rather than simply optimizing existing homes, HABITAT//NULL aims to turn imagined ways of living—things that do not yet exist—into visible spaces. How I Built It The floor plan is managed as structured data representing rooms, walls, openings, furniture, and equipment. The visual floor plan is generated from this underlying data. I created WebMCP tools that allow AI to inspect the current layout, propose modifications, validate the result, and apply an approved proposal. This allows the AI to understand and manipulate the structure of the floor plan instead of relying on screen coordinates or button positions. Changes are first created as proposals rather than being applied immediately. After the proposal has been reviewed, the exact change can be committed to the current floor plan. The visual design combines understated science fiction with the nostalgic feeling of a hand-drawn architectural plan. I wanted the interface to suggest a quiet, deteriorated future where advanced equipment still survives among worn materials and old records. Challenges The most difficult challenge was translating ambiguous natural-language requests into precise floor-plan operations. For example, “Make the kitchen larger” raises several questions: Which wall should move? How much space should be taken from the neighboring room? What should happen to doors, furniture, and connected spaces? Changing a room’s size requires more than updating its dimensions. The relationships among walls, openings, routes, and placed objects must remain consistent. Another challenge was making the entire workflow possible through WebMCP. Creating a proposal was not enough—the AI also needed to inspect, validate, and apply the change without requiring unnecessary manual interaction. It was also important to avoid adding too many unrelated features. I continually returned to the project’s essential experience: letting users reshape a floor plan through conversation. What I Learned This project taught me that WebMCP is more than a way to automate browser interactions. It can become a structured communication layer between an AI agent and a web application. When the AI understands the meaning of rooms, walls, and openings—not just their appearance on the screen—users can express their intentions naturally without learning specialized software controls. I also learned that giving an AI freedom is not enough to create a trustworthy experience. Users need to see proposed changes, verify the results, and clearly understand what will be applied. A proposal-and-approval workflow makes collaboration with AI both safer and easier to understand. What’s Next Next, I want to give users more freedom to create and place their own furniture, machines, and imagined future systems. I would also like to support multi-story buildings and unconventional environments such as fantasy homes, spacecraft, and underground shelters. My goal is to develop HABITAT//NULL into more than a tool for selecting or editing existing floor plans. I want it to become a place where users and AI can invent new ways of living together. Prompt Lab — an agent-ready prompt library where humans and AI can create, organize, and reuse prompts together through WebMCP.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Prompt engineering is becoming an important part of how people work with AI, but good prompts are often scattered across documents, chats, notes, and different AI tools. 

 We wanted to build a place where prompts could be treated as reusable assets rather than disposable messages. 

 That led to Prompt Lab — an agent-ready prompt library where humans can create, organise, improve, and reuse prompts, while AI agents can interact with the same library through WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Prompt Lab helps users: 

 
 Create and organise reusable prompts 
 Group prompts into categories 
 Build specialised AI agents 
 Generate prompts through agent conversations 
 Select and save useful prompts directly from the chat 
 Search, update, and manage an existing prompt library 
 

 With WebMCP, Prompt Lab also exposes structured actions to AI agents. 

 Instead of an agent visually interpreting the interface and guessing which buttons to click, it can discover supported actions such as creating, searching, retrieving, or updating prompts and execute them directly through the website. 

 This creates a shared workspace where both humans and agents can work with the same underlying prompt library. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Prompt Lab is a strong fit for WebMCP because the product contains many structured actions that are useful to both people and AI agents. 

 Traditionally, an AI interacting with a website may need to rely on screenshots, DOM interpretation, or browser automation. 

 WebMCP allows us to expose the capabilities of Prompt Lab explicitly. 

 For example, an agent can understand that the application supports actions such as: 

 
 search_prompts 
 get_prompt 
 create_prompt 
 update_prompt 
 delete_prompt 
 create_agent 
 get_agent_prompts 
 

 This makes agent interactions more reliable, understandable, and efficient. 

 It also creates a better user experience because a user can describe what they want naturally while the agent performs structured operations within Prompt Lab. 

 How we built it 

 Prompt Lab was built as a modern web application using React, TypeScript, Vite, and supporting backend/data services. 

 We designed the product around two main experiences: 

 
 A human-facing prompt management interface 
 An agent-facing capability layer powered by WebMCP 
 

 For the WebMCP implementation, we registered application capabilities using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 Each tool includes a clear description, input schema, validation, execution logic, and structured output. 

 Where possible, the WebMCP tools reuse the same underlying application logic as the normal user interface rather than creating a completely separate system. 

 This means both humans and agents operate on the same prompt data and workflows. 

 We also designed the agent chat so generated prompts can become interactive content directly inside the AI response. Users can select the prompts they want and save them into their library without switching to a separate workflow. 

 Challenges we faced 

 One of the biggest challenges was understanding how WebMCP should fit into an existing product architecture. 

 It was tempting to treat WebMCP as a separate integration layer with duplicated application logic, but we learned that a better approach is to expose existing product capabilities through shared services. 

 We also faced challenges around: 

 
 Detecting whether WebMCP was available in the current browser environment 
 Preventing duplicate tool registration during development 
 Keeping the application functional in browsers without WebMCP support 
 Designing tool schemas that were simple for agents to understand 
 Making agent-generated prompts interactive without duplicating the same content elsewhere in the UI 
 Maintaining a consistent experience between human-driven and agent-driven actions 
 

 Another challenge was designing the demo itself. We wanted to demonstrate WebMCP as more than browser automation, so we focused on showing an agent interacting with Prompt Lab through clearly defined application capabilities. 

 What we learned 

 The project changed how we think about websites designed for AI agents. 

 A website no longer has to expose functionality only through buttons, forms, and visual interfaces. 

 With WebMCP, applications can expose their capabilities directly to agents while still maintaining a normal interface for humans. 

 We learned that the strongest implementation is not about adding as many tools as possible. It is about exposing a small set of useful, well-defined actions that map directly to real product capabilities. 

 We also learned that designing for humans and agents together creates new product possibilities. Instead of replacing the human interface, the agent becomes another way of interacting with the same application. 

 What's next 

 We would like to continue developing Prompt Lab into a broader collaborative prompt workspace. 

 Future improvements could include: 

 
 Prompt version history 
 Shared team libraries 
 Agent-created prompt collections 
 Prompt performance and evaluation data 
 More advanced search and filtering 
 Additional WebMCP capabilities 
 Cross-agent prompt sharing 
 Collaborative workflows where humans review and approve agent-generated changes 
 

 Our broader goal is to explore what software looks like when websites are designed from the beginning for both humans and AI agents .
