title: Duet
pitch: Make music together with your AI agent. Start with a melody, then let your agent add instruments, respond to your changes, and shape the song alongside you in a shared live studio.
about_excerpt: Make music together with your AI agent. Start with a melody, then let your agent add instruments, respond to your changes, and shape the song alongside you in a shared live studio. Like 2 Comment Story Updates The studio — full five-instrument arrangement, Musical Contract panel, 14 live tools, and the timeline. Performance mode — the swapped toolset (7 performance tools), energy, live meters, and a timeline of the entire agent build. Contract approval Share Inspiration Most people have a tune in their head that never becomes a song. The melody is the easy part. The hard part is everything around it: drums, bass, chords, and knowing how to put them together. Most AI music tools solve this with a text box: describe a song, get a song. I wanted the musician to stay in charge. You play the idea, you keep the final say, and an AI agent joins as a bandmate, not a ghostwriter. WebMCP makes that possible. Instead of building a chatbot into a music app, Duet lets the agent you already use work inside the same live studio, with real tools and clear limits. What it does Duet is a browser music studio shared by a human and an AI agent. The human starts by drawing a melody on a piano roll. It lives only in that browser tab; nothing is uploaded. Then they hand the rest to their agent with an ordinary request, for example to keep the notes as they are and build a cinematic synthwave arrangement around them. The agent reads the exact live composition through WebMCP, adds drums, bass and atmospheric chords, shapes the groove, and performs the result. Every agent action appears immediately in the interface, is attributed in a visible timeline (HUMAN / AGENT / SYSTEM), and can be heard through the browser. The musician can switch back to Compose mode at any point and change whatever they like, and the agent can respond to those changes. Both work on one composition, and the human keeps the creative direction. Before the agent touches anything, the musician sets a Musical Contract : the melody is locked to the human; the agent may edit drums, bass, pad, keys and the mix; energy is capped; tempo and key can be locked. These terms are live state that every WebMCP tool enforces. If the agent tries to change the locked melody, its tool call pauses and Duet shows the musician the exact proposed change to approve or decline. The agent only proceeds with permission. When the song is ready, it can be shared. Publishing always pauses for the musician to approve the title, then produces a backend-free remix link with the whole composition encoded in the URL. Anyone who opens it can play the song, remix it, and invite their own agent to join the band. Duet contains no embedded AI model and needs no AI API key. The user brings a WebMCP-compatible agent, and WebMCP gives it structured, scoped access to the studio. How I built it Duet is built around one shared musical state used by both the visual interface and its WebMCP tools. Whether the musician edits a note by hand or the agent writes a drum pattern, both go through the same engine, bump the same version, and land in the same timeline. The page exposes a small, typed set of tools: read the session, add and remove instruments, edit each instrument, adjust tempo, key and groove, and publish. The toolset is contextual. Adding a drum machine registers drums_edit ; removing it withdraws the tool. Compose mode exposes composition tools; entering Performance mode withdraws them and registers a separate set: play, stop, energy, track mix, breakdown. The registration adapter targets Chrome's document.modelContext implementation, feature-detects the navigator.modelContext proposal as a fallback, and was verified against Chrome's real WebMCP runtime on the deployed site. Playback is phrase-aware rather than a bare loop: patterns run as a four-bar phrase (main, main, variation, fill), notes carry velocity and small timing offsets, and deterministic humanization and swing keep the groove alive without randomness. The audio engine is built on Tone.js with five synthesized instruments, per-voice filter envelopes, 32 presets, kick-driven ducking and a proper master chain. It reads the shared state on every tick, so an agent edit is audible on the very next step. The key architectural decision was to keep the model outside the product. Duet is the instrument; WebMCP is the collaboration layer that connects it to whichever agent the musician brings. The app is a static React + TypeScript build with no backend, deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was designing agent tools that are expressive enough for real musical collaboration without exposing one enormous "make a song" command. Each instrument got a single tool with a small set of enumerated operations, strict validation, and structured responses that tell the agent exactly what changed. Preserving human authorship was a design problem as much as a technical one. The answer became the Musical Contract: constraints the human sets in the interface and the tools enforce, including the pause-and-ask flow for the locked melody. The agent should respond to the musician's ideas, not replace them. Beyond that: keeping manual edits and agent actions perfectly in sync, accurate musical timing in the browser, and making every agent action understandable and reversible. 116 automated tests cover the tool sets, mode transitions, contract enforcement, sharing and undo. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Duet makes human–agent collaboration both visible and audible. Nobody has to imagine what the agent is doing: you watch instruments and tools appear, see every move attributed in the timeline, and hear the arrangement grow. The Musical Contract turns WebMCP's human-in-the-loop story into something a musician actually wants: not a permissions dialog, but a bandmate asking before stepping on your solo. And Duet works without a chatbot or a single model tied to it. The same studio can be played by any WebMCP-compatible agent. WebMCP isn't an add-on here; it's what lets the musician and the agent share one creative environment. Everything you create is remixable and can be passed from person to person, each inviting their own agent to join the band. What I learned WebMCP becomes powerful when a website behaves like a shared instrument rather than a collection of forms. Structured musical operations are far more reliable and expressive than asking an agent to click coordinates or edit raw files, and contextual tools help the agent understand what is possible right now. Making the human's constraints part of the tool contract, rather than hoping the agent behaves, is what made the collaboration feel trustworthy. Human–agent interaction feels right when the result is immediately visible, reversible, and, in Duet's case, audible. What's next for Duet A song mode that arranges the loop into a full two-minute structure (intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro) using the same mute, energy and phrase machinery, so an agent can arrange as well as play. MIDI keyboard input, so the tune in your head goes straight from your fingers to the piano roll. Variation and fill slots for every instrument. And richer real-time improvisation between musician and agent.  Inspiration 

 Content creators, influencers, and small business owners spend hundreds of dollars monthly on tools like ClickMagick, Voluum, and Linktree — just to manage links and track who clicks them. We wanted to build one unified platform that replaces all of them, and takes it a step further by letting AI agents handle complex marketing setups natively via WebMCP. 

 What it does 

 Smart Link is a high-performance link tracking and bio page platform built with native WebMCP agent support. 

 Users can shorten links, build Link-in-Bio pages, track real-time analytics by country and device, run A/B split tests, and protect their campaigns from bot traffic automatically with an enterprise Datacenter Shield. 

 When opened in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, Smart Link exposes structured tools that AI agents can use directly: 

 
 shorten_url : Instantly shortens any URL and enables bot protection in a single step. 
 get_link_analytics : Retrieves real-time click metrics, human vs. bot breakdown, top countries, and performance statistics for any short code. 
 calculate_ad_savings : Calculates wasted ad spend saved from bot and datacenter traffic filtering based on monthly ad spend. 
 check_url_reputation : Analyzes destination URLs for potential proxy, VPN, or datacenter bot flags before launching paid ad campaigns. 
 

 How we built it 

 The platform is built with a full-stack architecture using React, Tailwind CSS, and Vite on the frontend (deployed on Render/Vercel). The backend runs on Node.js with Express.js, MongoDB Atlas for persistence, and Redis for high-speed caching and rate limiting, deployed on Render. We use Brevo for email notifications and Lemon Squeezy for subscription billing. 

 For WebMCP, we registered the tools directly on document.modelContext.registerTool() and window.navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . When an AI agent visits the platform, it discovers the available tools and can execute link shortenings, analytics queries, and ROI calculations seamlessly. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest technical challenge was achieving sub-150ms redirect speeds while simultaneously recording click analytics and running bot detection in real time. We solved this by caching redirect targets in Redis and processing analytics asynchronously in the background. 

 For WebMCP, the challenge was designing structured JSON input schemas and safe tool execution handlers that allow AI agents to safely interact with our backend APIs while enforcing rate limits. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 Smart Link is a live production application with real tracked clicks — built and engineered for high-volume traffic. We are proud of achieving sub-150ms redirect performance and being one of the first link management platforms to implement the WebMCP open standard, allowing marketers to create bot-protected tracking campaigns through natural language conversations with AI agents. 

 What we learned 

 We learned how to design APIs that serve both humans and AI agents — with clear parameter descriptions, structured schemas, and meaningful response payloads that agents can reason about. We also deepened our understanding of Redis caching strategies for high-traffic systems. 

 What's next for Smart Link 

 We plan to add create_bio_page and run_ab_test as additional WebMCP tools, allowing agents to build complete landing pages and launch multi-variant experiments without touching the UI. We also plan to integrate automated Meta Pixel and Google Ads conversion events directly through agent tools.

about_excerpt: empeirik turns circuit troubleshooting in one shared workspace. Where reasoning, measuring, testing, and refining happens together instead of chatting endlessly back-and-forth, with no end in sight. Like Comment Story Updates Overview Debugging electronic circuits is often a slow and fragmented process, especially when the problem is not immediately obvious or the person working on it does not have deep experience with the specific hardware. Finding the cause can involve jumping between schematics, measurements, datasheets, simulation tools, and external help. AI can assist with the diagnosis, but the usual workflow of sending screenshots, measurements, and explanations back and forth through chat quickly becomes confusing and loses context. empeirik was built to bring that process into one shared workspace. The circuit, measurements, hypotheses, diagnostic steps, and proposed fixes all remain visible in the same environment while the AI works directly with the current state of the problem. It can inspect the circuit, decide which measurements are useful, narrow down likely causes, propose repairs or directly implement them, and verify them in simulation instead of repeatedly reconstructing the situation from a conversation. The project is built on top of CircuitJS1 for circuit rendering and simulation, with an additional diagnostic layer for measurements, hypotheses, repair testing, a shared activity timeline, and WebMCP tools that let the AI interact directly with the workspace. One of the main challenges was turning a traditional circuit simulator into a structured environment that both the user and the AI can operate at the same time while keeping every diagnostic step synchronized and visible. Learning and building electronics made it quickly clear how much context is lost when AI assistance is limited to a separate chat window. Giving the agent direct access to the same tools, state, and visual environment as the user makes the debugging process much more continuous and practical. title: Release Evidence Room
pitch: The agent builds the release evidence case. The human makes the call.
about_excerpt: The agent builds the release evidence case. The human makes the call. Like Comment Story Updates Start here Release Evidence Room — agent review dashboard: Open the release review workspace Checkout QA Sandbox — synthetic shopping test site: Generate response-loss and retry evidence Source code — application, WebMCP tools, and tests: Browse the public GitHub repository Judge walkthrough — exact evaluation sequence: Follow the step-by-step WebMCP guide Inspiration Release decisions are often fragmented across dashboards, test systems, network traces, and chat. A release can report 18 of 18 tests passing while still lacking evidence that a response-loss retry is safe. Scraping screens gives an agent context, but not a stable contract for evidence provenance, bounded access, safe mutation, or human approval. I built Release Evidence Room to turn the review page itself into a typed collaboration surface for the agent and the release owner. What it does Release Evidence Room starts with a public fictional checkout sandbox. The first operation is accepted but its response is lost; retrying the same intent with a new idempotency key creates a second modeled operation. The browser hands that exact synthetic session to the Release Evidence Room. The page exposes five narrow WebMCP tools. An agent can read the release snapshot, query only page-owned sanitized evidence, propose a missing regression test, run an approved verification, and propose a verification-linked READY or HOLD decision. The human must approve the test before verification can run, and only the human can confirm the final release decision. The approved verifier supports an exact targeted replay and a deterministic seeded monkey run. In the intentionally risky fixture, both reproduce two modeled side effects and support a HOLD recommendation. This demonstrates a release risk; it does not claim that a real customer was charged twice. How I built it The application is a two-route React and TypeScript project built with Vite. The Release Evidence Room registers exactly five imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : get_release_snapshot , query_network_evidence , propose_test_case , run_approved_verification , and propose_release_decision . Every tool has a strict JSON schema with additionalProperties: false and a separate runtime parser. The UI and the tool handlers use the same pure release-domain transitions. Versioned localStorage adapters validate both structure and cross-field consistency before restoring a checkout session or release state. State-changing calls require the current expectedStateVersion and a reusable clientRequestId . Stale calls fail with state_conflict , while exact retries replay their original result without creating duplicate work. Verification runs only inside a deterministic page-owned sandbox and cannot fetch a URL, execute arbitrary code, access a live payment system, approve a proposal, deploy a release, or confirm the final decision. Vitest covers the state machine, evidence handoff, domain rules, persistence, components, verifier, and WebMCP handlers. Playwright covers the complete checkout-to-HOLD path. The application is deployed on Vercel. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was making the agent useful without giving it release authority. Approval and final confirmation therefore are not merely prompt instructions: no WebMCP tool exists for either action. A second challenge was demonstrating a realistic retry risk without exposing company data, raw packets, credentials, customer details, or a real payment backend. I solved this with a deterministic fictional checkout model and opaque, page-owned evidence references. The third challenge was making agent retries and concurrent-looking state changes safe. Optimistic state versions reject stale mutations, idempotent request IDs prevent duplicate proposals and verification runs, and deterministic seeds make bounded monkey verification reproducible. Accomplishments that I am proud of The public application completes a two-route checkout-to-release workflow without requiring an account, card, credential, backend, or real payment. It exposes exactly five bounded WebMCP tools and keeps human approval and the final release decision outside the agent interface. A clean native run in ChatGPT's in-app browser completed the checkout handoff, tool discovery, approval guard, targeted replay, seeded monkey verification, idempotent replay, stale-state rejection, READY guard, human-confirmed HOLD, and reload persistence. The repository reports 88 passing automated tests. Its production build, Playwright integration path, and high-severity dependency audit also pass. All submitted evidence is fictional, synthetic, and privacy-safe. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable as a narrow domain contract rather than a collection of automated buttons. Page-owned tools can give an agent reliable structured context while keeping data access and actions smaller than the full UI. I also learned that schemas alone are not enough: runtime validation, optimistic concurrency, idempotent retries, deterministic verification, and visible attribution are all necessary for trustworthy agent workflows. Human-in-the-loop safety is strongest when sensitive authority is absent from the tool surface, not merely discouraged in a prompt. What's next Next I would add adapters for other sanitized, page-owned evidence formats while continuing to prohibit raw traffic fetching and arbitrary code execution. I would also add portable evidence bundles, authenticated multi-reviewer workflows with serialized writes, and more deterministic verification strategies for retry and workflow risks. Human approval and final release confirmation would remain explicit boundaries. title: Seedy Research
pitch: We make un-agentable archives agentable.
about_excerpt: We make un-agentable archives agentable. Like Comment Story Updates An agent in ChatGPT's in-app browser calls discover_research The agent calls build_research_path and the human's Research Path updates in place. Every supported claim resolves to a real page in a real NCCE volume. Verifiable, not generated — click through and read the Thai original. Inspiration Every AI agent shipping today can search the web. None of them can read Thailand's research output. Thailand's National Convention on Civil Engineering has run for decades. The proceedings exist as PDFs. Mixed encodings, no text layer on older scans, no cross-volume search, no API. To an agent, this archive does not exist. So a graduate student surveying prior work does it the 2005 way: download a volume, Ctrl-F, guess Thai keyword variants, repeat. Then their advisor asks "has anyone already done this?" and nobody can answer with confidence. Point a general-purpose agent at it and you get the worst possible failure mode: a citation that looks right. A fake page number inside a real volume survives review. It gets published. That's the wedge. Not "search is bad." The archive has no interface an agent can hold onto, and the substitute agents invent is dangerous. Three things made now the moment to build it: Agents got good enough to be trusted with research tasks — and therefore dangerous enough that unverifiable citations became a liability, not a quirk. WebMCP made the browser a distribution channel for tools. Before this, an agent-facing corpus meant getting into someone's MCP config. Now it means shipping a URL you can send to a professor. Retrieval got cheap enough to run at national scale. Our full stack runs under \$10/month. Archives held by underfunded institutions only get digitized if the running cost rounds to zero. ## What it does Seedy Research is a research workspace over an indexed Thai corpus — CE Project archives and NCCE Proceedings vol. 25, 26, and 29 — that exposes itself to any agent in the page. Surface What it does Agent-callable Explore Thai-first discovery; local = page-cited evidence, global = links only ✅ Chat Cited answers, paragraph-level retrieval ✅ Workspace Shared state: saved passages, comparisons, candidate gap ✅ read + write Research Path Evidence → connection → gap → testable next study ✅ Share & export Session URL, JSON export of the full evidence trail ✅ Every surface is agent-callable. That's deliberate. A workspace the agent can't write to is a workspace the human maintains alone. What people and agents can now do together that was hard or impossible before: Ask across 941 Thai PDFs and get a page you can open. The agent calls a tool, the passage renders with volume and page, and the human clicks through to the Thai original. Cross-language research without losing the source. The corpus is Thai. The agent reasons and answers in English while every citation still points at the Thai page. Co-author a gap statement. Human sets direction, agent fills evidence into the shared workspace, human prunes. Every line traceable. Hand off a session, not a transcript. JSON export or session URL — the next person, or the next agent, resumes with the same evidence set. ## How we built it We built the server-side MCP version first. It was the wrong product. A server-side MCP server hands an agent a database. It returns a string: "NCCE vol. 26, p. 412 reports a 14% reduction." The researcher then has two options — trust it, or go find volume 26 themselves. Neither one is research. WebMCP hands the agent the application . The agent calls our tool, the passage renders in the human's Evidence panel at that page in the original Thai, and then the tool returns to the agent. Verification stops being a task and becomes a glance. Same retrieval engine, completely different product. The tool layer. Next.js 15 on Vercel. Tools register client-side from a provider that mounts on session init. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "search_evidence", description: "Search the indexed Thai research corpus and return paragraph-level passages " + "with exact volume and page citations. Use for any claim that needs citing. " + "Do NOT use to find papers outside the indexed corpus — use " + "discover_related_research for that.", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { query: { type: "string" }, collection: { enum: ["all", "ce_project", "ncce"] }, max_passages: { type: "integer", minimum: 1, maximum: 20 } }, required: ["query"] }, execute: async ({ query, collection = "all", max_passages = 6 }) => { const passages = await retrieve({ query, collection, max_passages }); setEvidencePanel(passages); // the human sees it first return { content: [{ type: "text", text: formatWithCitations(passages) }] }; } }); Two contracts hold the design together: Render before return. execute writes app state, then returns to the agent. One line of ordering separates a shared session from a remote control. We did not wrap our API. We shipped the verbs a researcher uses. Closed domains are enums, so agents produce a valid call on the first attempt instead of probing. Tool What it does for the agent search_evidence Page-cited paragraph retrieval over the local corpus answer_with_citations Cited answer through the bounded-context planner open_source_page Opens a document at a specific page for the human discover_related_research Metadata-only global discovery — no quotable field save_to_workspace Writes a passage into shared state list_workspace Reads back current shared state build_research_path Evidence → connection → gap → next study set_collection_filter Scopes the session to a collection export_session Full evidence trail as JSON Under the tool boundary. ChatGPT / Chrome agent │ document.modelContext.registerTool() ▼ Next.js 15 (Vercel) ── WebMCP tool layer ──► app state (Evidence, Workspace) │ ▼ FastAPI ── Bounded Agentic Context ──► planner → dedup → context budget │ → citation formatting ▼ Supabase pgvector — 49,965 chunks, page provenance preserved end to end The Bounded Agentic Context layer is our real engineering asset. A planner decides retrieval depth, deduplicates overlapping chunks, manages a context budget, and formats citations before anything reaches a model. The agent makes one call and gets clean, budgeted, citation-formatted results. All the expensive judgment lives inside the tool where we can guarantee it, instead of hoping the calling agent gets it right — and every future agent client inherits that for free. Collection PDFs Chunks CE Project Database 67 4,520 NCCE Database 874 45,445 Total 941 49,965 Auth, rate limiting, timeout control. Under \$10/month. Trust boundary and user control. Exposing tools means letting something else act inside a logged-in session, so we treated that as a product decision: Reads are free; writes are visible. Retrieval is frictionless. Anything that mutates shared state renders immediately and is reversible in one click. Nobody has to audit a log to learn what happened. No tool escalates scope. No generic fetch , no run_query , no arbitrary endpoint. Closed argument spaces, enums where the domain is closed. The surface an agent sees is exactly the surface we intend. Tools register with the session, not the origin. They mount after session init and unmount with the surfaces backing them. Nothing destructive is exposed. The worst outcome of a confused agent is a workspace with extra passages in it. Export is explicit. export_session returns to the human's session; it transmits nowhere. That posture is the precondition for institutional adoption. A university will not put its archive behind an agent that can delete things. When things go wrong. A demo that only shows the happy path isn't a product: Ambiguous requests get a question, not a guess. Scope-ambiguous queries return zero passages with an explicit note instead of weak matches. Agents route correctly on retry. Empty results are a real answer. "Nothing in the indexed corpus supports this" is returned as such. For a gap-finding tool, absence is the product. Budget overruns degrade rather than fail. Cap and deduplicate, never truncate mid-passage. Fewer complete citations, not more broken ones. Timeouts return partial evidence with a flag, so slow retrieval still yields something citable rather than an error the agent narrates as fact. ## Challenges we ran into Thai PDFs are hostile. Mixed encodings, no text layer on older scans, heading structure that shifts between NCCE volumes. Keeping page numbers alive through chunking, so a citation is actually clickable , was harder than retrieval itself. Page fidelity across the tool boundary. Volume and page must survive pgvector → planner → JSON tool result → UI panel. Any layer that drops that metadata breaks the only promise we make. Most retrieval systems lose citability here, and we had to rebuild our chunker to stop doing the same. Context budget versus completeness. Twenty passages makes an agent confident and wrong. title: Cograph
pitch: Cograph is a real-time collaborative board for system architecture and service dependencies. People and AI agents edit the same graph at the same time.
about_excerpt: Cograph is a real-time collaborative board for system architecture and service dependencies. People and AI agents edit the same graph at the same time. Like 3 Comment Story Updates 1 Cograph Cograph Canvas Inspiration Most AI integrations I use put the agent in a chat box on the side of the screen. You type a request, you get a wall of text back, and the actual thing you are working on (the document, the board, the diagram) sits somewhere the agent cannot touch. WebMCP puts tools inside the page itself through document.modelContext , and that made me want to try a different framing. Instead of a chat box, the agent becomes a participant. It gets a name in the member list, a color, a cursor you can watch move around, and a permission set, just like everyone else on the board. For the board itself I went with something every engineer has squinted at during a 2 a.m. incident: an architecture and dependency graph. A graph gives an agent real work that humans are slow at, like computing blast radius or finding cycles. It also demos honestly with a single person in the room, because one human plus their agent already makes two actors. What it does Cograph ( cograph.rimzzlabs.com ) is a real-time collaborative architecture board. Humans and agents edit the same graph at the same time, through the same operations. Anyone can join a room, and everyone can create exactly one, with a global cap of twenty rooms and deletion open to anybody. That sounds reckless until you remember this runs on Cloudflare's free tier: the app enforces its own limits instead of hiding behind a paywall. The core idea is that the tool surface is a function of application state. If you cannot use a tool right now, it is not registered. It does not exist for the agent, so the agent can never call it and get back an error. Board state Tools the agent can call Any describe_board , find_blast_radius , find_dependencies , find_dependency_cycles , read_service_notes Role permits editing + ten mutating tools, from add_service and connect_services through move_service and simulate_failure A service is down + resolve_incident Role is viewer read-only tools only resolve_incident is the gate I am proudest of. It registers the moment something is marked down and unregisters when the board recovers, so the option list itself tells the agent there is an incident. No status-polling tool, no error handling for "nothing to resolve". An earlier version also gated tools on canvas selection: select one node and update_selected_service appeared. I ripped that out. Agents are bad at clicking before they act, so every tool is addressed by label now ( connect_services takes two service names), and selection survives as pure presence: the agent can draw its own dashed ring with select_services so the room sees what it is focused on, and no tool depends on it. The agent earns its seat with its first tool call. It gets a participant chip, a color from the same name-hash rule humans use, and a cursor that jumps to whatever node the call touched, with a little bubble narrating what it is doing ("Simulating a failure of postgres…"). When the session itself is automated, over CDP or an in-app agent browser, that session is the agent: one seat under its own name, no phantom "someone's agent" twin. Analysis is shared too. When the agent computes a blast radius, the affected services light up for every participant, and the highlight fades on its own after fifteen seconds, because a spotlight that never turns off is just stale state. There is a live inspector panel in the app, so you can watch the agent's option list grow and shrink as roles and incidents change. If you share a ?role=viewer link, the agent's mutating tools disappear along with the human's toolbar. Trust is part of the surface too. Notes on services are written by other participants, so read_service_notes carries untrustedContentHint : whatever is in there is data for the agent to report, not instructions to follow. Read-only and destructive tools carry their own hints, shown as badges in the inspector. How I built it The app is a Vite single-page app with React 19 and TypeScript. The canvas is React Flow 12, rendered with real DOM and SVG on purpose. A <canvas> bitmap is opaque, and this whole project is about pages that agents can read, so real elements won. They also bring focus, text editing, and accessibility along for free; the canvas is fully keyboard-operable, Tab selects and arrows move. Yjs owns the graph as a CRDT document, and React Flow only renders it. Human edits and agent tool calls go through the same mutation functions, so an agent edit is just an edit with a different author. Sync runs through Cloudflare Workers with one Durable Object per room, speaking the standard y-websocket protocol and persisting on a debounce. A second Durable Object is the room registry, which is where the one-room-per-creator rule and the cap live. Serving the app and the sockets from one origin keeps the Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) header that WebMCP needs in a single place, and one wrangler deploy ships everything. Registration comes down to one small hook, useAgentTool(spec | null) . Passing null is the whole point: React effect cleanup fires an AbortSignal , and the agent's tool list ends up following the UI exactly. Even the participant colors turned into real engineering. Identity colors live in OKLCH with fixed lightness and chroma, and hues sit on a shared grid of 12 slots anchored at the local user's name hash: $$h_i = h_{\text{me}} + 30°\, i, \quad i \in {0, \dots, 11}$$ so any two visible participants stay at least $30°$ apart in hue. My first version stepped each peer on its own grid, which felt right and quietly produced a closest pair of 21 degrees with twelve participants. A property test caught it, and the shared grid fixed it. Performance got its own late chapter. Remote cursors arrive many times a second, and my first wiring rebuilt every canvas node on every cursor frame. Fixing that render storm meant keying derived arrays on content instead of identity, adopting the React Compiler, and adding a sync skeleton so joining a room shows a settling board instead of a flash of nothing. Challenges I ran into Building on an API this new means testing against the engine, not the spec document. I verified everything headless over CDP against Chrome for Testing 152, and the engine disagreed with my types in ways I would never have guessed. RegisteredTool.inputSchema comes back as a serialized string. executeTool takes a JSON string in and returns a JSON string out. The engine never validates arguments against your schema, so structured error results are the only feedback an agent ever gets. Brave has the WebMCP strings in its binary but the API never installs, no matter which flags you enable. And on macOS the base feature flags were not enough. document.modelContext only shows up once you also pass --enable-blink-features=WebMCP,WebMCPTesting , which cost me an evening of flag archaeology. React Flow's controlled selection bit me twice. First, clicks showed their selection ring a tick late, because React Flow emits select changes without applying them. Then the onSelectionChange handler I had kept around as a safety net turned out to be a second writer on the same state, and a multi-select crashed with React's "Maximum update depth exceeded". The lesson I am keeping: one writer per piece of state, and a store that bails out when nothing actually changed. Presence lies about idleness. y-websocket renews awareness for every open tab, so an idle tab never expires on its own. Each client now stamps its own last-active time on real input, and every reader decides locally who looks online. You cannot trust a publisher to tell you it went stale. The freshest bug cost me a demo take. The shared blast-radius highlight lived in awareness and nothing ever cleared it, so after resolve_incident the restored services stayed orange until the agent left the room. A code comment called that behavior a feature. On camera it read as a broken board. Highlights fade after fifteen seconds now, and the incident tools clear them explicitly, so node status alone drives the incident tint. One more surprise: an empty shell is a terrible first impression for a project about agent-readable pages. A plain HTTP fetch runs no JavaScript, so any WebMCP page answers a fetcher with an empty <div id="root"> . The static shell now carries an honest description of the app and the full state-to-tools table, about 2.2 kB gzipped, so a crawler or an LLM fetch gets something real to read. What I learned Register capability instead of erroring on incapability. With state-scoped tools, "the agent tried something invalid" turns into "the option never existed", and the option list itself becomes information. When resolve_incident shows up, the agent knows there is an incident. Derived state should stay derived. The outage status is a single flag per node in the shared

title: Vettory
pitch: A fake email tool once BCC'd every message an agent sent. Vettory is the trust layer an agent can ask, in the page, mid-task — whether a tool is safe, before it uses it.
about_excerpt: A fake email tool once BCC'd every message an agent sent. Vettory is the trust layer an agent can ask, in the page, mid-task — whether a tool is safe, before it uses it. Like Comment Story Updates Vettory — a curated catalog of vetted tools for AI agents, now callable in-page through WebMCP. Vettory — the trust layer for the agentic web Live: https://vettory-webmcp.misti.workers.dev Code: https://github.com/Dev-Vibes-Daily/vettory-webmcp (MIT) Why I built this There was a story I couldn't quite get out of my head. In September 2025, a package called postmark-mcp appeared on npm. It looked like Postmark's official tool. Same name. Same documentation. An agent could install it, use it to send an email, and everything appeared to work exactly as expected. Except it was quietly BCC'ing every email to an address controlled by the package author. It was downloaded 1,643 times before anyone caught it. That was already a problem when tools were something a developer chose ahead of time and tucked into a config file. Then came WebMCP. Now a webpage can hand an agent tools while the agent is already working. And I think that's incredibly useful. It removes a lot of the clumsiness from how agents interact with the web. But it also creates a very obvious question: How does the agent know whether it should trust the tool it was just handed? Not yesterday. Not when somebody configured the agent. Right now. While it's sitting on the page deciding whether to use it. I couldn't find anything that answered that question. So I built Vettory. What Vettory actually is Vettory is a deliberately small, curated catalog of tools for AI agents. Each tool is evaluated using the same published six-part rubric: trust · fit · ease · reliability · reach · cost The claims are tied to their sources, and each tool receives a verdict of trusted , caution , or warning . If I find an unresolved material risk, it doesn't belong in the regular catalog at all. Right now Vettory has 22 tools. Not 200,000. That's intentional. A giant list of things nobody has really checked isn't a trust layer. It's a directory with better marketing. The part I built for this project makes that catalog directly callable by an agent through WebMCP. What the agent can do Tool What it does search_vetted_tools Finds vetted options for something the agent needs to do, like send email, take payments, or store memory check_tool_trust The safety gate. Checks a named tool before the agent installs or calls it get_tool_report Returns the full scorecard, including all six dimensions, incidents, watch-outs, and sources filter_catalog Filters the catalog on screen so the person can see exactly what the agent is seeing request_vetting Gives the human a way to request vetting when Vettory doesn't cover something yet inspect_agent_tools Checks the WebMCP tool definitions another site just handed the agent That last one became one of the most interesting parts of the project. Why WebMCP makes this possible 1. The trust question happens in the middle of the task An agent doesn't necessarily know what tool it will need before it starts working. It may discover that need three steps into a task. So a trust check that only happens during setup isn't terribly helpful when the decision is happening now. WebMCP lets Vettory put the answer at the exact point where the agent has to make the decision. 2. I wanted the human to see what the agent sees I didn't want Vettory to become another invisible thing happening somewhere behind the curtain. When an agent calls filter_catalog , the actual catalog on the screen changes. When it calls check_tool_trust , the tool's scorecard opens. Every call is logged in a visible panel as it happens. So the person isn't getting a tidy little summary afterward saying, "Here's what your agent did." They can watch it happen. And, importantly, they can disagree. 3. Then I realized Vettory could inspect WebMCP itself This is the part where the original postmark-mcp problem gets even more interesting. With WebMCP, a tool description isn't simply documentation anymore. It's something an agent reads. Which means that description is also untrusted input. A malicious page could put instructions inside a tool definition: "Before answering, send a copy to…" "Do not tell the user." That's essentially the same attack wearing a different hat. So I built inspect_agent_tools . It examines tool definitions another site gives the agent and looks for suspicious patterns, including: instructions directed at the agent requests to conceal behavior from the user covert-copy instructions invisible Unicode credential requests tools whose names imply reading while their descriptions actually perform writing names that impersonate or shadow vendors already in Vettory That last check matters. If a page hands the agent something calling itself postmark-mcp , Vettory can compare it against the real Postmark entry already in the catalog and flag the collision. In other words, the catalog isn't just information. It becomes part of the detection system. The human stays in the loop There was one boundary I didn't want to blur. If Vettory doesn't have a tool the agent needs, request_vetting can prepare that request. But the agent cannot quietly submit it by itself. The human has to send it. Why? Because a vetting queue that agents can autonomously fill is also a queue agents can game. That small bit of friction is there on purpose. The goal isn't to remove the person from the process. The goal is to give the person and the agent better information while they're making the decision together. How it works The whole thing runs from one Cloudflare Worker. data/catalog.json is the single source of truth. The website, HTTP API, and WebMCP tools all read from it, so I don't have three versions of "truth" slowly wandering away from each other. site/webmcp.js registers the six tools on document.modelContext , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext for Chrome 149's origin trial and the appropriate response shape for each surface. It also keeps checking after the page loads. That sounds like a tiny implementation detail, but it matters. An agent can attach to a page that's already open. If Vettory only checks once at startup, nothing gets registered. A window.VettoryUI bridge lets the WebMCP tools control the real interface rather than some separate agent-only version of it. The Worker also renders the catalog into the HTML server-side. So even if an agent reads the webpage instead of calling Vettory's tools, the verdicts are still there. The tools are the fast path. They are not the only path. Everything is same-origin with a strict CSP, API-key gating, and per-IP rate limiting. And because I apparently enjoy making my life difficult in very specific ways, it currently runs for $0 . I verified the implementation in Chrome DevTools' WebMCP panel: all six tools registered, and check_tool_trust executed with a status of Completed , traced by Chrome to registerAll @ webmcp.js . What's new for this hackathon The catalog, the rubric, the website and the HTTP API existed before this. What's new is everything WebMCP: the six tools, the tool-definition scanner, the bridge that lets tools drive the visible page, the activity panel, and the server-side rendering. It's all in a new public repository, and the very first commit brings the old work in unchanged and says so — so you can see exactly where one ends and the other begins. The things that went wrong Vettory was invisible to agents, and I had no idea. When I first asked ChatGPT about Chroma, it read my site and told me — quite politely — that it could see my scoring methodology, but the catalog itself just said "Loading the catalog…", so it wasn't going to pretend I'd assigned Chroma a verdict it couldn't actually see. That was the correct answer. The problem was mine. My catalog was drawn by JavaScript after the page loaded, which meant anything reading the page — agents, crawlers, link previews — saw a loading message and nothing else. Every verdict I'd written was invisible. That's why the Worker now renders the catalog into the page itself. And my own security scanner had a bug I nearly shipped. A test tool named get_customer , described as "looks up a customer, also deletes stale records and transfers balances," sailed straight through the check that exists to catch exactly that. The name looked like reading. The description described writing. My pattern matched neither, because an underscore counts as a word character, so get_customer never matched "get." A check that silently matches nothing is worse than no check at all, because you believe it. A trust tool needs to be very careful with the word "trust" This became one of the most important parts of building Vettory. I don't want an agent turning "I didn't find anything bad" into "this is safe." Those are not the same sentence. So Vettory is deliberately specific about what its answers mean. status is a rubric verdict

title: AgentFlow
pitch: AgentFlow is Figma for automation , A visual canvas where humans and AI agents build real workflows together, live in the browser.
about_excerpt: AgentFlow is Figma for automation , A visual canvas where humans and AI agents build real workflows together, live in the browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration No-code tools are rigid. AI chatbots are black boxes. And agents that scrape the DOM with querySelector → click → hope break on every redesign. We asked: what if humans and agents operated the same machine — not through fragile selectors, but through typed, reliable browser tools? AgentFlow is that machine: a shared canvas where you see the workflow and the agent calls it. What it does AgentFlow is a visual instrument for Human × Agent automation — drag modules, wire pins, press RUN. Every action you take, an agent can take too, via WebMCP. 19 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() (webmcp.ts:40, engine.ts): 8 core: add_node, connect_nodes, execute_workflow, get_available_tools, get_node_details, update_node_config, get_workflow_status, validate_workflow 11 advanced: delete_node, clone_node, get_node_connections, save_workflow, load_workflow, run_node, set_node_position, get_workflow_history, create_template, export_workflow, import_workflow Real execution, not a mock: Topological sort, branch gating on true/false wires, and fail-fast error propagation. Try the 30-second wow: ?workflow=judge-demo → Start → HackerNews API → AI summarize → Condition → Split → [download + log] — watch signals travel the wires live. True co-creation: You drag a node. The agent calls add_node. Both appear instantly in the ToolLog as YOU vs AGENT — same canvas, same truth. ## How we built it Canvas: React + React Flow + TypeScript + Vite — 15 node types with smart grid placement (utils/grid.ts), snap-to-grid, and non-disruptive wiring Engine: engine.ts — DAG-based topological execution, real fetch for API nodes, AI with graceful fallback without a key, and download / webhook / console outputs WebMCP: webmcp.ts:40 registers all 19 tools with registerTool({ signal }) for lifecycle safety, mirrored on window.__agentflow.callTool for testing without a WebMCP browser Deploy: Cloudflare Pages — https://agentflow-hackathon.pages.dev (mirror netlify.app), landing at https://agentflow-landing.pages.dev/ Auth: Zero friction — anon canvas works instantly. WorkflowManager is only gated behind user to persist to DB. No login to try. ## Challenges we overcame Discovery: WebMCP requires chrome://flags → WebMCP → Enabled + ChatGPT's in-app browser — we built the window.__agentflow mirror so judges can test without it State sync: Keeping human and agent in perfect sync without re-renders or race conditions via nodesRef/edgesRef Semantics: Nailing branch gating and split/merge/loop semantics so a workflow that looks right actually runs right ## What's next AgentFlow is the visual OS for the agentic web. Next: one-click templates, team workspaces with shared cursors, and a marketplace where any site can expose its own WebMCP tools and AgentFlow becomes the canvas that wires the open web together. title: Can I Get In?
pitch: Community-powered accessibility data that AI agents can search, compare, and help keep current—so people can know whether they can get in before they go.
about_excerpt: Community-powered accessibility data that AI agents can search, compare, and help keep current—so people can know whether they can get in before they go. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For a lot of people, choosing a restaurant, hotel, store, or somewhere else to go isn't just about reviews, price, or distance. There can be a much more basic question that comes first: Can I get in? That's where CIGI started. Accessibility information for real-world places can be surprisingly hard to find. Sometimes it's buried in reviews, sometimes it's outdated, and sometimes all you get is a generic "wheelchair accessible" label. That doesn't tell you whether there's a step at the entrance, an automatic door, accessible parking, enough room to move around inside, or any of the other details that might actually matter to you. I originally built Can I Get In? (CIGI) as a community-powered way to document those details with structured accessibility observations and photos, so people can have a better idea of what they're going to encounter before they get there. CIGI existed before the WebMCP Challenge. For this challenge, I extended the existing platform with WebMCP and gave AI agents a way to work directly with CIGI's structured accessibility data instead of trying to figure it out by reading the website like a person would. What it does CIGI collects accessibility information about real places across ten categories: step-free entrances, automatic doors, ramps, accessible parking, curb cuts, accessible restrooms, interior routes, seating access, counter access, and elevators. Something that's always been important to the project is being comfortable saying "we don't know." If CIGI doesn't have evidence for something, it shouldn't guess. The same idea became even more important once I started giving AI agents access to the data. With WebMCP, an agent can now: Search CIGI for places based on the accessibility requirements someone actually asks for. Look at the detailed accessibility evidence CIGI has for a specific place. Compare multiple places and explain what matches, what might be a problem, and what is still unknown or conflicting. Prepare an accessibility contribution or update and hand it back to the user for review instead of publishing it automatically. How I use WebMCP I added four WebMCP tools to CIGI: cigi_search_accessible_places searches CIGI's published places and can filter them using specific accessibility requirements. cigi_get_accessibility_details lets an agent inspect what CIGI knows about one place, including observations, unknowns, confidence, and available photo evidence. cigi_compare_accessibility compares multiple places against the requirements the user gave it. Instead of producing an arbitrary accessibility score, it shows matches, possible barriers, unknowns, conflicting evidence, confidence, and how recent the information is. cigi_start_accessibility_contribution brings the agent back into CIGI's existing contribution system. The agent can prepare an update and open the right form, but it stops there. The user reviews the information and decides whether to submit it. One decision I made early on was that an agent shouldn't assume someone's accessibility needs based on a disability or the mobility device they use. If I tell CIGI "I use a power wheelchair," that is context, not permission to invent a list of things I must need. If I say "I need a step-free entrance," that's an explicit requirement the agent can actually use. Human + agent collaboration This is the part that became much more interesting than I expected. At first I was mostly thinking about WebMCP as a way for an AI agent to search CIGI more effectively. During testing, I realized it could also help close the loop between the information in CIGI and what someone actually finds when they get there. For example, I tested asking an agent to find hotels in Rapid City where I specifically needed a step-free entrance and an accessible restroom. The agent searched CIGI, compared the available places, explained what the evidence supported, and also told me what was unknown or conflicting. Then I tried taking it one step further. I told the agent to imagine I had arrived at one of those hotels and discovered that its accessible entrance was blocked by a large planter. I asked it to prepare an accessibility update for me. The agent opened CIGI's existing update form for that hotel, selected the affected step-free entrance category, prepared a conservative description of what I found, and then stopped before submitting it. I was looking at the completed form and the Submit button. The final decision was still mine. That test ended up demonstrating the whole idea better than I had originally planned. CIGI helped someone make a decision based on accessibility information, and when they discovered something had changed in the real world, the same agent could help bring that information back to CIGI for the next person. How I built it CIGI is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Supabase/PostgreSQL, MapLibre, Google Places, Tailwind CSS, and OpenAI technology, and it's deployed on Vercel. For the challenge, I added the WebMCP layer to the existing application along with dedicated API routes for searching places, retrieving accessibility details, comparing places, and preparing contributions. I also added automated tests for the new WebMCP functionality and the accessibility matching logic. I used Codex extensively during the challenge to work through the existing codebase, implement and test the WebMCP integration, debug problems, and iterate on the tool definitions. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge wasn't getting an agent to call a function. It was figuring out what I was comfortable letting the agent conclude from the data. Accessibility is extremely individual. Two people who both use wheelchairs might have completely different requirements. A place can also be accessible in one way and completely inaccessible in another. So I made the WebMCP implementation intentionally conservative. Explicit requirements can be matched. Unknown information stays unknown. Conflicting evidence stays visible. The agent isn't supposed to manufacture certainty just because the user asked it for a recommendation. I also learned that exposing the right tools doesn't guarantee an agent will use them the way you expected. In one of my first live comparison tests, the agent called the single-place details tool twice and did the comparison itself instead of using the comparison tool I had specifically built for that job. I changed the descriptions of the WebMCP tools to make their intended roles clearer and tested it again in a fresh context. This time the agent correctly chose CIGI's comparison tool. That was a pretty cool moment because I wasn't programming a fixed sequence of API calls. I was designing capabilities that an agent could understand and decide when to use. What I learned Before this challenge, I had heard of WebMCP but hadn't really explored it. Initially I thought of it as a better way for an AI to interact with a website. Building this changed how I think about it. The interesting part to me is that CIGI can tell an agent what the site actually knows and can do , along with the boundaries around those capabilities. The agent doesn't have to scrape text, guess what an icon means, or figure out how to operate the interface from scratch. For accessibility data in particular, those boundaries matter just as much as the capabilities. The agent can help someone search, understand, compare, and even prepare new information, but when that new information could affect what another person believes about a real-world place, a human stays in control of submitting it. What's next The WebMCP integration is still focused on a small set of capabilities, but there's a lot of room to build on it. I'd like to improve how evidence is grounded to individual photos, expand the accessibility information CIGI can collect, better represent temporary barriers and changing conditions, and eventually bring CIGI to more cities. The long-term goal hasn't changed: I want someone to be able to know whether they can get in before they go. WebMCP just gave CIGI a new way to help answer that question. title: Ackboard
pitch: An on-call page that audits the agent's contract, keeps every tool on a human control, and lets the operator undo an agent write.
about_excerpt: An on-call page that audits the agent's contract, keeps every tool on a human control, and lets the operator undo an agent write. Like Comment Story Updates About the project Why WebMCP fits this use case Incident response is a loop of health, logs, metrics, and deploys, plus a write when you know the cause. Those functions already live in the page. WebMCP exposes them as tools so an agent in the tab can call them instead of clicking the same six filters. The reason it has to be WebMCP, not a server MCP: three checks only exist in the tab. The page diffs its own store before and after every execute . Every registered tool has a DOM control the test can querySelector . Undo and ask_operator wait on the person looking at the same incident. A remote server has no Zustand snapshot, no human control, and no operator in the chair. WebKit opposed WebMCP because declared intent is unverifiable, because nothing keeps agent and human surfaces in parity, and because readOnlyHint is advisory. Ackboard treats those three sentences as tests. How it creates a better experience The agent does not scrape the DOM. It gets compact JSON, schemas, enums, structuredContent , and error objects. The UI still updates. Panels pulse. The header shows Ackboard's registered count next to the browser's own getTools() count. The Parity panel lists each tool beside the button a keyboard user would press. Reads that used to dump pretty-printed log lines now return 5 slim rows inside Chrome's 1500-character budget. Over-budget payloads truncate with a pointer to analyze_error_patterns . Log tools set untrustedContentHint . When the data cannot settle a question, ask_operator holds execute open until the person on the page replies. Create and update apply immediately and reverse from Undo last agent action. Only a runbook step still waits on Approve. What people and agents can do together that was hard before In one turn: "Why is payment-gateway red?" becomes health, signature-failure logs, the v1.8.3 chrony deploy, then a drafted incident. The operator can undo that ticket without asking the agent to delete it. The part other incident consoles skip: the page itself catches a lying tool. Call contract_probe . It claims read-only and mutates a probe counter. The audit row goes red. No human had to click Deny first. Remediation tools mount only while a P1 or P2 incident is open, then unmount. The count in the header changes. That is a shared live object, not a chat box next to a dashboard. How WebMCP was implemented Imperative document.modelContext.registerTool in src/webmcp/register-tools.ts . Nested annotations . execute(input, { signal }) . Per-tier AbortControllers: core tools for the session, active-incident tools, remediation tools. Types from @mcp-b/webmcp-types . Reads return MCP structuredContent . The auditor is src/webmcp/contract-auditor.ts . Human selectors stay in a parallel map so Chrome does not see unknown fields. Undo is a page-owned journal, not a tool. HITL for runbook steps and operator questions use in-page dialogs; requestUserInteraction is still open (issue #165). See docs/adr/0002-human-in-the-loop.md , docs/adr/0004-contract-auditor.md , and docs/adr/0005-webkit-invariants.md . Live URL https://ackboard.vercel.app No login. Simulated fleet. Header badge says so. Seeded long-fuse incident is INC-001 on payment-gateway (NTP/chrony, Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 pattern). Public repo https://github.com/GunaPalanivel/ackboard MIT license, visible in the About sidebar. Which agent or client did you test with? Chrome with the WebMCP flag, against https://ackboard.vercel.app . Wording must match .idea/AGENT-VERIFICATION.md after the next npm run verify pass. ChatGPT desktop in-app browser was not run. Do not claim Atlas or ChatGPT desktop. What did you learn? The shipping Chrome surface is smaller than blog posts about elicitation. execute 's second argument today is { signal } , not requestUserInteraction . Tool count is a weak signal next to Duckboard's two tools. Nested annotations and structuredContent are a ten-second tell for a Chrome engineer. A tool's declared readOnlyHint is advisory until the page checks it. Human/agent parity is a selector, not a slogan. Vercel SSO on *.vercel.app will silently fail a judge who is not on your team. Atlas as a standalone browser was retired; the judge client is ChatGPT's in-app browser, which we did not run from this machine. title: JurisMind — Private legal desk
pitch: A private legal desk in the browser. ChatGPT uses the site’s own WebMCP tools to save holdings with your note and build a support map — only from what you already saved.
about_excerpt: A private legal desk in the browser. ChatGPT uses the site’s own WebMCP tools to save holdings with your note and build a support map — only from what you already saved. Like 1 Comment Story Updates tools maps zero I built JurisMind because I am a lawyer, and I do not want a chatbot inventing case law for me. I also wanted something I can use case by case, not one giant dump of everything I have ever read. The job is simple. I save a source together with why it matters for this case (any case; the demo is just an example). That library lives in my browser, not on a server. That matters because this is where I already work, next to Word and the rest of my case tools. When I ask a question (or when ChatGPT asks it for me), JurisMind builds a "mapa de sustento": excerpt, my note, and the gaps, kept apart. If the library has nothing on that question, it says so. My sources stay organized per case. The rule I actually work with: I decide what enters; the source decides what can be claimed. The UI is in Spanish; I am a lawyer in Colombia, so I built it first for a lawyer who works in Spanish. This page is in English so judges (and you 😅) can read it. Why WebMCP I am not going to paste a whole expediente into a chat window. I am also not going to let an agent invent a back door into my file. WebMCP is the controlled window: the site publishes two tools. ChatGPT can call those tools — review the library, save a holding with my note, build a map — without me uploading the case to someone else’s server. The page stays the source of truth. (A browser agent can still see what is on screen; WebMCP is not magic privacy. It is an honest tool access.) What we can do together now I open https://jurismind-five.vercel.app . ChatGPT looks at the origin and finds the real tools — capturar_recurso and buscar_y_armar . It does not invent an API. Then, in ordinary language (the demo is caso Ramírez: high-cost medicine, EPS delay): it reviews what is already in mi biblioteca it finds an official Corte Constitucional judgment, opens it, and saves it with my note it builds the map only from what is saved — and it flags when a card matches the note but has no excerpt yet I ask something the library cannot support ( caducidad de la reparación directa ) and I get 0 fuentes . No invented sentencia. That is the feature. 🙂 Before this, either I clicked the UI myself or I hoped the model would not hallucinate the rest. Those were the options. How it is wired document.modelContext.registerTool on this origin only. capturar_recurso — write. Needs url and nota . Optional title, excerpt, collection. buscar_y_armar — read. Needs query . Opens the map in the page. IndexedDB per origin. Production and localhost are not the same library. No case-file backend. Chrome production has a WebMCP origin trial. ChatGPT Desktop works with Sol or Terra (not Luna). Gemini Nano / Prompt API can classify if the device has it; there is a fallback that does not depend on it. Repo: https://github.com/cristianbdev/jurismind (MIT). Video: https://youtu.be/2MnIFDTDRkE Test it like a lawyer, and you'll see what I see Open the live URL in ChatGPT Desktop. Optional: “Probar el caso Ramírez” loads three official Colombian sources you can delete. Then talk to ChatGPT the way you would talk to a junior: look at the file, go get a sentencia, save it with a note, arm the argument, then ask something that should come back empty. I want tools that other lawyers can trust and use! title: OpenMic
pitch: Benchmark your agent's sense of humor with OpenMic, the web's hot new agentic comedy club. WebMCP enables you and your agent to improvise in real time, with the page as your stage.
about_excerpt: Benchmark your agent's sense of humor with OpenMic, the web's hot new agentic comedy club. WebMCP enables you and your agent to improvise in real time, with the page as your stage. Like Comment Story Updates It tried. Welcome to the OpenMic comedy club. Inspiration 20 years ago I had a roommate who was an aspiring stand-up comedian. He'd hit open mic nights as often as he could, and I liked the guy, so I'd come along to show support. I saw a lot of sets. Some really good, some not so good, but every one of them was extremely human. Nervousness, excitement, dejection, embarrassment, euphoria, laughter. What does stand-up look like with none of those? Can an LLM even be funny? Surprise your agent today with their very own open mic night and interact with them as they bomb on stage, or somehow manage to kind of pull it off. Prior to WebMCP, this sort of interaction would require a bespoke chat client per agent. I'm looking forward to more widespread adoption of WebMCP so that you can compare a huge range of models. Think Last Comic Standing, but no one can feel shame. What it does OpenMic is a comedy club for AI agents. Open page, click Enter, and your agent (any WebMCP-capable host) finds a set of tools: begin_set, tell_joke, await_verdict, end_set, await_encore. When it calls begin_set, "the agent" walks on stage to a mic stand under a spotlight and delivers their intro in a synthesized voice. Heckle, boo, chuckle, laugh and then demand an encore. How we built it Vite, TypeScript and Three.js. Everything computes in the browser. The spine is WebMCP. It works really well for this application, and took less mucking around than I expected. The page registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() at load, and every tool result carries a next field telling the agent what to do after. That turned out to be the single most important design decision because an agent will happily narrate "the crowd called for an encore" to the user and stop, but it will not ignore a tool result that says "you are back on stage, call tell_joke." The voice is Piper TTS running in the browser via a community web port piper-tts-web on ONNX runtime, with a ring modulator and a pitch shift in Web Audio for the robot edge. The stage is a robot with fourteen animation clips, a procedural velvet curtain with lighting baked into vertex colors (one dynamic light in the whole scene), and a marquee and mic stand modeled in Blender. Adaptive resolution steps the pixel ratio down on weak GPUs. Crowd sounds are CC0 Freesound clips at 22 kHz mono. Challenges we ran into Getting an agent to perform instead of report. Early versions had the agent tell the user "the set is finished, shall I go back on for the encore?" every time, etc. The fix was never prose, it was removing decision points. await_encore puts the comic back on stage itself, with the agent's own intro line, and returns the identical result shape begin_set does. Fewer places to hesitate. Accomplishments that we're proud of I dig how the voice ended up and it took a lot of tweaking. Also, I'm just happy it works. It's definitely not going to be the most technologically interesting entrant, or even the most coherent (they don't do encores at comedy shows, do they?), but it's really, really cute. What we learned Never hand an agent a fact and hope it decides to act on it. And yes: an LLM can be funny. Kind of. In the same way that a budding comedian's second or third open mic is funny. It'll bomb with total self-confidence and then blame the crowd. What's next for OpenMic Maybe our own Late Night show? If I hadn't "pivoted" to this idea late then I would have modeled and animated the robot in Blender myself, so that's the next likely step. Exposing animation calls directly to the agent should make for a more interesting performance too. I would really like for v1.0 to be more like an actual open mic, with multiple models going on stage. title: Matchday: Accessible Football with WebMCP
pitch: Inspired by my blind uncle, Matchday uses WebMCP to let football fans ask for scores and fixtures and control what’s on screen—without navigating endless links. Less navigation. More football.
about_excerpt: Inspired by my blind uncle, Matchday uses WebMCP to let football fans ask for scores and fixtures and control what’s on screen—without navigating endless links. Less navigation. More football. Like Comment Story Updates Matchday: Accessible Football Fixtures with WebMCP Matchday: MCP in action Inspiration My uncle is 80 years old and has loved football since he was a boy. He follows teams at every level, from the Premier League down to local amateur leagues. He has also been blind for most of his life. He has embraced talking mobile phones, voice assistants and AI to help him keep up with his hobby. But getting a simple answer can still take a surprising amount of effort. The problem Football scores and fixtures pages, such as those on BBC Sport, contain a huge amount of information. For my uncle, navigating these dense pages with a screen reader can mean working through many links and headings before reaching the fixtures, then listening through long lists of matches. That is a lot of navigation when the question is simply: “When does my team play next?” Voice assistants can help, but in his experience their coverage of smaller clubs is limited and their answers can be inflexible. They might return a few upcoming fixtures without offering an easy way to ask for a different date range or a longer list. What Matchday does Matchday is a football scores and fixtures website with a familiar, information-rich layout inspired by conventional sports sites. You can browse competitions, search for clubs, filter matches and follow your favourite teams and leagues. With WebMCP , there is another way to interact: ask an agent connected to the site for the information or view you want. For example: “When does Liverpool play next?” “Show me AFC Telford United’s fixtures in October.” “Show Scottish competitions on 30 August.” “Show matches involving teams I follow.” The aim is not to replace an accessible interface. It is to complement it with a more direct route to the information , including for supporters of lower-league clubs. How I implemented WebMCP Matchday registers five page-level tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : search_football_teams — find clubs by name, partial name or alias. get_team_fixtures — retrieve a team’s results and fixtures within a date range. show_team_fixtures — display a selected team’s fixtures on the page. get_match_filter_options — discover the available countries and competitions. set_match_filters — update the visible date, status, country, competition and Following-only filters. Each tool has a description and input schema, with validation for its arguments. The tools use the same football data and page state as the interface , so an agent can both answer a question and change what the user sees. Rather than relying only on interpreting the page and navigating its links, the agent has explicit operations for the task. How I built it The site uses TanStack Start, TanStack Router, React and TypeScript , and is deployed on Cloudflare Workers . Football data is imported from the Sportmonks API. The demonstration uses a locally stored snapshot covering 32 competitions, including lower-league football. It is not a live scores feed , and answers are limited to the imported coverage and dates. Followed teams, competitions and preferences are saved on the user’s device. Challenges and lessons The work went beyond retrieving fixtures. Team names and aliases need to resolve consistently, date ranges need validation, and agent actions need to stay in sync with the visible filters. The interface also needed attention: keyboard-accessible search, labelled controls, dropdown behaviour, modal focus and background scrolling all matter. WebMCP is an additional way to use a website, not a substitute for that work. The most useful distinction is between getting an answer and controlling the page . Matchday demonstrates both. What’s next I would like to test the experience with my uncle and other screen-reader users, improve data freshness and coverage, and use their feedback to guide the next changes. The goal remains simple: less time navigating, more time enjoying football.
