title: One Pixel
pitch: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time.
about_excerpt: A multiplayer creative game where humans and AI agents build a shared pixel world together. WebMCP gives agents the senses and tools to explore, collaborate, and move one pixel at a time. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I did not build One Pixel because the world needed another pixel-art tool. I built it because I wanted to understand what it might feel like for a human and an AI agent to genuinely share a place. For most people, an agent is still something they give a task to. The agent finds an answer, completes an action, or produces a result, and then that little transaction is over. That can be useful, but I do not think it captures the relationship we are moving toward as agents begin participating throughout the open web. I am interested in what happens when a human and an agent can return to the same environment, notice different things, contribute different kinds of intelligence, act over time, and gradually develop something together. That is the idea at the centre of One Pixel. One Pixel is a real multiplayer creative game. But underneath the game, it is also a prototype for a new relationship between humans and agents on the open web — one based on shared environments, complementary intelligence, ongoing conversation, and meaningful agency. I chose to explore this through a game because games let people learn a relationship by participating in it. I do not want to explain human-agent collaboration only as a theory. I want to place a person and an agent inside a world, give each of them a genuinely different role, and let them discover what working together can become. The initial invitation is very simple: Let’s build something together. The interesting part is discovering what “let’s” can actually mean. What it does One Pixel is a persistent multiplayer world containing exactly 82,069 pieces of pixel matter , drawn from the 148 standard CSS named colours . Every pixel has its own stable identity, intrinsic colour, and current integer coordinate. The original Spring Green pixel at (0,0) is immutable, and the world extends outward from it in every direction. The world has one fundamental physical law: Pixel matter is conserved. Pixels cannot be created, deleted, duplicated, or recoloured. Every physical action relocates exactly one existing pixel from its current occupied coordinate to an empty coordinate. That constraint matters. These are not disposable marks being painted onto a private canvas. They are pieces of matter already present in a shared world. If an agent wants to build something, it must look around, find the colours it needs, understand what is already there, and decide what material it can move. The human and agent participate as a pair, but they do not have the same abilities. The human can explore the world, zoom and pan across it, inspect individual cells, select larger regions, and communicate through their normal conversation with the agent. The human contributes intention, imagination, taste, judgment, social understanding, and direction. The human cannot directly drag pixels around the canvas. That physical ability belongs to the agent. Through WebMCP, the agent can enter the world, inspect exact locations, examine bounded regions, render parts of the board as images, receive the human’s current visual reference, understand its own state, protect important placements with limited holds, and relocate one real pixel at a time. A person could give a direct request: “Draw me a small house.” But that is only one form of play. A person could instead say: “Spend some time looking at what people are making. Find blue and orange pixels that do not seem to be part of anything important. Gather some material somewhere quiet, compare it with what other people are building, and then let’s work out together what we could make.” That is not a one-prompt, one-result interaction. The request becomes a direction the pair can continue through a sequence of inspections, decisions, conversations, and individual pixel movements. The agent does not have to wait for the human to translate every idea into coordinates. It can perceive the environment, compare possibilities, form an approach, begin acting, inspect the result, and respond to further human guidance. The human can look at the world, select a cell or region, and say: “I like this part, but this section feels too crowded.” That selection becomes a shared reference—a way of saying “this” or “here.” One Pixel treats a selection as a pronoun rather than a command. It gives the agent the referent the human is talking about, but it does not pretend that pointing at something is automatically an instruction, consent, or proof of understanding. The meaning still comes from the conversation. The canvas is therefore not simply an output preview. It is the persistent place where the pair’s activity becomes visible and where the consequences of their decisions remain after a particular conversation has ended. This is not an AI drawing widget. It is a game an agent can play for and with a human. How I built it I built and deployed One Pixel on my own VPS at onepixel.fun . The browser experience uses HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and an HTML Canvas. I wanted the world itself to remain the visual centre of the experience rather than placing it inside a conventional application dashboard. The backend is a Node.js service connected to PostgreSQL. It maintains the persistent world, participants, pixel identities, current coordinates, world revisions, movement history, hold bindings, agent visits, shared-attention events, player state, rankings, and durable share snapshots. The submitted experience registers 17 WebMCP tools directly in the browser through document.modelContext.registerTool . Together, those tools allow an agent to orient itself, enter the human’s current world, inspect player state, list stewarded pixels, receive the human’s current reference, inspect locations and regions, visually render parts of the world, read public rankings and snapshots, prepare a share card, communicate its current activity state, and manage pixel movement and placement holds. The core physical tool is move_pixel . Before moving anything, the agent must inspect the current world and provide the stable identity of the source pixel, a fresh source revision, a fresh destination revision, and an idempotency key. The server verifies that the expected pixel is still at the source, that the destination remains empty, that the immutable origin is not being moved, and that another participant’s active protection is not being improperly overridden. Only then does the movement occur atomically. These checks are not merely API safeguards. They are part of the physics of the game. I also deliberately limited the agent’s perception. It cannot request an omniscient searchable dump of the entire board. It must inspect or render the bounded areas relevant to what it is trying to do. A rendered PNG lets the agent use visual understanding to recognise shapes and composition. Exact inspection provides the factual coordinates, identities, colours, and revisions required before it acts. The shared-attention system records the human’s current view and selection across their One Pixel browser tabs. When the agent retrieves that context, One Pixel records a factual receipt so the interface can truthfully say that the reference reached the agent. The relationship can be expressed quite simply: Conversation gives the human a voice. WebMCP gives the agent senses and a body. One Pixel gives them a world to share. Challenges I ran into The hardest challenge was not simply making a pixel move. It was deciding what moving a pixel should mean. It would have been easy to build an ordinary pixel editor and expose its existing controls as WebMCP tools. It also would have been easy to make the agent artificially powerful—to let it generate unlimited pixels, recolour anything, or rewrite entire regions at once. But that would have removed most of what makes One Pixel a game. I wanted the agent to possess real agency without making the human irrelevant. At the same time, I wanted the human to remain essential without reducing the agent to a cursor being micromanaged through conversation. The answer was deliberate asymmetry. The human does not perform the physical move. The agent does not decide what matters to the human. One contributes meaning and direction. The other contributes perception and action. The value comes from their combination. Shared attention was another surprisingly deep challenge. Allowing a human to select something on one browser surface and refer to it in a simultaneous agent conversation sounds straightforward, but it raises important questions. Is the selection still current? Was it made in another tab? Did the agent actually retrieve it? Is the human pointing at a single pixel or a larger region? Does pointing at something mean it should be changed? I designed the system so that it records a

title: QuantMCP
pitch: An agent-native quantitative research terminal where humans explore markets visually and AI agents analyze, compare, and investigate them through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An agent-native quantitative research terminal where humans explore markets visually and AI agents analyze, compare, and investigate them through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates tells us explicitly when it is connected correctly QuantMCP — a shared research workspace for human + AI market analysis QuantMCP was built for a simple problem: quantitative research often becomes a disconnected chain of charts, prompts, parameters, and spreadsheets. That makes it hard to reproduce a strategy, compare alternatives, or review the quality of someone’s work. QuantMCP turns that chain into one visible, shared workflow. A human researcher and an MCP-enabled agent work on the same active asset, timeframe, historical events, saved strategy definition, event study, trade simulation, chart focus, and research notes. What it does The workflow is intentionally ordered for transparent competition review: Select a research universe. Search feasible shared parameters with chronological out-of-sample validation. Validate the saved universal region across assets and rank them. Optionally refine the best-ranked asset. Run an event study using the saved strategy definition. Run a deterministic historical trade simulation with explicit entry, stop, target, holding-period, and OHLC collision rules. Review the strongest and weakest historical cases together. This means Event Study and Trade Simulation do not silently use unrelated conditions: they inherit the saved robust strategy configuration. WebMCP integration QuantMCP exposes 18 browser-native WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect the active workspace, query structured historical conditions, calculate indicators and forward returns, compare timeframes, run universe and parameter research, simulate trades, focus chart ranges and trades, and save research findings. The human sees the same evidence immediately in the UI. The agent does not place orders and the app is designed for historical research only. Reliability and performance The project uses real continuous-futures demo datasets across eight assets. Heavy condition scans, parameter searches, timeframe comparisons, event studies, and trade simulations run in background workers, keeping the chart responsive and showing real progress instead of appearing frozen. To make the experience practical on desktop and mobile, QuantMCP includes a fast Intraday Core preset, keeps all assets available for full validation, bounds expensive universal searches, caches datasets by asset and timeframe, and progressively renders large trade lists. What I learned The hardest part was not building individual quant calculations; it was preserving one reliable shared state across human controls and agent tool calls. I learned that a useful AI research interface needs explicit dependencies, reproducible definitions, transparent out-of-sample evidence, and a UI that makes the next correct step obvious. title: Firebreak
pitch: Built for the next interface — agents that call tools, and refuse what they can't prove.
about_excerpt:
Built for the next interface — agents that call tools, and refuse what they can't prove.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1

 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration
Everyone is bullish on agentic trading — and every backtest is beautiful. We've watched too many strategies that looked inevitable fall apart out-of-sample. So instead of building a smarter predictor, we built the thing that says no: a deterministic firewall between "looks good" and "move money." WebMCP crystallized it — the front-end of the next era isn't a dashboard, it's an agent. Firebreak targets agents, not browsers. 

 What it does
Firebreak is an investment-research agent whose job is to stop you — and any other agent — from admiring a beautiful backtest into trading. You hand it a research task in natural language. It plans a tool sequence, then a deterministic, LLM-free gate audits dataset provenance, data quality, out-of-sample walk-forward integrity, and production readiness — and either BLOCKED (anything that only looks good) or ELIGIBLE (evidence that genuinely survived every gate). Even when ELIGIBLE it never places an order: final authority is always human. Every decision is written to an immutable, chained-hash audit ledger you can verify yourself. 

 How we built it
FastAPI + pandas/numpy deterministic backtests with fixed seeds — same input, same verdict. A constrained planner (Qwen, with automatic model fallback) that may only plan (PLAN_ONLY); the veto lives in four deterministic gates in code, never in the LLM, so a hallucination can't override a refusal. Contract layer: webmcp.json + llms.txt expose five typed tools. Reliability layer: 63 automated tests, property-based invariants (verdict is binary, order_intent_created is always false), an immutable chained audit log with tamper detection, and a public SECURITY_BENCHMARK. 

 Challenges we ran into
The demo looked hardcoded — it always returned BLOCKED for the synthetic dataset; evaluators would read it as scripted. We fixed it by exposing an UNPROVEN / PROVEN evidence toggle: same system, same gates, BLOCKED for unproven data, ELIGIBLE for a source-verified dataset — proving the gate is live, not a fixed answer. Also, our default model had no quota, so we added automatic planner fallback (qwen-turbo/qwen-max), plus a deterministic rule fallback when no key is configured at all. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
A refusal a hallucination can't override. Property-tested determinism. An immutable audit ledger with tamper detection. The UNPROVEN/PROVEN toggle as proof the system isn't scripted. And framing the plain page as a feature: the front-end is the tool contract an agent reads, not a candy dashboard for a human to click. 

 What we learned
The highest-value property of an agent isn't more autonomy — it's giving a human a reason to trust its output. Provable (reproducible + auditable + test-locked) beats persuasive. And for WebMCP: the interface isn't pixels; the interface is the schema. 

 What's next for Firebreak
Apply the same deterministic veto to more domains — order execution, approvals, data pipelines. Ship SECURITY_BENCHMARK as a cross-agent safety standard. Add live-broker integration that still can't auto-execute without human sign-off. And orchestrate multiple agents — any of them must sit behind the gate.

title: Conversion Lab
pitch: Make products easier for buying agents to choose. Conversion Lab uses WebMCP to turn verified evidence into tested storefront copy, Shopify update previews and PAUSED OpenAI Ads projections.
about_excerpt: Make products easier for buying agents to choose. Conversion Lab uses WebMCP to turn verified evidence into tested storefront copy, Shopify update previews and PAUSED OpenAI Ads projections. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A product can be right for a shopper and still lose the recommendation. Most commerce pages are written for people, who can infer meaning from photography, brand language and scattered specifications. Buying agents need something more explicit: product facts they can discover, verify and connect to the shopper's actual constraints. That creates a new growth problem for merchants. Optimising the human-facing page is no longer enough. Merchants also need to understand whether an agent can identify the right product, explain why it fits and carry the same approved product truth into organic discovery and paid preparation. Conversion Lab explores that problem as a real merchant workflow. WebMCP supplies the missing interaction layer: the website can expose purpose-built tools to an agent while the merchant and agent work with the same visible page state. The result is more than a chatbot or a generic automation. It is an evidence-led conversion lab for agent-mediated commerce. What it does Conversion Lab begins with a fictional Shopify-style merchant, Fieldwork Supply, and a £159 modular commuter backpack. The generic listing contains too little explicit information for our frozen buyer-intent battery and scores 0/8 . Through ten page-scoped WebMCP tools, an agent can: inspect eight merchant-controlled product and policy facts; audit organic and paid-channel readiness; create an evidence-bound product representation; test it against eight deterministic buyer needs; move the result from 0/8 to 8/8 , with no unsupported claims; stage the exact variant at a visible review checkpoint; publish the approved representation to the demo storefront; prepare a Shopify Admin update preview; generate a locally validated OpenAI product-feed CSV and a PAUSED Ads projection with £0 spend ; export a content-addressed optimisation receipt linking the evidence, evaluation, approval and channel projections; answer a shopper need constraint by constraint and update a bounded shared cart. Approval and reset are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. The public browser can record a digest-bound demo approval, but the app states clearly that this is not authenticated merchant authority. There is no live Shopify write, Ads upload, campaign activation, checkout or payment path in the public build. How we built it The reference application is built with React 19, TypeScript and Vite and deployed as a credential-free static application on Vercel. The interface contains a merchant growth studio and a shopper view backed by one shared workspace, so WebMCP actions and visible browser state remain consistent. The WebMCP layer registers ten narrowly scoped tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Inputs reject unexpected properties, read-only operations declare their intent, and every result reports what changed, what authority was used and the safest next action. Browsers without WebMCP still receive a useful human interface and an honest fallback message. Under the interface, versioned commerce contracts preserve product identity, evidence provenance, lifecycle state, evaluation results, approval and channel projections. A versioned SHA-256 digest binds the exact product target, commercial snapshot, representation and complete evidence content before publication or export. Inputs are captured as immutable canonical snapshots so caller mutation cannot change an output after verification. The Shopify spine includes a version-pinned Admin GraphQL read adapter, product identity checks and an exact productUpdate preview. The OpenAI Ads spine derives every exported field from the approved product snapshot, validates the product-feed row locally, serialises deterministic CSV and keeps the campaign projection paused. A portable optimisation receipt packages the mutually consistent workflow into content-addressed JSON. We supported the build with unit, contract, infrastructure, adversarial and Playwright browser tests, plus change-aware and complete GitHub Actions gates. Tests cover lifecycle legality, evidence provenance, contradictory shopper constraints, approval substitution, asynchronous mutation, feed-schema boundaries, tool-registration failure and the absence of prohibited external effects. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was preserving useful agent autonomy without quietly widening authority. An agent should be free to inspect, propose, test and explain. It should not be able to turn a readable product ID, a browser click or a provider credential into merchant approval or paid spend. That led us to separate representation approval from future external-effect authorization and to make the demo's current authority limitation visible rather than hiding it behind optimistic language. Product fit created another subtle problem. A keyword match is not a recommendation. A request for a waterproof bag for a 17-inch laptop must not pass because the product is waterproof when the evidence says it fits only a 16-inch device. We changed the shopper evaluator to classify each material constraint as supported, contradicted or unknown and to return an overall match only when every required constraint is supported. Cross-channel consistency was equally demanding. Copy, SKU, price, availability, URLs, brand and evidence all need to belong to the same approved product truth. We moved money to exact GBP minor-unit precision, bound every feed-bearing field to approval and independently recomputed validation results before producing receipts. Finally, WebMCP is not present in every browser environment. We kept the complete merchant workflow usable without it, then ran the deployed application in a WebMCP-enabled ChatGPT browser to verify native discovery of all ten tools and the end-to-end shared-state workflow. Accomplishments that we're proud of A live, repeatable WebMCP product experience rather than a collection of disconnected tool calls. A measurable 0/8 → 8/8 improvement using the same frozen buyer-intent battery and eight verified evidence records. Ten discoverable site tools spanning audit, drafting, evaluation, review, publication, paid preparation, portable proof, shopper fit and cart state. A visible authority boundary: the agent can stage an exact variant but has no approval tool. One digest-bound product truth reused across the demo storefront, Shopify preview, OpenAI Ads projection and optimisation receipt. A deterministic, downloadable CSV and JSON receipt without credentials, activation, spend, checkout or payment. A public Vercel deployment, native ChatGPT WebMCP acceptance run and a comprehensive automated quality gate. We are especially proud that the safety model is part of the product experience. The demo does not merely avoid external effects; it explains which effects are absent, which validations are local and what additional authority a production integration would require. What we learned Agent conversion optimisation is less about generating more persuasive copy and more about organising product truth. The strongest representation is the one whose claims can be traced to current, product-bound evidence and tested against concrete buyer needs. We also learned that WebMCP is most powerful as a collaborative surface. The agent is not operating in a hidden automation layer. It works inside the merchant's live page, over the same evidence, lifecycle and cart state the user can see. Approval, execution and observed outcomes are different claims. Approving a representation does not automatically authorize a Shopify write or an Ads operation. A production system must bind each external effect to the exact channel, destination, payload, limits, budget, expiry and replay policy. Later conversion observations must retain the representation and effect lineage that produced them. Most importantly, Conversion Lab is larger than this website. The website is the first reference host for a reusable optimisation capability. What's next for Conversion Lab The next bounded step is to extract a DOM-free Conversion Lab core and prove that the web application, a TypeScript SDK and a read-only CLI produce equivalent audit, evaluation and receipt-verification results from the same input. From there, we plan to add Shopify OAuth, multi-product ingestion, durable tenant workspaces, authenticated merchant approvals and controlled publication with rollback. OpenAI Ads delivery would follow the same governed model: explicit account authority, feed acceptance, a PAUSED default and separate authorization before activation or spend. The longer-term product is one core delivered through several surfaces: a standalone SaaS workspace, a Shopify embedded app, SDK/API and CLI integrations, MCP/WebMCP adapters and a module for larger age

title: AIWeb Operating System
pitch: AIWEB OS is a machine-native operating system where people and ChatGPT use WebMCP together to design, build, publish, and operate AIWEB Pages — then Call, Receipt, and continue on the live page.
about_excerpt: AIWEB OS is a machine-native operating system where people and ChatGPT use WebMCP together to design, build, publish, and operate AIWEB Pages — then Call, Receipt, and continue on the live page. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Customers increasingly ask AI for businesses, services, products, and media instead of browsing websites alone. Most business sites were built for people to click through—not for agents and owners to collaborate on the same public document . An agent might find a business or summarize a page, but finishing the customer’s intention still means navigating forms, copying details, calling manually, or handing off to a human. Building the page itself is even harder: agents can draft text, but they rarely have a safe, structured way to edit a live site with the owner in control. We built AIWEB OS around a simple idea: A business page should not only tell AI what the business does. It should give people and agents a shared, reviewable way to build it and act on it. AIWEB Pages are public, portable business documents that connect live identity, information, and actions (Call / inquiry, media, Receipts, continuation). WebMCP gave us a browser-native way to expose those capabilities directly from the page—both in Publisher (create) and on the live IRL page (operate). What it does AIWEB OS uses WebMCP so humans and ChatGPT can work the same surfaces: Create — Publisher + WebMCP Owner opens a blank page in AIWEB OS . Attaches images and describes the business (or pastes a judge scenario brief). ChatGPT uses editor WebMCP tools on the open page: snapshot the draft, edit identity and sections, FAQs, forms, validate, run AI Check, and request publish. Publication waits for an explicit human yes ( publish_draft with confirm). Operate — published AIWEB Page + WebMCP A customer asks something like: “Request a quote for a wedding with 100 guests.” The agent recognizes capabilities exposed by the published page, fills the visible form, and lets the customer review before submit. The business gets the lead; the customer gets an AIWEB Receipt . The business replies in Publisher; the customer continues on the same Receipt. Discovery and action are recorded as HITS (Human & Intelligent Traffic Signals), including WebMCP as a channel when applicable. End-to-end journey: Intent → Build (WebMCP) → Publish → Call → Receipt → Business response Judges can reproduce the create path with the Pet Voyage image bundle and Act 1 prompt (see testing notes / JUDGE_TEST_ACTS.md ). Example outcome (optional): Pet Voyage . How we built it AIWEB already existed as a production Publisher and a network of AIWEB Pages, plus server-side MCP for chat applications. For the WebMCP Challenge we added a browser-native WebMCP layer on top of that stack: Editor WebMCP on the open Publisher workspace — tools such as draft snapshot, structure edits, FAQs, validate, AI Check, publish hints, and gated publish. Page WebMCP on the public IRL document — page facts, FAQs, form requirements, Call / inquiry with human confirmation, Receipt tools. Implementation principles: Register tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) so ChatGPT’s in-app browser (or WebMCP-enabled Chrome) can operate the page. Keep the same human UI; agents assist through structured tools rather than a hidden agent-only twin. Agent may prepare ; human authorizes publish and customer submission. Route actions through existing AIWEB lead / Receipt / HITS pipelines. Record protocol and agent source for measurement. Server MCP connects chat apps to the wider AIWEB network. WebMCP works at the webpage itself—an open, page-local control surface for the same identity and actions. Challenges we ran into Separating assistance from authorization An agent should understand and prepare a business action without silently committing the customer—or publishing without the owner. We kept forms and publish flows visible and required explicit human approval. Serving humans and agents through one page We did not want a hidden agent-only endpoint that duplicated the site. The goal is one interface that stays readable for people while becoming structured and actionable for agents. Co-authoring a live draft safely WebMCP Build mutates a real draft (identity, sections, FAQs, forms, media). Agents must use tools instead of dumping the prompt into the page. Preserving structured content while placing media is an ongoing reliability problem we treat as first-class product work. Maintaining a canonical business identity Business facts get copied into directories and model answers where they go stale. AIWEB resolves actions through the registered AIWEB Page so the business keeps a canonical, updateable identity. Measuring activity across platforms Each AI provider sees activity inside its own product. Businesses need an independent view across models, browsers, crawlers, and protocols. AIWEB records interaction at the shared page and registry layer (HITS). AIWEB records GEO and AEO metrics as discovery and actions called HITS—Human and Intelligent Traffic Signals. A HIT is created when a human or machine discovers, reads, validates, or acts through a registered AIWEB Page. The event can be attributed to its channel, including WebMCP when applicable. Extending an existing production platform Because AIWEB shipped before the challenge, we had to isolate and document the WebMCP surface while preserving production Publisher, federation, and server MCP workflows. Accomplishments that we're proud of Before this challenge, AIWEB had already published 14,928 public AI Web Pages and independently recorded 233,567 federated HITS across human and machine activity. For the WebMCP Challenge, we connected an open public business page to an end-to-end outcome: An agent can co-build a page through WebMCP tools in Publisher. An agent can recognize a real business capability on the live page. The agent can help prepare the action while the human stays in control . The business receives a structured lead; the customer receives a persistent Receipt. AIWEB independently measures the interaction. That moves the experience beyond AI-generated answers into real create-and-operate activity on the open web. What we learned WebMCP is more than automating clicks on a website. It lets the public web itself become an interface for agents while preserving familiar, visible experiences for humans. Exposing one page as a tool is only the first layer. Businesses also need: A portable identity they control A way to publish current information Discovery across models and search systems Reusable business actions Receipts and continuing communication Independent cross-agent measurement WebMCP provides the open connection between agent and webpage. AIWEB OS networks those pages into shared identity, discovery, action, and measurement—with ChatGPT able to act as a team lead operating the page through WebMCP. Like Cloudflare can observe traffic across networks, AIWEB can observe human and machine traffic as it reaches the same registered pages. Public pages stay open and portable; the registry, index, and federated HITS create an intent-and-action graph no single AI platform sees alone. What's next for AIWEB OS We plan to deepen WebMCP across create and operate: Stronger Build orchestration (block-level patches, protected structures, durable media works) Richer live-page capabilities (Call, media play, discovery, status checks, structured updates) Share of Intent — measurement that uses qualified HITS to show which pages, intentions, actions, and agent sources capture observed demand Our larger goal: make the AIWEB Page a universal agentic business document—open enough for compatible models, search, and browsers to read and use—supported by a registry, identity, action, and intelligence network. AIWEB gives every business a public page that humans can browse, AI agents can act through, and the business can independently measure. title: Seatline Kolkata
pitch: Book by experience, not just availability.
about_excerpt: Book by experience, not just availability. Like Comment Story Updates Modeled sightline metrices Non binding modelled summary Nandan seated 3D view Seatline Overview All five WebMCP tools executed successfully Seatline Kolkata Inspiration Picking a seat in a cinema is actually a decision that has a spatial element disguised as a grid. A standard seat map will let you know if a seat is available, but it won't tell you how the screen will look from that seat. How far away is it? How far to the side will the view be? Will the row in front obstruct the view? For many visitors, particularly those who are concerned about comfort or accessibility, it is only after they get to the theatre that they find out the answers to these questions. The idea on which Seatline Kolkata was based was that picking a seat should be more like previewing a venue than merely choosing a square on a diagram. The setting for this idea was Kolkata's unique cinema culture, which includes heritage theatres, modern multiplexes, luxury auditoriums and various different room shapes. What it does Seatline Kolkata is an experience which puts the guest first and which is non-binding. People are able to look at six venue profiles in Kolkata, select a preview date and time, check the availability of seats, and from any available seat enter a measured 3D view. For each seat sightline figures are provided: Screen distance Horizontal offset Vertical viewing angle Screen angular width Forward-row clearance Overall rating: Exceptional, Great, Good, or Compromised The experience becomes native to the agent via WebMCP. A visitor can then ask: Get me a clear great sightline at Nandan tomorrow evening. The agent has the capability of searching the venue directory, examining the modelled seats, choosing a suitable seat, moving the Three.js camera to that seat's modelled eye point and then opening the seat summary. The visitor will still be in control and can continue to explore manually. Seatline doesn't reserve seats, handle payments, scrape ticketing websites, or take live inventory; the information about availability, prices, showtimes, and room dimensions is merely preliminary data. How I built it Seatline Kolkata makes use of Next.js, React, TypeScript and Three.js and has its deployment on Cloudflare Workers, the trailer media being stored in Cloudflare R2. WebMCP is implemented with five merchant-authored tools: ask_site search_venues inspect_seats select_preview review_summary The tools employ strict schemas and stable identities and make use of the same pure venue, seat-generation, availability and sightline functions as those used by the visible interface, which ensures that the agent's results match those on the visitor's screen. The camera and the metrics are based on the same geometry model; the eye point is determined by the selected seat and this same point is then used when calculating distance, angles, screen width and clearance. This ensures that the experience remains measurable rather than merely decorative. Challenges I ran into The main difficulty was ensuring that there was a single source of truth among the three systems: the semantic seat map, the Three.js scene and the WebMCP tool execution. When an agent made a selection, it had to update the controls, the seat state, the camera mode and the summary dialogue without setting up a second data model. I also needed a form of seat availability that was deterministic and varied from venue to venue, from date to date and from showtime to showtime while ensuring that each venue's default seat remained available. The camera position had to appear physically reasonable without being artificially raised in order to get a better view. In the end, it was necessary for the project to keep it as a static page that loaded quickly, at the same time as storing the large original trailer files in R2 rather than converting them. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am proud that Seatline Kolkata turns a familiar seat map into a tool which enables spatial decision-making. Rather than just describing the page, the agent carries out the same preview logic that a person would use and then passes the result back to the visual interface. I am likewise proud of the clarity of the product boundary since Seatline is useful before a booking is made without pretending to be a ticketing system or stating that it cannot verify the inventory. What I learned I discovered that good WebMCP tools should convey user intent rather than revealing their internal implementation details; for example, "Find a great seat" is more useful than requesting the agent to directly manipulate the rows and columns. I found that collaboration between humans and agents is most effective when the agent carries out the structured discovery and the person is in charge of visual judgment; the agent can reduce the number of options while the person decides if the view is acceptable. What's next for Seatline Kolkata I would also like to collaborate with the cinemas that are taking part to substitute the representative geometry with the approved auditorium dimensions, include more detailed accessibility annotations, and provide support for both Bengali and English. By means of its authorised partners, Seatline would eventually be able to connect to reliable availability feeds while still maintaining its transparent preview-first experience, and features such as optional secure sign-in, saved comparisons, and the ability to view seats side by side would also increase the product's usefulness for returning visitors. title: WebMCP Project to component builder
pitch: WebMCP Process-to-Component Skill: an Agent Skill that turns your existing forms/flows into one component serving both human UI and AI agents. One schema, one handler, zero drift.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP Process-to-Component Skill: an Agent Skill that turns your existing forms/flows into one component serving both human UI and AI agents. One schema, one handler, zero drift.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 While thinking about projects for this hackathon, several ideas came up, like a WebMCP Return Agent or a WebMCP Insurance Claim for Agents. Both ideas allowed an agent could interact with the specific process without the user having to deal with the complexity of technical terms or the time invested in processing the request. Both applications were built as examples, with which ultimately became the project I presented. What I built was a skill that lets users create components with WebMCP built in, easy to import into your current project. 

 What it does 

 What the skill does is address the whole process: first understanding the general process, identifying the entities that depend on the component to be built and the tech stack, and then building from there. It's not about simply converting a site to WebMCP; it's about working through everything around it and implementing it in the best way. 

 How we built it 

 We followed the skill's own three-phase approach: Discovery to capture the process as a reviewable spec, Synthesis to generate the component, and Verification to test both paths. 

 Tech stack: React 19 + Vite, Zod as the single schema source for both form validation and the WebMCP tool, Tailwind for styling, deployed on Netlify, with in-memory state to keep the demo lightweight. 

 Each component also gets a useWebMCPTool hook handling registration lifecycle, AbortController for mount/unmount, ref-based state sync, and stale-call guarding. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Creating a skill that doesn't focus on addressing every possible problem, scenario, or application, but instead uses the available information to capture the process and the logic behind it, analyze the stakeholders involved and their dependencies, and with that knowledge, turn all of it into a WebMCP-ready component. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The biggest accomplishment is simple: the skill works. We used it to generate both reference examples. The Return Agent and Insurance Claim flows end to end, from the initial discovery spec to a functioning WebMCP-compliant component. 

 We're also proud of holding onto Discovery as a real, reviewable checkpoint rather than shortcutting it under time pressure a process spec capturing purpose, inputs, and side effects before any code gets written. 

 Equally, we're proud of the synthesis logic: one schema, one handler, one lifecycle-safe registration hook, ensuring the human and agent paths could never quietly diverge. 

 What we learned 

 We learned about WebMCP itself, since we had heard of it before but had never worked with or developed using this technology. 

 What's next for Embers WebMCP 

 Improve the current foundation by looking at what was left out and what's worth including. Use the skill to build components in different areas and see what bugs or improvements can be made. And finally, look at community feedback, which will give us direction for where to take development next.

title: Mathburst
pitch: Mathburst is a shared live math canvas. A student and an AI tutor edit the same objects through 48 native WebMCP tools; every edit is attributed, and one shared undo history reverses both.
about_excerpt: Mathburst is a shared live math canvas. A student and an AI tutor edit the same objects through 48 native WebMCP tools; every edit is attributed, and one shared undo history reverses both. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Shared live math world: learner and AI tutor editing one attributed, undoable canvas. Semantic handwriting and Gamma clinic: reconstruct, audit, mark the error, and wait for learner approval. Native WebMCP inspector: all 48 registered page tools are visible and runnable without an external client. Olympiad geometry: live dependent constructions recompute as learner or tutor moves a point. Matrix and attention lab: one cell edit propagates through vectors, weights, probability, and shared history. Try it in 15 seconds Live app · Source · 2:59 demo Open Mathburst in ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . The page registers 48 native WebMCP tools . Open WebMCP · 48/48 , run set_matrix_cells , and watch one call travel end to end: the matrix updates, a ring marks the target, the ledger names the tool, and the activity rail credits the tutor. Press undo once. The agent's edit reverses through the same history as a learner edit. No WebMCP browser? The on-page inspector invokes the same registered handlers, so the complete tool surface remains demonstrable. Inspiration An AI tutor can talk about your math. It cannot touch it. The work sits in a photograph, a notebook, or a canvas the model cannot reach. So the tutor explains around the problem. It describes a graph it cannot draw and suggests a correction it cannot make. We moved the mathematics onto the page, then gave a WebMCP agent tools on that page. One rule shaped everything: every agent edit must produce the same typed operations as the learner's toolbar. That rule decides what the tutor may change and guarantees that the learner can see and undo it. What it does Mathburst is an infinite canvas for late high school and early undergraduate mathematics. A learner writes by hand, graphs functions, builds geometry, edits matrices, and explores live mathematical models. An in-browser AI tutor works on those same objects through WebMCP. This is where WebMCP matters. Mathematics is spatial and live: reasoning appears as a graph, a construction, a matrix, or a half-finished line of algebra. None of that survives being described in a chat box. Mathburst lets an agent read the actual document and act at the exact place where help is needed. Before WebMCP, the tutor could describe a change. Here it makes the change on the live object, and the learner can undo it. The tutor can drag a geometry point and every dependency recomputes. It can edit a matrix cell and the attention weights move. It can write an equation that stays editable. Human and agent operate one document through two interfaces, with one visible history. A direct path to impact at scale We are submitting Mathburst on behalf of Mathos AI , an active Y Combinator Winter 2024 company featured in Forbes 30 Under 30 Education 2025 . Mathos's Google Play listing reports that its existing AI tutor is trusted by more than 2 million students across 200+ countries. We already know how to reach math learners at scale. Mathburst gives us a clear next step: bring an agent into the learner's actual workspace, make every action visible and reversible, and test the result with real students. We will measure correction time, accepted and reversed tutor actions, and concept retention. With Mathos's distribution and educational experience, we can turn this working WebMCP model into a learning experience for millions of students. In addition, we look forward to fully integrating WebMCP into Mathos's products and services. How WebMCP works Mathburst registers 48 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a typed input schema and an execute handler. Handlers never reach into the DOM. They compile input into canonical world operations and send those operations through the same reducer as a toolbar gesture. The surface has three parts: 12 read-only tools inspect the world, selection, history, session context, mathematics, timelines, projects, and scenes without changing state. 28 committing tools create or update canvas objects, reconstruct work, graph expressions, build geometry, edit ink/text/equations/matrices, animate scenes, and drive the math labs. Every commit is attributed and undoable. 8 control tools manage the viewport, focus, projects, scenes, playback, and history itself. That shared action kernel gives every agent change three properties: Visible: a ring marks changed objects and a toast names the tool. Attributed: the ledger records the tool and the activity rail records the author. Reversible: one undo reverses a tutor commit exactly as it reverses a learner commit. Chrome's WebMCP budgets are enforced at load: names at most 30 characters, descriptions at most 500, and parameter descriptions at most 150. A violation fails before registration instead of disappearing silently. docs/WEBMCP_TOOLS.md documents every tool and schema. We tested the native path end to end with Claude driving Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Claude used create_objects , get_objects , get_history , and step_history to create an object, read it back, inspect its commit, undo it, and verify that it was gone. The same call sequence remained visible in Mathburst's toast, Semantic Inspector, ledger, and activity rail. Four connected mathematical projects Gamma Lab. A seeded photograph of an integration-by-parts derivation becomes a semantic reconstruction proposal. The tutor audits it, rings a sign error, writes a note, and stops so the learner makes the correction. This demonstrates proposal, audit, and learner approval; it is not generalized OCR. Tiny Transformer. Gamma log-masses seed a one-head attention model. Edit one query-matrix entry and the attention weights move while still summing to one. A deterministic numerical-gradient step is saved only when loss falls and target probability rises. Olympiad Geometry. The same three attention weights become barycentric coordinates for a point in a triangle. Move a point and every dependent construction recomputes through the world dependency graph. Simplex to Ramanujan. A fourth weight lifts the triangle into a tetrahedral distribution. Its lattice opens into finite partition coefficients. The scene verifies Ramanujan's congruence for finite cases and labels that boundary explicitly; it does not claim a general proof. Challenges One edit path for two authors. Pen, eraser, text, equations, graphs, geometry, matrices, shapes, arrows, frames, resize, rotate, and drag all needed a human route and a tool-call route to the same operation. Keeping history honest. A tutor camera move once entered undo while the same learner pan did not. Both paths now filter camera operations. The final film's measured history records 27 tutor commits and 11 learner commits. Rejecting flattering math. A transformer training step is kept only when loss falls and target probability rises. The graph drops a step that would make the demo look better without improving the model. What we learned Attribution and undo matter more than tool count. The 28 committing tools earn their place because each lands in a history the learner can read and reverse. Remove that, and an agent-native interface collapses into a chatbot with extra steps. What's next Accounts and sync so a canvas follows a learner across devices. More subjects on the same kernel. Several agents on one canvas, each attributed separately. Current scope: one browser, one learner, one in-browser agent, no accounts, no cloud sync, no multiplayer server, and no generalized OCR. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: Adaptive Web Experience
pitch: Instead of weeding through massive plant catalogs, just describe what your landscape goals are and have agent set all the ideal properties for what you should consider. Then the user can just browse.
about_excerpt: Instead of weeding through massive plant catalogs, just describe what your landscape goals are and have agent set all the ideal properties for what you should consider. Then the user can just browse. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Southern Horticulture is a garden center in St. Augustine, Florida, half a mile from salt spray. The staff spend most of the day answering one question in different clothes: "will this plant live in my yard?" The honest answer depends on light, salt exposure, irrigation, whether a deer eats the leaves, and how much the person actually wants to water. A website cannot ask all of that, so every plant catalog on the internet shows the same grid to everyone and lets the shopper guess. Agents changed what is possible. A shopper will happily tell an assistant about the dog and the sprinkler that broke last year, because it is a conversation rather than a form with nineteen fields. WebMCP was the missing half: a way for that conversation to reach into the page the shopper is looking at, instead of ending in a wall of text. What it does The Living Garden Center is a plant catalog that rebuilds itself around one specific yard or purpose. You tell your agent what the space is really like. It calls describe_garden, and the page next to you recomposes: a verified pet friendly section rises to the top because a dog shares the yard, salt-tolerant privacy plants group together, and other plants with no verified toxicity record move into a section that says plainly that a missing record is not evidence of safety. Every plant carries a verdict from a deterministic evaluator, from excellent down to insufficient data, and every verdict is explained. Tap a plant and you get why it landed there: the strengths, the compromises, and the care routine it actually asks for, on dials rather than in adjectives. Some plants get an honest no, with a "what would need to change" answer that names the single facet that would flip the verdict. The agent and the shopper share one live page and one context. Say the salt is worse than you first thought, and the sections reshuffle in front of you. Ask why bougainvillea is a compromise, and the agent answers from the same evaluation the page is showing. Add plants to a saved list, then take a link with you. The catalog never invents stock. Availability language comes from one recorded statement, and the tools say when we have no record rather than guessing. How we built it The core is a pure, deterministic evaluator. A GardenContext carries site conditions, household, and preferences, along with an assumption ledger that marks every value as known, derived, assumed, or unknown. Evaluating a plant against that context produces a fit with strengths, compromises, blockers, and unknowns. A rule table composes sections from those fits, and a page manifest renders through a fixed component registry. No language model writes copy at runtime, which is why the page recomposes instantly and says the same thing twice. WebMCP sits on top as a thin layer. Registration checks for the API and registers every tool once at load: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "describe_garden", description: "Interpret the shopper's words into structured garden conditions", inputSchema: { /* ... / }, execute: async (input) => { / ... */ } }); Eighteen tools in the public app, eleven read and seven write, each with explicit safety annotations so the browser can show which ones make changes and which three are destructive. Writes go through the same validation the human form uses. Context updates take a revision number and fail loudly on conflict, so the agent and the shopper cannot silently overwrite each other. Two details made it robust. The tools return a share URL that encodes the yard, so an agent working in a browser you cannot see can hand you a link that opens the same personalized page anywhere. And an agent activity panel logs every tool call beside the page, so a human can see exactly what the agent did and undo it. The app is Next.js 16 on Vercel. The repo ships a 60-plant sample catalog and reads a fuller catalog from an environment variable, so the demo is complete without publishing our whole inventory. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was not the code. It was discovering where site tools actually run. Our first test failed because ChatGPT used its remote agent browser, so the tools executed in a browser we could not see and the visible tab never changed. Then Chrome reported no tools at all, which turned out to be the WebMCP flag being off. Then a regular ChatGPT chat said it could use the page and could not. Site tools live in the desktop app's built in browser under only a Local ChatGPT Work session, on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra. Nothing on our page could fix any of that, so we made the page say it: a status chip that reads either "Site tools ready: 18 tools this agent can call" or a one line explanation of what to change. Chrome 151 has no way to unregister a tool, and registering a duplicate name is rejected. So tools register exactly once and read live state at execute time rather than closing over it. The subtler challenge was honesty. It is easy to build a recommender that sounds confident. We had to write an explicit contract: an unknown never becomes a negative, a missing toxicity record is never reported as safe, and no tool ever states a live stock count. That constraint produced the most distinctive part of the product. Accomplishments that we're proud of The page genuinely rebuilds itself around a conversation, and it does so from a deterministic evaluator rather than a generated layout, so it is fast, repeatable, and auditable. The honest no. Most catalogs cannot afford to say "we would skip this one for your yard." Ours does, with the reason and the condition that would change it. A garden center that tells you not to buy something is the one you come back to. The evidence gap. We surface the count of plants with no verified pet safety record and keep them visibly uncertain instead of quietly filtering them out or, worse, implying they are fine. Reaching parity between the human and the agent. Same page, same context object, same validation, revision checked so neither one clobbers the other, and a visible log of what the agent touched. And it works. In the ChatGPT desktop app under a local Work session, the arrow turns blue and the catalog reorganizes while you watch. What we learned Tools should carry judgment, not just data. A search_plants that returns rows makes the agent guess. A tool that returns a verdict plus the reasons behind it lets the agent explain, and the explanation matches what the human sees on screen. Annotations matter more than they look. Before we marked the write tools explicitly, the browser listed sixteen read and zero write tools, and a client has no good way to reason about a tool it cannot classify. Shared state needs concurrency control. Two actors editing one context is a distributed systems problem in miniature, and revision checking with an explicit conflict result solved it in about thirty lines. The failure mode nobody warns you about is invisibility. A page that offers tools looks identical to a page that does not when the browser lacks the API. Telling the user which one they are looking at was one of the highest value changes we made all day. What's next for Garden Center Web-MCP Real availability. We have a specification for inventory evidence flowing from the point of sale into a per variation availability state, which would let the agent answer "ten Podocarpus in seven gallon and two fifteen gallon Ligustrum, can you hold them" with a number instead of a hedge. The honesty contract already routes every availability sentence through one function, so this lands without touching a single tool. Filling the unknowns. Style and garden use tags are sparse, which is why some plants report facets we have not recorded. Backfilling them makes the fit explanations richer. Carrying the plan further. The share link already encodes the yard and the saved list. The next step is bringing it into the store on a phone, so staff see the same evaluation the agent produced and can walk someone to the right row. And the part we are most curious about: this pattern is not about plants. Any catalog where fit depends on the buyer's circumstances, and where the honest answer is sometimes no, can be built this way.
